illustration_description: Absolute value is distance from zero: negative four and four both sit four units from zero, so both have absolute value four.
accompanying_text: |x| is almost always taught as “make it positive,” and that description survives exactly as long as the numbers stay simple. The honest definition is geometric: |x| is the DISTANCE from x to 0 on the number line. Distance has no direction, which is why it is never negative — not because a sign was deleted.

illustration_description: Negative six and six share a distance of six from zero but sit on opposite sides, so they are not equal.
accompanying_text: So two numbers can share a distance while disagreeing about everything else. |−6| = |6| = 6, but −6 ≠ 6. Absolute value throws away the side and keeps the size; the number itself is unharmed by being measured.

illustration_description: Plotting absolute value: inputs on the right rise along y equals x, while inputs on the left have positive distances, so that arm folds upward into a V.
accompanying_text: Feed every input to |x| and plot the results. Inputs on the right rise along y = x. Inputs on the left are negative, but their DISTANCES are positive, so the left half rises too — mirror-imaging the right. Two rising branches meeting at the origin: a V.

illustration_description: The V has two slopes: it falls at slope negative one until the origin, then climbs at slope positive one. The corner is where the slope switches.
accompanying_text: The corner is the signature. A line has one constant slope; the V has two — it falls at slope −1 until the origin, then climbs at slope +1. The switch happens exactly where the inside of the bars changes sign, and that is the vertex.

illustration_description: y equals the absolute value of x minus 2, minus 3. The inside minus two moves the V right; the outside minus three moves it down, putting the vertex at two, negative three.
accompanying_text: y = |x − 2| − 3 is still the same V, standing somewhere else. The −2 INSIDE the bars moves it horizontally; the −3 outside moves it vertically. The vertex is wherever the inside of the bars equals 0 — that is the one input the shift is built around.

illustration_description: A minus in front of the bars flips the V upside down into a peak, so the vertex becomes the highest point instead of the lowest.
accompanying_text: A minus in FRONT flips instead of shifts. y = −|x| takes every height and negates it, turning the V upside down into a peak — the vertex becomes the highest point rather than the lowest. Inside the bars: horizontal. Outside: vertical. In front: reflection.

illustration_description: The equation absolute value of x equals five asks which numbers sit five units from zero; there are two, one on each side.
accompanying_text: |x| = 5 asks which numbers sit five units from zero. Phrased that way the answer is obvious — there are two, one per side. Phrased as “remove the bars,” only one shows up. The distance reading is what keeps the second solution from disappearing.

illustration_description: Treat the whole expression inside the bars as one object: the quantity x minus one is four from zero, so it equals four or negative four, giving x equals five or negative three.
accompanying_text: The method generalizes by treating whatever sits inside the bars as one object. |x − 1| = 4 says the QUANTITY x − 1 is four units from zero, so x − 1 = 4 or x − 1 = −4. Solve both, and you get both answers.

illustration_description: The equation absolute value of x equals k has two solutions when k is positive, exactly one when k is zero, and none when k is negative.
accompanying_text: The pair is the usual case, not the only one. |x| = k has two solutions when k > 0, exactly one when k = 0 (zero is its own mirror), and NONE when k < 0 — because no point on the line sits a negative distance from anywhere.

illustration_description: The number on the right decides the solution count before any case-splitting begins: positive gives a pair, zero gives a single solution where the inside is zero, negative gives none.
accompanying_text: So the count is decided by the number on the right, before any case-splitting begins. Positive right side: a pair. Zero: a single solution where the inside vanishes. Negative right side: nothing. Reading the right-hand side first saves the whole procedure.

illustration_description: Absolute value of x less than three is a band between negative three and three; absolute value of x greater than three is two rays heading outward.
accompanying_text: |x| < 3 asks which points are CLOSER than three units to zero — a band around the origin, from −3 to 3. |x| > 3 asks the opposite: points farther out than three units, which is everything beyond −3 on the left and beyond 3 on the right. One band, or two rays.

illustration_description: Less-than gives one connected sandwich written as a single chain; greater-than gives two separate pieces joined by the word or.
accompanying_text: So the direction of the sign decides the SHAPE of the answer, not just its edges. Less-than gives one sandwich, written with a single chain. Greater-than gives two separate rays, joined by ‘or’ — and it cannot be written as a chain, because no number is on both rays at once.

illustration_description: A phone plan charging one rate up to five gigabytes and another beyond it is one function with two formulas, each labelled with the inputs it governs.
accompanying_text: Some rules change formula partway along. A phone plan charges one rate up to 5 GB and another beyond it; that is one function with two formulas, each labelled with the inputs it governs. The labels are what keep it a function: every input is handed to exactly one formula.

illustration_description: Evaluating a piecewise rule takes two moves in order: first find which condition the input satisfies, then apply that branch's formula.
accompanying_text: So evaluating happens in two moves, and the order matters: first find which condition the input satisfies, THEN apply that branch's formula. Reaching for the nearest formula and checking the condition afterwards is what produces most piecewise errors.

illustration_description: Each formula is drawn only over the inputs it governs, and the branches meet at the boundary where a decision must be made about which one owns that point.
accompanying_text: Graphing a piecewise rule means drawing each formula only over the inputs it governs, then deciding what happens where the branches meet. At the boundary exactly one branch owns the point — the one whose condition includes it — and the graph marks that with a filled dot and the other with an open one.

illustration_description: A filled circle marks a height the branch attains; an open circle records a height it approaches but never reaches. When both branches meet at the same height the dots coincide and the graph is connected.
accompanying_text: The open circle is not decoration — it records that the branch approaches a height it never attains. When the two branches meet at the same height the dots coincide and the graph is continuous; when they do not, the graph jumps, and the size of that jump is visible on the page.

illustration_description: Postage, parking and tax brackets are flat between jumps: the graph is a staircase of level treads with a jump at each boundary.
accompanying_text: Some real rules are piecewise with many pieces, all of them flat. Postage charges by the ounce, parking by the hour, tax by the bracket. Between the jumps the price does not move at all; at each jump it leaps. Graphed, these rules look like a staircase.

illustration_description: Within one step the price carries no information about the exact input: three different weights on the same tread all cost the same, so the cost cannot tell them apart.
accompanying_text: Flat between jumps has a consequence worth naming: within one step the price carries no information about the exact input. Learning a letter cost $3 tells you the weight was more than 2 oz and at most 3 oz — a range, never a number. Steps trade precision for simplicity, on purpose.

illustration_description: A triangle sits inside a rectangle of the same base and height; the triangle covers exactly half the rectangle's area.
accompanying_text: Any triangle sits inside a rectangle sharing its base and height — and it always covers exactly **half** that rectangle. So a triangle's area is **1/2 × base × height**: base 6, height 4 gives 1/2 × 6 × 4 = **12**. The rectangle would be 24; the triangle is exactly half of it.

illustration_description: The height of a triangle is the perpendicular distance from the base to the top vertex, shown as a dashed line meeting the base at a right angle. Height is the perpendicular distance to the base.
accompanying_text: **Height** always means the PERPENDICULAR distance from the base to the opposite vertex — a straight up-and-down measurement, never a slanted side. A tall, tilted triangle can have a short height if its apex leans far to one side; height is about the drop, not the slant.

illustration_description: A parallelogram's area is base times height: cutting a right triangle off one end and moving it to the other turns it into a rectangle of the same area. Parallelogram area = base × height.
accompanying_text: A **parallelogram** slices a triangle off one side and reattaches it to the other, forming a rectangle of the SAME base and height — no halving needed. Area = **base × height**: base 6, height 4 gives 6 × 4 = **24**. Unlike a triangle, a parallelogram is already the full rectangle in disguise.

illustration_description: A trapezoid with a longer bottom base and shorter top base, split by a diagonal into two triangles — one using the bottom base, one using the top base, both sharing the same height.
accompanying_text: A **trapezoid** has two parallel bases of DIFFERENT lengths. Split it diagonally into two triangles — one using the long base (b1), one the short base (b2), both sharing the height. Adding those triangle areas gives the formula: **1/2 × (b1 + b2) × height**. Average the two bases, then apply the triangle rule.

illustration_description: Same base and height give different areas: a rectangle is base times height, a triangle is half of that, and a parallelogram equals the rectangle. Same base and height, three area formulas.
accompanying_text: Same base, same height, three different answers — the SHAPE decides the rule. Base 9, height 4: a **triangle** gives 1/2 × 9 × 4 = 18; a **parallelogram** gives 9 × 4 = 36 (exactly double the triangle); a **trapezoid** needs a second base too. Identify the shape FIRST, then pick its formula.

illustration_description: Same base and height give different areas: a rectangle is base times height, a triangle is half of that, and a parallelogram equals the rectangle. Same base and height, three area formulas.
accompanying_text: A trapezoid needs one more piece of information than the others: a SECOND base. Given base 9, second base 5, height 4: 1/2 × (9 + 5) × 4 = **28** — between the triangle's 18 and the parallelogram's 36, which makes sense since a trapezoid is a blend of the two.

illustration_description: An L-shaped figure formed from a large rectangle with a smaller rectangle cut from its top-right corner; a dashed line splits the L into a bottom rectangle and a top rectangle.
accompanying_text: An L-shaped figure isn't a single rectangle — but it splits into two. Cut it with one straight line and you get a bottom rectangle and a top rectangle; **add their areas** for the total. A 10-by-8 L with a 4-by-3 corner missing splits into a 10×5 rectangle (50) plus a 6×3 rectangle (18): total **68**.

illustration_description: An L-shaped figure formed from a large rectangle with a smaller rectangle cut from its top-right corner; a dashed line splits the L into a bottom rectangle and a top rectangle.
accompanying_text: There's a second, equally valid path: picture the L-shape's **bounding box** — the full rectangle it would be without the missing corner — then **subtract the cut-out** piece. The 10-by-8 example: bounding box 10×8 = 80, minus the 4×3 cut = 12, giving 80 − 12 = 68. Same answer, different route — a genuine check on your work.

illustration_description: A house-shaped figure splits into a rectangle body plus a triangle roof; adding their areas gives the total. House = rectangle + triangle.
accompanying_text: A house-shaped figure is a rectangle topped with a triangular roof — two DIFFERENT shape rules, added together. Walls 8 wide, 5 tall: rectangle area 8 × 5 = 40. Roof: base 8, height 3, so 1/2 × 8 × 3 = 12. Total house area: 40 + 12 = **52**. Identify each piece's shape before computing its area.

illustration_description: Some composite areas subtract: find the area of a large rectangle, then remove the area of a cut-out rectangle to leave the shaded region. Composite by subtracting a cut-out.
accompanying_text: Not every composite figure ADDS its pieces — some SUBTRACT a piece that's been cut away. A rectangle with a triangular notch removed (like a corner sliced off) LOSES that triangle's area: 10×6 rectangle (60) minus a base-4-height-3 triangle notch (6) leaves **54**. Look for whether a shape is attached (add) or removed (subtract).

illustration_description: An L-shaped figure formed from a large rectangle with a smaller rectangle cut from its top-right corner; a dashed line splits the L into a bottom rectangle and a top rectangle.
accompanying_text: Real floor plans often need THREE or more pieces: a main room, an extension, maybe a nook. The rule scales up perfectly — identify every piece's shape, compute each area, then combine with add or subtract as each piece demands. A main room (12×8=96) plus an extension (4×5=20) plus a triangular reading nook (1/2×4×3=6) totals **122**.

illustration_description: Some composite areas subtract: find the area of a large rectangle, then remove the area of a cut-out rectangle to leave the shaded region. Composite by subtracting a cut-out.
accompanying_text: The ORDER you add pieces never changes the total — 96 + 20 + 6 gives the same result as 20 + 6 + 96. Group however makes the arithmetic easiest, especially when a subtraction is mixed in: compute every piece first, THEN combine with the correct signs (+ for attached, − for removed).

illustration_description: Finding a side length from coordinates: a horizontal segment from x equals 2 to x equals 7 has length 7 minus 2, which is 5. Horizontal length = difference of x-values.
accompanying_text: When a side is perfectly horizontal or vertical, its length comes straight from the coordinates: **subtract the coordinate that changes, and take the distance (never negative)**. From (3, 2) to (8, 2), the y stays at 2 but x goes from 3 to 8 — length 8 − 3 = **5**. The unchanging coordinate tells you the side is horizontal (same y) or vertical (same x).

illustration_description: Finding a side length from coordinates: a horizontal segment from x equals 2 to x equals 7 has length 7 minus 2, which is 5. Horizontal length = difference of x-values.
accompanying_text: The same rule works for **vertical** sides, just swap which coordinate you're reading: the x stays the same, and you subtract the y's. It also works with **negative coordinates** — the distance is still the difference, taken as a positive number: from (2, −4) to (2, 3), length = 3 − (−4) = **7**.

illustration_description: Area of a polygon on a grid: with side lengths read from coordinates, a 5 by 3 rectangle on the grid has area 15 square units. Polygon area on the grid: 5 × 3 = 15.
accompanying_text: Once you can find side lengths from coordinates, area follows the same rules from earlier chapters. A rectangle with corners (2,2), (6,2), (6,4), (2,4): width = 6−2 = 4, height = 4−2 = 2, area = 4 × 2 = **8**. Find the sides first, THEN apply the shape's area formula.

illustration_description: Area of a polygon on a grid: with side lengths read from coordinates, a 5 by 3 rectangle on the grid has area 15 square units. Polygon area on the grid: 5 × 3 = 15.
accompanying_text: The right angle at a shared corner is what makes this easy: when two sides of a triangle are horizontal and vertical, they're the triangle's **legs**, and you already know how to find their lengths from coordinates. Read the legs first, then apply 1/2 × leg1 × leg2 exactly as before.

illustration_description: Area of a polygon on a grid: with side lengths read from coordinates, a 5 by 3 rectangle on the grid has area 15 square units. Polygon area on the grid: 5 × 3 = 15.
accompanying_text: Everything from this chapter combines: read side lengths from coordinates, identify each shape, and — if the figure is composite — add or subtract pieces exactly as in Chapter 2. A rectangle (1,1)-(6,1)-(6,4)-(1,4) plus an attached triangle gives one combined coordinate-based composite area.

illustration_description: Area of a polygon on a grid: with side lengths read from coordinates, a 5 by 3 rectangle on the grid has area 15 square units. Polygon area on the grid: 5 × 3 = 15.
accompanying_text: Combine exactly as before: since the triangle is ATTACHED to the rectangle (not cut from it), **add** the two areas. 15 + 4.5 = **19.5** total. The coordinate reading and the combine-the-pieces skill from Chapter 2 work together on any figure, however it's described.

illustration_description: A rectangular prism unfolded flat into six connected faces: front, top, back, and bottom stacked in a column, with the two side faces attached left and right of the top face.
accompanying_text: Unfold a box flat and you get its **net** — six connected rectangles. **Surface area** is the total area of all six faces. A 4×3×2 box has three PAIRS of matching faces: two 4×3 (top/bottom), two 4×2 (front/back), two 3×2 (sides). Sum: 24 + 16 + 12 = **52** square units.

illustration_description: A rectangular prism unfolded flat into six connected faces: front, top, back, and bottom stacked in a column, with the two side faces attached left and right of the top face.
accompanying_text: The shortcut formula packages the three pairs: **SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)**. For 4×3×2: 2(12 + 8 + 6) = 2 × 26 = 52 — identical to adding all six faces. The two most common slips: counting each pair only once (getting half), or computing l×w×h (that's VOLUME, a different thing entirely).

illustration_description: The surface area of a triangular prism is two triangular ends plus three rectangular sides, found from its unfolded net. Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles.
accompanying_text: A **triangular prism** (like a tent or a Toblerone box) has 5 faces: **2 triangle bases** at the ends, plus **3 rectangles** wrapping around. Each face keeps its OWN formula from Chapter 1 — triangles halve, rectangles don't. Compute all five, then add.

illustration_description: The surface area of a triangular prism is two triangular ends plus three rectangular sides, found from its unfolded net. Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles.
accompanying_text: Total surface area = 2 triangle ends + 3 rectangles. For the (3,4,5)×6 prism: 12 + 72 = **84**. Verify by listing all five faces individually — 6, 6, 18, 24, 30 — which also sums to 84. Two routes, same answer, exactly like the L-shapes in Chapter 2.

illustration_description: A rectangular prism unfolded flat into six connected faces: front, top, back, and bottom stacked in a column, with the two side faces attached left and right of the top face.
accompanying_text: Surface area answers real questions: **how much wrapping paper covers a gift, how much paint coats a room, how much cardboard makes a box.** The key reading skill: does the problem cover ALL faces (a wrapped gift) or only SOME (painting walls but not the floor)? Count exactly the faces the situation includes.

illustration_description: How many small boxes fit inside a big one: divide the big box's volume by the small box's volume to count them. Boxes that fit = big volume ÷ small volume.
accompanying_text: Volume and surface area answer DIFFERENT questions: volume is what fits **inside** (cubic units); surface area is what covers the **outside** (square units). "How much water fills the tank" is volume; "how much paint coats the tank" is surface area. The units are the tell: cubic for inside, square for outside.

illustration_description: A box built from unit cubes: a base layer of 3 by 2 cubes, stacked 3 layers high; the highlighted bottom layer shows the base.
accompanying_text: **Volume** counts the unit cubes that fill a box: a 2×3 base holds 6 cubes per layer, and 4 layers stack to 24 cubes — which is exactly **V = length × width × height** = 2×3×4 = 24 cubic units. The formula is layer-counting, compressed.

illustration_description: A box built from unit cubes: a base layer of 3 by 2 cubes, stacked 3 layers high; the highlighted bottom layer shows the base.
accompanying_text: Volume and surface area part ways here for good: volume is **cubic units** (what fits inside); surface area is **square units** (what covers outside). One box, two numbers: the 4×3×6 box holds 72 cubic units inside and wears 108 square units of surface. Keep the units straight and you'll never mix them.

illustration_description: Volume with a fractional edge: a box 3 and a half by 2 by 2 uses V equals length times width times height, giving 14 cubic units. Volume with a fractional edge: 3½ × 2 × 2 = 14.
accompanying_text: The formula V = l × w × h keeps working when an edge is a **fraction** — you just pack with SMALLER cubes. A box 3 × 2 × 3/2 fits half-unit cubes: 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 of them, each with volume 1/8, totaling 72/8 = **9** — exactly what 3 × 2 × 3/2 gives directly. Fractions don't break the formula; they refine the cubes.

illustration_description: Volume with a fractional edge: a box 3 and a half by 2 by 2 uses V equals length times width times height, giving 14 cubic units. Volume with a fractional edge: 3½ × 2 × 2 = 14.
accompanying_text: For a **mixed number** edge like 3½, convert to an improper fraction first: 3½ = 7/2. Then V = 7/2 × 2 × 4 = **28**. The most common slip is quietly dropping the fraction and computing 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 — always convert the mixed number before multiplying.

illustration_description: How many small boxes fit inside a big one: divide the big box's volume by the small box's volume to count them. Boxes that fit = big volume ÷ small volume.
accompanying_text: Volume questions hide in everyday objects: **how much water an aquarium holds, how much soil fills a planter, how many boxes fit in a moving van.** Read the three dimensions (converting any mixed numbers), multiply, and label the answer in cubic units. The whole course's toolkit comes together here.

illustration_description: How many small boxes fit inside a big one: divide the big box's volume by the small box's volume to count them. Boxes that fit = big volume ÷ small volume.
accompanying_text: "How many smaller boxes fit inside" is volume DIVISION: total space ÷ space per box. A van with 48 cubic units of cargo space fits 48 ÷ 2 = **24** boxes of 2 cubic units each — as long as the shapes stack cleanly. Divide volumes to count containers.

accompanying_text: You do not need counters forever: the ONES digit tells you. 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 end even numbers; 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 end odd ones.

accompanying_text: The tens pair up automatically — every ten is five pairs — so only the ones digit can leave a leftover.

accompanying_text: A double like 7 + 7 pairs every counter with its twin across the groups — so a double can never leave a leftover.

accompanying_text: Doubles are the even numbers wearing their construction on their sleeve: two equal groups, zero leftovers.

accompanying_text: Every even number can be written as a double: split it into two equal groups and name the sum, like 14 = 7 + 7.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Finding the double is un-doubling — asking which number, taken twice, rebuilds the total.

accompanying_text: An array lines counters into ROWS (across) and COLUMNS (up and down). Every counter sits in exactly one row and one column.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The grid is not decoration — rows and columns are two honest ways to slice the same total.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: To count an array by rows, take one row's number and add it again for every row: 3 rows of 4 is 4, then 8, then 12.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The running total climbs by the same step each time — that steady step IS the row size.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The SAME array counts by columns too: 3 rows of 4 is also 4 columns of 3 — the totals must agree because the counters never moved.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Two counting paths, one answer. When they disagree, a counting mistake happened, not a mathematical one.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The repeated sum is the array written as arithmetic: 3 rows of 4 becomes 4 + 4 + 4. The addend is the row size; the number of addends is the row count.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Reading it back works too — see 5 + 5 + 5 and picture 3 rows of 5 before computing a thing.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Twelve counters make a 2-by-6 array, a 3-by-4, a 6-by-2 — the shape changes freely while the count stands still.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: That freedom is useful: choose the slicing that makes the adding easiest, since every honest slicing agrees.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Egg cartons, garden beds, window panes — the world stacks things in rows and columns, and your row-by-row sum totals every one of them.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Spot the array, name the rows and row size, write the repeated sum, and stage the addition. Four moves, any array.

illustration_description: The square of a plus b is an area split into four pieces: a squared, b squared, and two identical cross rectangles a b that the wrong answer forgets.
accompanying_text: (a + b)² is not a² + b². Squaring a sum means multiplying the whole sum by itself, and the cross terms that appear are the entire content of this course. Drawn as a rectangle, (a + b)² is one a-square, one b-square, and TWO identical strips — and the strips are what the wrong version throws away.

illustration_description: Raising the power adds a term each time: the square has three terms, the cube four, the fourth power five — n plus one in general.
accompanying_text: Push the exponent up and the pattern keeps going. (a + b)³ has four terms, not two; (a + b)⁴ has five. In general (a + b)ⁿ expands into n + 1 terms, whose a-powers count down from n while the b-powers count up — and whose coefficients are what the rest of this chapter is about.

illustration_description: Stacking the coefficient rows builds Pascal's triangle: one; one one; one two one; one three three one; one four six four one. Each entry is the sum of the two above it.
accompanying_text: Stack the coefficient rows and a triangle appears. Row 0 is a lone 1; row 1 is 1 1; row 2 is 1 2 1; row 3 is 1 3 3 1. Every interior entry is the sum of the two directly above it, and every row begins and ends with 1. The rows are numbered from ZERO, which is the single most common place to slip.

illustration_description: Two facts make the triangle trustworthy: every row reads the same backwards, and each entry is the sum of the two entries above it.
accompanying_text: Two facts make the triangle worth trusting. Every row is symmetric, so reading it backwards changes nothing. And the entries of row n add to 2ⁿ — row 3 sums to 8, row 4 to 16 — which is a fast way to check a row you have just built.

illustration_description: Expanding four brackets means taking either a or b from each one; a term with two b's arises from every way of choosing which two brackets supply the b.
accompanying_text: Expanding (a + b)⁴ means multiplying four brackets, and from EACH bracket you take either an a or a b. Every term of the answer is one such choice sequence. So the coefficient of a²b² is simply the number of ways to choose which two of the four brackets contribute the b — a counting question, not an algebra one.

illustration_description: The entry in row n position k is exactly C of n choose k, and Pascal's addition rule is the same statement as the counting identity.
accompanying_text: That identification is the theorem's engine: the entry in row n, position k, IS C(n, k). Pascal's addition rule is the same statement in disguise — choosing k things from n either uses the last item or does not, which is exactly C(n−1, k−1) + C(n−1, k), the two entries above.

illustration_description: The binomial theorem in one line: the sum over k from zero to n of C n k times a to the n minus k times b to the k, with the exponents always adding to n.
accompanying_text: Written out, the identification of the last lesson becomes one line: (a + b)ⁿ is the sum, over k from 0 to n, of C(n,k)·aⁿ⁻ᵏ·bᵏ. Three moving parts — a combination, a falling power of a, a rising power of b — and their exponents always total n, which is the fastest check that a term was written correctly.

illustration_description: For two x plus three to the fourth, take a to be the whole block two x and b to be three, then apply the formula unchanged.
accompanying_text: The theorem also handles binomials that are not bare letters. For (2x + 3)⁴, take a = 2x and b = 3 and apply the formula unchanged — but every power now acts on the whole quantity, so a² means (2x)² = 4x², coefficient included. Forgetting to raise the 2 is the standard slip.

illustration_description: To get only the b cubed term of a plus b to the seventh, set k to three and evaluate one term — the other seven never need expanding.
accompanying_text: The theorem's real power is selective. If you want only the b³ term of (a + b)⁷, you need not expand the other seven — set k = 3 and write C(7,3)·a⁴·b³. The whole skill is deciding what k is, and reading it off the power of b every time.

illustration_description: Because rows are symmetric, C of seven three and C of seven four are equal, so mixing up which exponent supplies k can give the right number by luck and the wrong exponents.
accompanying_text: Because rows are symmetric, C(n,k) and C(n,n−k) agree — so mixing up which exponent supplies k sometimes yields the right number by luck. Depending on that luck is how the error survives. Anchor k to the power of b and it never matters.

illustration_description: With p the chance of success and q equals one minus p, expanding p plus q to the n gives one term per success count, and the terms sum to one.
accompanying_text: Let p be the chance of a success and q = 1 − p the chance of a failure. Then (p + q)ⁿ expands into terms C(n,k)pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ, and each one is the probability of exactly k successes in n trials. Since p + q = 1, the whole expansion sums to 1ⁿ = 1 — the distribution accounts for every outcome.

illustration_description: With a fair coin every path is equally likely, so the chance of exactly k heads is C n k over two to the n; when p is not one half the paths stop being equally likely.
accompanying_text: With a fair coin every path is equally likely, so the probability of exactly k heads is C(n,k)/2ⁿ. When p is not ½ the paths stop being equally likely and each carries weight pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ instead — but the COUNT of paths is still C(n,k), unchanged. The combination counts; the powers weigh.

illustration_description: Three scatter plots. On the left, points rise from lower-left to upper-right — a positive association. In the middle, points fall from upper-left to lower-right — a negative association. On the right, points are scattered with no pattern — no association.
accompanying_text: A **scatter plot** shows **paired data** — two numbers measured on each thing. Each dot uses one measurement for its across-position (x) and the other for its up-position (y). One dot per item.

illustration_description: An ordered pair plots as across then up. The point 3 across and 2 up sits three units right and two units above the origin.
accompanying_text: The two measurements must stay in order: the first number is always the across-value, the second the up-value. Swapping them puts the dot in the wrong place and can hide the real pattern in the data.

illustration_description: Three scatter plots. On the left, points rise from lower-left to upper-right — a positive association. In the middle, points fall from upper-left to lower-right — a negative association. On the right, points are scattered with no pattern — no association.
accompanying_text: **Association** is the overall direction of the dots. **Positive**: as x goes up, y tends to go up (dots rise to the right). **Negative**: as x goes up, y tends to go down (dots fall). **No association**: no clear direction.

illustration_description: Positive versus negative association. On the left the dots rise together; on the right they fall as one value grows and the other shrinks.
accompanying_text: Think about what the pairing means. More hours of studying and more problems solved rise together — positive. More time driving and less fuel left in the tank move oppositely — negative. Shoe size and test score have no real link — no association.

illustration_description: On the left, a straight line: the output rises by the same amount at each step, so it is linear. On the right, a curve: the output rises by more and more at each step, so it is nonlinear.
accompanying_text: Beyond direction, look at three things. **Clusters**: groups of dots bunched together. **Outliers**: lone dots far from the rest. **Form**: whether the pattern follows a straight line (**linear**) or a curve (**nonlinear**).

illustration_description: Form decides the model. On the left dots follow a straight path, so a line fits; on the right they bend, so a curve fits.
accompanying_text: Form tells you what kind of model fits. If the dots follow a straight path, the form is linear and a straight line summarizes them. If they bend — leveling off or curving up — the form is nonlinear and a line would miss the shape.

illustration_description: A scatter plot of about a dozen points trending upward, with a single straight line drawn through the middle of the cloud. The line of best fit passes close to the points, with roughly as many points above it as below it.
accompanying_text: When a scatter plot's form is roughly linear, a single straight line can summarize the trend. This **line of best fit** runs through the middle of the cloud, staying as close as possible to all the dots at once.

illustration_description: The line of best fit sits in the middle of the cloud, with roughly as many dots above it as below — it need not touch any dot.
accompanying_text: A good fit doesn't have to touch any dots. What matters is that the line sits in the **middle** of the cloud — roughly as many dots above it as below, each one not too far away. It's a summary, not a connect-the-dots.

illustration_description: A scatter plot of about a dozen points trending upward, with a single straight line drawn through the middle of the cloud. The line of best fit passes close to the points, with roughly as many points above it as below it.
accompanying_text: To compare two candidate lines, look at the **gaps** between the dots and each line. The better fit has smaller gaps overall — the dots huddle closer to it. Bigger gaps mean a worse summary of the trend.

illustration_description: A tight cloud gives small gaps to the line — a strong fit; a spread-out cloud leaves bigger gaps — a weak fit.
accompanying_text: A tightly clustered cloud can be summarized by a line with very small gaps — a strong fit. A widely spread cloud leaves bigger gaps no matter how you draw the line, so even the best line is a looser summary.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: Once you have a good line, describe it with an equation **y = mx + b** — the same form from functions. The **slope m** is the line's steepness, and the **intercept b** is where it crosses the up-axis (its value when x = 0).

illustration_description: In the line y equals 2 x plus 3, the intercept 3 is where the line starts on the up-axis, and the slope 2 means y rises 2 for each step of 1 in x.
accompanying_text: The slope tells you how much y changes for each step of x. In y = 2x + 3, every increase of 1 in x raises y by 2. The intercept, 3, is the starting height where the line meets the up-axis.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: A line of best fit does more than describe — it **predicts**. To predict y for a new x, plug that x into the equation **y = mx + b**. The line fills in a likely y-value for an x you didn't measure.

illustration_description: Predicting with y equals 3 x plus 1 at x equals 4: multiply 3 by 4 to get 12, then add 1 to get 13.
accompanying_text: The steps are always the same: multiply the slope by the new x, then add the intercept. For y = 3x + 1 at x = 4: 3 × 4 = 12, then 12 + 1 = 13. Order matters — multiply before you add.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: In a real situation, the **slope** is a rate: how much y changes for each extra unit of x. The **intercept** is the starting value of y when x = 0. Reading them tells the data's story in words.

illustration_description: In y equals 2 x plus 10, the intercept 10 is the base value at x equals 0, and the slope 2 is the amount added for each unit of x.
accompanying_text: The intercept anchors the story at x = 0. In y = 2x + 10, the 10 is the base cost before any data is used — the fee you pay at 0 gigabytes. Slope = per-unit change; intercept = starting amount.

illustration_description: A scatter plot of about a dozen points trending upward, with a single straight line drawn through the middle of the cloud. The line of best fit passes close to the points, with roughly as many points above it as below it.
accompanying_text: Predictions are most reliable **inside** the range of the data. Stretching far **beyond** it — called **extrapolation** — is risky: the trend may not continue. A line fit to weeks 1–6 may say little about week 50.

illustration_description: Extrapolation risk. Real data grows then levels off, but a straight line keeps predicting upward past the measured range — so predictions outside the data can be wrong.
accompanying_text: Data can also curve outside the range you measured. A plant grows steadily for weeks, then stops at full height — a straight line would keep predicting impossible growth. Real trends often bend once you leave the data.

illustration_description: A two-way table. Columns are labeled dog and cat; rows are labeled child and adult. The four inner cells hold counts: 20 and 10 in the top row, 5 and 15 in the bottom row. The right margin shows row totals 30 and 20, and the bottom margin shows column totals 25 and 25, with a grand total of 50.
accompanying_text: Some data is **categorical** — not numbers, but groups like dog/cat or child/adult. A **two-way table** sorts each person into a row-and-column box, counting how many fall into each combination.

illustration_description: A two-way table with margin totals. Children have 20 dogs and 10 cats, totaling 30; adults have 5 dogs and 15 cats, totaling 20. The dog column totals 25, the cat column 25, and the grand total is 50.
accompanying_text: The margins hold the **totals**. The child row totals 30 (20 dogs + 10 cats); the dog column totals 25 (20 children + 5 adults). The bottom-right corner, 50, is the **grand total** — everyone surveyed.

illustration_description: A two-way table. Columns are labeled dog and cat; rows are labeled child and adult. The four inner cells hold counts: 20 and 10 in the top row, 5 and 15 in the bottom row. The right margin shows row totals 30 and 20, and the bottom margin shows column totals 25 and 25, with a grand total of 50.
accompanying_text: A **relative frequency** turns a count into a fraction or percent of a total: divide the cell by the total you care about. Of all 50 people, the 20 dog-loving children are 20 ÷ 50 = 0.40, or **40%**.

illustration_description: Relative frequency depends on the total you divide by. The same cell divided by the whole survey of 50 gives one rate; divided by just the 20 adults gives another.
accompanying_text: The total you divide by depends on the question. **Of the whole survey?** Divide by 50. **Of just the adults?** Divide by 20. Same cell, different total — so always ask which group the percent is 'out of'.

illustration_description: A two-way table. Columns are labeled dog and cat; rows are labeled child and adult. The four inner cells hold counts: 20 and 10 in the top row, 5 and 15 in the bottom row. The right margin shows row totals 30 and 20, and the bottom margin shows column totals 25 and 25, with a grand total of 50.
accompanying_text: Two-way tables reveal **association** between categories. Compare relative frequencies across rows: if children and adults prefer dogs at very different rates, age and pet-preference are **associated**. Similar rates mean little or no association.

illustration_description: Compare rates, not raw counts. Two groups of different sizes are only fairly compared by turning each count into a percent of its own group total.
accompanying_text: The key move is comparing **rates, not raw counts**. Two groups of different sizes can't be compared by counts alone. Turning each into a percent of its own row makes a fair comparison possible.

illustration_description: Real points do not sit on the line: each one misses by a vertical gap called its residual.
accompanying_text: Chapter 2 fit a line; chapter 3 used it to predict. But real points don't sit ON the line — each one misses by some amount. That miss has a name: the residual, observed minus predicted. It is the line's error, measured point by point.

illustration_description: Every point gets a residual: positive above the line, negative below, zero on it. Fitting a line does not erase the misses, it records them.
accompanying_text: Every data point gets a residual: positive above the line, negative below, zero on it. A fitted line doesn't erase the misses — it chooses where to put them. Reading those leftovers is how you audit the line.

illustration_description: Plotting residuals against x flattens the line into a horizontal axis, so a shapeless scatter means the model fits and a pattern means it does not.
accompanying_text: One residual judges one point. All the residuals together judge the MODEL. Plot each residual against x — flip the line down to a flat zero-axis — and look for a pattern. A good fit leaves patternless scatter; a pattern means the line missed something systematic.

illustration_description: Three diagnoses: a U shape means curvature, all residuals on one side means a misplaced line, and growing spread means the relationship loosens as x grows.
accompanying_text: Three diagnoses so far: U = curvature, one-sided = misplaced line, growing spread = the relationship loosens with x. Different diseases, one instrument — and none of them are visible from the fitted line alone. The scatter plot can look fine while the residual plot screams.

illustration_description: Residuals can steer a line as well as judge it: move the line and every leftover changes, so the best line is the one that makes the leftovers smallest overall.
accompanying_text: If residuals diagnose a line, they can also steer one. Move the line and every leftover changes; the best line is the one that makes them small AND balanced — some up, some down, summing to about zero, with no pattern. Fit by leftover.

illustration_description: The line of best fit is chosen to make the squared residuals as small as possible, which is why squaring stops positives and negatives from cancelling.
accompanying_text: This is the idea behind the 'line of best fit' your tools compute: they choose the slope and intercept that make the residuals collectively smallest (squaring them so ups and downs can't cancel). You've been doing by eye what least squares does by algebra.

illustration_description: A circle with center marked. A radius is drawn from the center to the edge, and a diameter crosses the whole circle through the center — twice the radius. The distance around the circle is the circumference, 2 pi r, and the space inside is the area, pi r squared.
accompanying_text: Circles measure turning, and the ruler is the **central angle** — vertex at the center, sides on two radii. The piece of circle it cuts off is an **arc**, and we simply DEFINE the arc's measure to equal its central angle. A 140° central angle stands on a 140° arc; the whole circle is 360°.

illustration_description: Naming keeps the two arcs straight: minor arcs under one hundred eighty degrees use two letters, major arcs over one hundred eighty use three.
accompanying_text: Naming keeps the two arcs straight: **minor arcs** (under 180°) use two letters — arc AB — while **major arcs** (over 180°) borrow a third point to force the long way around — arc ACB. A 180° arc is a **semicircle**, cut off by a diameter. Adjacent arcs simply add, like segment lengths on a bent ruler.

illustration_description: A circle with a central angle of 80 degrees standing on arc AB. An inscribed angle from a point on the far side of the circle measures 40 degrees on the same arc, and moving the vertex to a second position keeps it at 40 degrees: any inscribed angle is half its central angle.
accompanying_text: Slide the vertex from the center out to the circle itself: that's an **inscribed angle** — vertex ON the circle, sides two chords. The **Inscribed Angle Theorem**: an inscribed angle measures **half** the arc it opens onto (half the central angle on that arc). An 80° arc is seen at 40° from the circle.

illustration_description: Why half: drawing the radius to the inscribed vertex splits the problem into isosceles triangles that reveal the inscribed angle is half the central angle.
accompanying_text: Why half? Draw the radius to the inscribed vertex: it splits the picture into isosceles triangles (two sides are radii), and each base angle gets doubled by the exterior angle at the center. The doubling at the center IS the halving at the rim. One proof, endless mileage.

illustration_description: Every inscribed angle is half of the central angle that subtends the same arc.
accompanying_text: The animated figure's punchline is a theorem of its own: **every inscribed angle on the same arc is congruent** — slide the vertex anywhere along the major arc and the angle refuses to change, because it always halves the SAME arc. Photographers call it the viewing-angle circle; geometers call it free congruence.

illustration_description: A circle with a horizontal diameter A B. A point C on the circle connects to both ends of the diameter, and the angle at C is exactly 90 degrees: the diameter subtends a right angle from anywhere on the circle.
accompanying_text: Point the inscribed angle at a **diameter** and the theorem sings: the diameter's arc is a semicircle, 180°, so the inscribed angle is half of that — **exactly 90°, from anywhere on the circle**. That's Thales' theorem, arguably the oldest proved statement in mathematics.

illustration_description: Thales turns every triangle on a diameter into a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the diameter.
accompanying_text: Thales turns every such triangle into a RIGHT triangle whose hypotenuse is the diameter — so the whole right-triangle toolkit (Pythagoras, the trig course) boards the circle. And the two remaining angles? They must complete 180° past the right angle: complements of each other.

illustration_description: A chord is a segment with both endpoints on the circle; the diameter is the longest chord.
accompanying_text: A **chord** is a segment with both endpoints on the circle — the diameter is just the chord that happens to pass through the center. Every chord cuts off an arc, and the two are locked together: **congruent chords cut congruent arcs**, and vice versa (in the same circle, or in congruent circles).

illustration_description: The lock runs through the central angle: congruent chords match congruent central angles and congruent arcs.
accompanying_text: The lock runs through the **central angle**: chord ↔ central angle ↔ arc, each pair matched. A 60° central angle is special: its two radii and the chord form a triangle with two equal sides and 60° between them — equilateral, so **the chord of a 60° arc equals the radius**.

illustration_description: A circle with two congruent chords. The perpendicular from the center meets each chord at its midpoint, and both perpendicular distances are equal. Radius, distance, and half-chord form a right triangle.
accompanying_text: Drop a perpendicular from the center onto any chord: it lands on the chord's **midpoint** — and bisects the chord's arc too. Proof: the two endpoint triangles share the perpendicular leg and have matching radius hypotenuses — HL congruence, then CPCTC. One perpendicular, two halves.

illustration_description: Given the chord, find its distance: half the chord, the distance to the center, and the radius form a right triangle, so half chord squared plus distance squared equals radius squared.
accompanying_text: Run it backward: given the chord, find its distance. Half the chord and the distance are the legs; the radius is always the hypotenuse. Radius 13, chord 24: half-chord 12, so d = √(169 − 144) = 5. The 5-12-13 triple lives inside every such circle problem.

illustration_description: The converse is a center-finder: the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center.
accompanying_text: The converse is a center-finder: **the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center** — the center is equidistant from the chord's endpoints, and the bisector is exactly the set of such points. Two chords, two bisectors, one intersection: the lost center, found. Restorers rebuild broken plates this way.

illustration_description: A circle with two congruent chords. The perpendicular from the center meets each chord at its midpoint, and both perpendicular distances are equal. Radius, distance, and half-chord form a right triangle.
accompanying_text: Put the right-triangle engine to comparative work: **congruent chords sit at equal distances from the center, and equal-distance chords are congruent.** The equation (chord/2)² + d² = r² makes it plain — fix r, and chord length determines distance exactly, both ways.

illustration_description: Unequal chords trade off: from half chord squared plus distance squared equals radius squared, a longer chord sits closer to the center.
accompanying_text: Unequal chords trade off: from (chord/2)² + d² = r², a LONGER chord forces a SMALLER distance — **the closer the chord, the longer it runs**, peaking at the diameter (distance zero). Ranking chords by length is ranking their distances in reverse.

illustration_description: A circle with an external point P. Two tangent lines from P touch the circle at T1 and T2. Each radius to a tangent point meets its tangent at 90 degrees, and the two tangent segments from P are congruent.
accompanying_text: A **tangent line** touches the circle at exactly ONE point — the point of tangency. (Different creature from the tangent RATIO in trigonometry; the shared name is historical.) The headline theorem: **a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of tangency** — and conversely, a line perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint is tangent.

illustration_description: The tangent meets the radius at a right angle, which recruits Pythagoras: from an external point, the tangent, radius, and distance to the center form a right triangle.
accompanying_text: That right angle recruits Pythagoras. From an external point P, the segment to the center (OP), the radius to the tangency point (r), and the **tangent segment** PT form a right triangle with the right angle AT T — so **PT = √(OP² − r²)**. The hypotenuse is OP, always.

illustration_description: A circle with an external point P. Two tangent lines from P touch the circle at T1 and T2. Each radius to a tangent point meets its tangent at 90 degrees, and the two tangent segments from P are congruent.
accompanying_text: From any external point, exactly TWO tangent lines reach the circle — and their tangent segments are **congruent**: PT₁ = PT₂. Proof in one breath: triangles OT₁P and OT₂P share hypotenuse OP and have equal legs (radii), so HL congruence — then CPCTC hands over the tangent segments.

illustration_description: Zoom out to the whole figure: two radii and two congruent tangent segments from one external point form a kite.
accompanying_text: Zoom out to the whole figure OT₁PT₂: two radii, two congruent tangent segments — **a kite**, straight from the quadrilateral course, with its right angles at T₁ and T₂. Its angle sum forces a clean supplement: **angle P + central angle T₁OT₂ = 180°**, since the two right angles spend the other 180.

illustration_description: Wrap a triangle around a circle so every side is tangent: the circle is the inscribed circle, or incircle.
accompanying_text: Wrap a triangle around a circle so every side is tangent — the circle is **inscribed** in the triangle. The two-tangent theorem fires at all three vertices: each vertex owns a matched pair of tangent lengths, call them x, x at A, y, y at B, z, z at C. Every side is then a SUM of two tangent lengths.

illustration_description: Run it in reverse to find unknown pieces: the two tangent segments from each vertex are equal, letting you solve for lengths.
accompanying_text: Run it in reverse to find unknown pieces. If AB = 12 and the tangent length from A is 4, then B's tangent length is 12 − 4 = 8 — and B carries that same 8 onto side BC. Tangent lengths are a bookkeeping system: each vertex's number is fixed, and sides just add adjacent entries.

illustration_description: Chapter one priced angles on the circle as half their arc; now the vertex moves elsewhere.
accompanying_text: Chapter 1 priced angles ON the circle (half their arc). Move the vertex and the price changes. Two chords crossing **INSIDE** the circle make an angle equal to **half the SUM of the two arcs** they and their vertical partner intercept — the average of the two arcs. Arcs 100° and 40°: angle = 70°.

illustration_description: Push the vertex outside and the formula flips its sign: the angle is half the difference of the two intercepted arcs.
accompanying_text: Push the vertex **OUTSIDE** and the formula flips its sign: two secants (or tangents) from an external point make an angle equal to **half the DIFFERENCE of the far and near arcs**. Arcs 130° and 30°: angle = 50°. Inside averages; outside takes half the spread. The vertex's location picks the sign.

illustration_description: One hybrid remains: a tangent and a chord meeting at the point of tangency.
accompanying_text: One hybrid remains: a **tangent and a chord** meeting at the point of tangency. The angle between them equals **half the intercepted arc** — the same rate as an inscribed angle, because it IS an inscribed angle in the limit: slide one chord endpoint around until the chord becomes the tangent, and the half-arc rule survives the slide.

illustration_description: The two angles the chord makes with the tangent, one on each side, each equal half their intercepted arc.
accompanying_text: The two angles the chord makes with the tangent — one on each side — halve the two arcs the chord creates, and those arcs sum to 360°. So the two tangent-chord angles sum to 180°: supplements, exactly as a straight line demands. The circle's arithmetic and the line's arithmetic agree.

illustration_description: Two chords crossing inside a circle at point P cut each other so that the products of their two pieces are equal.
accompanying_text: From angles to lengths. Two chords crossing at P inside a circle obey **PA · PB = PC · PD**: the products of the two pieces match. Why: joining the endpoints creates two triangles with equal inscribed angles (same arcs) — similar by AA, from the similarity course — and the proportion cross-multiplies into the product rule.

illustration_description: Outside the circle the same law holds in costume: for two secants, the whole length times its external piece is equal for both.
accompanying_text: Outside the circle the same law holds in costume: for two secants from P, **PA · PB = PC · PD**, where both distances are measured FROM P — so each product is the secant's **external part times its whole length**. Same AA-similarity engine, same matched products.

illustration_description: Let one secant rotate until its two points merge: it becomes a tangent, and the tangent squared equals the whole secant times its external piece.
accompanying_text: Let one secant rotate until its two intersection points merge: it becomes a **tangent**, and near × far collapses to **PT · PT = PT²**. The tangent-secant law: **PT² = PA · PB** (external × whole). One law, three costumes — chords, secants, tangent — all called the *power of the point* P.

illustration_description: A circle with a shaded 60-degree sector, one sixth of the whole. The arc length is theta over 360 times the circumference, and the sector area is theta over 360 times the full area.
accompanying_text: Arc MEASURE counts degrees; arc LENGTH measures distance — and the bridge is a fraction. An arc of θ degrees claims θ/360 of the circle, so it claims that same fraction of the circumference (2πr, from your Grade 7 circle work): **arc length = (θ/360) · 2πr**. Degrees price the share; the radius prices the whole.

illustration_description: The trigonometry course prices the same arc as s equals r theta, with theta measured in radians.
accompanying_text: The trigonometry course prices the same arc as **s = rθ** with θ in radians — and the two formulas are one. Convert 60° = π/3 rad: s = 9 · π/3 = 3π, exactly the fraction route's answer. Radians BUILD the fraction into the angle unit; degrees keep it explicit. Same arc, two bookkeeping systems.

illustration_description: A circle with a shaded 60-degree sector, one sixth of the whole. The arc length is theta over 360 times the circumference, and the sector area is theta over 360 times the full area.
accompanying_text: The same fraction that priced the arc prices the **sector** — the pie slice between two radii. A θ-degree sector claims θ/360 of the circle's area πr² (Grade 7 again): **sector area = (θ/360) · πr²**. One fraction, two purchases: rim distance and interior area.

illustration_description: Radian bookkeeping compresses the sector too: with theta in radians, the sector area is one half r squared theta.
accompanying_text: Radian bookkeeping compresses this one too: with θ in radians, sector area = **½r²θ**. Check it on the quarter-circle: ½(36)(π/2) = 9π — the same 28.27. And notice the pleasing echo: arc s = rθ, sector = ½r·(rθ) = ½ · radius · arc, just like a triangle's ½ · base · height.

illustration_description: A circle with a central angle of 80 degrees standing on arc AB. An inscribed angle from a point on the far side of the circle measures 40 degrees on the same arc, and moving the vertex to a second position keeps it at 40 degrees: any inscribed angle is half its central angle.
accompanying_text: A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on one circle. Its signature: **opposite angles are supplementary.** Why: opposite angles are inscribed angles opening onto complementary arcs — the two arcs together make the whole 360°, so the two angles halve it: 180° between them.

illustration_description: The proof in one line: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral each halve arcs that together make the whole circle, so they are supplementary.
accompanying_text: The proof in one line: angle A halves arc BCD, angle C halves arc DAB, and those arcs tile the whole circle — A + C = ½(360) = 180. The CONVERSE holds too: if a quadrilateral's opposite angles are supplementary, a circle passes through all four vertices. Supplementarity is the entrance ticket.

illustration_description: Two concentric-looking circles of different sizes, both labelled with their circumference over diameter, showing the same ratio pi regardless of size — the reason any two circles are related by a single scale factor.
accompanying_text: For similarity, most shapes need conditions checked — matching angles, proportional sides. A circle needs none of that. Every circle's circumference is 2πr and every circle's area is πr² — the SAME two formulas, for every circle there is. Only the radius changes from one circle to the next, and that single number is enough to connect any two circles by exactly one dilation.

illustration_description: A bar chart comparing how circumference and area respond when the radius doubles: circumference doubles in step with the radius, while area quadruples, growing with the square of the scale factor.
accompanying_text: Area's formula is πr² — built from r SQUARED, not r alone. That one difference changes everything about how it scales: double the radius and the '2r' piece doubles, but the 'r²' piece quadruples. Circumference and area are both built from the same radius, but they answer to that radius in genuinely different ways.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Two groups can hold MORE, FEWER, or the SAME. Those three words are all of comparing — the rest is finding out which is true.

accompanying_text: More means leftovers on that side after pairing. Fewer means running out first. Same means the pairing comes out even.

illustration_description: Completing the square as area: a large square labeled x squared, with a strip labeled three x attached to its right and another strip labeled three x attached below. Together they form a bigger square of side x plus three, except one small dashed corner square labeled nine is missing. Caption: add nine to complete the square.
accompanying_text: A **perfect square trinomial** is a squared binomial in disguise: (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p². Read it backward: given x² + bx, the constant that completes the square is **(b/2)²** — half the middle coefficient, squared. The picture: two b/2 strips wrap the x² square, leaving one small corner to fill.

illustration_description: Spotting a perfect-square trinomial: x squared plus ten x plus twenty-five works because twenty-five is ten halved, then squared.
accompanying_text: Spotting one in the wild: x² + 10x + 25 has 25 = (10/2)², so it folds up as **(x + 5)²**. The number inside the parentheses is always **b/2** — the same half that got squared.

illustration_description: Completing the square as area: a large square labeled x squared, with a strip labeled three x attached to its right and another strip labeled three x attached below. Together they form a bigger square of side x plus three, except one small dashed corner square labeled nine is missing. Caption: add nine to complete the square.
accompanying_text: You already know how to solve (x + 3)² = 4 — square roots. Completing the square lets you **build** that form from any quadratic. Solve x² + 6x + 5 = 0: move the constant, x² + 6x = −5; add (6/2)² = 9 to **both sides**: (x + 3)² = 4.

illustration_description: Finish with square roots: x plus three squared equals four gives x plus three equals plus or minus two, so x is negative one or negative five.
accompanying_text: Finish with square roots: (x + 3)² = 4 gives x + 3 = ±2, so x = −3 ± 2 — that's **x = −1 or x = −5**. Check: (−1)² + 6(−1) + 5 = 0. ✓ The whole method is: isolate, add (b/2)² to both sides, root, undo the shift.

illustration_description: An upward-opening parabola: its lowest point is the vertex, and the dashed vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, mirroring the two sides.
accompanying_text: You've read vertices FROM vertex form — now derive it. For y = x² − 6x + 5, add and subtract (6/2)² = 9 **on the same side**: y = (x² − 6x + 9) − 9 + 5 = **(x − 3)² − 4**. Add-and-subtract keeps y unchanged — there's no other side to balance on.

illustration_description: Why completing the square is legal: adding nine then subtracting nine is adding zero, so the value never changes, it only regroups.
accompanying_text: Why it's legal: +9 − 9 = 0, so y never changed — it just regrouped. The payoff is instant: (x − 3)² − 4 hands you the vertex **(3, −4)** and the minimum value −4 with no formula at all.

illustration_description: x squared equals negative one has no real solution, because every real number squares to zero or a positive value.
accompanying_text: x² = −1 has no real solution — every real number squares to zero or more. Mathematicians' fix: invent a new number. Define **i** by **i² = −1**. With it, square roots of negatives make sense: √(−9) = √9 · √(−1) = **3i**.

illustration_description: The rule in general: the square root of negative k is i times the square root of k, pulling the negative one out as i.
accompanying_text: The rule in general: **√(−k) = i√k** for k > 0 — pull the −1 out as i, then root the rest. And equations follow: x² = −16 now HAS solutions, x = ±4i, because (4i)² = 16 · i² = −16 and (−4i)² does the same.

illustration_description: The powers of i arranged on a circle: 1 on the right, i on top, negative 1 on the left, negative i on the bottom. Curved arrows labeled times i step counterclockwise from each value to the next, showing the repeating four step cycle 1, i, negative 1, negative i, back to 1.
accompanying_text: Keep multiplying by i and a pattern locks in: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = i²·i = **−i**, i⁴ = i²·i² = (−1)(−1) = **1** — and then it repeats. Every power of i is one of just four values, cycling like a quarter turn.

illustration_description: For big exponents, ride the cycle: since i to the fourth is one, only the remainder when the exponent is divided by four matters.
accompanying_text: For big exponents, ride the cycle: since i⁴ = 1, only the **remainder of n ÷ 4** matters. i¹⁰: 10 = 4·2 + 2, remainder 2, so i¹⁰ = i² = −1. Remainder 0 means a whole number of laps: the value is 1.

illustration_description: The complex plane: a horizontal real axis and a vertical imaginary axis. The number 3 plus 2 i is plotted as a single point, reached by moving 3 units right along the real axis and 2 units up along the imaginary axis, with dashed guide lines showing each move.
accompanying_text: A **complex number** mixes both kinds: **a + bi**, with real part a and imaginary part b. Since it takes two numbers to describe, it lives on a **plane**: real part along the horizontal axis, imaginary part up the vertical. 3 + 2i is the point 3 right, 2 up.

illustration_description: On the complex plane, a purely real number sits on the horizontal axis while a purely imaginary number sits on the vertical axis.
accompanying_text: Special positions: a purely **real** number like 5 sits ON the horizontal axis (its b is 0); a purely **imaginary** one like 5i sits ON the vertical axis (its a is 0). Every other complex number floats off both axes.

illustration_description: Adding complex numbers works like combining like terms: real with real and imaginary with imaginary.
accompanying_text: Adding complex numbers works like combining like terms: **real with real, imaginary with imaginary**. (3 + 2i) + (1 + 4i) = (3 + 1) + (2 + 4)i = 4 + 6i. The two parts never mix — just as 3 + 2x stays 3 + 2x.

illustration_description: Subtraction distributes the minus sign to both parts of the second complex number.
accompanying_text: Subtraction distributes the minus to **both parts** of the second number: (6 + 2i) − (4 + 5i) = (6 − 4) + (2 − 5)i = 2 − 3i. The classic slip is subtracting the real part but forgetting to subtract the imaginary one.

illustration_description: Area model for multiplying two binomials: a rectangle with sides split into a plus b across and c plus d down forms four smaller rectangles — ac, bc, ad, and bd — whose areas add to the product.
accompanying_text: Multiply complex numbers like binomials — distribute everything (FOIL) — then apply **i² = −1**. (2 + i)(3 + 2i) = 6 + 4i + 3i + 2i². The 2i² becomes **−2**, a real number, so the product is (6 − 2) + 7i = **4 + 7i**.

illustration_description: Multiplying: FOIL as usual, but the Last term carries i squared, which becomes negative one and merges into the real part.
accompanying_text: The pattern to internalize: the **First** and **Last** FOIL terms build the real part (with the Last flipped by i²), and the **Outer + Inner** build the imaginary part. In symbols: (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.

illustration_description: The conjugate of a plus b i is a minus b i: same real part, flipped imaginary part, a mirror across the real axis.
accompanying_text: The **conjugate** of a + bi is a − bi — same real part, flipped imaginary sign. Multiply a number by its conjugate and the i vanishes: (a + bi)(a − bi) = **a² + b²**, always a real number. For 3 + 2i: (3 + 2i)(3 − 2i) = 9 + 4 = 13.

illustration_description: The real product is the key to division: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate to clear the imaginary part from the denominator.
accompanying_text: That real product is the key to **division**: to divide by a complex number, multiply top and bottom by the **bottom's conjugate**. Example: (3 + i)/(1 − i). Multiply by (1 + i)/(1 + i): bottom becomes 1 + 1 = 2, top becomes (3 + i)(1 + i) = 2 + 4i, so the answer is **1 + 2i**.

illustration_description: What was once a dead end now solves: x squared equals negative sixteen gives x equals plus or minus four i.
accompanying_text: In Algebra 1, x² = −16 was a dead end: 'no real solutions.' Now you can finish it: x = ±√(−16) = **±4i**. Every equation of the form x² = −k has two purely imaginary solutions, ±i√k — the square-root method never stalls again.

illustration_description: Shifted squares work the same way: x minus two squared equals negative nine gives x minus two equals plus or minus three i, so x is two plus or minus three i.
accompanying_text: Shifted squares work the same way: (x − 2)² = −9 gives x − 2 = ±3i, so **x = 2 ± 3i** — a real shift plus an imaginary spread. The answers come as a matched pair, one +3i and one −3i around the center 2.

illustration_description: Three parabolas over a horizontal x-axis: when the discriminant is positive the curve crosses the axis at two points (two roots); when it is zero the curve just touches the axis (one root); when it is negative the curve stays above the axis (no real roots).
accompanying_text: The quadratic formula never needed the discriminant to be positive. For x² − 4x + 13 = 0: D = b² − 4ac = 16 − 52 = **−36**. Then √D = √(−36) = 6i, and x = (4 ± 6i)/2 = **2 ± 3i**. Same formula, new number system.

illustration_description: Finishing matters: x equals four plus or minus six i over two divides both parts by two, giving two plus or minus three i.
accompanying_text: Finishing matters: x = (4 ± 6i)/2 divides **both parts** by 2, giving 2 ± 3i. Notice the answers are **conjugates** — same real part, opposite imaginary signs. Real-coefficient quadratics always deliver complex roots in conjugate pairs.

illustration_description: Three parabolas over a horizontal x-axis: when the discriminant is positive the curve crosses the axis at two points (two roots); when it is zero the curve just touches the axis (one root); when it is negative the curve stays above the axis (no real roots).
accompanying_text: Algebra 1's discriminant chart had a hole: 'D < 0: no real solutions.' The full story: **every** quadratic has exactly **two** roots. D > 0: two distinct reals. D = 0: one real, counted twice. D < 0: two complex conjugates. Nothing is ever missing — it just moves off the real line.

illustration_description: Classifying is a one-number job: compute the discriminant b squared minus four a c, then read the sign for real or complex roots.
accompanying_text: So classifying is a one-number job: compute D = b² − 4ac and read its **sign**. Positive → two real crossings. Zero → the vertex kisses the axis. Negative → the parabola floats clear and the pair goes complex.

illustration_description: The old shortcuts survive: for x squared plus b x plus c equals zero, the roots sum to negative b and multiply to c.
accompanying_text: The old shortcuts survive the trip: for x² + bx + c = 0, the roots still **sum to −b** and **multiply to c** — even when they're complex. x² − 4x + 13 has roots 2 ± 3i: sum (2 + 3i) + (2 − 3i) = 4 = −b. ✓

illustration_description: The product uses the conjugate pattern: two plus three i times two minus three i equals four plus nine, which is thirteen, a real number.
accompanying_text: The product uses the conjugate pattern: (2 + 3i)(2 − 3i) = 4 + 9 = **13** = c. ✓ In general a ± bi sums to **2a** (the imaginary parts cancel) and multiplies to **a² + b²** (always real — which is exactly why c is real).

illustration_description: Run the shortcuts backward: a monic quadratic with roots r and s is x squared minus the sum times x plus the product.
accompanying_text: Run the shortcuts backward: a monic quadratic with roots r and s is **x² − (sum)x + (product)**. Roots 3 ± 2i: sum 6, product 9 + 4 = 13, so the quadratic is **x² − 6x + 13**. Note the sign: minus the sum.

illustration_description: Complex roots of real quadratics must come in conjugate pairs, mirrored across the real axis.
accompanying_text: This is also why complex roots of real quadratics **must** come in conjugate pairs: only then do the sum (2a) and product (a² + b²) come out real. One root 4 − i immediately tells you the other is 4 + i.

illustration_description: Four solving methods, one decision: choose based on the form of the quadratic in front of you.
accompanying_text: Four solving methods, one decision: bare x² = k or a ready-made square → **square roots**; friendly integer factors → **factoring**; even middle term, stubborn factors → **completing the square**; anything at all → the **formula**. The discriminant predicts the root type before you commit.

illustration_description: Complex roots are not tied to any one method: they appear whenever the discriminant is negative.
accompanying_text: Complex roots aren't tied to any one method — they appear whenever **D < 0**, whichever route you take. x² + 10x + 29: completing the square gives (x + 5)² = −4, so x = **−5 ± 2i** — the negative square announces the complex pair.

illustration_description: Two overlapping circles for event A (multiple of 3, six cards) and event B (greater than 15, five cards). The overlap holds one card, 18. Ten cards lie outside both.
accompanying_text: Two words do all the work. **And** (∩) keeps an outcome only if it passes **both** tests. **Or** (∪) keeps it if it passes **at least one**. So the intersection is always the smaller set — it lives inside the union.

illustration_description: Twenty cards numbered 1 to 20 laid out in a grid; the six multiples of 3 (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18) are shaded to show the event as a subset of the sample space.
accompanying_text: Draw one card from twenty cards numbered 1–20. The twenty outcomes are the **sample space**. An **event** is just a subset of it: "multiple of 3" is the set {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}. Because every card is equally likely, a probability is a count: P(A) = (outcomes in A) ÷ 20.

illustration_description: Two overlapping circles for event A (multiple of 3, six cards) and event B (greater than 15, five cards). The overlap holds one card, 18. Ten cards lie outside both.
accompanying_text: Picture the two events as overlapping circles. The middle holds outcomes in **both**; the outer petals hold outcomes in only one; everything outside is in **neither**. That picture is why counting a union means adding the two circles and then removing the middle once — it was counted twice.

illustration_description: A bar of total probability 1 split into event A on the left and not-A on the right, showing that P(A) plus P(not A) equals 1.
accompanying_text: "At least one" means **one or more** — one, two, all of them. It fails in exactly one way: **zero**. So always ask "how many outcomes have zero?" and subtract that from the total.

illustration_description: A bar of total probability 1 split into event A on the left and not-A on the right, showing that P(A) plus P(not A) equals 1.
accompanying_text: Every outcome either is in A or is not. So P(A) + P(not A) = 1, giving the **complement rule**: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). This is the workhorse for "at least one", because the opposite of *at least one* is the much smaller, much easier event: **none**.

illustration_description: The 36 outcomes of rolling two dice as a 6 by 6 grid. The last row and last column are shaded because they contain a six; they share the corner cell, so 6 plus 6 minus 1 equals 11 shaded outcomes.
accompanying_text: Notice the pattern. Counting "at least one" directly means adding overlapping cases and repairing double-counts. Counting **none** is one clean multiplication — every trial must miss. That is why the complement route is almost always the short road.
