illustration_description: On the left, two separate circles for even and odd share no outcome, so they are mutually exclusive. On the right, even and multiple of five overlap at 10 and 20, so they can happen together.
accompanying_text: One test decides it. Try to name a **single outcome** that is in both events. If you can name even one, the events are not mutually exclusive. If no such outcome exists, they are.

illustration_description: On the left, two separate circles for even and odd share no outcome, so they are mutually exclusive. On the right, even and multiple of five overlap at 10 and 20, so they can happen together.
accompanying_text: Two events are **mutually exclusive** when they share no outcome: A ∩ B is empty, so they cannot both happen. Even and odd. Rain all day and dry all day. When events are exclusive, counting a union is pure addition — there is nothing to remove. Most real pairs of events are **not** exclusive.

illustration_description: Adding the size of circle A to the size of circle B counts the overlapping middle region twice, so the union subtracts that middle once.
accompanying_text: That subtraction has a name coming in Chapter 4: the **addition rule**. For now, hold the picture. Add the two counts, then remove the middle once. Exclusive events just happen to have an empty middle, so nothing gets removed — they are the easy special case, not the rule.

illustration_description: Adding the size of circle A to the size of circle B counts the overlapping middle region twice, so the union subtracts that middle once.
accompanying_text: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts everything in the middle **twice** — once from each event. The rule fixes that by subtracting the middle once. If the events cannot co-occur, the middle is empty and there is nothing to subtract.

illustration_description: Two overlapping circles for hearts and face cards in a 52-card deck: 10 hearts that are not face cards, 3 cards in both, 9 face cards that are not hearts, giving 22 cards in the union.
accompanying_text:
Counting outcomes and finding probabilities are the same move, divided by the total. If every card is equally likely, P(A) is just |A|/52. So the overlap correction you learned for **counts** carries straight over to **probabilities**:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

illustration_description: On the left, two separate circles for even and odd share no outcome, so they are mutually exclusive. On the right, even and multiple of five overlap at 10 and 20, so they can happen together.
accompanying_text:
When the overlap is empty, P(A ∩ B) = 0 and the subtraction does nothing:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

That is the *special* case, not the default. Adding without checking the overlap is the single most common error in this chapter — so before you add, always ask: **can both happen at once?**

illustration_description: A two-way table of 200 students. Inside cells: bus and sport 40, bus and no sport 60, walks and sport 70, walks and no sport 30. Row totals 100 and 100, column totals 110 and 90, grand total 200.
accompanying_text: A joint probability answers **both** questions at once, so it lives in a single inner cell — never a row, never a column. Its denominator is always the grand total, because the student could have landed anywhere in the table.

illustration_description: A two-way table of 200 students. Inside cells: bus and sport 40, bus and no sport 60, walks and sport 70, walks and no sport 30. Row totals 100 and 100, column totals 110 and 90, grand total 200.
accompanying_text:
A two-way table sorts one group by **two questions at once**. Each of the 200 students lands in exactly one inner cell, so the four inner cells add to 200. The edge totals are just those cells summed along a row or a column.

You met these tables in Grade 8. Now every count in one becomes a probability: divide by the grand total.

illustration_description: The same table with one inside cell highlighted as a joint probability, 40 out of 200, and one edge total highlighted as a marginal probability, 110 out of 200.
accompanying_text:
Two names for two shapes:

**Joint** probability — one inner cell over the total. P(bus and sport) = 40/200.

**Marginal** probability — a whole edge total over the total. P(sport) = 110/200.

Same denominator, different shaded region. Marginals ignore the second question entirely.

illustration_description: The bus row and the sport column are both shaded. The single cell where they cross, 40, is shaded darkest because adding the row total to the column total counts it twice.
accompanying_text: Row total + column total always overshoots, because the crossing cell lives in both. Subtract that cell once and you are left with exactly the shaded students. A quick sanity test: if your "or" probability exceeds 1, you forgot the subtraction.

illustration_description: The bus row and the sport column are both shaded. The single cell where they cross, 40, is shaded darkest because adding the row total to the column total counts it twice.
accompanying_text:
"Bus **or** sport" on a table means: shade the whole bus row, then shade the whole sport column. The cell where they cross gets shaded twice — once by the row, once by the column.

That is the addition rule in picture form. Add the row total and the column total, then take the crossing cell back once.

illustration_description: A bar of total probability 1 split into event A on the left and not-A on the right, showing that P(A) plus P(not A) equals 1.
accompanying_text:
"**Neither**" is the complement of "or". Every student is either inside the shaded union or outside it, so:

P(neither) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).

On a table it is the one cell you never shaded. That gives you a free check: the union and the "neither" cell must add to the whole group.

illustration_description: Six die faces. The three odd faces are greyed out because we are told the roll is even, leaving only 2, 4 and 6 in play, and one of those three is the 6.
accompanying_text: When you are told B happened, cross out every outcome where B is false. Then just count: how many of the survivors are also A? That count over the number of survivors **is** the conditional probability.

illustration_description: Six die faces. The three odd faces are greyed out because we are told the roll is even, leaving only 2, 4 and 6 in play, and one of those three is the 6.
accompanying_text:
P(roll a 6) = 1/6. Now someone tells you the roll came up **even**. The three odd faces are gone — they were never possible after all — and the 6 is one of the three faces still standing.

Information does not change the die. It changes the **set of outcomes you are choosing among**.

illustration_description: A Venn diagram where circle B is shaded as the new universe. Everything outside B is faded away, and the part of A inside B is highlighted. The conditional probability is that highlighted part divided by all of B.
accompanying_text:
Written as a formula:

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

Read it as: *of the B-world, how much is also A?* The numerator must be the part of A **inside** B — an outcome outside B is no longer on the table. Both parts are measured against the same original total, so that total cancels.

illustration_description: Two copies of the same table. On the left the bus row is highlighted so 40 is divided by 100. On the right the sport column is highlighted so the same 40 is divided by 110. The two conditional probabilities are different.
accompanying_text: The bar in P(A | B) is not symmetric. Whatever stands to the **right** of the bar is the group you are standing inside; whatever stands to the left is what you are counting there. Swap them and you have changed the question.

illustration_description: Two copies of the same table. On the left the bus row is highlighted so 40 is divided by 100. On the right the sport column is highlighted so the same 40 is divided by 110. The two conditional probabilities are different.
accompanying_text:
The same 40 students sit in the crossing cell. But *what you are told* decides what you divide by.

Told they take the bus → divide by the bus row: 40/100.
Told they play a sport → divide by the sport column: 40/110.

Same numerator, different denominator, different answer. P(A | B) and P(B | A) are **not** the same number.

illustration_description: A Venn diagram where circle B is shaded as the new universe. Everything outside B is faded away, and the part of A inside B is highlighted. The conditional probability is that highlighted part divided by all of B.
accompanying_text:
Swapping the two sides is the most expensive mistake in probability.

*Almost every flu patient has a cough* does **not** mean *almost every cougher has flu*. The first divides by the flu patients; the second divides by the far larger crowd of coughers.

When a claim conditions on something, ask: **which group is underneath?**

illustration_description: A unit square. Half its width is the bus riders, and two fifths of that strip's height are the ones who play a sport, so the shaded rectangle has area zero point two — the joint probability.
accompanying_text: Think of it as a two-stage journey. Stage one: how likely is B at all? Stage two: **given you got there**, how likely is A? Multiply the two stages. The second probability must be measured inside the world the first one created.

illustration_description: A unit square. Half its width is the bus riders, and two fifths of that strip's height are the ones who play a sport, so the shaded rectangle has area zero point two — the joint probability.
accompanying_text:
Multiply both sides of P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) by P(B):

P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B).

In words: to get **both**, first get B, then get A *in the world where B already happened*. Half the students ride the bus; 40% of those play a sport; so 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20 do both.

illustration_description: A Venn diagram where circle B is shaded as the new universe. Everything outside B is faded away, and the part of A inside B is highlighted. The conditional probability is that highlighted part divided by all of B.
accompanying_text:
The rule works from either end:

P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = P(A) × P(B | A).

Use whichever conditional you actually know. That freedom is what makes the rule usable — and it is the seed of Bayes' rule, since both products describe the same overlap.

illustration_description: A probability tree for drawing two marbles from a bag of five red and three blue without replacing the first. The first branches are five eighths and three eighths, and the second-draw branches use denominators of seven because one marble is gone.
accompanying_text: Take the draws one at a time. Write the bag's contents before each draw, and read the probability off *that* bag. Without replacement the bag changes between draws, so the second fraction is never a copy of the first.

illustration_description: A probability tree for drawing two marbles from a bag of five red and three blue without replacing the first. The first branches are five eighths and three eighths, and the second-draw branches use denominators of seven because one marble is gone.
accompanying_text:
A tree turns the multiplication rule into a picture. Each branch carries a conditional probability, so you **multiply along a path** to reach a leaf.

The second-draw branches use denominators of 7, because one marble is already gone. Removing it also changes *which* marble is likelier next — the branches differ depending on the path you took.

illustration_description: A probability tree for drawing two marbles from a bag of five red and three blue without replacing the first. The first branches are five eighths and three eighths, and the second-draw branches use denominators of seven because one marble is gone.
accompanying_text:
Multiply **along** a path; add **across** paths.

"One of each colour" happens two ways — red-then-blue and blue-then-red — and those two leaves are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add. Every leaf of the tree is exclusive of every other, which is why the four leaves sum to 1.

illustration_description: Left panel: two separate circles, mutually exclusive, where learning that A happened makes B impossible. Right panel: two overlapping circles that are independent, where learning A happened leaves B's chance unchanged.
accompanying_text: Ask one question: *does the news change my estimate?* If P(A) was 0.3 before you heard about B and it is still 0.3 after, B was worthless news and the events are independent. If it moves at all — up or down — they are dependent.

illustration_description: The deck grid with the hearts row and the kings column shaded. One in thirteen hearts is a king, and four in fifty-two cards are kings — the same one-thirteenth, so suit tells you nothing about rank.
accompanying_text:
Two events are **independent** when learning one leaves the other's probability exactly where it was:

P(A | B) = P(A).

A card's suit and its rank are like this. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. Told the card is a heart, the world shrinks to 13 cards — but exactly one is a king, so it is still 1/13.

illustration_description: A Venn diagram where circle B is shaded as the new universe. Everything outside B is faded away, and the part of A inside B is highlighted. The conditional probability is that highlighted part divided by all of B.
accompanying_text:
Independence is **symmetric**. If B tells you nothing about A, then A tells you nothing about B:

P(A | B) = P(A)  ⟺  P(B | A) = P(B).

So you may test whichever direction is easier. Careful: independence is a claim about *information*, not about causation, and it must be checked — never assumed because two things "feel unrelated".

illustration_description: Two tables compared. On the left, the joint count equals the product of the marginal probabilities, so the events are independent. On the right, the actual joint count of forty is well below the fifty-five the product predicts, so the events are dependent.
accompanying_text: The product test has two steps. **Predict:** multiply the two rates and scale by the total. **Compare:** look at what the cell actually holds. Equal means independent. Any difference at all means dependent.

illustration_description: Two tables compared. On the left, the joint count equals the product of the marginal probabilities, so the events are independent. On the right, the actual joint count of forty is well below the fifty-five the product predicts, so the events are dependent.
accompanying_text:
Put P(A | B) = P(A) into the multiplication rule and the conditional disappears:

P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)  — **only when A and B are independent.**

That gives a one-line test. Predict the cell from the two edge totals; then look at the cell. If the prediction is wrong, the events are dependent.

illustration_description: Two tables compared. On the left, the joint count equals the product of the marginal probabilities, so the events are independent. On the right, the actual joint count of forty is well below the fifty-five the product predicts, so the events are dependent.
accompanying_text:
The product test works in **both directions**:

– Given a table, compare the actual cell with P(A) × P(B) × total.
– Given that events *are* independent, use the product to **build** the missing cell.

A gap in either direction — cell above or below the prediction — is dependence. Only an exact match means none.

illustration_description: Left panel: two separate circles, mutually exclusive, where learning that A happened makes B impossible. Right panel: two overlapping circles that are independent, where learning A happened leaves B's chance unchanged.
accompanying_text: Picture the Venn diagram. Mutually exclusive events are **drawn apart** — no shared region at all. Independent events **must overlap**, and the overlap has to be exactly the product size. Separate circles can never be independent.

illustration_description: Left panel: two separate circles, mutually exclusive, where learning that A happened makes B impossible. Right panel: two overlapping circles that are independent, where learning A happened leaves B's chance unchanged.
accompanying_text:
These two words sound similar and mean nearly opposite things.

**Mutually exclusive:** A happening makes B *impossible*. P(B | A) = 0.
**Independent:** A happening leaves B *untouched*. P(B | A) = P(B).

So if both events have a real chance of happening, being exclusive is the strongest possible dependence — the news is devastating, not useless.

illustration_description: Left panel: two separate circles, mutually exclusive, where learning that A happened makes B impossible. Right panel: two overlapping circles that are independent, where learning A happened leaves B's chance unchanged.
accompanying_text:
A test you can apply in one second: could both events happen at once?

– If **no**, they are mutually exclusive, hence dependent (assuming each has a real chance).
– If **yes**, they overlap, and you must still check the product to know whether they are independent.

Overlapping is necessary for independence, but it is not enough.

illustration_description: Three medal slots. The first can be filled 5 ways, the second 4 ways because one runner is already used, and the third 3 ways, so there are 5 times 4 times 3 equals 60 podiums.
accompanying_text: Draw one empty box per slot. Write in each box how many candidates are still available when you reach it. Then multiply the boxes. If a chosen item is used up, the next box holds one fewer.

illustration_description: Three medal slots. The first can be filled 5 ways, the second 4 ways because one runner is already used, and the third 3 ways, so there are 5 times 4 times 3 equals 60 podiums.
accompanying_text:
Sometimes the sample space is far too big to list. Then you **count** it instead.

Fill the slots one at a time and multiply. Five runners, three medals: 5 choices for gold, then only 4 runners remain for silver, then 3 for bronze.

5 × 4 × 3 = 60 possible podiums.

illustration_description: Three medal slots. The first can be filled 5 ways, the second 4 ways because one runner is already used, and the third 3 ways, so there are 5 times 4 times 3 equals 60 podiums.
accompanying_text:
Two names for the same machinery:

**n!** — arrange **all** n items: n × (n−1) × … × 1.
**nPk** — fill only **k** slots from n items: n × (n−1) × … , k factors in total.

Both assume order matters: swapping two chosen items produces a different result.

illustration_description: Six different orderings of the same three people all collapse into one team, so the number of ordered picks must be divided by six to count the teams.
accompanying_text: Count as if order mattered, then repair. Any k chosen items can be arranged in k! ways, and those arrangements all describe the same group — so the ordered count is exactly k! times too big. Divide by k!.

illustration_description: Six different orderings of the same three people all collapse into one team, so the number of ordered picks must be divided by six to count the teams.
accompanying_text:
A podium of gold-silver-bronze cares about order. A **team** does not: {A, B, C} is the same team however you list it.

Those 60 ordered picks contain each team exactly 3! = 6 times — once per ordering. So divide:

60 ÷ 6 = 10 teams.

illustration_description: Six different orderings of the same three people all collapse into one team, so the number of ordered picks must be divided by six to count the teams.
accompanying_text:
The formula records that division:

C(n,k) = nPk / k! = n! / (k! (n−k)!).

Ask one question before you compute: **would swapping two of my chosen items give a different outcome?** If yes, use a permutation. If no, use a combination.

illustration_description: A long bar of fifty-six equally likely three-marble groups, with the ten all-red groups shaded, giving a probability of ten fifty-sixths.
accompanying_text: Write down two counts before touching a calculator. **Total:** how many equally likely groups exist? **Favourable:** how many of them satisfy the event? Then divide. Use the same counting style for both.

illustration_description: A long bar of fifty-six equally likely three-marble groups, with the ten all-red groups shaded, giving a probability of ten fifty-sixths.
accompanying_text:
When every group is equally likely, probability is just a ratio of two counts:

P = (favourable groups) / (all groups).

Grab 3 marbles from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue. There are C(8,3) = 56 possible groups, and C(5,3) = 10 of them are all red. So P(all red) = 10/56 ≈ 0.179.

illustration_description: A long bar of fifty-six equally likely three-marble groups, with the ten all-red groups shaded, giving a probability of ten fifty-sixths.
accompanying_text:
Two habits make these problems easy.

**Split the favourable count** into independent choices and multiply: pick the girls, then the boys.
**Use the complement** when the event says "at least one": count the single way to fail, and subtract from 1.

illustration_description: A parabola opening upward with its focus marked above the vertex and its directrix drawn as a horizontal line below. A point on the curve is joined to both the focus and the directrix by two segments of equal length, showing the defining equal-distance rule. The focus-directrix definition of a parabola.
accompanying_text: A **parabola** is the set of all points equidistant from a fixed point (the **focus**) and a fixed line (the **directrix**). Every point on the curve is balanced exactly between them. This single rule — equal distances — carves out the familiar U-shape, no equation required yet.

illustration_description: Vertex at the origin, focus at zero p, directrix at y equals negative p: the standard parabola is x squared equals four p y.
accompanying_text:
Place the vertex at the origin, focus at (0, p), directrix y = −p. The equal-distance rule becomes the equation

x² = 4py,  or  y = x²/(4p).

The number **p** is the **focal length** — the vertex-to-focus distance. Larger p means a wider, gentler parabola; smaller p, a tighter one.

illustration_description: Move the vertex to h k and the equation shifts: x minus h squared equals four p times y minus k.
accompanying_text:
Move the vertex to (h, k) and the equation shifts too (recall transformations):

(x − h)² = 4p(y − k).

The vertex is (h, k); the focus sits p units above it at (h, k + p); the directrix is the line y = k − p. Everything rides along with the vertex.

illustration_description: Parabolas can open sideways too: when y is squared, x is the one that opens, giving y squared equals four p x.
accompanying_text:
Parabolas can open **sideways** too. When y is squared, x drives the opening:

(y − k)² = 4p(x − h)

opens right (p > 0) or left (p < 0), with the focus at (h + p, k). Which variable is squared tells you the axis of symmetry — squared y means a horizontal axis.

illustration_description: A parabolic reflector: several vertical rays come straight down, strike the curve, and all reflect to a single focus point above the vertex, illustrating why dishes concentrate signals at the focus. Parallel rays reflecting to a parabola's focus.
accompanying_text: A parabola has a remarkable property: **every ray coming straight in, parallel to the axis, reflects to the focus** — and rays from the focus reflect out parallel. This is why satellite dishes, headlights, and solar cookers are parabolic: they concentrate incoming signal at the focus, or beam a source outward.

illustration_description: The focal length p sets how deep the dish is: a small p gives a narrow, deep parabola.
accompanying_text: The focal length p sets how deep the dish is. A small p gives a deep, tightly-curved dish with the focus close to the vertex; a large p gives a shallow dish with a distant focus. Designers choose p to place the receiver conveniently while capturing the beam.

illustration_description: An ellipse with two foci marked on its horizontal major axis. From a point on the curve, two line segments run to the foci; their lengths always sum to 2a, the major axis length. The semi-major axis a, semi-minor axis b, and focus distance c form a right triangle with c squared equal to a squared minus b squared. An ellipse as the locus where distances to two foci sum to a constant.
accompanying_text: An **ellipse** is every point whose distances to **two fixed foci** add up to a constant. Pin a string at both foci, pull it taut with a pencil, and trace: the constant string length is the sum. That sum equals **2a**, the length of the long (major) axis.

illustration_description: Centered at the origin, the ellipse has the tidy equation x squared over a squared plus y squared over b squared equals one.
accompanying_text:
Centered at the origin, the ellipse has the tidy equation

x²/a² + y²/b² = 1,

with **a > b**. Here a is the semi-major axis (half the long way) and b the semi-minor (half the short way). For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1: a = 5, b = 3 — the curve reaches 5 along x and 3 along y.

illustration_description: An ellipse with two foci marked on its horizontal major axis. From a point on the curve, two line segments run to the foci; their lengths always sum to 2a, the major axis length. The semi-major axis a, semi-minor axis b, and focus distance c form a right triangle with c squared equal to a squared minus b squared. An ellipse as the locus where distances to two foci sum to a constant.
accompanying_text:
Where are the foci? For an ellipse, a right triangle links the three lengths:

**c² = a² − b²**,

where c is the focus distance from the center. The foci sit ON the major axis, c units from center. For a = 5, b = 3: c² = 25 − 9 = 16, so c = 4 — foci at (±4, 0).

illustration_description: The ellipse relationship subtracts: c squared equals a squared minus b squared, so the foci sit inside.
accompanying_text: Notice the ellipse relationship **subtracts** (c² = a² − b²), which forces c < a: the foci always sit INSIDE the ellipse. This is the opposite of the hyperbola's rule (coming next), and it's why a bigger gap between a and b pushes the foci further out toward the vertices.

illustration_description: Move the center to h k and every x and y shifts inside the equation.
accompanying_text:
Move the center to (h, k) and every x, y shifts inside the equation (recall the circle's shift):

(x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1.

Everything else — a, b, c, the foci offsets — stays the same; only the center relocates. The foci become (h ± c, k) for a horizontal ellipse.

illustration_description: Eccentricity e equals c over a measures how far from circular an ellipse is, always between zero and one.
accompanying_text: **Eccentricity** e = c/a measures how far from circular an ellipse is. e is between 0 and 1: near **0** it's almost a circle (foci nearly together); near **1** it's long and cigar-shaped (foci near the vertices). For a = 5, c = 4: e = 4/5 = 0.8 — quite elongated.

illustration_description: A hyperbola opening left and right, with two branches. A central box of half-width a and half-height b has diagonals that extend into the asymptotes the branches approach. The vertices sit where each branch turns, and the foci lie further out on the horizontal axis, since c squared equals a squared plus b squared. A hyperbola with its guiding box, asymptotes, foci, and vertices.
accompanying_text: A **hyperbola** flips the ellipse's rule: instead of a constant SUM of focal distances, it's a constant **difference**. Every point satisfies |r₁ − r₂| = 2a. This splits the curve into **two separate branches**, one hugging each focus.

illustration_description: Centered at the origin and opening left-right, the standard hyperbola is x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals one.
accompanying_text:
Centered at the origin and opening left-right, the standard form is

x²/a² − y²/b² = 1

— note the **minus sign**, the hyperbola's signature. The vertices are at (±a, 0); the curve never crosses the y-axis. For x²/9 − y²/16 = 1: a = 3, so vertices at (±3, 0).

illustration_description: A hyperbola opening left and right, with two branches. A central box of half-width a and half-height b has diagonals that extend into the asymptotes the branches approach. The vertices sit where each branch turns, and the foci lie further out on the horizontal axis, since c squared equals a squared plus b squared. A hyperbola with its guiding box, asymptotes, foci, and vertices.
accompanying_text:
Far from center, each branch races toward a straight-line **asymptote**. For x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 the asymptotes are

y = ±(b/a)x.

Draw the a-by-b **guiding box** (±a wide, ±b tall); its diagonals ARE the asymptotes. The branches open through the box's sides and hug those diagonals forever.

illustration_description: For a hyperbola the focus relationship adds: c squared equals a squared plus b squared, so the foci sit outside.
accompanying_text: For a hyperbola the focus relationship **adds**: **c² = a² + b²** (opposite of the ellipse's minus). Because c² = a² + b² > a², the foci sit BEYOND the vertices, further out. For a = 3, b = 4: c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5.

illustration_description: The foci sit on the opening axis, c units from the center, farther out than the vertices.
accompanying_text: The foci sit on the opening axis, c units from center — for a horizontal hyperbola, at (±c, 0), always BEYOND the vertices (±a, 0) since c > a. For x²/9 − y²/16 = 1: c = 5, so foci at (±5, 0), outside the vertices (±3, 0).

illustration_description: Eccentricity e equals c over a again, but for a hyperbola c is greater than a, so e is greater than one.
accompanying_text: **Eccentricity** e = c/a again — but for a hyperbola c > a, so **e > 1** always. The bigger e, the more sharply the branches flare open (wider asymptote angle). This single number > 1 is the hyperbola's fingerprint (recall: ellipse had e < 1).

illustration_description: A classification table for conics from the general form A x squared plus C y squared. Equal A and C gives a circle; same sign but unequal gives an ellipse; opposite signs give a hyperbola; one squared term missing gives a parabola. Classifying a conic from its squared coefficients A and C.
accompanying_text:
Every axis-aligned conic hides in the **general second-degree form**:

Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0.

You can name the conic just from the two squared coefficients **A and C** — before doing any algebra. The linear terms only shift it around; A and C set its shape.

illustration_description: The telltale signs: opposite signs on A and C mean a hyperbola, matching signs mean an ellipse.
accompanying_text: The two telltale signs: **opposite signs** on A and C mean a **hyperbola** (one term is subtracted); **exactly one squared term missing** (A = 0 or C = 0) means a **parabola** (only one variable is squared). These two rules complete the classification.

illustration_description: Completing the square as area: a large square labeled x squared, with a strip labeled three x attached to its right and another strip labeled three x attached below. Together they form a bigger square of side x plus three, except one small dashed corner square labeled nine is missing. Caption: add nine to complete the square.
accompanying_text: To find a conic's center and size, **complete the square** (recall the technique) on the x-terms and y-terms separately. Group them, add the square that finishes each perfect-square trinomial, and balance the other side. This turns the messy general form into the clean standard form.

illustration_description: For an ellipse, after completing the square you must divide through to make the right side equal one.
accompanying_text: For an **ellipse**, after completing the square you must **divide** to make the right side equal 1. From x² + 4y² − 2x − 15 = 0 you complete to (x − 1)² + 4y² = 16, then divide by 16: (x − 1)²/16 + y²/4 = 1 — now a and b are readable.

illustration_description: A hyperbola in general form needs the same divide-to-one step after completing the square.
accompanying_text: A **hyperbola** in general form needs the same divide-to-1 finish, keeping the minus sign. From 9x² − 4y² − 36 = 0: move the constant (9x² − 4y² = 36), then divide by 36 to get x²/4 − y²/9 = 1 — a clean hyperbola with a = 2, b = 3.

illustration_description: A parabola has only one squared variable, so there's no dividing step, just isolate and read.
accompanying_text: A **parabola** has only one squared variable, so there's nothing to divide — just isolate. From y² − 8x = 0: y² = 8x, matching y² = 4px with 4p = 8, so p = 2. Completing the square handles any shift, but the core move is isolating the lone square.

illustration_description: Four conics arranged left to right along an eccentricity axis: a circle at e equals 0, an ellipse at e equals 0.5, a parabola at e equals 1, and a hyperbola at e equals 1.5. As eccentricity increases the curve grows more open, from a closed circle to two flying-apart branches. Eccentricity morphs a circle into an ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.
accompanying_text: One number — **eccentricity e** — organizes ALL the conics on a single scale. As e climbs from 0 upward, the curve morphs: **e = 0** is a circle, **0 < e < 1** an ellipse, **e = 1** a parabola, and **e > 1** a hyperbola. They're one family, not four separate shapes.

illustration_description: Reading the scale physically: a small eccentricity means nearly round, while one approaching one means very stretched.
accompanying_text: Reading the scale physically: small e means 'nearly round' (a circle barely stretched); e approaching 1 means a long, thin ellipse; past 1 the curve breaks open into a hyperbola's two flying-apart branches. The bigger e, the more 'open' the conic.

illustration_description: Four conics arranged left to right along an eccentricity axis: a circle at e equals 0, an ellipse at e equals 0.5, a parabola at e equals 1, and a hyperbola at e equals 1.5. As eccentricity increases the curve grows more open, from a closed circle to two flying-apart branches. Eccentricity morphs a circle into an ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.
accompanying_text:
Why does one number rule them all? Because every conic obeys the **same** rule: for a fixed focus and a fixed line (the **directrix**),

(distance to focus) / (distance to directrix) = e.

That single ratio, held constant, traces a circle-to-hyperbola depending only on e. The parabola (Ch1) was this with e = 1.

illustration_description: The directrix location depends on the eccentricity and the size of the conic.
accompanying_text: The directrix location depends on e and the size. For a horizontal ellipse the directrix is the vertical line x = a/e (equivalently a²/c). For a = 5, e = 0.8: x = 5/0.8 = 6.25 — just outside the vertex at x = 5. As e → 0 the directrix races off to infinity (a circle has none).

illustration_description: Four conics arranged left to right along an eccentricity axis: a circle at e equals 0, an ellipse at e equals 0.5, a parabola at e equals 1, and a hyperbola at e equals 1.5. As eccentricity increases the curve grows more open, from a closed circle to two flying-apart branches. Eccentricity morphs a circle into an ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.
accompanying_text: Conics run the solar system. **Kepler's first law**: every planet orbits the Sun on an **ellipse** with the Sun at ONE focus (not the center). The orbit's eccentricity says how oval it is — and the same e-scale from this course classifies every path through space.

illustration_description: Comets show the other extreme: Halley's Comet has eccentricity about zero point nine seven, a very elongated ellipse.
accompanying_text: Comets show the other extreme. Halley's Comet has e ≈ 0.97 — a long, cigar-shaped ellipse swinging far out and back. Objects with **e ≥ 1** (parabolic or hyperbolic paths) visit ONCE and never return: they aren't bound to the Sun.

illustration_description: A compass with two legs meeting at a hinge beside a straightedge ruler A compass with two legs meeting at a hinge beside a straightedge ruler
accompanying_text: Two tools, strict rules. A **straightedge** draws a line through two points — but it has NO marks, so it never measures. A **compass** draws a circle (or arc) given a center and a radius, and it holds that radius as you swing. Constructions use only these two — no ruler numbers, no protractor. Every length comes from a compass setting.

illustration_description: The compass's superpower is holding a radius: set it to span two points, then swing that fixed distance anywhere.
accompanying_text: The compass's superpower is **holding a radius**. Set it to span two points, lift it, and every arc you swing keeps that exact length. This single ability — transfer a distance without reading a number — is what makes copying segments and building equal parts possible.

illustration_description: Constructions are recipes with guarantees: follow the steps and the result is exact, not approximate.
accompanying_text: Constructions are **recipes with guarantees**: follow the steps and the result is exact by the geometry of circles, not by careful drawing. A shaky hand makes a messy picture — but the LOGIC still proves the lengths and angles are exactly right.

illustration_description: The line through the two arc crossings X and Y meets AB at its midpoint M at a right angle, cutting AB into two equal marked halves The line through the two arc crossings X and Y meets AB at its midpoint M at a right angle, cutting AB into two equal marked halves
accompanying_text: The workhorse construction. To bisect segment AB perpendicularly: open the compass **wider than half of AB**, swing an arc from A, swing the SAME radius from B, and connect the two crossing points. That line is the **perpendicular bisector** — it hits AB's midpoint at a right angle.

illustration_description: Segment AB drawn horizontally; a wide compass arc swung from center A, more than half of AB Segment AB drawn horizontally; a wide compass arc swung from center A, more than half of AB
accompanying_text: Build it, arc by arc.

illustration_description: The four compass radii XA, XB, YA, YB are all equal, so X and Y are each equidistant from A and B and must lie on the perpendicular bisector The four compass radii XA, XB, YA, YB are all equal, so X and Y are each equidistant from A and B and must lie on the perpendicular bisector
accompanying_text: **Why it works** is the real lesson. Both X and Y were drawn at the same radius from A AND from B, so XA = XB and YA = YB. A point equidistant from A and B must lie on the perpendicular bisector — so the line through X and Y IS it.

illustration_description: Angle at vertex V; an arc crosses its two sides at D and E; equal arcs from D and E meet at F; ray VF splits the angle into two equal marked parts Angle at vertex V; an arc crosses its two sides at D and E; equal arcs from D and E meet at F; ray VF splits the angle into two equal marked parts
accompanying_text: To split an angle in half: from the vertex V, swing one arc crossing both sides at D and E. Then swing equal arcs from D and from E; where they meet is F. The ray **VF bisects the angle** — two exactly equal halves, built with no protractor.

illustration_description: Angle at vertex V; an arc crosses its two sides at D and E; equal arcs from D and E meet at F; ray VF splits the angle into two equal marked parts Angle at vertex V; an arc crosses its two sides at D and E; equal arcs from D and E meet at F; ray VF splits the angle into two equal marked parts
accompanying_text: Bisect it, step by step.

illustration_description: The angle bisector and the perpendicular bisector are cousins: both are built by planting equal arcs from two points.
accompanying_text: The angle bisector and the perpendicular bisector are cousins: both plant **two equidistant points** and connect them. Perpendicular bisector: points equidistant from two ENDPOINTS. Angle bisector: a point equidistant from two SIDES. Equidistance is the engine of both.

illustration_description: A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle
accompanying_text: The perpendicular-bisector trick has a cousin. To raise a **perpendicular at a point P that lies ON a line**, first make P the midpoint of a little segment, then bisect it. Two compass openings, and a clean 90° rises from P — no protractor, no guessing.

illustration_description: A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle
accompanying_text: Mark equal distances Put the compass point on P. Swing one opening to cut the line on BOTH sides, marking A and B. Now PA = PB — P is the midpoint of AB.

illustration_description: A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle
accompanying_text: Widen and arc from A Open WIDER than PA. With the point on A, swing an arc above the line.

illustration_description: A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle
accompanying_text: Same-radius arc from B Keep that opening. Arc from B; it crosses the first arc at Q.

illustration_description: A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle A horizontal line with point P on it; equal arcs mark G and H on either side of P; a perpendicular line rises from P at a right angle
accompanying_text: Draw PQ The straightedge line through P and Q is perpendicular to the original line at P.

illustration_description: A perpendicular at a point makes two right angles, because the original straight line splits into two ninety-degree halves.
accompanying_text: One perpendicular, two right angles. Because the original line is straight, the perpendicular splits the straight angle at P into two equal parts. Each must be **half of 180°** — so raising a perpendicular is really the same move as bisecting a straight angle.

illustration_description: Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P
accompanying_text: Now P floats ABOVE the line and we drop a perpendicular down to it. One arc from P crosses the line at two points; equal arcs from those two points meet below; the line from P through that meeting point lands on the original line at 90° — the **shortest** path from P to the line.

illustration_description: Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P
accompanying_text: Arc across the line Point on P, open wide enough to reach the line. Swing an arc that cuts the line at two points, C and D.

illustration_description: Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P
accompanying_text: Arc from C Now open past halfway. With the point on C, swing an arc on the FAR side of the line from P.

illustration_description: Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P
accompanying_text: Same-radius arc from D Keep the opening. Arc from D; it meets the C-arc at point E.

illustration_description: Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P Point P above a horizontal line; an arc from P crosses the line at G and H; the perpendicular from P meets the line at foot F directly below P
accompanying_text: Draw PE The line through P and E crosses the original line at a right angle — the foot of the perpendicular.

illustration_description: The perpendicular from a point is the shortest segment from that point to the line; any slanted path is longer.
accompanying_text: That perpendicular is special: it's the **shortest segment** from P to the line. Any other path from P slants down and forms the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose leg is the perpendicular — and a hypotenuse always beats its leg. "Distance from a point to a line" always means this perpendicular length.

illustration_description: The construction builds a reflection for free: point E is exactly P mirrored across the line, the same distance on the far side.
accompanying_text: The construction also builds a reflection for free: point E is exactly **P mirrored over the line**. The line is the perpendicular bisector of PE — precisely the reflection property from geometry-foundations. Construction and transformation are two views of one picture.

illustration_description: A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows
accompanying_text: To draw a line through P **parallel** to a given line, borrow a transversal. Draw any line from P crossing the given line; then **copy the angle** it makes, up at P, in the matching (corresponding) position. Equal corresponding angles force the two lines parallel — the converse you'll prove later, used here as a builder.

illustration_description: A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows
accompanying_text: Draw a transversal Draw any line through P that also crosses the given line, meeting it at Q. This transversal makes an angle at Q.

illustration_description: A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows
accompanying_text: Arc the angle at Q With the compass, draw an arc across both sides of the angle at Q — the standard copy-an-angle first move.

illustration_description: A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows
accompanying_text: Copy that arc to P Using the same radius and the copy-angle steps, reproduce the identical angle at P, opening in the corresponding direction.

illustration_description: A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows A line with a transversal through external point P; the angle at the line is copied at P as a corresponding angle, and the new line through P is parallel to the original, marked with matching arrows
accompanying_text: Draw the parallel The new ray through P makes the same corresponding angle with the transversal — so it is parallel to the given line.

illustration_description: Copying an angle onto a transversal builds a parallel line: equal corresponding angles force the two lines to never meet.
accompanying_text: The copied angle is your choice of position, but the fact is fixed: with a transversal, **corresponding angles are equal** exactly when the lines are parallel. Its partners follow — alternate interior angles equal, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles summing to 180°.

illustration_description: Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel to that line.
accompanying_text: One elegant payoff: through a point NOT on a line, there is **exactly one** parallel to it. Existence — the construction just built it. Uniqueness — any second line through P would make a different angle with the transversal, so it would have to cross the given line. One point, one parallel.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: The compass hides a gift: **the radius of a circle steps around it exactly six times**. Keep the compass set to the circle's radius, walk it point-to-point around the circle, and the six marks are the vertices of a perfect regular hexagon. No measuring — the radius IS the side.

illustration_description: To inscribe a hexagon, the radius equals the chord: two radii and the chord form a triangle with a sixty-degree central angle.
accompanying_text: That center triangle is the key: two radii plus the chord, with a 60° angle between the radii. Two equal sides and a 60° angle between them force an **equilateral** triangle — so all three sides, chord included, equal the radius. Six such triangles tile the hexagon like pizza slices.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: The square comes from **perpendicular diameters**. Draw a diameter, construct its perpendicular through the center (a diameter too), and the four points where these cross the circle are the square's vertices — four equal 90° slices of the circle.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: Draw a diameter Draw any line through the center, meeting the circle at two opposite points.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: Perpendicular diameter Construct the perpendicular to that diameter through the center — it hits the circle at two more points.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: Four points The four crossing points are 90° apart around the circle.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: Connect them Join consecutive points: an inscribed square.

illustration_description: Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides Segment AB; arcs of radius AB from A and from B meet at apex C; triangle ABC has three equal marked sides
accompanying_text: The equilateral triangle uses **three 120° arcs**. One way: inscribe a hexagon and keep every other vertex. Another: from any circle point, an arc of the circle's radius marks two neighbors 60° away — the three alternate marks span 120° each and form the triangle.

illustration_description: One engine drives all: equal central angles make equal chords, which make equal sides of the inscribed polygon.
accompanying_text: All three share one engine: **equal central angles make equal chords make a regular polygon**. Divide 360° into n equal slices and the n chords are forced equal, so the figure is regular. The compass just delivers the equal slices — 60° by radius-stepping, 90° by perpendicular diameters.

illustration_description: A two-column proof layout: left column headed Statements, right column headed Reasons, with each statement row paired to a justifying reason row, flowing from givens to the conclusion A two-column proof layout: left column headed Statements, right column headed Reasons, with each statement row paired to a justifying reason row, flowing from givens to the conclusion
accompanying_text: A construction is only as good as its REASON. Every compass move creates a fact you can trust: a circle guarantees all its radii are **equal**. That single guarantee — equal radii — is the seed of nearly every construction proof. Spot the equal radii and the reason usually follows.

illustration_description: Equal radii feed the congruence engine: once enough equal segments appear, the triangles must be congruent.
accompanying_text: Equal radii feed the congruence engine. Once you see enough equal segments (and shared sides), triangles become **congruent by SSS** — and congruent triangles hand you equal angles and equal sides for free. Construction proofs are usually: equal radii → congruent triangles → the property you wanted.

illustration_description: A careful drawing suggests a truth, but only a proof settles it beyond doubt.
accompanying_text: This is the leap the chapter has been building toward: a careful drawing SHOWS; a proof GUARANTEES. "It looks perpendicular" could hide a tiny error forever. "XY is the perpendicular bisector because △AXY ≅ △BXY by SSS" is true no matter how shaky the hand that drew it.

illustration_description: A conjecture is a pattern you believe but have not proven, even after it holds in many examples.
accompanying_text: You've seen a pattern hold ten times — is it always true? A **conjecture** is a pattern you suspect; a **proof** is a chain of reasoning that makes it certain. The gap between them is the whole game: no matter how many examples agree, one counterexample can still sink a conjecture. Examples build belief; only proof gives knowledge.

illustration_description: No number of examples ever proves a universal conjecture; but a single counterexample disproves it.
accompanying_text: Flip it around: how many examples PROVE a universal conjecture? **None ever can.** A million confirming cases still leave the million-and-first unchecked. Proof escapes the trap by reasoning about ALL cases at once — usually from definitions and established facts, not from a pile of instances.

illustration_description: This is why constructions needed proofs, not just careful drawings: a drawing can hide a tiny error.
accompanying_text: This is why constructions needed proofs, not just careful drawings. A drawing is one more confirming example; a proof — equal radii, congruent triangles, done — settles every case. The rest of this chapter builds the machinery: how to write a proof that a skeptic can't wriggle out of.

illustration_description: A two-column proof layout: left column headed Statements, right column headed Reasons, with each statement row paired to a justifying reason row, flowing from givens to the conclusion A two-column proof layout: left column headed Statements, right column headed Reasons, with each statement row paired to a justifying reason row, flowing from givens to the conclusion
accompanying_text: A **two-column proof** puts every claim on the left (**Statements**) beside its justification on the right (**Reasons**). Rules: start from the GIVEN, end at what you're PROVING, and every statement's reason must be a definition, postulate, given, or an already-proven line. No reason may point forward.

illustration_description: Reasons in a proof come from a fixed toolbox: givens, definitions, postulates, and already-proven theorems.
accompanying_text: Reasons come from a fixed toolbox: **givens, definitions, postulates, and theorems already proved.** Three properties of equality earn constant use — **Reflexive** (a = a), **Symmetric** (a = b ⇒ b = a), and **Transitive** (a = b and b = c ⇒ a = c). A shared side is reflexive; that's the workhorse of construction proofs.

illustration_description: The golden rule of ordering: no line may use a fact not yet established above it.
accompanying_text: The golden rule of ordering: **no line may use a fact not yet established.** Each reason points only backward — to the given, a definition, a postulate, or a line already written above. A proof read top to bottom should never make you ask "but how do we know that yet?"

illustration_description: Two lines crossing at a point; the two vertical angle pairs are marked with matching single and double arcs, and one linear pair is highlighted to show why the vertical angles must be equal Two lines crossing at a point; the two vertical angle pairs are marked with matching single and double arcs, and one linear pair is highlighted to show why the vertical angles must be equal
accompanying_text: Your first real theorem — one you already believe: **vertical angles are equal.** When two lines cross, the opposite angles match. You've used this since Grade 7; now you'll see WHY it can't fail. The engine is the **linear pair**: two angles on a straight line always sum to 180°.

illustration_description: Two lines crossing at a point; the two vertical angle pairs are marked with matching single and double arcs, and one linear pair is highlighted to show why the vertical angles must be equal Two lines crossing at a point; the two vertical angle pairs are marked with matching single and double arcs, and one linear pair is highlighted to show why the vertical angles must be equal
accompanying_text: Here's the whole argument in one breath. Two lines cross, making angle **1** next to angle **2**, and angle **2** next to angle **3**. Then ∠1 + ∠2 = 180° and ∠2 + ∠3 = 180° (two linear pairs). Both equal 180°, so ∠1 + ∠2 = ∠2 + ∠3 — subtract ∠2 and **∠1 = ∠3**. The vertical angles are equal.

illustration_description: Two parallel lines crossed by a slanted transversal. At each crossing the same pattern of angles appears. Angles in matching positions (corresponding angles) are equal, and alternate interior angles are equal too — shown here by shared colors.
accompanying_text: One transversal cutting two **parallel** lines makes eight angles — but only two distinct sizes. Every angle is either the base size a or its supplement 180 − a. The named pairs just tell you WHICH: **corresponding** and **alternate** angles are EQUAL; **same-side (co-interior)** angles are SUPPLEMENTARY.

illustration_description: The interior region between two parallel lines holds the angle pairs students most often mix up.
accompanying_text: The interior region — between the two lines — holds the pairs students mix up most. **Alternate interior** (opposite sides of the transversal) are EQUAL; **co-interior / same-side interior** (same side) are SUPPLEMENTARY. Opposite sides ⇒ equal; same side ⇒ sum to 180°. That one distinction settles most problems.

illustration_description: One transversal fact anchors the rest: corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel.
accompanying_text: One transversal fact anchors the rest: **corresponding angles are equal** (the Corresponding Angles Postulate for parallel lines). From it, alternate and co-interior relationships all FOLLOW by pairing with vertical angles and linear pairs — which is exactly what the next lesson proves.

illustration_description: Two parallel lines crossed by a slanted transversal. At each crossing the same pattern of angles appears. Angles in matching positions (corresponding angles) are equal, and alternate interior angles are equal too — shown here by shared colors.
accompanying_text: Time to prove what the last lesson listed. Take the Corresponding Angles relationship as the starting postulate. From it, the **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** falls out in two lines: an alternate interior angle is the VERTICAL angle of a corresponding one, and vertical angles are equal — so alternate interior angles are equal.

illustration_description: The co-interior, or same-side interior, theorem proves those angles supplementary, summing to one hundred eighty degrees.
accompanying_text: The **Co-Interior (Same-Side Interior) Theorem** proves supplementary instead of equal. A same-side interior angle and an alternate interior angle form a LINEAR pair (they sit on one line), summing to 180°; since the alternate one equals the far angle, the same-side pair sums to 180°. Equal-family proofs use vertical angles; supplementary-family proofs use linear pairs.

illustration_description: The pattern across these proofs: start from one postulate, corresponding angles, and derive all the other angle relationships.
accompanying_text: Notice the pattern across all these proofs: start from ONE postulate (corresponding angles), then reach every other relationship by adding a single vertical-angle step (to stay equal) or a single linear-pair step (to become supplementary). A big theorem family, grown from one seed.

illustration_description: Every theorem has a converse, its arrow reversed: parallel lines give equal angles, and equal angles give parallel lines.
accompanying_text: Every theorem has a **converse** — its arrow reversed. Theorem: parallel lines ⇒ equal corresponding angles. Converse: equal corresponding angles ⇒ parallel lines. The converse is what makes the parallel-line CONSTRUCTION valid — copying an angle forces the lines parallel. But a converse must be proved separately; reversing an arrow doesn't guarantee truth.

illustration_description: A true statement's converse need not be true: every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
accompanying_text: A true statement's converse **need not be true.** "If it's a square, it's a rectangle" is true; its converse "if it's a rectangle, it's a square" is false. So each transversal converse is its own theorem — luckily, all of them ARE true for lines, which is what powers parallel constructions and proofs of parallelism.

illustration_description: The toolkit is symmetric: the forward direction, parallel implies angle relationships, complements the reverse, angle relationships imply parallel.
accompanying_text: So the toolkit is symmetric. FORWARD (parallel ⇒ angle relationships) computes unknown angles when you know lines are parallel. BACKWARD, via the converses (angle relationships ⇒ parallel) proves lines parallel when you know the angles. Same facts, arrows both ways.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: The **coordinate plane** is two number lines crossed at a point called the **origin**. The **x-axis** runs to the right; the **y-axis** runs up. Every point gets an address called an **ordered pair (x, y)**: first how far **right** from the origin, then how far **up**. The point (3, 2) sits 3 right and 2 up.

illustration_description: Order matters: the point two comma five and the point five comma two are different, like an address where street and number can't swap.
accompanying_text: **Order matters.** (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points — like an address where the street number and the floor got swapped. The first number always travels along the x-axis (right), the second always climbs the y-axis (up). Walk the street first, then take the elevator.

illustration_description: To plot a point, walk its address: start at the origin, go right to the x-number, then up to the y-number.
accompanying_text: To **plot** a point, walk its address: start at the origin, go **right** to its x-number, then **up** to its y-number, and mark the spot. Our practice grids label the gridlines 1 through 6 on each axis — the origin sits just below-left of the numbered corner. Plot (3, 2): column 3, then up to row 2.

illustration_description: Plotted points can belong together: two points make the ends of a segment, and three or four can be the corners of a polygon.
accompanying_text: Plotted points can **belong together**. Two points make the ends of a segment; three or four make the corners of a shape. And on a grid you can **measure along a gridline**: between (2, 2) and (6, 2) — same height — the distance is the difference of the x-numbers, 6 − 2 = 4 units. Count the **spaces** between them, not the dots.

illustration_description: Coordinates can mean things: on a town map, x counts blocks east of the square and y counts blocks north.
accompanying_text: Coordinates can **mean** things. On a town map, x can count blocks **east** of the town square and y blocks **north**. Then the library at (2, 3) is a real place: 2 blocks east, 3 blocks north. The axes' meanings — east and north here — turn every pair into a location you could walk to.

illustration_description: Graphs tell stories over time: Maya saves three dollars every week, plotting one comma three, two comma six, three comma nine.
accompanying_text: Graphs tell stories over time, too. Suppose Maya saves $3 every week and plots her total: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9). Here x is the **week** and y is the **dollars saved so far**. Reading a point answers a question — at week 2, the height 6 says she had $6.

illustration_description: A rule makes a pattern: Rule A says start at zero and add two, making zero, two, four, six, eight.
accompanying_text: A **rule** makes a pattern. Rule A says *start at 0, add 2*: it makes 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Rule B says *start at 0, add 4*: it makes 0, 4, 8, 12, 16. Run both rules **side by side**, one step at a time, and each step gives you one number from each pattern.

illustration_description: Pair the terms that happen at the same step: zero comma zero, two comma four, four comma eight, six comma twelve, eight comma sixteen.
accompanying_text: Now **pair the terms that happen at the same step**: (0, 0), (2, 4), (4, 8), (6, 12), (8, 16). A-term first, B-term second. Look across each pair — the B-number is always **double** the A-number. Two separate rules, one hidden relationship.

illustration_description: Every pair from two rules is an ordered pair, so it can be plotted on the coordinate plane.
accompanying_text: Every pair from two rules is an **ordered pair** — so it can be **plotted**. Rule A (*start at 1, add 1*) makes 1, 2, 3; rule B (*start at 2, add 2*) makes 2, 4, 6. The pairs are (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6): A gives the x, B gives the y. Plot them and watch what appears.

illustration_description: The points line up straight, because from each point to the next you always move the same way — right two, up four — the doubling rule.
accompanying_text: The three points **line up straight**. Why: from each point to the next, you always move **right 1** (rule A adds 1) and **up 2** (rule B adds 2). The same move, repeated, can only walk a straight path. Steady rules draw straight lines — that's the two rules made visible.

illustration_description: Shape categories nest like a family tree, and attributes are inherited: if every member of a big category has a property, so does every shape below it.
accompanying_text: Shape categories nest like a **family tree**, and attributes are **inherited**: if EVERY member of a category has an attribute, then every member of any subcategory inside it has that attribute too. Every rectangle has 4 right angles; a square is a kind of rectangle; so every square has 4 right angles — no measuring needed.

illustration_description: The inheritance arrow points only downward: what is true of the big category is true of the small one, but not the reverse.
accompanying_text: The arrow points **only downward**. What's true of the big category is true of the small one inside it — never the reverse. Every square has 4 equal sides, and squares are rectangles; that does NOT make every rectangle equal-sided. Counterexample: a 5-by-2 rectangle has sides 5, 2, 5, 2 — a fine rectangle, sides not all equal.

illustration_description: The quadrilateral family tree: quadrilateral splits into parallelogram and trapezoid; parallelogram splits into rectangle and rhombus, which meet at square.
accompanying_text: Meet the family. Any 4-sided shape is a **quadrilateral**. Two pairs of parallel sides make it a **parallelogram**. A parallelogram with 4 right angles is a **rectangle**; with 4 equal sides, a **rhombus**; with BOTH, a **square**. Each level keeps everything from its parent and adds one new attribute.

illustration_description: The trapezoid stands apart: in this course it means exactly one pair of parallel sides.
accompanying_text: One cousin stands apart: the **trapezoid**, which in this course means **exactly one pair of parallel sides**. (Some books say "at least one pair" — we use "exactly one.") Under our definition, a trapezoid is never a parallelogram, and a parallelogram is never a trapezoid: two pairs is one too many.

illustration_description: Triangle side families: scalene has no equal sides, isosceles has two marked equal sides, equilateral has all three marked equal.
accompanying_text: Triangles get **two family systems at once**. By **sides**: scalene (no equal sides), isosceles (at least two equal — that's our definition), equilateral (all three equal). By **angles**: acute (all under 90°), right (one exactly 90°), obtuse (one over 90°). Every triangle earns one label from EACH system.

illustration_description: The systems combine: a ninety, forty-five, forty-five triangle is a right isosceles triangle — one right angle and two equal sides.
accompanying_text: The systems **combine**: that 90-45-45 triangle is a **right isosceles** triangle — one label from each system, worn together. And since equilateral means all three sides equal, every equilateral triangle is automatically **isosceles** too (three equal sides certainly contains two). One more tool: a triangle's angles always add to **180°**.

illustration_description: Classification runs both ways: given a list of properties, name the most specific shape that fits them all.
accompanying_text: Classification runs **both ways**. Given a list of properties, name the **most specific** shape they force — walk down the family tree as far as the clues push you, and no farther. Given a shape's name, you get back every property its whole ancestry promises. The clues decide; never assume a property you weren't given.

illustration_description: The reverse direction: say a shape's name and you have promised its full inheritance — a square is also a rectangle and a quadrilateral.
accompanying_text: The reverse direction: say a shape's **name** and you've promised its full inheritance. "Square" promises 4 sides, two parallel pairs, 4 right angles, 4 equal sides — the whole chain. And **cross-cutting rules** like "has a right angle" can gather shapes from totally different families: a square and a right triangle both pass.

illustration_description: The quadrilateral family tree: quadrilateral splits into parallelogram and trapezoid; parallelogram splits into rectangle and rhombus, which meet at square.
accompanying_text: Family claims get one of three verdicts. **Always**: true of every member ("a square is a rectangle"). **Sometimes**: true of some, false of others — proving it takes one example AND one counterexample ("a rectangle is a square": an all-sides-4 rectangle yes, a 5-by-2 no). **Never**: a fact blocks every possible example.

illustration_description: Never verdicts need a blocker: one fact that kills every possible example, such as a trapezoid having only one pair of parallel sides so it can never be a parallelogram.
accompanying_text: **Never** verdicts need a **blocker** — one fact that kills every possible example. "A trapezoid is a parallelogram": never, because ours has exactly one parallel pair and a parallelogram needs two. "An equilateral triangle is a right triangle": never, because equilateral angles are locked at 60° and right demands a 90°. A blocker beats any amount of searching.

illustration_description: Two points, A at one two and B at seven ten, on a grid. A horizontal run of 6 and a vertical rise of 8 form the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse joins A to B. By the Pythagorean theorem the distance is the square root of 6 squared plus 8 squared, which is 10.
accompanying_text: Coordinates turn geometry into arithmetic — starting with length. Between A(1, 2) and B(7, 10), draw the horizontal **run** Δx = 6 and vertical **rise** Δy = 8: they're the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse IS the segment AB. The Pythagorean theorem (your Grade 8 workhorse) prices it: d = √(6² + 8²) = 10.

illustration_description: The distance formula: d equals the square root of the change in x squared plus the change in y squared, the Pythagorean theorem on the plane.
accompanying_text: In general: **d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)**. The squares erase every sign worry — measuring from B to A negates both differences, but (−6)² = 6², so the distance comes out identical. Distance is unsigned, a pure length, exactly like the segment measures of your first geometry course.

illustration_description: A segment from A at two three to B at eight seven. Its midpoint M sits at five five: the average of the x-coordinates, two plus eight over two, and the average of the y-coordinates, three plus seven over two.
accompanying_text: Halfway along a segment is halfway along in x AND halfway along in y — so the midpoint is a pair of **averages**: **M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)**. From A(2, 3) to B(8, 7): M = (5, 5). Each coordinate splits its own gap evenly, independently of the other.

illustration_description: Run the midpoint machine in reverse to find a missing endpoint: the midpoint is the average, so double it and subtract the known end.
accompanying_text: Run the machine in reverse to find a missing **endpoint**: if M is the midpoint of A and B, then each M-coordinate is an average, so **B = (2Mₓ − Aₓ, 2Mᵧ − Aᵧ)** — double the middle, subtract the known end. Averages are easy to invert, and that inversion earns its keep in proofs.

illustration_description: Formulas become proof tools the moment they classify: measure all three sides, and two equal lengths prove an isosceles triangle.
accompanying_text: Formulas become PROOF TOOLS the moment they classify. Is triangle ABC isosceles? Don't squint at a sketch — **measure all three sides with the distance formula** and compare. Numbers don't wobble the way drawings do; a coordinate computation is a proof, not an impression.

illustration_description: Right triangles surrender to the same treatment: if two sides' slopes are negative reciprocals, the angle between them is right.
accompanying_text: Right triangles surrender to the same treatment: measure the three sides, then check the **converse of Pythagoras** — if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the angle opposite c is right. Distance gives sides; Pythagoras-in-reverse gives angles. No protractor touches the page.

illustration_description: A segment from A at one one to B at seven ten, divided in the ratio two to one by point P at five seven. P sits two thirds of the way from A: A plus two thirds of the run and two thirds of the rise. Tick marks show two equal parts from A to P and one from P to B.
accompanying_text: The midpoint splits a segment 1 : 1 — but any ratio is buyable. To divide AB in the ratio **m : n from A**, walk the fraction k = m/(m + n) of the way: **P = A + k(B − A)**, applied to each coordinate. For 2 : 1, k = 2/3: two parts down, one to go.

illustration_description: The coordinate walk matches the geometric ratio because similar triangles share proportional sides.
accompanying_text: Why does the coordinate walk match the geometric ratio? **Similar triangles** again: the run-rise triangle from A to P is a k-scaled copy of the full A-to-B triangle, so AP is k of AB along the segment itself — the same 1/2-argument that justified the midpoint, generalized to any k. Direction matters: the ratio counts **from the first-named point**.

illustration_description: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so matching slopes prove two segments parallel.
accompanying_text: Algebra 1 handed you the rule: **parallel lines have equal slopes**. Here's the missing WHY. Take any slope triangle on line ℓ and **translate** it (a rigid motion from Grade 8) until its corner lands on line ₘ. Translations preserve direction, so the image triangle's hypotenuse still points along ℓ's direction — if ₘ is parallel, it runs along ₘ exactly: same run, same rise, same slope.

illustration_description: Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, multiplying to negative one.
accompanying_text: The converse needs one more idea: through a given point there's only ONE line with a given slope (pick the point, the slope forces every other point). So if two DISTINCT lines share a slope, neither can cross the other — a crossing point would put two same-slope lines through one point, collapsing them into one line. Equal slopes ⇔ parallel (or identical).

illustration_description: A slope triangle with run 3 and rise 2 for a line of slope two thirds. Rotating it ninety degrees about its corner turns the run into a rise and the rise into a leftward run: the new line has slope negative three halves. The product of the slopes is negative one.
accompanying_text: The perpendicular rule — slopes multiply to −1 — falls to a **quarter-turn**. Rotate a slope triangle 90° about its corner (a rigid motion): the run (a, 0) turns into a rise, the rise (0, b) into a LEFTWARD run — displacement (a, b) becomes (−b, a). New slope: a/(−b). Old times new: (b/a)(−a/b) = **−1**, always.

illustration_description: Care at the edges: the slope rule serves every pair except when one line is vertical, where the slope is undefined.
accompanying_text: Care at the edges: the rule serves every pair EXCEPT when one line is vertical — vertical lines have no slope, yet they're perpendicular to every horizontal (slope 0) line.
