A complete perpendicularity test: slopes multiply to −1, OR one is vertical and the other horizontal. Coordinate proofs must remember the exception.

illustration_description: Now combine the tools: distances measure side lengths and slopes measure angles, together classifying any figure.
accompanying_text: Chapter 1 measured; Chapter 2 proved slopes. Now combine them into **coordinate proofs**: compute, then CONCLUDE by a definition or theorem. Triangle classification runs two audits — **sides** by the distance formula (scalene / isosceles / equilateral) and **angles** by slopes or the Pythagorean converse (right or not). Squared distances suffice: comparing d² avoids every root.

illustration_description: Four vertices, same discipline: use the quadrilateral course's tests on the coordinates to name the shape.
accompanying_text: Four vertices, same discipline — and the quadrilateral course's tests become CHECKLISTS. Parallelogram: both slope pairs match (or diagonal midpoints coincide). Upgrade to **rectangle**: adjacent slopes multiply to −1 (or diagonals congruent). Upgrade to **rhombus**: all four sides equal (or diagonals perpendicular). Both upgrades at once: **square**.

illustration_description: Numbers prove one figure, but variables prove them all: place a general point with letters for coordinates.
accompanying_text: Numbers prove ONE figure; **variables prove them all**. Place a general rectangle at (0, 0), (a, 0), (a, b), (0, b) — chapter 1's “cheap placement” advice paying off — and both diagonals compute to √(a² + b²). No specific rectangle was harmed: the congruent-diagonals theorem is proved for every rectangle at once.

illustration_description: A quadrilateral with the midpoint of each side marked. Joining the four midpoints makes a parallelogram whose sides are parallel to the quadrilateral's diagonals — one pair copies each diagonal at half length.
accompanying_text: Placement is strategy. Put a vertex at the origin; run a side along an axis; exploit symmetry (an isosceles triangle as (−a, 0), (a, 0), (0, b) makes the equal slants √(a² + b²) automatic). Good placement costs nothing — rigid motions from the transformations course guarantee the figure is the same — and buys zeros everywhere.

illustration_description: Perimeter is the distance formula on a lap: sum every side by walking around the figure.
accompanying_text: Perimeter is the distance formula on a lap: sum every side, walking the vertices IN ORDER. Two disciplines carry the chapter — keep radicals EXACT until the final step (√20 + √20 = 2√20, never 4.47 + 4.47), and never skip a side: n vertices, n sides, back to the start.

illustration_description: Mixed laps demand exact bookkeeping: a trapezoid mixes horizontal sides with slanted ones, each measured separately.
accompanying_text: Mixed laps demand exact bookkeeping. The trapezoid (0,0), (8,0), (6,4), (2,4): bases 8 and 4 are free reads; each leg is √(2² + 4²) = √20 = 2√5. Perimeter: 12 + 4√5 exactly — decimalize (≈ 20.94) only at the very end, if at all.

illustration_description: Slanted figures resist base times height, so box them: draw the bounding rectangle and subtract the corner triangles.
accompanying_text: Slanted figures resist base-times-height — so BOX them. Draw the smallest axis-aligned rectangle containing the figure, then subtract the right-triangle corners (each a half-rectangle, trivially priced). Box minus corners = area. Every subtracted piece has axis-aligned legs: no distance formula needed at all.

illustration_description: Cross-check with the classification: the same triangle proved right earlier should give the same area both ways.
accompanying_text: Cross-check with chapter 3's classification: this triangle was RIGHT and ISOSCELES with legs √20 — so its area is ½(√20)(√20) = ½(20) = 10. Two completely different routes, one answer. Coordinate geometry keeps auditing itself; when routes disagree, one of them is lying.

illustration_description: The box method industrialized is the shoelace formula: list the coordinates in order and cross-multiply down the columns.
accompanying_text: The box method industrialized: the **shoelace formula**. List the vertices counterclockwise, cross-multiply each pair like lacing a shoe — x₁y₂ − x₂y₁ for every edge, wrapping around — sum, halve, take absolute value. Area = ½|Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)|. One sweep, any polygon.

illustration_description: Each cross-term one half x i times y i plus one minus x i plus one times y i is the signed area of a triangle to the origin.
accompanying_text: Why it works: each cross-term ½(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ) is the SIGNED area of the triangle from the origin to that edge — positive when the edge runs counterclockwise around the origin, negative clockwise. Summing sweeps the whole boundary: outside cancels, inside survives. It's the box method's subtraction, automated by signs.

illustration_description: A circle with center three two and radius five on a grid. A point on the circle at six six connects to the center by a radius, with a run of 3 and a rise of 4 forming a right triangle: three squared plus four squared is twenty-five, so the circle's equation is x minus 3 squared plus y minus 2 squared equals 25.
accompanying_text: A circle is pure distance: every point (x, y) sitting exactly r from the center (h, k). Chapter 1's formula IS the equation — square both sides once and forever: **(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²**. The figure's circle: center (3, 2), radius 5 — every point obeys (x − 3)² + (y − 2)² = 25.

illustration_description: The circle equation is a judge: substitute any point into x minus h squared plus y minus k squared, and compare to r squared to see inside, on, or outside.
accompanying_text: The equation is a JUDGE. Substitute any point into (x − h)² + (y − k)² and compare the result to r²: **equal ⇒ on the circle; less ⇒ inside; greater ⇒ outside.** It's chapter 3's d² discipline again — squared distances compare perfectly well without ever taking a root.

illustration_description: Expand x minus three squared plus y minus two squared equals twenty-five and the disguise appears: x squared plus y squared minus six x minus four y minus twelve equals zero.
accompanying_text: Expand (x − 3)² + (y − 2)² = 25 and the disguise appears: x² + y² − 6x − 4y − 12 = 0. To reverse it, **complete the square** — the algebra course's move, now with a geometric payoff: group x-terms, group y-terms, add (half the linear coefficient)² to each side, and the center-radius form steps out.

illustration_description: The unmasked form makes every earlier tool available once you complete the square back to center and radius.
accompanying_text: The unmasked form makes every earlier tool available: center and radius feed the position judge, the distance and midpoint formulas, even cr's tangent theorems. One completed square converts an opaque quadratic into geometry you've been computing with for five chapters.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: Counting keeps going past 20. After 20 comes 21, 22, 23 — the same pattern as 1, 2, 3.

illustration_description: Counting past twenty repeats the pattern: twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-six go just like four, five, six, with a two in front.
accompanying_text: Each ten counts the same way. 24, 25, 26 goes just like 4, 5, 6 — with a 2 in front.

illustration_description: Two number windows like an odometer. The number twenty-nine rolls to thirty: the ones digit rolls from nine to zero and the tens digit ticks from two to three.
accompanying_text: Counting to 29, then one more, is tricky. The 9 rolls back to 0 and the ten goes up: 30.

illustration_description: The nine always rolls to a new ten: after forty-nine comes fifty.
accompanying_text: It happens at every ten. After 49 comes 50. After 59 comes 60. The nine always rolls.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: You can count all the way to 50. Past 20 the order never changes: 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, and on.

illustration_description: Missing numbers are filled by keeping the count in order: forty-two, forty-three, then forty-four, forty-five.
accompanying_text: Missing numbers are easy — just keep the count going in order.

illustration_description: The first three rows of the 120 chart: one to ten, eleven to twenty, twenty-one to thirty. Each row holds ten numbers and ends in a zero — ten, twenty, thirty.
accompanying_text: The 120 chart is rows of ten. Each row has 10 numbers and ends in a 0: 10, 20, 30.

illustration_description: A hundred-chart row reads left to right counting up by one, from twenty-one to thirty; the next row starts the next ten.
accompanying_text: Read a row left to right, counting up by one. The next row starts the next ten.

illustration_description: The full one to one hundred twenty chart in twelve rows of ten. Forty-seven is highlighted; its row of forties and its column of sevens are tinted, showing a number is found by its row and its spot across.
accompanying_text: Find a number by its row and spot. 47 is in the row of forties, 7 spots across.

illustration_description: The column a number sits under shows its ones digit: forty-seven sits under seven, fifty-two sits under two.
accompanying_text: The spot across is the ones digit. 47 sits under 7. 52 sits under 2.

illustration_description: Two rows of the chart: thirty-one to forty above forty-one to fifty. Thirty-four sits directly above forty-four. Moving down one row adds ten, so ten more than thirty-four is forty-four.
accompanying_text: Move down one row and you add ten. 34 is above 44. Ten more than 34 is 44.

illustration_description: Going down a row adds ten; a whole column shares the same ones digit: four, fourteen, twenty-four, thirty-four.
accompanying_text: Up a row takes ten away. A whole column shares the same ones digit: 4, 14, 24, 34.

illustration_description: The number forty-seven built from blocks: four ten-rods and seven one-cubes. The four matches the tens digit and the seven matches the ones digit of forty-seven.
accompanying_text: A two-digit number is tens and ones. 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones.

illustration_description: In sixty-two the six means sixty, not six: the place a digit sits in gives its size.
accompanying_text: The digit's place gives its size. In 62, the 6 means 60 — not just 6.

illustration_description: Thirteen hides a ten: a full ten-frame of ten dots plus three more makes thirteen, one ten and three ones.
accompanying_text: Teen numbers hide a ten. 13 is 1 ten and 3 ones — 'thir-TEEN' means three and ten.

illustration_description: Thirteen and thirty-one flip their digits: thirteen is one ten and three ones, thirty-one is three tens and one one.
accompanying_text: Careful: 13 and 31 flip the digits. 13 = 1 ten 3 ones. 31 = 3 tens 1 one.

illustration_description: The number one hundred thirteen built from blocks: one hundred-square, then one ten-rod and three one-cubes. One hundred and thirteen more ones make one hundred thirteen.
accompanying_text: Ten tens make 100. Past it, count on: 100 and 13 more is 113.

illustration_description: One hundred thirteen is one hundred and thirteen more: write the one hundred, then the rest.
accompanying_text: Numbers like 113 are 100 and more: 113 is 100 and 13. Write 1, then the rest.

illustration_description: Skip-counting by ten from twenty-three: twenty-three, thirty-three, forty-three, fifty-three. Each jump adds ten, and the ones digit stays three the whole way.
accompanying_text: Skip-counting by ten jumps ten each time. Start at 23: 23, 33, 43, 53. The ones digit stays 3 — only the tens grow.

illustration_description: Skip-counting by tens can start anywhere: from seven, jump to seventeen, twenty-seven, thirty-seven, forty-seven — each jump is a ten.
accompanying_text: You can start the tens-count anywhere. From 7: 7, 17, 27, 37, 47. Each jump is a ten.

illustration_description: The number forty-seven built from blocks: four ten-rods and seven one-cubes. The four matches the tens digit and the seven matches the ones digit of forty-seven.
accompanying_text: A big pile is easy in groups of ten. 47 is 4 full tens and 7 leftover ones: count 10, 20, 30, 40… 47.

illustration_description: Counting a pile of eighty-five: eight ten-rods count the tens, and five single dots count the leftover ones.
accompanying_text: The tens digit counts the ten-groups; the ones digit counts the leftovers. In 85: 8 tens, 5 ones.

illustration_description: The number one hundred thirteen built from blocks: one hundred-square, then one ten-rod and three one-cubes. One hundred and thirteen more ones make one hundred thirteen.
accompanying_text: Ten tens make one hundred. After 90 comes 100, then keep going: 100, 110, 120. A hundred is just 10 tens bundled.

illustration_description: One hundred fourteen is one hundred, one ten, and four ones: a hundred-square, a ten-rod, and four single dots.
accompanying_text: Numbers past 100 still have tens and ones. 114 is 1 hundred, 1 ten, and 4 ones.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: One more means the next number; one less means the number before. After 45 comes 46; before 45 is 44.

illustration_description: One more than thirty-nine rolls to forty, and one less than forty goes back to thirty-nine.
accompanying_text: Sometimes one more rolls a ten. One more than 39 is 40; one less than 40 is 39. The ones roll over.

illustration_description: Two rows of the chart: thirty-one to forty above forty-one to fifty. Thirty-four sits directly above forty-four. Moving down one row adds ten, so ten more than thirty-four is forty-four.
accompanying_text: On the chart, ten more is straight below; ten less is straight above. Ten more than 31 is 41 — the ones stay 1.

illustration_description: Ten more keeps the ones digit and grows the tens: forty-five and fifty-five both end in five.
accompanying_text: Ten more keeps the ones digit and grows the tens. That's why 45 and 55 both end in 5. Only the tens change.

illustration_description: Mixing jumps from thirty-four: ten more makes forty-four, then one more makes forty-five.
accompanying_text: Now mix the jumps. From 34, ten more then one more: 34 → 44 → 45. Do each jump in order, watching tens and ones.

illustration_description: Jumps can go down: from fifty-eight, ten less makes forty-eight, then one less makes forty-seven.
accompanying_text: Jumps can go down too. From 58, ten less then one less: 58 → 48 → 47. Down for less, up for more.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: Counting keeps going past 20. After 20 comes 21, 22, 23 — the same pattern as 1, 2, 3.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: Every new ten counts the same way. 21, 22, 23 goes just like 1, 2, 3 — with a 2 in front.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: Some jumps land in a brand-new ten. After 29 comes 30 — a new ten begins.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: Every ten ends in 9, then a new ten starts: 29 then 30, 39 then 40, 49 then 50.

illustration_description: A number track showing eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Counting keeps going past twenty in order.
accompanying_text: The count climbs on: thirties, then forties, up to fifty. The pattern never changes.

accompanying_text: Differentiate. Set it to zero. Solve. Then also ask: is there anywhere f′ fails to exist — a corner, a cusp, a vertical tangent? Every such x is a suspect, and no other x is.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
In C1 you learned that **f′ = 0 is a suspect, not a conviction**. This course is where the suspects get tried.

A **critical point** is any x where f′(x) = 0 **or f′ does not exist**. Those are the only places an interior extremum can hide — everywhere else the curve is visibly climbing or falling, and a climbing curve is not at a peak.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So the procedure has two halves, and the second is the hard one:

**Find** the critical points: solve f′ = 0, and find where f′ is undefined.
**Classify** them: peak, valley, or neither.

Finding is algebra. Classifying is calculus — and it is where the rest of this chapter lives.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Look at f′ just LEFT of the critical point, and just RIGHT of it. Positive then negative: the curve climbed and then fell, so it is a peak. Negative then positive: a valley. Same sign twice: nothing happened.

illustration_description: A cubic above, and the sign chart of its derivative below. Where the derivative is positive the curve climbs; where it is negative the curve falls; and the two sign changes mark the peak and the valley.
accompanying_text:
The verdict is decided by what f′ does on **either side** of the critical point.

**f′ goes + → −** : the curve climbs then falls. A **maximum**.
**f′ goes − → +** : falls then climbs. A **minimum**.
**f′ does not change sign** : no extremum at all. A flat pause.

That is a **sign chart** — the exact machinery you built in `polynomial-rational-analysis`, pointed at f′ instead of f.

illustration_description: A cubic above, and the sign chart of its derivative below. Where the derivative is positive the curve climbs; where it is negative the curve falls; and the two sign changes mark the peak and the valley.
accompanying_text:
So the whole first-derivative test is one habit:

**Draw the sign chart of f′. Read the story of f off it.**

+ then − is a peak. − then + is a valley. No change is a saddle. You already own this machinery; it has simply been pointed at a new function.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Make a list. Every critical point INSIDE the interval, plus both endpoints. Evaluate f at each. The biggest number on the list is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum. There is nowhere else to look.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
On a **closed interval**, the biggest and smallest values are guaranteed to exist — and they can hide in only two places:

**at a critical point**, or **at an endpoint**.

That is the Extreme Value Theorem, and it turns optimisation into a finite checklist. Compute f at every critical point and at both ends; the largest wins.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So the **closed-interval method** is a three-line recipe:

1. Find every critical point inside the interval.
2. Evaluate f there, and at both endpoints.
3. Pick the largest and the smallest.

No sign charts, no second derivatives. On a closed interval you simply compare a finite list of numbers.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Concave up holds water; concave down spills it. The test is the sign of f″, and nothing else — not whether the curve is rising, not whether it is above the axis.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
f′ tells you whether the curve is rising. **f″ tells you which way it BENDS.**

**f″ > 0** — the slope is increasing. The curve bends upward: *concave up*, holding water.
**f″ < 0** — the slope is decreasing. The curve bends downward: *concave down*, spilling it.

Note what this is not: a curve can be falling and concave up at the same time. Direction and bend are independent.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
So there are now **three** sign charts, and they answer three different questions:

**f** — is the curve above or below the axis?
**f′** — is it rising or falling?
**f″** — is it bending up or down?

Three functions, three charts, one machine.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: At a flat point, ask which way it bends. Bending UP at a flat point means the flat point is the bottom of a bowl — a minimum. Bending DOWN means it is the top of a dome. And if it is not bending at all, the test has nothing to say.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
A critical point is flat. Ask which way it BENDS and the verdict is instant:

**f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) > 0** → flat, bending upward → a **minimum**.
**f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0** → flat, bending downward → a **maximum**.
**f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = 0** → **inconclusive**. Fall back on the sign chart of f′.

One substitution instead of a whole chart — when it works.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So choose your tool:

**Second-derivative test** — fast, and it works whenever f″(c) ≠ 0. One substitution.
**First-derivative test** — slower, and it NEVER fails. It also handles critical points where f′ does not exist, which f″ cannot even reach.

Try the shortcut. When it shrugs, do the work.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Two independent questions at every point. **Which way am I going?** — the sign of f′. **Is that intensifying or easing?** — the sign of f″. Four combinations, and every point on every curve is one of them.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
You now have three sign charts and they answer three separate questions:

**f** — above or below the axis?
**f′** — rising or falling?
**f″** — bending up or down?

Stack them and you have the curve. Not an approximation of it — the actual shape, deduced rather than plotted.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
So sketching is a procedure, not an art:

**Zeros of f** — where it crosses the axis.
**Sign chart of f′** — where it rises and falls; mark the extrema.
**Sign chart of f″** — where it bends; mark the inflections.
**Ends** — what happens as x → ±∞.

Join the dots consistently with all four, and there is only one curve that fits.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: If you leave home and come back to the same height, you must have stopped climbing at some point. That is the whole theorem — and the flat spot is guaranteed strictly BETWEEN the two ends, never at them.

illustration_description: A curve with the chord joining two of its points, and a tangent drawn parallel to that chord at a point in between. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a point exists.
accompanying_text:
If a curve starts and ends at the **same height**, it must have turned round somewhere.

**Rolle's theorem:** if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one c inside where **f′(c) = 0**.

It sounds too obvious to be worth a name. It is the engine of everything in this chapter.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
Rolle also counts your roots for you.

Between any two roots of f there must be a root of f′. So if f′ has only **two** zeros, f can have at most **three** roots — because four roots would force three flat spots.

The derivative constrains the function, which is the reverse of the usual traffic.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text: Two steps. **One:** compute the secant slope, [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a). **Two:** solve f′(c) = that slope. The theorem guarantees a solution inside the interval; your only job is to find it.

illustration_description: A curve with the chord joining two of its points, and a tangent drawn parallel to that chord at a point in between. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a point exists.
accompanying_text:
Now tilt the picture. The ends need not match — but the conclusion survives, tilted with it.

**MVT:** somewhere inside, the **tangent is parallel to the secant**:

f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)] / (b − a)

At some instant, your instantaneous speed equalled your average speed. Rolle is just the flat case of this.

illustration_description: A curve with the chord joining two of its points, and a tangent drawn parallel to that chord at a point in between. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a point exists.
accompanying_text:
Note what the MVT does NOT promise:

It does not say **where** c is. It does not say there is only **one**. And it does not give any way to **find** it beyond solving f′(c) = the secant slope.

It is an **existence** theorem. Its power is that it lets you argue about a function you cannot see.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text: The MVT converts a fact about the DERIVATIVE into a fact about the FUNCTION. If the slope is always positive, the function must rise. If the slope is always zero, it cannot move at all. If the slope is bounded, the function's growth is bounded too.

illustration_description: A curve with the chord joining two of its points, and a tangent drawn parallel to that chord at a point in between. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a point exists.
accompanying_text:
Every lesson so far has ASSUMED that f′ > 0 means the curve rises. Nobody proved it. The MVT does.

Take any x₁ < x₂. The MVT gives a c with f(x₂) − f(x₁) = f′(c)(x₂ − x₁). If f′ is positive everywhere, the right-hand side is positive — so f(x₂) > f(x₁).

**f′ > 0 ⇒ increasing.** Not a picture. A proof.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text:
And it settles the last loose end from C4.

If F′ = G′ everywhere, then (F − G)′ = 0, so **F − G is constant**. That is *why* every antiderivative of f has the form F + C, and why the + C is a complete description of the family rather than a hedge.

The theorem you almost skipped is the one holding up the integral.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: At the far ends, only the biggest term matters. For a polynomial, that is the leading term. For a rational function, it is the ratio of the leading terms — and everything else fades to nothing.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
A sketch needs one more thing the derivatives cannot tell you: **what happens at the far ends.**

For a polynomial, the highest-power term wins as |x| → ∞. For a rational function, compare the degrees:

**top < bottom** → y = 0. **top = bottom** → y = the ratio of leading coefficients. **top > bottom** → no horizontal asymptote (it runs away).

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
For a polynomial the ends are simpler, and the **leading term decides everything**:

**Even degree, positive lead** → both ends up.
**Even degree, negative lead** → both ends down.
**Odd degree, positive lead** → down on the left, up on the right.

At large |x| every other term is a rounding error.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Work the checklist in order and never skip ahead. Zeros. Ends. Where it rises and falls. Where it bends. Then draw the ONE curve that agrees with everything you have written down.

illustration_description: A cubic above, and the sign chart of its derivative below. Where the derivative is positive the curve climbs; where it is negative the curve falls; and the two sign changes mark the peak and the valley.
accompanying_text:
A complete sketch is a **checklist**, and the curve is whatever satisfies all of it:

1. **Zeros and intercepts** — where is f = 0?
2. **Ends** — what happens as x → ±∞? Any asymptotes?
3. **Sign chart of f′** — rising, falling, extrema.
4. **Sign chart of f″** — bending, inflections.

No plotting. Only one curve fits.

illustration_description: A cubic above, and the sign chart of its derivative below. Where the derivative is positive the curve climbs; where it is negative the curve falls; and the two sign changes mark the peak and the valley.
accompanying_text:
Now the consistency check, which is where errors surface.

Between two extrema the curve must **change direction exactly once**. Between two inflections the bend must **flip exactly once**. And the ends must agree with the leading term.

If your sketch violates any of these, one of your charts is wrong — and you will know which.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Say it before every question: **this graph is the SLOPE of f, not f.** So its height tells you how steeply f is going, and its sign tells you which way. Where it crosses zero, f stops and turns.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
Now the hardest reading of all: you are shown a graph, and told **it is f′, not f**.

Every instinct will read it as the function. Resist that.

Where the graph is **above** the axis, f is rising. Where it **crosses** the axis, f has an extremum. Where the graph is **rising**, f is concave up. The graph's HEIGHT is f's SLOPE.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
A translation table, worth memorising:

**f′ above the axis** → f rising.
**f′ crosses zero** → f has an extremum.
**f′ rising** → f concave up.
**f′ has a peak or valley** → f has an inflection.

Every statement about the HEIGHT of f′ is a statement about the SLOPE of f, and every statement about the SLOPE of f′ is a statement about the BEND of f.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Two variables cannot be differentiated. The constraint exists to KILL one of them — solve it for the variable you do not want, substitute, and only then reach for calculus.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Optimisation is not a calculus problem. It is a **translation** problem with a calculus step in the middle.

1. Name what you are maximising. Write it as a formula.
2. Use the constraint to eliminate variables until **one** is left.
3. State the **domain** — the values that actually make physical sense.
4. *Then* differentiate.

Most marks are lost in steps 2 and 3, before any calculus happens.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Once you have one variable and a domain, the rest is chapter 1:

Differentiate. Set to zero. Find the critical points **inside the domain**. Compare their values with the values at the ends.

That is the **closed-interval method**, and it is the whole of the calculus in an optimisation problem.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Write the volume with one variable. State the domain. Differentiate, factor, find the critical points, throw away any outside the domain, and compare what survives with the two endpoints. The biggest number wins.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
The classic. From a 12-inch square sheet, cut a square of side x from each corner and fold up the sides.

**Volume** = base × height = (12 − 2x)² · x.
**Domain** = 0 < x < 6 (the cut must be positive; the base must survive).

One variable, one interval. Now the calculus is three lines.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Notice what the endpoints did.

V(0) = 0 — no cut, so no sides, so no box.
V(6) = 0 — the whole sheet cut away, so no base.

Both ends are **degenerate**, and the maximum is safely inside. But you had to CHECK. In another problem the answer sits at an endpoint, and skipping the check would have lost it.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Draw the picture and label it. Write the constraint from the picture, and the quantity you want from the picture. Then the algebra tells you what to differentiate — never the other way round.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
A farmer has 100 m of fence and a long straight wall. He wants the largest rectangular pen, using the wall as one side.

**Fence used** = 2x + y = 100, where x is the depth and y the width along the wall.
**Area** = xy = x(100 − 2x).

One variable, and a domain of 0 < x < 50. The wall is the whole point: it means only three sides need fencing.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Two habits that survive every problem of this kind:

**Check the endpoints, always.** Here they are degenerate (A = 0), but in a problem with a real constraint at the edge, the answer can live there — and a critical point that beats the interior can still lose to an edge.

**Sanity-check the shape.** Half the fence went to the two depths and half to the width. If your answer has a wildly lopsided pen, suspect an algebra slip.

illustration_description: A dot plot of ten quiz scores with a peak at 8 and 9 and one low outlier at 2, showing how a single distant value stretches the range and pulls the tail.
accompanying_text: A dot plot puts every value where it belongs on a number line, one dot per data point, stacked when values repeat. Nothing is summarized away yet — the whole dataset is right there, which is exactly why its **shape** is visible: where it peaks, whether it leans, and whether one value sits far from the rest.

illustration_description: Two box plots stacked for comparison: Class A is centred higher with a narrower box, Class B is centred lower with a wider box, showing that both the middle and the spread matter when comparing groups.
accompanying_text: Shape and range describe ONE dataset. Comparing TWO datasets needs the same two questions asked side by side: which is centred higher (or lower), and which is more spread out. A class that averages higher AND stays more consistent is doing better on both counts — a class that averages higher but swings wildly might not be, once you look past the average.

illustration_description: A scatter plot of about a dozen points trending upward, with a single straight line drawn through the middle of the cloud. The line of best fit passes close to the points, with roughly as many points above it as below it.
accompanying_text: When two quantities move together, a line drawn through the middle of the scatter can **predict** one from the other. Fitting that line by hand means dragging it until the gaps above and below balance out — a real skill, not a guess, and it is exactly what a spreadsheet's trendline button does automatically underneath.

illustration_description: Residuals can steer a line as well as judge it: move the line and every leftover changes, so the best line is the one that makes the leftovers smallest overall.
accompanying_text: A spreadsheet or calculator finds this SAME line — not by eye, but by testing every possible tilt and choosing the one where the leftover gaps, squared and added up, are as small as they can be. It is the identical goal fitting by hand chases; **technology just automates the search**, and lands on the same answer a careful hand-fit approximates.

illustration_description: A scatter plot with a fitted line; one point sits above the line and one sits below it, with a vertical dashed segment marking each gap — the actual value minus the line's prediction.
accompanying_text: Once a line is fitted, every point has a **residual**: its actual value minus what the line predicted. A point above the line has a positive residual; a point below has a negative one. Small residuals, scattered on both sides, mean the line is doing its job.

illustration_description: A number line from negative one to positive one showing the correlation coefficient: near negative one is a tight downward trend, near zero is a scattered cloud, near positive one is a tight upward trend.
accompanying_text: Checking every residual by hand doesn't scale. The **correlation coefficient**, r, compresses that whole pattern into one number from −1 to 1: close to ±1 means the residuals are tiny and the points hug the line; close to 0 means the points are scattered with barely any linear trend at all. The sign matches the slope's direction; the SIZE says how strong the relationship is.

illustration_description: Two measurements, one to the nearest whole unit and one to the nearest tenth, combined by a chain that is only as strong as its weakest link, illustrating that a computed result cannot be more precise than the least precise input.
accompanying_text: Every measurement has a limit to how finely it was taken. Combine two measurements — add them, subtract them, divide one by the other — and the result can be no MORE precise than the least precise input. A slope computed from whole-centimetre data cannot honestly claim five decimal places, however many the calculator displays.

illustration_description: A ruler marked only in whole centimetres next to a claimed reading of 3.14159 centimetres, showing that a tool cannot honestly report more decimal places than it can actually distinguish.
accompanying_text: The rule in one line: **a result is only as precise as its least precise input.** Add, subtract, multiply, or divide measurements together, and whichever one was measured most coarsely sets the ceiling for how many meaningful digits the answer can honestly claim — no arithmetic operation manufactures precision that wasn't in the data to begin with.

illustration_description: A statistical question expects variety: asking one person's height has a single answer, but asking a whole class's heights gives many varied answers. Statistical questions expect varied answers.
accompanying_text: "How tall is Maria?" has ONE answer. "How tall are the students in your school?" expects MANY different answers — heights vary from person to person. A **statistical question** is one that anticipates **variability**: you expect the answers to differ, and the interesting part is the PATTERN in those differences.

illustration_description: A statistical question expects variety: asking one person's height has a single answer, but asking a whole class's heights gives many varied answers. Statistical questions expect varied answers.
accompanying_text: The same topic can produce both kinds. "How old is your teacher?" — one answer, not statistical. "How old are the teachers at this school?" — many answers, statistical. Watch for the switch from ONE case to a GROUP: asking about a group is what invites variability.

illustration_description: A statistical question is answered by a whole data set, not a single number: many collected values together form the answer. A data set answers a statistical question.
accompanying_text: Ask a statistical question and collect the answers — that collection is your **data set**. Ask 5 classmates "how many pets do you have?" and get 0, 1, 1, 2, 3: five **data values**, one per person. Each value answers the SAME question; together they show the variability the question anticipated.

illustration_description: A statistical question is answered by a whole data set, not a single number: many collected values together form the answer. A data set answers a statistical question.
accompanying_text: A data set answers exactly ONE statistical question, with one value per **unit of observation** — here, per student. Mixing questions (some students report pets, some report siblings) ruins the set. Before collecting, fix two things: WHAT you're asking, and WHO you're asking.

illustration_description: The statistics pipeline runs in four steps: pose a statistical question, collect data, display it, then summarize what it shows. The stats pipeline: pose, collect, display, summarize.
accompanying_text: The full pipeline: **pose a statistical question → decide who to ask → collect one value per person → look for the pattern.** Every later tool in this course (plots, averages, spreads) works on data born this way. A weak question — or mixed-up collection — poisons everything downstream, so the pipeline's first step matters most.

illustration_description: The statistics pipeline runs in four steps: pose a statistical question, collect data, display it, then summarize what it shows. The stats pipeline: pose, collect, display, summarize.
accompanying_text: A well-run pipeline still produces MESSY-looking data — that's normal and good. "How many pets?" giving 0,1,1,2,2,2,3,4 isn't a mistake; the spread IS the finding. Variability isn't noise to eliminate — it's the signal the statistical question set out to capture.

illustration_description: A dot plot titled pets per student: one dot above 0, two dots above 1, three dots above 2, one dot above 3, and one dot above 4 — eight dots for eight students.
accompanying_text: A **dot plot** turns a data set into a picture: a number line for the possible values, one **dot per data value**, stacked when values repeat. The pets data 0,1,1,2,2,2,3,4 becomes stacks of height 1,2,3,1,1 — eight dots for eight students, and the tallest stack (at 2) shows the most common answer at a glance.

illustration_description: A dot plot titled pets per student: one dot above 0, two dots above 1, three dots above 2, one dot above 3, and one dot above 4 — eight dots for eight students.
accompanying_text: Building a dot plot has just two moves: draw a number line covering the smallest to largest value, then place one dot per data value, **stacking upward on repeats**. Nothing is lost — you can recover the entire data set by reading the dots back.

illustration_description: A histogram of quiz scores with four touching bars: scores 0 to 4 have one student, 5 to 9 have two, 10 to 14 have four, and 15 to 19 have three.
accompanying_text: When data spreads over many values, individual dots get crowded. A **histogram** groups values into equal-width **bins** and draws one bar per bin, its height showing how many values landed there. Ten quiz scores binned by fives — 0-4, 5-9, 10-14, 15-19 — give bars of height 1, 2, 4, 3. The bars **touch** because the bins share edges.

illustration_description: A histogram of quiz scores with four touching bars: scores 0 to 4 have one student, 5 to 9 have two, 10 to 14 have four, and 15 to 19 have three.
accompanying_text: Binning trades detail for clarity: the 10-14 bar says four scores landed between 10 and 14, but NOT which exact scores. Unlike a dot plot, a histogram can't be read back into the original data. Same-width bins are non-negotiable — uneven bins make bar heights lie.

illustration_description: The shape of data: a symmetric distribution balances around the middle, while a skewed one has a long tail stretching to one side. Data shape: symmetric versus skewed.
accompanying_text: Once data is plotted, describe its **shape** in plain words: where dots **cluster** (bunch up), where there are **gaps** (empty values), which values **peak** (tallest stack), and whether any point sits far from the rest (an **outlier**). The plot 1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,5 peaks at 3 and falls away evenly on both sides — roughly **symmetric**.

illustration_description: The shape of data: a symmetric distribution balances around the middle, while a skewed one has a long tail stretching to one side. Data shape: symmetric versus skewed.
accompanying_text: Not all data balances. The plot of 1,1,1,2,2,3,4,8 **clusters** at the low end (five dots at 1-2), then trails off — with a **gap** from 5 through 7 and a lone dot at 8 sitting far from the pack: an **outlier**. Naming cluster, gap, and outlier tells the data's story before any number is computed.

illustration_description: Three towers of blocks holding 2, 4, and 6 blocks. A dashed line crosses all three at a height of 4: moving two blocks from the 6-tower to the 2-tower levels every tower to 4, the mean.
accompanying_text: Three trail-mix bags hold 2, 4, and 6 raisins. Pool every raisin — 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 — then share them equally: each of the 3 bags gets 12 ÷ 3 = **4**. That level-out value is the **mean**: **mean = sum ÷ count**. In the picture, moving the extra blocks from the tallest tower to the shortest levels all three towers at exactly 4.

illustration_description: Three towers of blocks holding 2, 4, and 6 blocks. A dashed line crosses all three at a height of 4: moving two blocks from the 6-tower to the 2-tower levels every tower to 4, the mean.
accompanying_text: The mean doesn't have to be a value anyone actually had — 3, 5, 7, 9 has mean 6, and nobody read exactly 6 books. The formula also runs **backwards**: since **mean × count = sum**, a mean of 7 across 4 quizzes means the scores total 7 × 4 = 28. Knowing the total lets you hunt down a missing value.

illustration_description: The list 7, 2, 9, 4, 6 is sorted into 2, 4, 6, 7, 9. In the sorted row the middle value 6 is highlighted, with two values below it and two above it — the median.
accompanying_text: The **median** is the middle value — but only of the **sorted** list. Take 7, 2, 9, 4, 6. Sort it first: 2, 4, 6, 7, 9. Five values is an **odd** count, so one value stands exactly in the middle: **6**, with two values below it and two above. Skip the sort and you'd grab the 9 sitting mid-list — not a middle at all.

illustration_description: With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values: for 4, 5, 7, 8 the middle pair 5 and 7 average to 6. Even count: median averages the two middle values.
accompanying_text: **Even** counts have no single middle — two values share the center, and the median is the **mean of those two**. Sorted data 3, 5, 8, 12, 14, 16 has 6 values; the middle pair is 8 and 12, so the median is (8 + 12) ÷ 2 = **10**. Like the mean, a median can be a number that never appears in the data.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 30 with data dots clustered at 4 through 8 and one outlier dot at 30. The median marker sits at 6.5 inside the cluster, but the mean marker is pulled out to 10, with an arrow showing the outlier dragging it away.
accompanying_text: Five hikers carry 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 pounds: mean 6 (sum 30 ÷ 5) and median 6 — the summaries agree. Now a sixth hiker hauls **30** pounds. The sum leaps to 60, so the mean jumps to 60 ÷ 6 = **10** — bigger than five of the six packs! The median barely moves: the middle pair is 6 and 7, so it becomes **6.5**.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 30 with data dots clustered at 4 through 8 and one outlier dot at 30. The median marker sits at 6.5 inside the cluster, but the mean marker is pulled out to 10, with an arrow showing the outlier dragging it away.
accompanying_text: That's the whole choice. The mean uses every value's **size**, so one extreme value — an **outlier** — can drag it far from the pack (6 → 10). The median uses only **position**, so it's **resistant**: it moved just half a step (6 → 6.5). Data with outliers or a strong skew? Report the **median**. Balanced, outlier-free data? The **mean** works — and the two will nearly agree anyway.

illustration_description: A number line from 2 to 13 with dots at 3, 5, 7, 9, and 12. A bracket stretches from the smallest dot at 3 to the largest dot at 12, labeled range equals 12 minus 3 equals 9.
accompanying_text: Centers say where data sits; **spread** says how far it stretches. The simplest spread measure is the **range**: **maximum − minimum**. Swim laps of 3, 5, 7, 9, and 12 stretch from a min of 3 to a max of 12, so the range is 12 − 3 = **9 laps**. One subtraction, two values — everything in between is ignored.

illustration_description: A number line from 2 to 13 with dots at 3, 5, 7, 9, and 12. A bracket stretches from the smallest dot at 3 to the largest dot at 12, labeled range equals 12 minus 3 equals 9.
accompanying_text: Because range ignores everything between the endpoints, two very different data sets can share one. Both 2, 6, 6, 6, 10 and 2, 3, 5, 8, 10 have range 10 − 2 = **8** — yet the first bunches tightly at 6 while the second scatters. Range is a fast first look at spread, but it can't tell these stories apart. (And it inherits a weakness: the endpoints might be outliers.)

illustration_description: The sorted data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 shown as a row of chips. The median line splits it at 9; quartile markers at Q1 equals 5 and Q3 equals 13 fence off the shaded middle half, whose width is the IQR of 8.
accompanying_text: The range trusts the wild endpoints. The **interquartile range (IQR)** measures the calm **middle half** instead. Sort the data and split it at the median into a lower and an upper half. **Q1** is the median of the lower half, **Q3** the median of the upper half, and **IQR = Q3 − Q1**. For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16: halves split at the median 9, Q1 = 5, Q3 = 13, IQR = **8**.

illustration_description: The sorted data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 shown as a row of chips. The median line splits it at 9; quartile markers at Q1 equals 5 and Q3 equals 13 fence off the shaded middle half, whose width is the IQR of 8.
accompanying_text: One convention question: with an **odd** count, the median is a real data value — does it join a half? **No.** Our rule (the standard one): the median is **left out**, and the halves are everything below and above it. For 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, the median 8 steps aside; lower half 3, 5, 6 gives Q1 = 5, upper half 10, 12, 14 gives Q3 = 12, so IQR = **7**.

illustration_description: Two dot plots on matching number lines. Class A's dots hug the center at 7; Class B's dots scatter from 1 to 13. A dashed line through both plots marks their shared center of 7 — same middle, very different spread.
accompanying_text: Two classes record hours of weekly reading. **Class A:** 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10. **Class B:** 1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13. Both sum to 42, so both means are 42 ÷ 6 = **7** — and both medians are (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = **7** too. Every center agrees the classes match. But look at the plots: A hugs its center; B scatters. Centers alone can hide the whole story.

illustration_description: Two dot plots on matching number lines. Class A's dots hug the center at 7; Class B's dots scatter from 1 to 13. A dashed line through both plots marks their shared center of 7 — same middle, very different spread.
accompanying_text: Spread is what those numbers mean **in context**. Class A (IQR 4): most students read a similar amount — a 7-hour-ish plan suits nearly everyone. Class B (IQR 10): the 'typical 7 hours' describes almost nobody; some students read barely at all while others devour books. Same center, opposite classrooms. A center without a spread is **half a description**.

illustration_description: A box plot above a number line. Whiskers run from the minimum at 2 to the maximum at 20. The box spans Q1 at 6 to Q3 at 15, with a line at the median of 10. Each of the four sections holds one quarter of the data.
accompanying_text: You already find the median, Q1 and Q3. Add the smallest and largest values and you have the **five-number summary**: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. A **box plot** draws that summary. The **box** runs from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median; the **whiskers** reach out to the min and the max. For 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14, 16, 19, 20 the summary is min 2, Q1 7, median 12, Q3 16, max 20.

illustration_description: The same box plot with each of its four sections labelled twenty-five percent. The two whisker sections are long and the two box sections are short, showing that equal shares of data can occupy very different widths.
accompanying_text: Every one of the four pieces — lower whisker, lower box, upper box, upper whisker — holds the **same quarter** of the data. So a **wide** piece does not mean more values; it means that quarter is **spread out**. A long whisker and a short whisker on the same plot hold equally many values, packed loosely on one side and tightly on the other.

illustration_description: Two box plots stacked on a shared scale. Class A runs from 8 to 18 with a narrow box from 11 to 15. Class B runs from 2 to 22 with a wide box from 9 to 17. Both have a median of 13, so the centres match while the spreads differ sharply.
accompanying_text: Two box plots on the **same scale** answer two questions at a glance. Line up the median lines to compare **centres**; compare box widths to compare **spread**. Class A runs 8 to 18 with a box from 11 to 15. Class B runs 2 to 22 with a box from 9 to 17. Both medians sit at 13 — identical centres — but B's box is 8 wide against A's 4. Same typical value, very different consistency.

illustration_description: The same box plot with each of its four sections labelled twenty-five percent. The two whisker sections are long and the two box sections are short, showing that equal shares of data can occupy very different widths.
accompanying_text: One warning when comparing. A box plot hides the **individual values** — it shows only five numbers. Two very different data sets can produce the **same** box plot: one with values evenly sprinkled, one with values clumped at each end. If the question is about gaps, clusters or repeated values, go back to the dot plot; the box plot answers centre and spread.

illustration_description: A number line with five dots at 2, 4, 6, 9 and 9, and a vertical line at the mean of 6. An arrow runs from each dot to the mean, labelled with its distance: 4, 2, 0, 3 and 3. The mean absolute deviation is the average of those five distances.
accompanying_text: The IQR uses quartiles. Here is a second measure, built on the **mean**. For each value, find how far it sits from the mean — always a positive distance. Average those distances. That average is the **mean absolute deviation**, or **MAD**: the typical distance from centre. For 2, 4, 6, 9, 9 the mean is 6 and the distances 4, 2, 0, 3, 3 average to **2.4**.

illustration_description: Two spread measures compared on one data set. The interquartile range is drawn as a bracket spanning the middle half from Q1 to Q3. The mean absolute deviation is drawn as a band of equal width on each side of the mean. IQR pairs with the median, MAD pairs with the mean.
accompanying_text: Two spread measures, two partners. The **IQR** is built from quartiles, so it pairs with the **median** and, like the median, shrugs off wild values. The **MAD** is built from distances to the mean, so it pairs with the **mean** and, like the mean, an extreme value pulls it upward. Report median with IQR, or mean with MAD — matching the centre to the spread that was built from it.

illustration_description: A dot plot of minutes to get to school: one dot at 5, two at 10, three at 15, two at 20, one at 25. Callouts name its shape as symmetric with a peak at 15, its center as median 15, and its spread as range 20.
accompanying_text: You now own three lenses, and a real description uses **all of them**. Minutes to get to school: 5, 10, 10, 15, 15, 15, 20, 20, 25. **Shape:** one peak at 15, symmetric. **Center:** median 15 (the mean is 15 too — symmetric data agrees with itself). **Spread:** range 25 − 5 = 20, IQR 20 − 10 = 10. One plot, three questions, one honest paragraph.

illustration_description: A dot plot of minutes to get to school: one dot at 5, two at 10, three at 15, two at 20, one at 25. Callouts name its shape as symmetric with a peak at 15, its center as median 15, and its spread as range 20.
accompanying_text: Assemble it **in context, with units**: 'Trips to school center around **15 minutes** (median), with the middle half between 10 and 20 (**IQR 10**); the shape is **symmetric** with a single peak at 15 and no outliers.' Notice what's missing from bad descriptions: a bare '15' answers nothing — fifteen *what*, of *what data*, how *spread out*?

illustration_description: Summaries travel in pairs matched to shape: symmetric data uses mean with a spread measure, and skewed data uses median with the interquartile range. Match summaries: mean+spread or median+IQR.
accompanying_text: Weekly allowances (dollars): 10, 12, 12, 14, 14, 16, 18, **64**. The 64 is a lone outlier past a huge gap. Mean: 160 ÷ 8 = **20** — larger than seven of the eight allowances! Median: (14 + 14) ÷ 2 = **14**, right among the pack. The shape you see decides the summary you trust: **outliers or skew → median (and IQR); symmetric → mean works fine**.

illustration_description: Summaries travel in pairs matched to shape: symmetric data uses mean with a spread measure, and skewed data uses median with the interquartile range. Match summaries: mean+spread or median+IQR.
accompanying_text: The summaries travel in **pairs**. The mean and range both feel every extreme — use them together on **symmetric, outlier-free** data, where they're honest and familiar. The median and IQR both read positions, not sizes — the **resistant pair** for **skewed or outlier-carrying** data. Mixing (say, median with range) half-fixes the problem: the range still hands the outlier the microphone.

illustration_description: A dot plot of minutes to get to school: one dot at 5, two at 10, three at 15, two at 20, one at 25. Callouts name its shape as symmetric with a peak at 15, its center as median 15, and its spread as range 20.
accompanying_text: Course capstone: run the WHOLE pipeline on one fresh case. The question — *"How many books do students in our class borrow per week?"* — anticipates variability, so it's statistical. Ten students answer: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, **12**. Your job, detective: plot it, name its shape, choose the honest summaries, and report in context. Every tool from chapters 1–4 shows up once.

illustration_description: Summaries travel in pairs matched to shape: symmetric data uses mean with a spread measure, and skewed data uses median with the interquartile range. Match summaries: mean+spread or median+IQR.
accompanying_text: Shape decides the summaries. The 12 is an outlier, so the honest pair is the resistant one: **median with IQR**. Sorted halves — 0, 1, 1, 2, 2 and 2, 3, 3, 4, 12 — give median (2 + 2) ÷ 2 = **2**, Q1 = **1**, Q3 = **3**. Meanwhile the mean is 30 ÷ 10 = **3**, dragged a full book above the median by one avid reader.

illustration_description: Two bars lined up on the left. The top bar is nine; the bottom bar is five. The four extra units on the top bar are the difference. Nine minus five equals four more.
accompanying_text: Data starts with a question. A good survey question gives every person one choice you can sort and count.

accompanying_text: To multiply 23 × 4, split 23 into its places: 20 and 3. Multiply each by 4, then add. That's **20 × 4 = 80** and **3 × 4 = 12**, so 80 + 12 = 92. These are **partial products** — one piece per place, added back together.

accompanying_text: The standard algorithm is partial products, written compactly. For 47 × 6: multiply the ones, 7 × 6 = 42 — write the 2, **carry** the 4. Then the tens: 4 × 6 = 24, plus the carried 4 = 28. The answer is 282. The carry is just the tens part of the first partial product, waiting its turn.

accompanying_text: The carry matters most when the tens step would otherwise be wrong. For 35 × 4: ones give 5 × 4 = 20 — write 0, carry 2. Tens: 3 × 4 = 12, plus the carried 2 = 14. Answer 140. Forget the carry and you'd get 120 — off by exactly the carry's value.

accompanying_text: To multiply 23 × 45, multiply 23 by each part of 45. First by the 5 ones: 23 × 5 = 115. Then by the 4 tens: 23 × 40 = 920. Add the two rows: 115 + 920 = 1035. Two partial products, one for each digit of the second number.

illustration_description: Estimating a quotient with compatible numbers: 812 divided by 39 is about 800 divided by 40, which is 20. Estimate with compatible numbers: about 20.
accompanying_text: A compatible number is one that divides the rounded divisor cleanly. For 356 ÷ 58, round 58 to 60, then reach for a multiple of 60 near 356 — that's 360. So 360 ÷ 60 = 6. Choosing the multiple that divides evenly is the whole skill.

illustration_description: The long-division cycle of four repeating steps: divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down the next digit. Long division repeats four steps.
accompanying_text: Long division repeats four steps: **divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.** For 372 ÷ 12, look at 37 first. Your estimate says 12 fits about 3 times. Place the 3, multiply 3 × 12 = 36, subtract 37 − 36 = 1, then bring down the next digit. The estimate from last lesson picks each digit.

illustration_description: The long-division cycle of four repeating steps: divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down the next digit. Long division repeats four steps.
accompanying_text: After placing the 3: multiply 3 × 12 = 36, subtract 37 − 36 = 1. That 1 is what's left over so far. Now **bring down** the next digit of 372 — the 2 — beside the 1, making 12. The leftover joins the next digit to keep dividing.

illustration_description: The same division 27 divided by 4 answered two ways: needing whole buses rounds up to 7, while sharing evenly leaves 6 with 3 left over. A remainder means different things.
accompanying_text: A remainder means different things depending on the question. Divide 100 kids into buses of 15: that's 6 remainder 10. Six buses hold 90 kids — but 10 kids are still waiting. You can't leave them, so you **round up** to 7 buses. When everyone must fit, the leftover forces one more group.

illustration_description: The same division 27 divided by 4 answered two ways: needing whole buses rounds up to 7, while sharing evenly leaves 6 with 3 left over. A remainder means different things.
accompanying_text: Now the *same* division, a different question. You have 100 stickers and make full packs of 15. That's still 6 remainder 10 — but here you **drop** the remainder: only 6 full packs are possible, and 10 stickers are left over, not enough for a 7th pack. Same numbers, opposite rounding.

illustration_description: Adding decimals by lining up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths and ones under ones, with the point carried straight down into the answer. Line up the decimal points to add.
accompanying_text: To add or subtract decimals, line up the **decimal points**, not the right ends. Points aligned means places aligned — tenths over tenths, hundredths over hundredths. Adding 3.5 + 1.75, the 5 tenths sits over the 7 tenths, and the point keeps every digit in its true place.

illustration_description: Adding decimals by lining up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths and ones under ones, with the point carried straight down into the answer. Line up the decimal points to add.
accompanying_text: Once the points are aligned, **pad with trailing zeros** so both numbers have the same length. Write 3.5 as 3.50, then add straight down like whole numbers: 3.50 + 1.75. The zero holds the hundredths place so nothing drifts. Bring the point straight down into the answer.

illustration_description: Subtracting a decimal from a whole number: write 5 as 5.00 by padding zeros, then borrow across to compute 5.00 minus 1.75 equals 3.25. Pad with zeros, then borrow across.
accompanying_text: When the numbers have different lengths, padding does the heavy lifting. For 4.08 + 2.9, pad 2.9 to 2.90 so the hundredths line up. If you skip that, it's easy to slide the 9 into the wrong column and add 2.09 by mistake. Padding keeps every digit honest.

illustration_description: Subtracting a decimal from a whole number: write 5 as 5.00 by padding zeros, then borrow across to compute 5.00 minus 1.75 equals 3.25. Pad with zeros, then borrow across.
accompanying_text: Subtracting from a whole number means borrowing across zeros. For 10.0 − 3.47, pad to 10.00. There's nothing to borrow from in the tenths or hundredths, so the borrow travels all the way from the ones: 10 becomes 9, then the zeros become 9s and 10, and you subtract cleanly.

illustration_description: Adding decimals by lining up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths and ones under ones, with the point carried straight down into the answer. Line up the decimal points to add.
accompanying_text: Word problems just wrap the same skill. Words like *total*, *altogether*, or *combined* mean add; *change*, *difference*, or *how much more* mean subtract. Either way, line up the points and pad. Making change from $10.00 for a $6.75 item is 10.00 − 6.75 = $3.25.

illustration_description: Adding decimals by lining up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths and ones under ones, with the point carried straight down into the answer. Line up the decimal points to add.
accompanying_text: Some problems take two steps. To find change from $20 for several items, first **add** the items into a total, then **subtract** that total from $20. Do the steps in order — the total feeds the subtraction. Read carefully so you answer the question actually asked.

illustration_description: A hundredths grid where three shaded columns overlap four shaded rows in twelve cells, showing three tenths times four tenths equals twelve hundredths. 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12 on a hundredths grid.
accompanying_text: To multiply decimals, ignore the points at first: multiply as whole numbers. Then count the total decimal places in **both** factors, and put that many places in the answer. For 0.3 × 0.4: 3 × 4 = 12, and there are two decimal places total, so the answer is 0.12.

illustration_description: Multiplying decimals by ignoring the points, multiplying 12 by 5 to get 60, then counting the two decimal places to place the point, giving 0.60. Count decimal places: 1.2 × 0.5 = 0.60.
accompanying_text: Count the places first, then tidy up. 1.2 × 0.5: 12 × 5 = 60, two places gives 0.60 — and 0.60 is just 0.6, so a trailing zero can drop away. Always place by the count *before* removing any trailing zeros, or the point lands wrong.

illustration_description: Multiplying decimals by ignoring the points, multiplying 12 by 5 to get 60, then counting the two decimal places to place the point, giving 0.60. Count decimal places: 1.2 × 0.5 = 0.60.
accompanying_text: The rule scales to bigger numbers. For 2.5 × 1.4, multiply as wholes: 25 × 14 = 350. Both factors have one decimal place, so two total — place the point two from the right: 3.50, which is 3.5. Multiply first, count places second, every time.

illustration_description: Estimating a quotient with compatible numbers: 812 divided by 39 is about 800 divided by 40, which is 20. Estimate with compatible numbers: about 20.
accompanying_text: Estimation guards the point. For 2.5 × 1.4, round to about 3 × 1 = 3 — so the answer should be near 3, which 3.5 is. That instantly rules out 35 (way too big) and 0.35 (way too small). A quick estimate catches a misplaced point every time.

illustration_description: Multiplying decimals by ignoring the points, multiplying 12 by 5 to get 60, then counting the two decimal places to place the point, giving 0.60. Count decimal places: 1.2 × 0.5 = 0.60.
accompanying_text: To divide a decimal by a whole number, divide as usual and bring the decimal point **straight up** into the answer. For 4.8 ÷ 6, think 48 ÷ 6 = 8, and the point comes straight up to give 0.8. The point stays in its column — it doesn't move.

illustration_description: The equation zero point five x plus one point two equals three point seven. Multiplying every term by ten shifts each decimal point one place: five x plus twelve equals thirty-seven, so x equals five.
accompanying_text: Dividing by a *decimal* needs one move first: **shift both numbers** the same number of places until the divisor is a whole number. For 1.5 ÷ 0.5, shift each one place right: 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Shifting both the same way keeps the answer the same — it's like scaling a fraction up.

accompanying_text: One whole can be split into 10 equal parts. Each part is called one tenth of the whole.

accompanying_text: The count of shaded tenths becomes a decimal: write the count just after a dot called the decimal point. Three tenths is 0.3.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Every count of tenths has a decimal name. The digit after the decimal point counts the tenths.

accompanying_text: Zero point five, zero point nine — the pattern is always the same: the tenths digit counts the shaded columns.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: The strip is a piece of the number line: its left edge is 0 and its right edge is 1. The column edges mark the tenths.

accompanying_text: Each tenth is one step of the walk from 0 to 1. Shading 0.4 walks four of the ten steps.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: A tenths decimal and a tenths fraction name the same amount two ways: 0.7 and 7/10 are the same seven parts.

accompanying_text: The fraction shows the split (10 equal parts) and the count (7 of them). The decimal hides the 10 and keeps the 7.

accompanying_text: A count of hundredths gets a two-digit decimal: the count's last digit lands two places after the point.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: When the count is small, a zero holds the tenths place: nine hundredths is 0.09, not 0.9.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: The grid reads any hundredths decimal: full columns show the tenths digit, single cells show the hundredths digit.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: 0.37 is three full columns and seven more cells — 37 cells in all. The decimal's digits ARE the grid recipe.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Any tenths amount can be renamed in hundredths: each tenth is worth 10 hundredths, so multiply the count by 10.

accompanying_text: 0.4 = 40/100. Four full columns hold 40 cells — same shading, new name.

accompanying_text: To add tenths and hundredths, rename first: turn the tenths into hundredths, then add the counts.
