accompanying_text: 0.2 + 0.05: the 0.2 is 20 hundredths, so the sum is 20 + 5 = 25 hundredths — 0.25.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: A decimal is read by its last place: 0.62 is read “sixty-two hundredths,” because its digits end in the hundredths place.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: 0.07 is “seven hundredths” — the zero after the point is silent in the name, but it holds the tenths place open.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Each digit after the point has its own place name: first the tenths place, then the hundredths place.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: In 0.58, the 5 is in the tenths place — worth five full columns — and the 8 is in the hundredths place — eight single cells.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Fractions over 10 or over 100 convert straight to decimals: the denominator names the place, the numerator fills it.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: 62/100 becomes 0.62; 3/10 becomes 0.3. No arithmetic — just place the count.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Every hundredths decimal converts back to a fraction over 100: 0.43 is 43/100.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Watch the digit order — 0.43 is 43/100, not 34/100. The places carry the value.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: To compare decimals, line up the places: compare tenths digits first, and only check hundredths when the tenths tie.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: More digits does not mean more value: 0.5 beats 0.35, because 5 tenths beats 3 tenths before hundredths are even read.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: A zero added after the last decimal digit changes nothing: 0.60 and 0.6 shade exactly the same six columns.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: 0.60 says “60 hundredths” and 0.6 says “6 tenths” — two names for one amount, because 60 hundredths IS 6 tenths.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Ordering decimals is repeated comparison: place them by tenths digits first, using hundredths only for ties.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: In 0.09, 0.35, 0.4, 0.5 the digit counts vary, but the tenths digits 0, 3, 4, 5 already tell the whole story.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Money runs on hundredths: a dollar splits into 100 cents, so a dime is one tenth and a penny is one hundredth.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: 3 dimes and 7 pennies is $0.37 — the dimes fill the tenths place and the pennies fill the hundredths place.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Measurement uses hundredths too: one meter is 100 centimeters, so each centimeter is one hundredth of a meter.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: A 42-centimeter ribbon is 0.42 meters — the same renaming the grid has shown all along.

illustration_description: One whole bar split into ten equal parts; one highlighted part is one tenth, written 0.1 — the first rung below the ones place.
accompanying_text: You already climbed the ×10 ladder up to a million: each rung left is ten times bigger. Now climb the other way. Split one whole into 10 equal parts and each part is a **tenth** — the first rung *below* the ones place. We write one tenth as **0.1**, and the dot (the decimal point) marks where the ones place ends.

illustration_description: The place-value ladder continued below one: ones, then tenths, hundredths, and thousandths, each rung one tenth of the one above. The ladder below one: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
accompanying_text: The ladder rule still holds, both directions: the ones place is **ten times** one tenth, and one tenth is **one tenth of** the ones place. So 0.1 × 10 = 1, and 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1. Tenths are just the ladder's next rung down.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: Keep climbing down. Split one tenth into 10 equal parts and each is a **hundredth** — written 0.01, because it takes two places after the point. A 10×10 grid shows it: 100 tiny cells fill one whole, so each cell is one hundredth.

illustration_description: A hundred-square grid representing one whole; one small cell is one hundredth and one full column of ten cells is one tenth. One cell is a hundredth; a column is a tenth.
accompanying_text: One more rung: split a hundredth into 10 and you get a **thousandth** — written 0.001, three places after the point. The ladder never runs out downward, but Grade 5 stops here: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

illustration_description: The equation zero point five x plus one point two equals three point seven. Multiplying every term by ten shifts each decimal point one place: five x plus twelve equals thirty-seven, so x equals five.
accompanying_text: In Grade 4 the ×10 ladder ran through the whole numbers: ×10 slid a digit one rung **left** (bigger), ÷10 one rung **right** (smaller). Nothing new happens at the decimal point — the same two moves keep working straight through it. The point is just a landmark, not a wall.

illustration_description: The equation zero point five x plus one point two equals three point seven. Multiplying every term by ten shifts each decimal point one place: five x plus twelve equals thirty-seven, so x equals five.
accompanying_text: Chaining moves just repeats the slide. Two ×10 moves is one rung left, then another: 0.03 → 0.3 → 3. Two ÷10 moves is two rungs right: 7 → 0.7 → 0.07. Count the moves, count the rungs.

illustration_description: The digits of 3.47 named after the point: 4 is in the tenths place worth four tenths, and 7 is in the hundredths place worth seven hundredths. Place names after the point.
accompanying_text: Each rung below the point has a name that ends in **-ths**: the first place is **tenths**, the second **hundredths**, the third **thousandths**. So in 0.375 the 3 is 3 tenths, the 7 is 7 hundredths, and the 5 is 5 thousandths — read left to right, smallest name last.

illustration_description: The digits of 3.47 named after the point: 4 is in the tenths place worth four tenths, and 7 is in the hundredths place worth seven hundredths. Place names after the point.
accompanying_text: A digit's **name tells its value**. The 7 in 0.375 isn't just "7" — it's 7 *hundredths*, worth 7/100. The place name is the size of each piece, and the digit counts how many of those pieces you have.

illustration_description: The decimal 0.347 broken into its places: three tenths plus four hundredths plus seven thousandths. Expanded form: 0.347 = 0.3 + 0.04 + 0.007.
accompanying_text: A decimal is just its places, added up. Break 0.375 into what each digit is worth: **3/10 + 7/100 + 5/1000**. That's **expanded form** — the number pulled apart into one piece per place, so you can see exactly where each digit's value comes from.

illustration_description: The decimal 0.347 broken into its places: three tenths plus four hundredths plus seven thousandths. Expanded form: 0.347 = 0.3 + 0.04 + 0.007.
accompanying_text: Expanded form runs both ways. Given the pieces, add them back to rebuild the decimal: 2/10 + 4/100 puts a 2 in tenths and a 4 in hundredths, so it recomposes to **0.24**. Each fraction lands in its own place.

illustration_description: Reading a decimal in words: 0.47 is read as forty-seven hundredths, using the last digit's place name. 0.47 is forty-seven hundredths.
accompanying_text: To say a decimal in words, read the digits after the point as a whole number, then name the **last** (smallest) place. So 0.375 is "three hundred seventy-five **thousandths**" — because the last digit lands in thousandths. One place name covers the whole fractional part.

illustration_description: Reading a decimal in words: 0.47 is read as forty-seven hundredths, using the last digit's place name. 0.47 is forty-seven hundredths.
accompanying_text: Going the other way, the place name tells you the **last** place to fill — and you may need placeholder zeros to reach it. "Nine hundredths" ends in hundredths (2nd place), so the 9 goes there and a 0 holds the empty tenths: **0.09**.

illustration_description: Comparing decimals by lining up the points: 0.45 above 0.40 shows four tenths tie, then five hundredths beats zero, so 0.45 is greater. Compare by lining up places, so 0.45 beats 0.4.
accompanying_text: To compare two decimals, line up their points and check place by place, **left to right**. The first place where the digits differ decides it — a bigger digit there wins, no matter what follows. Start at tenths, the biggest place after the point.

illustration_description: Comparing decimals by lining up the points: 0.45 above 0.40 shows four tenths tie, then five hundredths beats zero, so 0.45 is greater. Compare by lining up places, so 0.45 beats 0.4.
accompanying_text: Here's the trap: more digits does **not** mean bigger. Compare 0.7 and 0.68 at the first place — tenths: 7 versus 6. 7 wins immediately, so **0.7 is greater than 0.68**, even though 0.68 has more digits. The first differing place is all that matters.

illustration_description: The trailing-zero rule: adding zeros to the right end of a decimal does not change its value, so one half equals 0.5 equals 0.50 equals 0.500. Trailing zeros don't change value: 0.5 = 0.50.
accompanying_text: Zeros added to the **right end** of a decimal change nothing: 0.5, 0.50, and 0.500 are the same value. Each extra zero just says "and no more of the next smaller piece." Half a whole is half whether you write one place or three.

illustration_description: The trailing-zero rule: adding zeros to the right end of a decimal does not change its value, so one half equals 0.5 equals 0.50 equals 0.500. Trailing zeros don't change value: 0.5 = 0.50.
accompanying_text: Padding is a **tool**: give two decimals the same number of places, then compare like whole numbers. To check 0.5 against 0.45, pad to 0.50 — now compare 50 and 45. So **0.5 is greater than 0.45**, even though 0.45 has more digits.

illustration_description: Comparing decimals by lining up the points: 0.45 above 0.40 shows four tenths tie, then five hundredths beats zero, so 0.45 is greater. Compare by lining up places, so 0.45 beats 0.4.
accompanying_text: To order a whole set of decimals, use one trick: **pad them all to the same number of places** with trailing zeros, then read them like whole numbers. Once every number has the same length, the smallest "whole number" is the least decimal.

illustration_description: The trailing-zero rule: adding zeros to the right end of a decimal does not change its value, so one half equals 0.5 equals 0.50 equals 0.500. Trailing zeros don't change value: 0.5 = 0.50.
accompanying_text: The padding trick shines when lengths are mixed. For 0.3, 0.25, 0.301, 0.31, pad to three places: 0.300, 0.250, 0.301, 0.310. Now compare 300, 250, 301, 310 — the order falls right out.

illustration_description: Rounding 3.7 to the nearest whole number on a number line from 3 to 4 with a mark at the halfway 3.5: 3.7 is past halfway, so it rounds up to 4. Round 3.7 to the nearest whole: 4.
accompanying_text: Rounding a decimal to the nearest whole asks: which whole number is it closest to? Look at the **tenths** digit — the first one after the point. If it's 5 or more, round up to the next whole; if it's 4 or less, stay at the current whole. So 3.8 rounds to 4, and 3.2 stays at 3.

illustration_description: Rounding 3.7 to the nearest whole number on a number line from 3 to 4 with a mark at the halfway 3.5: 3.7 is past halfway, so it rounds up to 4. Round 3.7 to the nearest whole: 4.
accompanying_text: What about an exact halfway, like 3.5? It sits the same distance from 3 and from 4. The agreed **convention** is: a tenths digit of exactly 5 rounds **up**. It's a rule people chose for consistency, not a law of nature — but everyone follows it, so 3.5 rounds to 4.

illustration_description: Rounding 3.7 to the nearest whole number on a number line from 3 to 4 with a mark at the halfway 3.5: 3.7 is past halfway, so it rounds up to 4. Round 3.7 to the nearest whole: 4.
accompanying_text: The same rule rounds to any place, not just wholes. Pick your target place, then look at the digit **one place to its right** — the *decider*. To round to the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: 5 or more rounds the tenths up, 4 or less leaves it. So 3.16 rounds to 3.2.

illustration_description: Rounding 3.7 to the nearest whole number on a number line from 3 to 4 with a mark at the halfway 3.5: 3.7 is past halfway, so it rounds up to 4. Round 3.7 to the nearest whole: 4.
accompanying_text: To round to the nearest **hundredth**, the target moves one place right — so the decider does too, becoming the **thousandths** digit. Look there: 5 or more rounds the hundredths up. The rule never changes; only which place you target and which you check.

illustration_description: Rounding 3.7 to the nearest whole number on a number line from 3 to 4 with a mark at the halfway 3.5: 3.7 is past halfway, so it rounds up to 4. Round 3.7 to the nearest whole: 4.
accompanying_text: Real problems tell you which place to round to. "Nearest dollar" means round to the ones place — and the **tenths** digit (the dimes) is the decider. So $4.60 rounds to $5, because 6 is 5 or more. The context names the place; the rule stays the same.

illustration_description: Rounding 3.7 to the nearest whole number on a number line from 3 to 4 with a mark at the halfway 3.5: 3.7 is past halfway, so it rounds up to 4. Round 3.7 to the nearest whole: 4.
accompanying_text: "Nearest tenth" shows up in measurements — a length to the nearest tenth of a meter, a time to the nearest tenth of a second. Target the tenths place; the **hundredths** digit decides. The context changes; the decider-one-place-right rule does not.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: f tells you **how high**. f′ tells you **how steep**. They are different questions about the same point, and their answers are unrelated: a curve can be high and falling, or low and climbing.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
In precalculus you squeezed the secant onto the tangent and got **one number**: the slope of f at one point.

Now do it at every x at once. Each input has its own slope, and a rule that hands one output to each input is a **function**.

That function is the derivative, f′.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text:
Three notations, one object:

**f′(x)** — Lagrange. Compact; good for stating rules.
**dy/dx** — Leibniz. It *looks* like a fraction, and in the chain rule it behaves like one.
**d/dx[ ]** — the operator. Read it as "differentiate what follows".

They are the same function wearing different clothes.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: A horizontal tangent says the curve has stopped climbing *for an instant*. It does not say it has changed its mind. To turn, f′ must go from one sign to the other — touching zero is not enough.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
The sign of f′ is the direction of f.

**f′ > 0** → f is rising.
**f′ < 0** → f is falling.
**f′ = 0** → f is momentarily flat.

And the *size* of f′ is the steepness. Nothing else about f matters to f′ — not its height, not its sign.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So f′ = 0 marks a **critical point** — a place worth investigating, not a verdict.

To know whether it is a peak, a valley, or a flat pause, you must ask what f′ does *either side* of it. That question is a whole course of its own (`curve-analysis`), and this is the moment it is born.

illustration_description: The absolute value graph has a corner at zero. The slope coming from the left is minus one and from the right is plus one, so no single tangent line fits and the derivative does not exist there.
accompanying_text: Ask the one question the definition asks: does [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h settle on a single finite number as h → 0? A corner gives two answers. A jump gives none. A vertical tangent gives infinity. Only a settled, finite value counts.

illustration_description: The absolute value graph has a corner at zero. The slope coming from the left is minus one and from the right is plus one, so no single tangent line fits and the derivative does not exist there.
accompanying_text:
A derivative is a **limit**, and limits can fail.

At a corner, the slope coming from the left and the slope coming from the right disagree. Two different answers means the limit does not exist — so f′ does not exist there, however smooth the curve looks elsewhere.

illustration_description: The absolute value graph has a corner at zero. The slope coming from the left is minus one and from the right is plus one, so no single tangent line fits and the derivative does not exist there.
accompanying_text:
So "differentiable" is a stronger promise than "continuous": it says the curve is **locally straight**. Magnify a differentiable point far enough and the curve becomes indistinguishable from its tangent.

Magnify a corner and it stays a corner, forever. That is the honest test.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Two moves, always in this order. **Drop** the exponent to the front as a multiplier. **Subtract one** from the exponent. Nothing else changes — and if the expression is a root or a reciprocal, write it as a power BEFORE you start.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
Take the limit by hand for x², x³, x⁴ and a pattern appears immediately:

x² → 2x · x³ → 3x² · x⁴ → 4x³

**The exponent drops in front, and the power falls by one:**

d/dx[xⁿ] = n·xⁿ⁻¹.

One rule retires an infinite family of limits.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
The rule does not care that n is a whole number.

**√x = x^(1/2)** → (1/2)x^(−1/2) = 1/(2√x).
**1/x² = x^(−2)** → −2x^(−3).

Rewrite as a power first, then apply the rule mechanically. Most 'hard' derivatives are just powers in disguise.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Differentiate a polynomial **term by term**. Each term is a coefficient times a power: the coefficient rides along, the power rule handles the rest, and any bare constant dies.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
Three rules that cost nothing:

**Constants have zero slope.** d/dx[7] = 0 — a horizontal line does not climb.
**Constants factor out.** d/dx[5f] = 5f′ — stretching a curve vertically stretches its slopes by the same amount.
**Sums split.** d/dx[f + g] = f′ + g′ — the slopes just add.

With these plus the power rule, every polynomial is now routine.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
Notice what is NOT here.

There is no rule that says the derivative of a **product** is the product of the derivatives, and none that says the derivative of a **quotient** is the quotient of the derivatives.

Both are false, and both are the next chapter. Sums are easy; products are not.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Do it in two separate passes. First differentiate f to get f′ — and then treat f′ as a brand-new function and differentiate THAT. There is no shortcut; there are just two applications of the same rules.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
f′ is a function. So differentiate it again.

**f″** is the derivative of the derivative — the rate at which the SLOPE is changing. If f is position and f′ is velocity, then f″ is acceleration.

A car can be moving forward (f′ > 0) while slowing down (f″ < 0). Direction and change-of-direction are different questions.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
The second derivative also has a shape meaning:

**f″ > 0** → the slope is increasing → the curve bends **upward** (concave up, holding water).
**f″ < 0** → the curve bends **downward**.

That is how a critical point gets convicted: flat *and* bending upward is a valley.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text: Say it out loud: **first times the derivative of the second, plus the second times the derivative of the first.** Two terms, always. If you have written one term, you are not finished.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
A rectangle has width u and height v, and its area is uv. Grow both a little.

The new area gains a **strip along the top** (u·dv), a **strip along the side** (v·du), and a **tiny corner** (du·dv) — a product of two tiny things, too small to survive the limit.

(uv)′ = u′v + uv′. The area grows on **two sides**, which is why one term is never enough.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
The rule is **symmetric**: u′v + uv′ is the same as v′u + vu′. It does not matter which factor you call u.

What does matter is that you take **both** turns. Every wrong answer in this chapter comes from taking one.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text: Write the four pieces down before you touch anything: u, u′, v, v′. Then assemble (u′v − uv′)/v² slowly. Almost every error in this chapter is a subtraction done in the wrong order.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
A quotient is a product in disguise: u/v = u·v⁻¹. Push that through the product rule and tidy up, and you get

**(u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′) / v²**.

The order matters now — the minus sign means **low·d-high minus high·d-low**, and swapping them flips the sign of the whole answer.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
Two habits worth keeping.

**Simplify before you differentiate.** x³/x is just x². Reaching for the quotient rule there is legal but foolish.

**Never simplify the denominator away.** v² stays as it is — expanding it usually makes the answer harder to read and easier to get wrong.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text: Ask what the expression IS before you ask how to differentiate it. Multiplied together → product rule. Divided → quotient rule, unless it cancels. Added → term by term. Getting the structure right is most of the battle.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
Before differentiating anything, ask one question: **what is this expression, structurally?**

A sum of terms → differentiate term by term.
A product of two things → product rule.
One thing over another → quotient rule (or simplify it away).

The rules are easy. Choosing the right one is where the marks go.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
When rules nest, work from the **outside in**.

For a product whose factors are themselves complicated, apply the product rule first and let each u′ and v′ be a smaller problem you solve afterwards.

Never try to do two rules in one line. That is where the errors live.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text: Two steps, and never skip the second. **One:** differentiate the outer function, leaving the inner bracket exactly as it is. **Two:** multiply by the derivative of what is inside the bracket. If your answer has no second factor, you have not finished.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
Three gears. x turns u three times as fast; u turns y five times as fast. How fast does x turn y?

Fifteen. **Rates multiply along a chain:**

dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx)

And the Leibniz notation is not a coincidence — the du really does cancel, exactly as it looks like it should.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
State it as a ritual and it stops being frightening:

**Differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.**

Say the last clause out loud every time. "Times the derivative of the inside" is the entire difference between a right answer and a wrong one.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, exactly as normal — but every time a y appears, remember it is secretly a function of x, so the chain rule attaches a dy/dx. Then collect the dy/dx terms and solve for it like any other unknown.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
Nothing changes when the chain gets longer. Peel one layer at a time, from the outside in, and multiply everything you collect.

For √((2x + 1)³): the outside is a square root, then a cube, then a linear bracket. Three layers, three factors.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text:
Some functions refuse to be written as y = f(x) at all. x² + y² = 25 defines a whole circle, and no single formula gives y.

**Differentiate the equation anyway.** Treat y as a function of x, and every time you differentiate a y, the chain rule makes you pay a dy/dx.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text: Three steps, always the same. **Differentiate** every term with respect to x, charging a y′ each time a y is differentiated. **Collect** every y′ term on one side. **Divide.** The algebra is ordinary; only the y′ bookkeeping is new.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text:
An implicit derivative usually comes out in terms of **both x and y** — and that is not a failure. It is the honest answer.

On a circle, dy/dx = −x/y. The slope depends on WHERE you are on the curve, and a circle has two points above most x-values with opposite slopes. Only a formula mentioning y can tell them apart.

illustration_description: A rectangle of width u and height v grows a little in each direction. The new area is a strip of width u times the growth in v, plus a strip of height v times the growth in u, plus a tiny corner that vanishes.
accompanying_text:
When a **product** of x and y appears, the product rule and the chain rule arrive together.

For xy: differentiate as a product — one term for each factor taking its turn — and the y-term picks up its dy/dx.

d/dx[xy] = 1·y + x·(dy/dx).

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text: Two facts, and everything else is the chain rule attached to them. **eˣ differentiates to itself.** **ln x differentiates to 1/x.** When there is an inside, multiply by its derivative — and for a log, that inner derivative goes on top.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
Differentiate 2ˣ from the definition and you get 2ˣ times a stubborn constant (about 0.693). Differentiate 3ˣ and you get 3ˣ times about 1.099.

Somewhere between 2 and 3 lies the base whose constant is exactly **1** — the base whose curve is its own derivative.

That number is **e ≈ 2.71828**, and (eˣ)′ = eˣ. That is what e is FOR.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
With the chain rule, the whole family follows:

**(e^u)′ = e^u · u′**
**(ln u)′ = u′/u**
**(aˣ)′ = aˣ · ln a** — the stubborn constant is ln a, and it is 1 exactly when a = e.

Every one of these is the base case times the derivative of the inside.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Learn the pair, and the sign. **sin → cos** (no minus). **cos → −sin** (minus). Then differentiate four times and check that you return to where you began — if you do not, a sign has gone astray.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
The sine wave's slope is the cosine wave. Not approximately — exactly.

**(sin x)′ = cos x** · **(cos x)′ = −sin x**

Differentiate four times and you are back where you started. The derivatives go round in a circle, which is precisely what you would expect of a function born on one.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
The rest of the library follows from the quotient and chain rules:

**(tan x)′ = sec² x** — always positive, which is why the tangent graph only ever climbs.

And with an inside: **(sin u)′ = cos u · u′**. The inner derivative is owed here exactly as everywhere else.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text: Two steps, in this order. **One:** find the a with f(a) = b — the point that reflects onto the one you care about. **Two:** take 1/f′(a). Almost every error here is evaluating f′ at b instead of at a.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text:
An inverse is a reflection across y = x. Reflecting a line **swaps its rise and its run** — so a tangent of slope 4 becomes a tangent of slope 1/4.

**(f⁻¹)′(b) = 1 / f′(a), where f(a) = b.**

You never need a formula for f⁻¹. You only need to know where the point came from.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text:
This is where the inverse trig derivatives come from — none of them need memorising as isolated facts.

**(arcsin x)′ = 1/√(1 − x²)** · **(arctan x)′ = 1/(1 + x²)**

Each is the reciprocal of the original's derivative, rewritten in terms of the new input. And each one is a clean algebraic expression: the trig has vanished entirely.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Differentiate once for velocity, twice for acceleration — and substitute only at the very end. The position tells you WHERE; only the velocity can tell you how fast; only the acceleration can tell you whether that is changing.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
One function, differentiated twice, answers three different questions.

**s(t)** — where the particle IS.
**v(t) = s′(t)** — how fast, and which way.
**a(t) = v′(t) = s″(t)** — whether that is changing.

The sign of v is direction. The sign of a is not — and confusing the two is the classic error.

illustration_description: A table of the four sign combinations of velocity and acceleration. When the two signs agree the particle speeds up; when they differ it slows down. The sign of the acceleration alone decides nothing.
accompanying_text:
Reading the motion is reading two signs:

**v > 0** — moving forward (right, up, positive direction).
**v < 0** — moving backward.
**a > 0** — the velocity is increasing.
**a < 0** — the velocity is decreasing.

Note that a > 0 does **not** mean 'speeding up'. A car reversing with positive acceleration is slowing down.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Write down the two signs and compare them. **Same** → the push is in the direction of travel → speeding up. **Different** → the push opposes the travel → slowing down. The sign of the acceleration on its own tells you nothing.

illustration_description: A table of the four sign combinations of velocity and acceleration. When the two signs agree the particle speeds up; when they differ it slows down. The sign of the acceleration alone decides nothing.
accompanying_text:
Here is the rule that settles it, and it is not the one people guess:

**Speeding up ⟺ v and a have the SAME sign.**
**Slowing down ⟺ they have OPPOSITE signs.**

A car reversing (v < 0) with a < 0 is speeding up — going backward, faster and faster. The sign of a alone tells you nothing about speed.

illustration_description: A table of the four sign combinations of velocity and acceleration. When the two signs agree the particle speeds up; when they differ it slows down. The sign of the acceleration alone decides nothing.
accompanying_text:
Speed is |v| — it has no direction and cannot be negative. Velocity has both.

So **speed increases exactly when v and a agree in sign**, and the sign of a on its own is never the answer. The word 'deceleration' is a trap for the same reason: it means a < 0, which slows a forward-mover and speeds up a reverser.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Find where the particle turns round (v changes sign). Measure each leg separately. Add the lengths as POSITIVE numbers for distance; subtract the ends for displacement.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
Two different questions, and they have different answers:

**Displacement** = s(b) − s(a). Where you ended up, relative to where you began.
**Total distance** = every mile you actually covered, forwards and backwards.

If the particle never reverses, they agree. The moment it turns round, they part company — and the turning points are exactly where v changes sign.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
So the recipe for total distance is:

**Find where v = 0 and changes sign.** Those are the turns.
**Compute |s| change on each leg.**
**Add them all as positive numbers.**

In integral language — which is the next course — displacement is ∫v dt and total distance is ∫|v| dt. The absolute value is doing exactly the work you just did by hand.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text: Every letter in the equation is secretly a function of time. So when you differentiate with respect to t, every letter pays a d/dt — just as every y paid a dy/dx in implicit differentiation. And substitute the numbers only at the very END.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
If two quantities are linked by an equation, then their **rates of change are linked too** — and the link is the chain rule, with **time as the hidden variable**.

Differentiate the equation with respect to **t**. Every variable is secretly a function of time, so every one of them picks up a dx/dt, exactly as implicit differentiation picked up a dy/dx.

It is the same move you already know, wearing a clock.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
So the procedure is four lines, always:

1. **Draw it.** Label what varies; do not put numbers on the picture.
2. **Find the relation** between the quantities (geometry, not calculus).
3. **Differentiate with respect to t** — every variable pays a d/dt.
4. **Substitute the instant's values** and solve for the rate you want.

Substituting at step 2 instead of step 4 is the mistake that ruins the problem.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text: Three steps. **Pythagoras** gives the relation. **d/dt** gives the rate equation, with every variable paying a d/dt. **Substitute** the instant's numbers last — and use the relation itself to find any missing side.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text:
A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall. The foot is dragged away at 2 ft/s. How fast is the top sliding **down**?

The relation is Pythagoras: **x² + y² = 100**, where x is the distance from the wall and y the height on it.

Both x and y change with time. The 100 does not.

illustration_description: A circle of radius five with the tangent drawn at the point three, four. The radius to that point has slope four over three, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, with slope minus three over four.
accompanying_text:
Solve for what you want, and read the **sign**.

dy/dt = −(x/y)·(dx/dt)

With x, y and dx/dt all positive, dy/dt comes out **negative** — the top is sliding DOWN. The minus sign is not an accident of algebra; it is the physics, reported honestly.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text: Before any calculus: what is changing, and what equation ties those things together? Right triangle → Pythagoras. Nested triangles → similar triangles. A solid filling up → its volume formula. Find the equation first; differentiate second.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
The calculus in a related-rates problem is three lines. The **hard part is finding the equation**, and nobody hands it to you.

Ask two questions:

**Which quantities are changing?** (label them)
**What ties them together?** (geometry, or a given formula)

And resist the urge to substitute numbers into the picture — a labelled diagram of *variables* is what you want.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
Two rules that will save you every time:

**Reduce to one variable BEFORE differentiating.** If your relation has two changing quantities and you only want one rate, use the geometry to eliminate the other first.

**Never put numbers on the diagram.** Label lengths x and h, not 6 and 8. The numbers belong in the last line, and nowhere else.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text: Start at a point you know exactly. Move along the TANGENT instead of the curve. The rise you get is f′(a) times how far you moved — and near a, that is almost the truth.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text:
Differentiable means **locally straight**. So near x = a, the curve is almost its own tangent line — and the tangent is something you can compute in your head.

**L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a)**

That is the linearisation. It is not an approximation of convenience; it is what having a derivative MEANS, cashed in.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Which side is the tangent on?

**f″ > 0 (concave up)** → the curve bends AWAY from the tangent, upward. The tangent lies below, so the estimate **under**-shoots.
**f″ < 0 (concave down)** → the tangent lies above, so the estimate **over**-shoots.

The second derivative does not just describe the bend — it tells you the DIRECTION of your error, before you make it.

accompanying_text: A small error in the input becomes an error in the output, and the derivative is the conversion factor: **dy = f′(x)·dx**. Big derivative, big amplification. That is all a differential says.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text:
Same idea, new notation — and the notation is what makes it useful.

**dy = f′(x) · dx**

Read it as: *a small change dx in the input produces a change of about f′(x)·dx in the output.* The derivative is the exchange rate between the two.

That is exactly how a small measurement error propagates into the answer.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
So there are two errors, and they answer different questions:

**Absolute error** — dV = 30 cm³. How far off, in real units.
**Relative error** — dV/V = 3%. How far off, as a proportion.

And the exponent rule: for V = sⁿ, the relative error in V is **n times** the relative error in s.

accompanying_text: Two questions before you trust a linearisation. **How far from a am I?** (the error grows like the square of that distance) and **how hard does the curve bend?** (the error is proportional to |f″|). Close in and gently curved: excellent. Far out and sharply curved: useless.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
The tangent is a good stand-in **near a**, and a bad one far from it. Two things ruin the approximation:

**Distance.** The error grows roughly like (x − a)².
**Curvature.** The bigger |f″|, the faster the curve peels away from its tangent.

So the error is governed by f″ — the same function that told you which SIDE the error was on.

accompanying_text:
There is one more way for it to fail, and it is fatal:

**If f is not differentiable at a, there is no tangent to use.**

No tangent, no linearisation. |x| at 0 has no linear approximation at all — you cannot approximate a corner with a line and expect it to work on both sides.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text: Substitute first. If you get 0/0 or ∞/∞ — and ONLY then — differentiate the top and the bottom **separately** and try again. If you get any ordinary number, you already have the limit and the rule must not be touched.

illustration_description: Two curves that both pass through zero at the same point. Magnified, each becomes its own tangent line, so the ratio of the two functions turns into the ratio of the two slopes.
accompanying_text:
In precalculus you met 0/0 and were told to **factor and cancel**. It worked. But nobody said WHY, and it only worked when something happened to cancel.

Here is why. Near x = a, both f and g are almost their tangent lines. So their RATIO is almost the ratio of the tangents — and if both vanish at a, that ratio is exactly **f′(a)/g′(a)**.

**L'Hôpital's rule:** if f/g gives 0/0, then lim f/g = lim f′/g′.

illustration_description: Two curves that both pass through zero at the same point. Magnified, each becomes its own tangent line, so the ratio of the two functions turns into the ratio of the two slopes.
accompanying_text:
Two warnings, and both are earned:

**Check the form FIRST.** L'Hôpital applies only to 0/0 or ∞/∞. Apply it to anything else and it produces confident nonsense.

**It is not the quotient rule.** You differentiate the top and the bottom **separately** — no minus sign, no square. Confusing the two is the commonest slip in this chapter.

accompanying_text: L'Hôpital needs a fraction. If you have a product, push one factor downstairs as its reciprocal. If you have a difference, put it over a common denominator. Manufacture the quotient FIRST, then check the form.

illustration_description: Two curves that both pass through zero at the same point. Magnified, each becomes its own tangent line, so the ratio of the two functions turns into the ratio of the two slopes.
accompanying_text:
L'Hôpital speaks only two languages: **0/0** and **∞/∞**.

But other forms are indeterminate too — 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞ — and every one of them can be **rewritten as a quotient**, and then handed over.

The skill is not the rule. It is the rewriting.

illustration_description: Two curves that both pass through zero at the same point. Magnified, each becomes its own tangent line, so the ratio of the two functions turns into the ratio of the two slopes.
accompanying_text:
For **∞ − ∞**, put it over a common denominator. For **1^∞**, take logarithms — the log turns an exponent into a product, and the product into a quotient.

In every case the move is the same: **manufacture a quotient**, check the form, then differentiate.

A narrow tool with a wide reach — and the reach is entirely in the rewriting.

accompanying_text: Read the right-hand side as a command: *at this point, head off with THIS slope.* Draw the command as a little segment at every point, and a solution is any curve that follows the segments wherever it goes.

illustration_description: A field of small segments, each tilted at the slope the differential equation demands there. Three solution curves thread through the field, one for each starting value, and all of them level off at the same ceiling.
accompanying_text:
A differential equation does not tell you what y IS. It tells you, at every point, **which way to go**.

dy/dx = f(x, y) is an instruction: *at this point, leave with this slope.*

Draw a tiny segment at every point with the prescribed slope and you have a **slope field** — a set of instructions. A solution is any curve that obeys them everywhere.

illustration_description: A field of small segments, each tilted at the slope the differential equation demands there. Three solution curves thread through the field, one for each starting value, and all of them level off at the same ceiling.
accompanying_text:
So this is the picture the + C has been waiting for.

**The differential equation gives the FAMILY.** (the field)
**The initial condition selects ONE.** (the starting point)

And the field exists even when no formula does. Most differential equations cannot be solved with symbols at all — but their slope fields can always be drawn, and their curves always exist.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text: Set the whole right-hand side to zero and solve for y. Every y you find is a horizontal line the solution can never leave — because the instruction there says *do not move*.

illustration_description: A field of small segments, each tilted at the slope the differential equation demands there. Three solution curves thread through the field, one for each starting value, and all of them level off at the same ceiling.
accompanying_text:
Some fields have a line along which **every segment is flat**.

Start there and the instruction says: *do not move.* So the solution is a horizontal line — forever. That is an **equilibrium solution**, and it is found by setting the whole right-hand side to zero:

**dy/dx = 0 ⟹ solve f(x, y) = 0 for y.**

It is not a curve that happens to be flat. It is the one curve the instructions forbid from going anywhere.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
And the field answers questions the formula would make you work for.

**What happens in the long run?** Follow the segments. Every solution starting above zero ends up at the ceiling.

**Where does it grow fastest?** Where the segments are steepest — for this logistic equation, at exactly HALF the ceiling, y = 2.

All of that, before a single line of algebra.

accompanying_text: Every y (including the dy) to the left. Every x (including the dx) to the right. Integrate both sides, put ONE + C on the right, and only then solve for y.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
Some differential equations can be **untangled**: get every y on one side, every x on the other, and integrate both.

dy/dx = 2xy → **(1/y) dy = 2x dx** → ∫(1/y) dy = ∫2x dx → ln|y| = x² + C

The dy and the dx are being treated like quantities you can move about — and the chain rule is what makes that legal. Substitution earned it for you in C4.

accompanying_text:
Two habits worth forming:

**Apply the initial condition EARLY.** Solve for the constant as soon as you have an equation containing it, rather than dragging C through three more lines of algebra.

**Watch for the equilibrium you divided away.** Dividing by y assumed y ≠ 0 — and y = 0 is a perfectly good solution that the algebra has just quietly discarded. The slope field would never have lost it.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text: Read the sentence, then write the equation. *'Grows in proportion to how much there is'* is dy/dt = ky. Separate it, integrate it, and out comes y = y₀e^(kt) — every time.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
In Algebra 1 you were HANDED exponential growth as a fact: some things grow like bˣ, and that is that.

Here is where it comes from.

**dy/dt = ky** — *the rate of growth is proportional to how much you already have.*

Separate and integrate: (1/y)dy = k dt → ln|y| = kt + C → **y = y₀e^(kt)**.

Exponential growth is not a species of function. It is what dy/dt = ky *forces*.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
Make k **negative** and the same equation becomes decay:

**dy/dt = −ky** → y = y₀e^(−kt)

Radioactive atoms, cooling coffee, drugs leaving the bloodstream — all obey *the rate of loss is proportional to what is left*. And the **half-life** is the time to fall by half:

y₀/2 = y₀e^(−kT) → **T = ln2 / k**

One equation, two behaviours, and the sign of k decides which.

accompanying_text: Read the bracket. **(1 − P/K)** is nearly 1 when P is small (so growth is nearly exponential) and nearly 0 when P nears K (so growth shuts down). The bracket is the ceiling, written as algebra.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Exponential growth is a lie told about the short term. Nothing grows forever — food runs out, space runs out.

So make k **stop being constant**. Let it shrink to zero as the population approaches a ceiling K:

**dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K)**

When P is small the bracket is nearly 1 and growth is nearly exponential. When P nears K the bracket goes to zero and growth stops. **The logistic equation is what happens when k stops being constant.**

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So the logistic curve has a shape you can now read entirely off the equation:

**Below K/2** — growing, and growing FASTER. (concave up)
**At K/2** — the inflection: fastest growth, and the moment it starts easing.
**Above K/2** — still growing, but slowing. (concave down)
**At K** — stopped.

An S-curve, and every feature of it is forced by kP(1 − P/K).

accompanying_text:
Most differential equations cannot be solved with symbols. At all. Ever.

But the **field** always exists — so **walk it**.

Stand at the starting point. Read the instruction (the slope). Take one small step in that direction. Read the new instruction. Step again.

**yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h·f(xₙ, yₙ)**

That is Euler's method, and it is nothing but the tangent-line approximation from C2, used over and over.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
Euler's answer is **wrong**, and it is wrong in a predictable direction.

Each step follows the tangent, and a tangent to a **concave-up** curve lies BELOW it — so Euler **undershoots**. For a concave-down curve, it overshoots.

That is the same f″ argument from C2's linearisation lesson, applied once per step. And halving h roughly halves the total error.
