Two big ones: **through any two distinct points there is exactly one line**, and **two distinct lines intersect in at most one point**. "Exactly one" is doing real work: at least one (you can always draw it) and at most one (no second line fits).

illustration_description: A segment DE, a ray FG, an angle HJK with an arc at J, and a circle centered at O with one radius drawn A segment DE, a ray FG, an angle HJK with an arc at J, and a circle centered at O with one radius drawn
accompanying_text: Now build. A **segment AB** is the part of line AB between A and B, endpoints included. A **ray AB** starts at A and runs forever through B — the ENDPOINT is written first. An **angle** is two rays sharing an endpoint (the **vertex**). A **circle** is the set of ALL points at one fixed distance (the radius) from one fixed point (the center).

illustration_description: Angle naming puts the vertex letter in the middle: angle A B C has its vertex at B.
accompanying_text: Angle naming: **the vertex letter goes in the middle**. The angle with vertex Y made by rays YX and YZ is ∠XYZ or ∠ZYX — never ∠YXZ. When only one angle sits at a vertex, the single letter ∠Y is enough; when several share the vertex, three letters keep them apart.

illustration_description: Ray order is strict: ray F G starts at F, while ray G F starts at G and points the opposite way.
accompanying_text: Ray order is strict: **ray FG starts at F**; ray GF starts at G — different objects, opposite tails. But two ray names CAN mean the same ray: if A, B, C sit on a line in that order, ray AB and ray AC both start at A and run the same way — same endpoint, same direction, same ray.

illustration_description: Three hats, three objects: a two-way arrow means the line, a bar means the segment, and a one-way arrow means the ray.
accompanying_text: Three hats, three objects: a two-way arrow over AB means the **line**, a one-way arrow the **ray**, a plain bar the **segment**. NO hat — plain AB — means a **number**: the segment's length. So segments are **congruent** (≅, same size and shape) while lengths are **equal** (=, same number). Write segment AB ≅ segment CD, but AB = CD.

illustration_description: The same discipline covers angles: angle A is a figure, while m angle A is a number, its measure.
accompanying_text: The same discipline covers angles: **∠A is a figure; m∠A is a number** (its measure in degrees). ∠A ≅ ∠B and m∠A = m∠B say the same thing in two registers — and swapping their symbols is the classic notation error graders hunt for.

illustration_description: Where things meet: two distinct lines intersect in at most one point.
accompanying_text: Where things meet: two distinct lines intersect in at most one **point**; a line meets a plane it doesn't lie in at exactly one point; two distinct planes intersect in a **line** (think of two walls meeting along their shared edge). The intersection is always a lower-rung object.

illustration_description: Top: points A, B, C on a segment with lengths AB and BC bracketed and summing to AC. Bottom: angle PQS split by interior ray QR into two smaller angles that add Top: points A, B, C on a segment with lengths AB and BC bracketed and summing to AC. Bottom: angle PQS split by interior ray QR into two smaller angles that add
accompanying_text: The **Ruler Postulate** lets every point on a line wear a number (its coordinate), and the distance between two points is the positive difference of their coordinates. From it comes the **Segment Addition Postulate**: if B is between A and C, then **AB + BC = AC** — the two pieces tile the whole with no gap and no overlap.

illustration_description: The midpoint M of segment A B splits it into two congruent halves.
accompanying_text: The **midpoint** M of segment AB is the point that splits it into two congruent halves: AM ≅ MB. On a number line the midpoint's coordinate is the **average** of the endpoints' coordinates — halfway between is exactly the mean.

illustration_description: Vocabulary upgrade: anything that passes through a segment's midpoint bisects it.
accompanying_text: Vocabulary upgrade: anything that passes through a segment's midpoint — a line, ray, or segment — is a **segment bisector**. Bisecting talk runs both directions: from the whole, each half is half; from one half, the whole is DOUBLE.

illustration_description: Top: points A, B, C on a segment with lengths AB and BC bracketed and summing to AC. Bottom: angle PQS split by interior ray QR into two smaller angles that add Top: points A, B, C on a segment with lengths AB and BC bracketed and summing to AC. Bottom: angle PQS split by interior ray QR into two smaller angles that add
accompanying_text: Angles copy the ruler's trick. The **Protractor Postulate** assigns each ray from a vertex a number 0–180, and an angle's measure is the positive difference of its rays' numbers. The **Angle Addition Postulate** follows: if R is in the interior of ∠PQS, then **m∠PQR + m∠RQS = m∠PQS**.

illustration_description: An angle bisector is a ray that splits an angle into two congruent angles.
accompanying_text: An **angle bisector** is a ray that splits an angle into two **congruent** pieces. "QR bisects ∠PQS" packs an equation: m∠PQR = m∠RQS, each exactly half the whole. Like midpoints, it runs both ways — halve the whole, or double a half.

illustration_description: Angle addition solves for missing pieces: inside a known whole angle, the parts sum to the whole.
accompanying_text: Angle addition solves for missing pieces too. Inside a known whole — say a right angle, 90° — one known piece pins down the other: **missing piece = whole − known piece**. The only trap is using the wrong whole.

illustration_description: B is between A and C still means A B plus B C equals A C, now with the pieces wearing algebra.
accompanying_text: Now the pieces wear algebra. "B is between A and C" is still AB + BC = AC — even when AB = 2x + 3 and BC = 3x − 7. **Translate the geometry sentence into an equation first**, then solve. The postulate chooses the equation; the algebra does the rest.

illustration_description: Answer the question asked: solving for x is usually only the halfway point, then substitute back to get the length.
accompanying_text: **Answer the question asked.** Solving for x is usually the halfway point — the question may want a LENGTH. Finish by substituting x back into the right expression, and sanity-check that the pieces really total the whole.

illustration_description: Bisectors write a different equation: Q R bisects angle P Q S means the two half-angles are equal.
accompanying_text: Bisectors write a DIFFERENT equation. "QR bisects ∠PQS" means the two pieces are **equal**: m∠PQR = m∠RQS. No whole is needed — the geometry word tells you whether to ADD the pieces (between/interior) or EQUATE them (bisects/midpoint).

illustration_description: Rule (x, y) maps to (x plus 5, y plus 2): triangle PQR slides right 5 and up 2 to its image P prime Q prime R prime, with dashed arrows joining each vertex to its image Rule (x, y) maps to (x plus 5, y plus 2): triangle PQR slides right 5 and up 2 to its image P prime Q prime R prime, with dashed arrows joining each vertex to its image
accompanying_text: A **transformation is a function on points**: feed in a point (the **preimage**), get out a point (the **image**, marked with a prime: P → P′). A **translation** slides every point the same amount, written as a coordinate rule: **(x, y) → (x + 5, y + 2)** means "add 5 to every x, add 2 to every y." One rule, applied to every point at once.

illustration_description: Finding the rule runs the machine backward: subtract the preimage from the image to get the shift.
accompanying_text: **Finding the rule** runs the machine backward: subtract preimage coordinates from image coordinates. A(3, 5) → A′(8, 2) gives shifts 8 − 3 = +5 and 2 − 5 = −3, so the rule is (x, y) → (x + 5, y − 3). Always image MINUS preimage — order matters.

illustration_description: Translations chain: doing plus two, minus five and then minus seven, plus one adds up to a single combined shift.
accompanying_text: Translations **chain**. Doing (x + 2, y − 5) and then (x − 7, y + 1) is one combined translation: the shifts just add, slot by slot: 2 + (−7) = −5 and −5 + 1 = −4, net rule (x − 5, y − 4). Two slides make a slide.

illustration_description: Reflections are functions too, using sign flips instead of shifts: across the x-axis, y changes sign.
accompanying_text: Reflections are functions too — with sign flips instead of shifts. Over the **x-axis**: (x, y) → (x, −y) (the y flips). Over the **y-axis**: (x, y) → (−x, y) (the x flips). Memory hook: reflecting over an axis flips the OTHER coordinate — the one measuring your distance from that axis.

illustration_description: Vertical mirror line m; point P at left and its image P prime at right; the segment P P prime crosses m at a right angle and is cut into two equal halves Vertical mirror line m; point P at left and its image P prime at right; the segment P P prime crosses m at a right angle and is cut into two equal halves
accompanying_text: What makes a mirror line a mirror? **The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of every segment joining a point to its image.** Perpendicular: PP′ crosses the line at 90°. Bisector: P and P′ sit at EQUAL distances from it. That single property pins down where every image lands.

illustration_description: One more mirror earns a rule: reflecting across the diagonal line y equals x swaps the coordinates.
accompanying_text: One more mirror earns a rule: the diagonal line **y = x**. Reflecting over it **swaps the coordinates**: (x, y) → (y, x). No signs change — first and second coordinates simply trade places.

illustration_description: Rotations about the origin get coordinate rules too: a counterclockwise quarter turn sends x, y to negative y, x.
accompanying_text: Rotations about the origin get coordinate rules too. Counterclockwise: **90°: (x, y) → (−y, x)** · **180°: (x, y) → (−x, −y)** · **270°: (x, y) → (y, −x)**. The 180° rule is the easiest — both signs flip. The quarter turns swap the coordinates AND flip exactly one sign.

illustration_description: Direction convention: positive rotations run counterclockwise.
accompanying_text: **Direction convention: positive rotations run counterclockwise.** A 270° counterclockwise turn lands exactly where a 90° CLOCKWISE turn does — same ending, two descriptions. When a problem says only "rotate 90°," read it as counterclockwise unless told otherwise.

illustration_description: Rotations compose by adding angles: a ninety-degree turn followed by another gives a one-hundred-eighty-degree turn.
accompanying_text: Rotations **compose by adding angles**: a 90° turn followed by another 90° turn is one 180° turn. The rules confirm it — push a point through (−y, x) twice and both coordinates come out negated, exactly the 180° rule. Function composition, wearing degrees.

illustration_description: A sky triangle is first translated to a faint leaf ghost position, then reflected over a dashed vertical line to its final berry image; arrows numbered 1 and 2 show the order A sky triangle is first translated to a faint leaf ghost position, then reflected over a dashed vertical line to its final berry image; arrows numbered 1 and 2 show the order
accompanying_text: Functions chain — so transformations do too. A **composition** applies one motion, then feeds its OUTPUT into the next: translate, THEN reflect. Because each rigid motion preserves distances and angles, any chain of them is still one rigid motion. Bookkeeping tip: track ONE point at a time through the chain.

illustration_description: Order can matter: reflect-then-translate and translate-then-reflect need not land in the same place.
accompanying_text: **Order can matter.** Reflect-then-translate and translate-then-reflect are DIFFERENT functions in general — like putting on socks and shoes. Some pairs do commute (two translations always do), but never assume it: check by pushing a test point through both orders.

illustration_description: One composition earns its own name: a glide reflection is a translation followed by a reflection along the same line.
accompanying_text: One composition earns its own name: a **glide reflection** — a translation followed by a reflection over a line PARALLEL to the slide (footprints in snow: step forward, mirror to the other foot). Together with translations, rotations, and reflections, that completes the full cast of rigid motions.

illustration_description: A shape has line symmetry when a mirror line maps the figure onto itself.
accompanying_text: Point a reflection back at its own figure. A shape has **line symmetry** when some reflection maps the shape **exactly onto itself** — the mirror line is its **line of symmetry**. The physical test: fold along the line; the two halves must match perfectly, edge for edge.

illustration_description: A regular pentagon with all five lines of symmetry drawn dashed from each vertex to the opposite side's midpoint, plus a badge reading rotation order 5, 72 degrees per turn A regular pentagon with all five lines of symmetry drawn dashed from each vertex to the opposite side's midpoint, plus a badge reading rotation order 5, 72 degrees per turn
accompanying_text: Counting lines is a search over mirror candidates: midlines, diagonals, vertex-to-opposite-edge folds. **Regular polygons are maximal**: a regular n-gon has exactly **n** lines of symmetry (through each vertex for odd n; alternating vertex-lines and edge-midpoint-lines for even n).

illustration_description: Two ends of the spectrum: a scalene triangle has zero lines of symmetry, while a regular figure has many.
accompanying_text: Two ends of the spectrum: a scalene triangle has **zero** lines (no fold ever matches unequal sides), while the extreme case is the circle — EVERY diameter is a mirror. Symmetry count is a fingerprint: it separates shapes that otherwise look alike.

illustration_description: A figure has rotational symmetry when some turn less than a full circle maps it onto itself.
accompanying_text: The turning version: a figure has **rotational symmetry** when some rotation of LESS than a full turn maps it onto itself. Its **order** is how many matching positions fit in one full turn, and the smallest matching angle is **360° ÷ order**. (Every figure trivially matches after 360° — that one doesn't count.)

illustration_description: Order and angle are two dials on one machine: the order times the smallest turn angle equals three hundred sixty degrees.
accompanying_text: Order and angle are two dials on one machine: **order × smallest angle = 360°**. Read either from the other. Order 2 means a half-turn match (180°) — the letters S, N, and Z have exactly that: turn them upside down and they read the same.

illustration_description: The two symmetry kinds are independent: a shape can have line symmetry, rotational symmetry, both, or neither.
accompanying_text: The two symmetry kinds are **independent**. A shape can have both (square), neither (scalene triangle), mirrors only (isosceles trapezoid) — or the sneaky fourth cell: **rotation only**. The plain parallelogram lives there: a perfect half-turn match, yet every candidate fold fails.

illustration_description: Sky triangle ABC and berry triangle DEF, marked with matching ticks and angle arcs; a curved arrow labeled rigid motion carries one onto the other Sky triangle ABC and berry triangle DEF, marked with matching ticks and angle arcs; a curved arrow labeled rigid motion carries one onto the other
accompanying_text: Here is the payoff of four chapters: **two figures are congruent exactly when some rigid motion (or chain of them) maps one precisely onto the other**. Not "they look alike" — a checkable claim: name a translation, rotation, reflection, or composition that carries every point of one onto the other.

illustration_description: Rigid motions preserve distance and angle, so the image is congruent to the preimage.
accompanying_text: Why THIS definition works: rigid motions **preserve distance and angle measure**. So the instant a motion maps figure 1 onto figure 2, every side and every angle automatically matches — congruence of all the parts comes free, no measuring required.

illustration_description: The club rules exclude dilations for a reason: a dilation with scale factor not one changes distances, so it is not rigid.
accompanying_text: The club rules exclude dilations for a reason: a dilation with scale factor k multiplies EVERY distance by k. The image keeps the shape but not the size — that's **similarity**, a different (weaker) relationship. One stretched distance is enough to sink a congruence claim.

illustration_description: Detective work: given both figures' coordinates, identify the motion that carried one onto the other.
accompanying_text: Detective work: given both figures' coordinates, identify the motion. **Compare a preimage point with its image and read the pattern**: both coordinates shifted by constants → translation. Signs flipped or coordinates swapped → reflection or rotation. Then CONFIRM the candidate on every remaining point — one point can lie, three can't.

illustration_description: Sign patterns are fingerprints: only x flipping sign is a reflection over the y-axis, only y flipping is over the x-axis.
accompanying_text: **Sign patterns are fingerprints.** Only x flips: reflection over the y-axis. Only y flips: reflection over the x-axis. BOTH flip: 180° rotation. Coordinates swap: the y = x mirror. Read the pattern off one pair, then verify it on the rest.

illustration_description: Sometimes the detective's answer is that no rigid motion exists, when the figures are not congruent.
accompanying_text: Sometimes the detective's answer is **no motion exists**. Rigid motions preserve distance, so if ANY pair of matched points sits at a different distance than its partners, no slide, turn, flip, or chain can ever connect the figures. Measure first; it can end the case immediately.

illustration_description: A congruence statement is a cipher: in triangle A B C congruent to triangle D E F, the letter order pairs the corresponding vertices.
accompanying_text: A congruence statement is a **cipher**. In ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF the letter ORDER carries the correspondence: A↔D, B↔E, C↔F — first with first, second with second, third with third. From it, matched parts read off by POSITION: AB ≅ DE, BC ≅ EF, ∠C ≅ ∠F. Never trust the picture; trust the order.

illustration_description: The cipher also moves numbers: since corresponding parts are congruent, matching sides and angles are equal.
accompanying_text: The cipher also moves **numbers**. Since corresponding parts of congruent figures are congruent, a measurement known on one triangle teleports to its positional partner on the other — and ONLY to its partner. The commonest slip: grabbing a measurement from the matching-looking side instead of the matching-POSITION side.

illustration_description: Statements can be rewritten, but every rewrite must respect the same vertex correspondence.
accompanying_text: Statements can be **rewritten** — but every rewrite must respect the same point pairing. If ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF, then listing the first triangle as ΔBCA forces the second into ΔEFD: each letter drags its partner to the same new position. Same fact, new outfit.

illustration_description: A scale drawing. On the left, a small rectangle labeled 3 centimeters wide represents a drawing. An arrow labeled scale, 1 centimeter equals 4 meters, points to a much larger rectangle on the right labeled 12 meters wide — the real garden.
accompanying_text: A **scale drawing** shows a real object shrunk (or enlarged) so it fits on paper. The **scale** says what each drawing unit stands for: a scale of **1 cm = 4 m** means every centimeter on paper is 4 real meters.

illustration_description: A scale as a unit rate. A drawing length of 3 centimeters is multiplied by the scale amount 4 to give the real length 12 meters.
accompanying_text: Drawing-to-real is a **multiplication**: real length = drawing length × the scale amount. The scale works like a unit rate — meters per centimeter — exactly the rate thinking from proportional relationships.

illustration_description: A scale drawing. On the left, a small rectangle labeled 3 centimeters wide represents a drawing. An arrow labeled scale, 1 centimeter equals 4 meters, points to a much larger rectangle on the right labeled 12 meters wide — the real garden.
accompanying_text: Going the other way — real length to drawing length — is a **division**. At 1 cm = 4 m, a 20 m real wall needs 20 ÷ 4 = **5 cm** on paper. Divide by the scale amount.

illustration_description: One scale, two directions. Going from drawing to real you multiply by 4; going from real back to drawing you divide by 4.
accompanying_text: One scale, two directions: **drawing → real multiplies**, **real → drawing divides**. Ask which way you're going before touching the numbers — the most common error is multiplying both ways.

illustration_description: A scale drawing. On the left, a small rectangle labeled 3 centimeters wide represents a drawing. An arrow labeled scale, 1 centimeter equals 4 meters, points to a much larger rectangle on the right labeled 12 meters wide — the real garden.
accompanying_text: Lengths scale by the scale factor — but **area scales by its square**. At 1 cm = 4 m, each 1 cm² of drawing stands for 4 × 4 = **16 m²** of real area, because both the width AND the height stretch by 4.

illustration_description: Area scaling. A 2 by 3 centimeter drawing at 1 centimeter equals 4 meters becomes 8 by 12 meters, so the real area is 96 square meters.
accompanying_text: The safest method for a scaled rectangle: convert each **side** to real units first, then multiply. A 2 cm × 3 cm drawing at 1 cm = 4 m becomes 8 m × 12 m, so the real area is 96 m².

illustration_description: A circle with center marked. A radius is drawn from the center to the edge, and a diameter crosses the whole circle through the center — twice the radius. The distance around the circle is the circumference, 2 pi r, and the space inside is the area, pi r squared.
accompanying_text: A circle has two key lengths. The **radius** r runs from the center to the edge; the **diameter** d crosses the whole circle through the center. The diameter is always **twice** the radius: d = 2r.

illustration_description: Pi is the circle's built-in ratio. The distance around any circle is pi, about 3.14, times its diameter — the ratio never changes.
accompanying_text: The number **π** (about 3.14) is the circle's built-in ratio: every circle's distance around is π times its diameter. Big or small, that ratio never changes — that's what makes π special.

illustration_description: A circle with center marked. A radius is drawn from the center to the edge, and a diameter crosses the whole circle through the center — twice the radius. The distance around the circle is the circumference, 2 pi r, and the space inside is the area, pi r squared.
accompanying_text: The **circumference** is the distance around a circle: **C = πd**, or equally **C = 2πr** (since d = 2r). We leave answers as a number times π (exact): a circle with radius 3 has C = 2 × 3 × π = **6π**.

illustration_description: Circumference from a diameter. With diameter 10, the distance around is C equals pi times d, which is 10 pi.
accompanying_text: With a **diameter**, skip the doubling: C = πd directly. Diameter 10 gives C = 10π. Given a radius, double it first; given a diameter, use it as-is. The two formulas are the same fact in two outfits.

illustration_description: A circle with center marked. A radius is drawn from the center to the edge, and a diameter crosses the whole circle through the center — twice the radius. The distance around the circle is the circumference, 2 pi r, and the space inside is the area, pi r squared.
accompanying_text: A circle's **area** — the space inside — is **A = πr²**: square the radius, then multiply by π. Radius 3 gives A = π × 3² = **9π**. This is the very πr² that lives inside the cylinder volume formula.

illustration_description: Circumference doubles but area squares. For radius 10, C equals 2 pi r is 20 pi, while A equals pi r squared is 100 pi — area grows much faster.
accompanying_text: Circumference and area are the classic mix-up: **C = 2πr doubles**, **A = πr² squares**. A quick sense-check: area answers grow much faster — radius 10 gives C = 20π but A = 100π.

illustration_description: Two angle-pair diagrams. On the left, two angles fit together into a square corner: complementary angles adding to 90 degrees. On the right, two lines cross, making two pairs of equal vertical angles across from each other.
accompanying_text: Two angles that fit together into a **square corner** are **complementary**: they add to **90°**. Two angles that fit along a **straight line** are **supplementary**: they add to **180°**.

illustration_description: Complementary makes a corner of 90 degrees; supplementary makes a straight line of 180 degrees.
accompanying_text: A memory hook: **C**omplementary makes a **C**orner (90°); **S**upplementary makes a **S**traight line (180°). To find a missing partner, subtract the known angle from the pair's total.

illustration_description: Two angle-pair diagrams. On the left, two angles fit together into a square corner: complementary angles adding to 90 degrees. On the right, two lines cross, making two pairs of equal vertical angles across from each other.
accompanying_text: When two lines cross, they make four angles. Angles **across** from each other are **vertical angles** — always **equal**. Angles **next to** each other are **adjacent** — they share a side and add to 180° along each line.

illustration_description: Two lines cross. One angle is 75 degrees, the angle across is also 75 degrees, and the two adjacent angles are each 105 degrees.
accompanying_text: At a crossing, you get everything from one angle. If one angle is 75°: across is 75° (vertical, equal); next to it is 180 − 75 = 105° (adjacent on a line); across from that is 105° again.

illustration_description: Two angle-pair diagrams. On the left, two angles fit together into a square corner: complementary angles adding to 90 degrees. On the right, two lines cross, making two pairs of equal vertical angles across from each other.
accompanying_text: Angle facts become **equations**. If x and 2x fit a square corner, then x + 2x = 90, so 3x = 90 and **x = 30**. Write the fact as an equation, combine the x's, divide.

illustration_description: Angles x and 3x sit on a straight line, so x plus 3x equals 180. Then 4x equals 180 and x equals 45, making the angles 45 and 135 degrees.
accompanying_text: The same recipe works on a straight line. If x and 3x are supplementary: x + 3x = 180, so 4x = 180 and x = 45. The only question is which total to use — 90° for corners, 180° for lines.

illustration_description: Two triangles built from the same three side lengths, four, five and six, drawn in different positions but identical in shape and size.
accompanying_text:
Hand three people the same three side lengths — 4, 5 and 6 — and tell them to build a triangle. They will all build the **same** triangle.

It may be flipped or turned, but no one can produce a different shape. Three sides leave nothing to choose, which is what mathematicians mean when they say the conditions **determine a unique triangle**.

illustration_description: Sides of length 2 and 3 cannot reach over a floor of length 6: two plus three is five, which is less than six, so the sides fall flat and never meet.
accompanying_text:
The failure case has a rule of its own. Two sides can only meet if together they are **longer** than the third.

2 and 3 cannot bridge a gap of 6: laid end to end they reach 5 and stop short. That is the triangle inequality, and it is why some lists of three lengths describe no triangle at all.

illustration_description: One fixed angle and two given sides produce two different triangles, because the swinging side can meet the base at either of two points.
accompanying_text:
Give two sides and an angle that is **not** between them, and the triangle stops being unique.

The second side swings like a door and can reach the base at two different points. Both landings satisfy every given, so the conditions describe *two* different triangles — this is the ambiguous case, SSA.

illustration_description: Three triangles with the same three angles but different sizes, showing that angles alone fix the shape but not the size, so infinitely many triangles fit.
accompanying_text:
Three angles that sum to 180° always describe a real shape — but never a single triangle.

With no length anywhere in the conditions there is nothing to set the scale, so the same shape can be drawn at every size. That is **infinitely many**, and it is a different kind of non-uniqueness from SSA's exactly two.

illustration_description: Two arcs of equal radius swung from each end of a segment cross above and below it; the line through those crossings is the perpendicular bisector.
accompanying_text:
A compass does one thing: it holds a distance. That single ability is enough to build every construction in this lesson.

Swing equal arcs from each end of a segment and they cross above and below it. Every crossing sits the same distance from both ends, so the line through them is the **perpendicular bisector** — proved, not measured.

illustration_description: Copying an angle with compass arcs: the same compass opening is swung on the original and on the new ray, so the crossing points sit at equal distances and the copied angle matches.
accompanying_text:
The same trick copies an **angle** without ever measuring it.

Swing one arc across the original angle and an identical arc on the new ray. Then step off the distance between the two crossing points. Because every distance was carried by the compass, the copied angle is exactly equal — no protractor, no rounding.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: Not every three lengths can form a triangle. The **triangle inequality** decides: the two **shorter** sides together must **beat** the longest side. Sides 3, 4, 5 work because 3 + 4 > 5. Sides 2, 3, 6 fail because 2 + 3 < 6.

illustration_description: Sides of length 2 and 3 cannot reach over a floor of length 6: two plus three is five, which is less than six, so the sides fall flat and never meet.
accompanying_text: Picture why: the longest side is the floor, and the two shorter sides must reach over it to meet. If they're too short to arch over — like 2 and 3 across a floor of 6 — the sides fall flat and never touch.

illustration_description: Cross-sections of a cylinder. On the left, a cylinder is sliced straight across, parallel to its base, and the cut face is a circle. On the right, the same cylinder is sliced straight down through its center, and the cut face is a rectangle.
accompanying_text: Slice a 3D solid with a flat cut and the cut face is a 2D shape — a **cross-section**. A cylinder cut **across** (parallel to its base) shows a **circle**; cut straight **down** through the center, it shows a **rectangle**.

illustration_description: Slicing a square pyramid. A cut parallel to the base makes a smaller square; a cut straight down through the tip makes a triangle.
accompanying_text: The same solid gives different sections depending on the cut. A rectangular box cut parallel to any face shows that face's rectangle. A square pyramid cut parallel to its base shows a smaller **square**; cut down through its tip, a **triangle**.

illustration_description: A circle with center marked. A radius is drawn from the center to the edge, and a diameter crosses the whole circle through the center — twice the radius. The distance around the circle is the circumference, 2 pi r, and the space inside is the area, pi r squared.
accompanying_text: One chapter left to close Grade 7 geometry: putting it all together. Scale drawings convert, circles measure, angle facts become equations, side lengths decide triangles, and cuts reveal cross-sections.

illustration_description: A circular pond of radius 6 meters. The fence around it is circumference C equals 2 pi times 6, which is 12 pi meters; the water is area A equals pi times 6 squared, which is 36 pi square meters.
accompanying_text: Skills chain together. That 6 m radius feeds straight into the circle formulas: circumference C = 2π × 6 = 12π meters of fence, area A = π × 6² = 36π square meters of water.

illustration_description: Cut a box along its edges and lay it flat: surface area is the total of the six flat faces of the net.
accompanying_text: Surface area is a flat question wearing a 3-D costume. Cut a box along its edges and lay it out: what you get is a NET, a flat arrangement of the same faces. Adding up the net's areas is adding up the solid's surface, because they are the same cardboard either way.

illustration_description: The formula two times l w plus l h plus w h is bookkeeping: each product is one face and each two accounts for that face's opposite twin.
accompanying_text: So the formula is bookkeeping, not magic: 2(lw + lh + wh). Each product is one face; each 2 is that face's opposite twin. If you ever forget it, unfold the box in your head and add the rectangles — the formula will reassemble itself.

illustration_description: The routine: find the three distinct face areas, add them, then double the total.
accompanying_text: With the net understood, surface area becomes a routine you can trust: find the three distinct face areas, add them, double. The only real hazard is mixing it up with volume — they use the same three numbers and answer completely different questions.

illustration_description: Surface area lands in square units because every face is a length times a length; volume lands in cubic units because it is length times length times length.
accompanying_text: Units settle the question when words do not. Surface area lands in square units because every face is a length times a length. Volume lands in cubic units because it multiplies three lengths. If your answer's units do not match the question's, the wrong measure was computed.

illustration_description: A triangular prism has two matching triangular ends and three rectangular sides, so the ends still pair up but the sides usually do not.
accompanying_text: A triangular prism has two triangular ENDS and three rectangular SIDES. The ends match each other, so they still come as a pair; the sides usually do not match at all. Surface area is the same idea as before — add every face — but the bookkeeping has to be done honestly rather than by doubling three products.

illustration_description: The shortcut worth keeping: lateral surface equals the perimeter of the end times the length, so a three four five triangle gives a perimeter of twelve.
accompanying_text: The shortcut worth keeping is lateral surface = perimeter of the end × length. Here the perimeter is 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 and the length is 10, giving 120 in one step. Add the two ends and the prism is finished. The same rule works for ANY prism, whatever polygon its end happens to be.

illustration_description: Volume of a right prism is one idea repeated: cover the base once, then stack that layer as many times as the height.
accompanying_text: Volume of a right prism is one idea repeated: cover the base once, then stack that layer as many times as the height allows. Base area times height. For a box the base is a rectangle, but the rule never mentions rectangles — it works for a triangular base, a hexagonal base, any base at all.

illustration_description: Because the rule is base area times height, a triangular prism needs no new formula: compute the triangle's area and multiply.
accompanying_text: Because the rule is base-area times height, a triangular prism needs no new formula at all. Compute the triangle's area, multiply by the length, done. The shape of the base changes what you compute FIRST; it never changes the stacking.

illustration_description: Real floor plans are not single rectangles: break the figure into rectangles, find each area, and add.
accompanying_text: Real floor plans are not single rectangles. The move that handles all of them is the same: break the figure into pieces you already know, find each area, then ADD the pieces that are there and SUBTRACT the ones cut away. A ledger, kept honestly, beats any formula.

illustration_description: There is usually more than one correct cut: the same L-shape can be sliced vertically, horizontally, or read as a big rectangle with a bite removed.
accompanying_text: There is usually more than one correct cut. The same L-shape can be sliced vertically or horizontally, or read as a big rectangle with a bite taken out. Every honest route gives the same total — which makes a second method the fastest way to check the first.

illustration_description: One crate, three questions: floor space is area, paint is surface area, and sand is volume.
accompanying_text: One crate, three questions. How much floor does it stand on? Area. How much paint wraps it? Surface area. How much sand fills it? Volume. The numbers are the same; the question decides which measure answers it — and the units confirm the choice.

illustration_description: The reliable check is units: floor space and paint are square units, sand is cubic units, and tape along an edge would be plain length.
accompanying_text: The reliable check is units. Floor space and paint are square units. Sand is cubic units. Tape along an edge would be linear units. When an answer's units do not match what the question is asking for, the wrong measure was computed — no matter how clean the arithmetic was.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Counting is a pairing game: touch one toy, say one number. Every toy gets a number, and no toy gets two.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The touch is what keeps the pairing honest — it marks which toys already have their number.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Two mistakes break a count: skipping a toy, and counting a toy twice. Skipping makes the answer too small; repeating makes it too big.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Careful counters go slowly enough that each toy is touched exactly once — speed is the enemy of the pairing.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A line is the friendliest arrangement to count: start at one end, touch each thing in turn, and stop at the other end.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The line does the organising for you — what has been counted sits behind your finger, and what remains sits ahead.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A circle has no ends, so the counter must invent one: remember the starting bead, and stop just before reaching it again.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Forget the start and the count sails past it, counting beads a second time — the circle's only trap.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Pictures on a page cannot move into a line — so mark them instead: each one gets a tick as its number is said.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Marking splits the page the way a line splits a row: ticked things are counted, clean things still wait.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Counting's biggest secret: the last number said is not just the last toy's name — it tells how many are in the WHOLE group.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Count five shells and the word “five” belongs to all of them together. That is what “how many” asks for.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Once a group is counted, its number sticks. Asked again, the counter answers from memory — nothing changed, so the count still holds.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Recounting is only needed when the group itself changes: something added, something taken away.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Count the same toys left-to-right, right-to-left, or hopping about — the answer never moves. Order is the counter's choice; the amount is not.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: As long as every toy is counted exactly once, the pairing ends at the same last number from any direction.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Spread five buttons far apart and the group LOOKS bigger — but looking bigger and being more are different. The count ends at five.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Space is not amount. Only adding or removing buttons can change how many there are.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Scattered things are hardest to count — nothing separates counted from uncounted. The oldest trick fixes it: mark each one as its number is said.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: With a mark on every counted thing, the mess cannot fool you — the clean ones are exactly the ones still waiting.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Add one more toy and the count does not start over — it simply says the NEXT number. One more than five is six, always.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This is why the counting song matters: each number is exactly one more than the number before it.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A group can grow one toy at a time, and the count grows with it: six, seven, eight — counting ON from where it stood.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Counting on is the fast counter's habit: never start over when you already know where the count stands.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: “One more” also compares: if Ben has one more grape than Ana's six, Ben has seven — the very next number.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Pairing the groups one to one shows it: every grape of Ana's matches one of Ben's, and Ben has a single grape left over.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Counting out reverses the game: instead of asking how many, you remove exactly the number asked for — and STOP when the count says so.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The pile's total does not matter. Seven crayons means the count stops at seven, however many remain behind.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Some amounts need no counting at all: a quick look at two dots, or a dice-style four, and the mind names it instantly.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: That instant naming is a skill — the eye learns the shapes small numbers make, the way it learns faces.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The ten-frame gives EVERY amount a shape: a full row is five at a glance, so seven reads as five-and-two with no counting.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: That is the frame's whole purpose — it turns any number up to ten into a picture the mind can name quickly.

illustration_description: The line y equals x plus one does more than hold its own points: it cuts the whole plane into an upper half and a lower half.
accompanying_text: An equation like y = x + 1 draws a line — every point ON it makes the two sides equal. But the line does more: it cuts the whole plane into two halves. Every point not on the line lives on one side or the other, and which side it's on is a fact you can COMPUTE.

illustration_description: The test is arithmetic, not eyesight: at the point's x, compute the line's y and compare. Bigger means above, smaller below, equal means on the line.
accompanying_text: So the test is arithmetic, not eyesight: at the point's x, compute the line's y. If the point's y is bigger, it's above; smaller, below; equal, on. Three outcomes, one subtraction.

illustration_description: An inequality does not pick a line, it picks a side: the solutions of y greater than 2x minus 1 are an entire half-plane of points.
accompanying_text: An inequality like y > 2x − 1 doesn't pick a line — it picks a SIDE. Its solutions are every point whose coordinates make the statement true: a whole half-plane of them. To find which side, you don't need theory. Pick any point not on the boundary and ask it.

illustration_description: One test point decides the side, because crossing the boundary flips the comparison and not crossing it cannot. All points on one side vote the same way.
accompanying_text: Why one witness suffices: crossing the boundary flips the comparison, and NOT crossing it can't. All points on one side vote the same way. So a single test point speaks for its whole side — choose (0, 0) whenever the boundary misses it, because zeros make the arithmetic trivial.

illustration_description: Two inequalities can shade the same side yet disagree about the boundary itself: strictly greater excludes the line, greater-or-equal includes it.
accompanying_text: Two inequalities can shade the same side and still disagree — about the boundary itself. y > x + 1 excludes the line: points ON it make the sides equal, and 'equal' isn't 'greater.' y ≥ x + 1 welcomes them. Graphs record the difference in the line's own body: dashed for excluded, solid for included.

illustration_description: Read the symbol and draw the line: strict inequalities give a dashed boundary you cannot stand on; or-equal inequalities give a solid boundary that belongs to the region.
accompanying_text: Read the symbol, draw the line: > and < mean dashed (the boundary is a fence you can't stand on); ≥ and ≤ mean solid (the fence is part of the yard). The shaded side is decided separately, by the point test — symbol style and side are two independent decisions.

illustration_description: A system demands both inequalities at once, so its solution is the overlap of the two shaded half-planes.
accompanying_text: A SYSTEM of inequalities demands both at once: y > x AND y < 4 keeps only points that pass both tests. Each inequality shades a half-plane; the system's solution is where the shadings overlap. Think of two fences — the region is the strip the fences trap between them.

illustration_description: One failed test disqualifies a point. The point five, two passes y less than four but fails two greater than five, so it is out with no partial credit.
accompanying_text: One failed test disqualifies. (5, 2) satisfies y < 4 easily, but 2 > 5 is false — so it's out, no partial credit. When a point fails, it helps to name WHICH fence it hit: that's the difference between being below the strip and being above it.

illustration_description: Where two boundary lines cross the region gets a corner, and that corner is found by algebra rather than by squinting at the picture.
accompanying_text: Where two boundary lines cross, the region gets a CORNER — a vertex. Corners are found by algebra, not squinting: the crossing of y = x and y = 4 is the point satisfying both equations at once. Corners matter because they're where regions are sharpest — and, soon, where best answers hide.

illustration_description: Different pairs of boundaries, same machine: substitute the known value into the other equation and solve. x plus y equals six with y equals two gives the corner four, two.
accompanying_text: Different pairs, same machine. x + y = 6 crossing y = 2: substitute the known y to get x + 2 = 6, so x = 4 — corner (4, 2). Every corner of every region falls to substitution or elimination, the tools you already own from systems of equations.

illustration_description: Real regions carry several fences at once — x at least zero, y at least zero, and x plus y at most six — and membership means passing every one of them.
accompanying_text: Real regions wear several fences: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 6 is three demands stacked. Membership is still a checklist — run the point through every inequality, and one failure evicts it. The skill is bookkeeping: test each fence, record each verdict, then combine.

illustration_description: When a point fails, say where: four, four passes both sign fences but breaks the cap because eight exceeds six, while negative one, two breaks x at least zero before the cap is even consulted.
accompanying_text: When a point fails, say where. (4, 4) passes both sign fences but breaks the cap: 8 > 6. (−1, 2) breaks x ≥ 0 before the cap is even consulted. Diagnosing the broken fence is what lets you FIX a plan, not just reject it.

illustration_description: In a planning problem the inequalities are constraints — limits on time, money or materials — and the region they trap is the feasible region.
accompanying_text: Rename the picture: in a planning problem, the inequalities are CONSTRAINTS — limits on time, money, materials — and the region they trap is the FEASIBLE region: every plan you could actually run. Nothing new mathematically; the fences just started meaning something.

illustration_description: The feasible region's shape comes from its boundaries: x equals zero, y equals zero and x plus y equals six cut a triangle with corners at the origin, six zero and zero six.
accompanying_text: The feasible region's SHAPE comes from its boundaries: here x = 0, y = 0, and x + y = 6 cut a triangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 6). You already know how to find those corners — solve boundary pairs. The corners are about to earn their keep.

illustration_description: Every feasible point has a score under the objective, and on a straight-fenced region the best score is always reached at a corner.
accompanying_text: Plans differ in value. If profit is P = 2x + y, every feasible point has a score — and we want the highest. Here's the gift: on a straight-fenced region, the maximum of a linear objective always lands ON A CORNER. So don't search the infinite interior; interview the two or three corners.

illustration_description: The algorithm is short: find the corners from boundary pairs, score each with the objective, and keep the best. Different objectives crown different corners.
accompanying_text: So the algorithm is short: find the corners (boundary pairs), score each with the objective, keep the best. Different objectives crown different corners — P = x + 3y on the same triangle pays (0, 6) eighteen, dethroning (6, 0). The region sets the menu; the objective picks the meal.

illustration_description: A stall sells trays of cookies and pans of brownies. Cookies take one oven slot and brownies two, with eight slots available, so the constraints cut a feasible region.
accompanying_text: The whole pipeline on one problem. A stall sells trays of cookies (x) and pans of brownies (y). Oven space: cookies take 1 slot, brownies 2, and 8 slots exist: x + 2y ≤ 8. Cookie dough limits x ≤ 4. And x, y ≥ 0. Profit: $3 per tray, $4 per pan.

illustration_description: Scoring profit equals three x plus four y at every vertex: zero, twelve, twenty and sixteen. The mixed plan of four trays and two pans wins with twenty dollars.
accompanying_text: Now the interview. P = 3x + 4y at each vertex: (0,0) → 0; (4,0) → 12; (4,2) → 12 + 8 = 20; (0,4) → 16. The mixed plan wins — four trays, two pans, twenty dollars. Neither all-in plan beats using BOTH resources fully.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text: Each rectangle has the same width, h = (b − a)/n. Only its HEIGHT is a choice — and the rule you pick just says where in the strip that height is measured. Left edge, right edge, or middle.

illustration_description: The same curve twice. On the left, rectangles taking their height from the left edge sit entirely under the curve. On the right, rectangles taking their height from the right edge poke out above it. The true area is caught between the two.
accompanying_text:
You can find the area of a rectangle. You cannot find the area under a curve — so **cover the curve in rectangles** and add them up.

The answer will be wrong. That is fine: the question is not whether it is wrong but **how** it is wrong, and whether the error can be made as small as you like.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text:
The rules differ only in **where each rectangle takes its height**:

**Left** — the left edge. Undershoots a rising curve.
**Right** — the right edge. Overshoots it.
**Midpoint** — the middle. Usually far better than either.
**Trapezoid** — join the two edges with a slanted top, which is the average of left and right.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: The two sums are walls. The true area is between them, and it cannot escape. Raise n and the walls move toward each other — never past the truth, always toward it. Whatever is left when they meet IS the area.

illustration_description: The same curve twice. On the left, rectangles taking their height from the left edge sit entirely under the curve. On the right, rectangles taking their height from the right edge poke out above it. The true area is caught between the two.
accompanying_text:
Here is the move that makes calculus possible.

On a rising curve, the left sum is **too small** and the right sum is **too big**. So the true area is caught between them:

**left sum ≤ true area ≤ right sum**

And the gap between the two is [f(b) − f(a)]·h — which shrinks to nothing as n grows. The trap closes.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
So the definite integral is **defined** as the number the trap closes on:

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = limit of the Riemann sums as n → ∞.

The elongated S is a stretched-out sum. The dx is the width of a strip that has shrunk to nothing. Every part of the notation is a fossil of the rectangles.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Three facts, and all three come straight from the rectangles. Zero width gives zero area. Sweeping backwards makes every width negative. And two adjacent piles of strips are one bigger pile.

illustration_description: The same curve twice. On the left, rectangles taking their height from the left edge sit entirely under the curve. On the right, rectangles taking their height from the right edge poke out above it. The true area is caught between the two.
accompanying_text:
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is not a formula. It is the **number the trap closes on** — the limit of the Riemann sums.

Three properties fall straight out of the rectangles:

∫ₐᵃ f = 0 (no width, no area).
∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦᵃ f (running backwards flips the sign of every dx).
∫ₐᶜ f + ∫꜀ᵇ f = ∫ₐᵇ f (the strips just join up).

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
And the integral is **signed**. Where f dips below the axis, the heights are negative — so those strips contribute negative area.

∫ₐᵇ f is not 'the area'. It is the area above the axis **minus** the area below it. If you want the geometric area, you must integrate |f|.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: A(x) answers one question: **how much area have I swept out so far?** Move the endpoint and you get a different answer, which is exactly what makes A a function of x.

illustration_description: The function f on top with the area under it shaded up to a point. Beneath, the accumulated area drawn as a second curve. The tangent to that second curve has exactly the height of f above it.
accompanying_text:
So far the area has been one fixed number: from a to b.

Now let the far end **move**. Define

**A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt** — the area so far, up to x.

A is a brand-new function, built out of f by sweeping. Feed it an x and it hands you back an area.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
The letter inside the integral does not matter.

∫₀ˣ 2t dt and ∫₀ˣ 2u du are the same number. **t is a dummy variable** — it runs across the interval and disappears.

But x, the upper limit, is real. It survives, and it is what A depends on. Writing ∫₀ˣ 2x dx is a genuine error: the x cannot be both the sweeping variable and the endpoint.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Ask only one question at each x: **is area being added, or taken away?** Above the axis, added — A climbs. Below it, taken away — A falls. On the axis, neither — A holds still.

illustration_description: The function f on top with the area under it shaded up to a point. Beneath, the accumulated area drawn as a second curve. The tangent to that second curve has exactly the height of f above it.
accompanying_text:
You can describe the accumulation without computing a single area, because the **sign of f decides what A does**:

**f > 0** → A is rising (area is piling on).
**f = 0** → A is momentarily flat (nothing is being added).
**f < 0** → A is falling (area is being subtracted).

If that list sounds familiar, it should. It is the list from `dr-01-02`, with f′ replaced by f.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So the whole shape of A is dictated by f, with no arithmetic at all:

f positive and large → A steeply rising.
f positive and small → A rising gently.
f zero → A flat.
f negative → A falling.

This is the same reading you did in C1 — only now f is playing the part that f′ played then.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Multiply the units. The height of a strip is a RATE — something per something. The width is that something. Multiply and the 'per' cancels, leaving a TOTAL. That cancellation is the entire meaning of the integral.

illustration_description: The function f on top with the area under it shaded up to a point. Beneath, the accumulated area drawn as a second curve. The tangent to that second curve has exactly the height of f above it.
accompanying_text:
If f is a **rate**, then the area under it is a **total**.

Velocity (miles per hour) × time (hours) = miles. That is exactly what a strip computes: height × width. Add the strips and you have the total distance.

**∫ₐᵇ (rate) dt = the total change over [a, b].** This is the single most useful sentence in the course.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
The pattern is everywhere, and it is always the same shape:

Integrate a **flow rate** → get a **volume**.
Integrate a **birth rate** → get a **population change**.
Integrate a **current** → get a **charge**.
Integrate **marginal cost** → get a **total cost**.

Each one is height × width, summed. Nothing new is happening.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Push the endpoint forward by h and you gain a thin sliver of area — nearly a rectangle, width h and height f(x). So the area grows at the RATE f(x). That is all the theorem says: **A′ = f**.

illustration_description: The function f on top with the area under it shaded up to a point. Beneath, the accumulated area drawn as a second curve. The tangent to that second curve has exactly the height of f above it.
accompanying_text:
Push the accumulation forward a hair. From x to x + h you gain a sliver of area — and that sliver is very nearly a rectangle of width h and height f(x).

So A(x + h) − A(x) ≈ f(x)·h. Divide by h and let h → 0:

**A′(x) = f(x).**

Differentiation and integration are inverse operations. That is the Fundamental Theorem, and it is why they are taught together.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
With the chain rule, the upper limit can be anything:

**d/dx[∫ₐ^(g(x)) f(t) dt] = f(g(x))·g′(x)**

The accumulation is being swept at a rate g′(x), so the area piles up that much faster. It is the gears again.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Two steps. **One:** find any F with F′ = f — undo the derivative. **Two:** compute F(b) − F(a). The commonest error in the entire chapter is doing step one and forgetting to subtract the lower limit.

illustration_description: The function f on top with the area under it shaded up to a point. Beneath, the accumulated area drawn as a second curve. The tangent to that second curve has exactly the height of f above it.
accompanying_text:
Part 1 said A′ = f, so A is **an antiderivative** of f.

But A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f is the area from a, so A(a) = 0 and A(b) = the area you want. And any other antiderivative F differs from A only by a constant — which cancels in a subtraction. Hence:

**∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)**, for ANY antiderivative F of f.

No rectangles. No limits. Just: undo the derivative, and subtract.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
So the antiderivative is the whole game, and you already have it.

Every derivative rule from C1 runs backwards. **Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power** — that is the power rule reversed, and it is the only antiderivative you need for the rest of this lesson.

Always check by differentiating your answer. It costs ten seconds and catches almost every error.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text: Ask what you are being asked to DO. Differentiating an accumulation? That is Part 1, and the answer is the integrand. Computing a definite value? That is Part 2: antiderivative, then subtract.

illustration_description: The function f on top with the area under it shaded up to a point. Beneath, the accumulated area drawn as a second curve. The tangent to that second curve has exactly the height of f above it.
accompanying_text:
Part 1: **differentiating an accumulation gives back the function.** (A′ = f)
Part 2: **the accumulation can be computed from any antiderivative.** (∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a))

These are not two facts. They are one fact, read in two directions: **differentiation and integration are inverse operations.** Part 2 is what you get by taking Part 1 seriously.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text:
And now the two courses are one course.

Every derivative rule you learned in C1 is now an **antiderivative rule**, read backwards. The power rule reversed gives xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). The chain rule reversed is about to give you substitution.

Differentiation was never a separate subject. It was the other half of this one.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Two moves, and then a check. **Raise** the exponent by one. **Divide** by the new exponent. Then **differentiate your answer** — if it does not give back what you started with, you have made an error and you will know instantly.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
Differentiation drops the exponent in front and lowers the power. So **run it backwards**: raise the power, then divide by the new power.

∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1.

And check by differentiating. It takes ten seconds and catches nearly every error.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
Why the **+ C**?

Because a constant has zero slope, x⁴/4 and x⁴/4 + 7 have the *same* derivative. Antidifferentiating cannot recover information the derivative destroyed.

So an indefinite integral is a whole **family** of parallel curves. For a definite integral, C cancels in the subtraction and you may ignore it.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Three steps. **Integrate**, keeping the + C. **Substitute** the given point. **Solve** for C. Only then answer the question that was actually asked.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
∫ 2x dx = x² + C is a **family**: a stack of identical parabolas, one for every C.

They all have the same slope at every x — which is exactly why the derivative could not tell them apart. To choose one, you need a single extra fact: **one point the curve passes through.**

That fact is called an *initial condition*, and it pins C.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
That is the shape of every problem in the next course:

**A rate + a starting value = the whole story.**

The rate gives the shape (the antiderivative). The starting value gives the height (the constant). Neither one alone is enough, and together they are always enough.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text: You are not learning new facts — you are reading old ones backwards. Take each derivative rule from C1, swap the sides, and add a + C. The only one that bites is sin, because its antiderivative carries a minus.

illustration_description: The exponential curve e to the x, with tangents drawn at three points. At each one the slope of the tangent equals the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
Every derivative from C1 is now an antiderivative, read backwards:

∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C
∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C
∫ cos x dx = sin x + C
∫ sin x dx = **−**cos x + C

The minus on the last one is where nearly every error lives. Check by differentiating: (−cos x)′ = +sin x ✓.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
With the chain rule running backwards, each library entry gains a partner:

∫ e^(kx) dx = e^(kx)/k + C
∫ cos(kx) dx = sin(kx)/k + C

The **division by k** is the price of the inner derivative. Differentiating would have MULTIPLIED by k, so antidifferentiating must divide by it.

That single observation is the whole of the next chapter, in embryo.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text: Look for an **inside function** and its **derivative**, sitting together. Name the inside u, write du = u′ dx, and swap everything over. If a piece of x is left over that is not a constant, the substitution was the wrong one.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
The chain rule left a fingerprint: **the derivative of the inside, multiplied on the outside.**

So when an integrand contains an inside function AND its derivative, you are looking at the output of a chain rule — and you can run it backwards.

Call the inside **u**. Then du = u′ dx, and the whole integral collapses into ∫ (something in u) du.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
If the inner derivative is present but with the **wrong constant**, fix it with a constant — never with an x.

∫ x(x² + 1)³ dx has an x where a 2x is wanted. Write du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2, and the ½ comes out front.

Constants may be moved across the integral sign. **Variables may not.** That single rule keeps substitution honest.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text: The moment you write du, the integral lives in u — so its limits must be u-values. Compute u at the old lower limit and u at the old upper limit, and write those instead. Mixing the two worlds gives a tidy answer that is simply wrong.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
A definite integral carries limits, and the limits are values of **x**. Change variable to u and they must change too.

∫ₓ₌ₐ^(x=b) → ∫ᵤ₌ᵤ₍ₐ₎^(u=u(b))

Otherwise you would be feeding x-values into a u-integral, which is a category error — and it silently gives the wrong number.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
Substitution also handles the plain **linear inside**, which is the commonest case of all:

∫ cos(3x) dx → u = 3x, du = 3 dx → (1/3)∫ cos u du = sin(3x)/3 + C.

That division by 3 is the same division you met at the end of the last lesson. It is the inner derivative, being paid back.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text: Write down the candidate u, then immediately write du. Now look at the integrand: **does it contain that du, up to a constant?** If yes, substitute. If a bare x is left over, stop — that substitution is the wrong one.

illustration_description: Three gears in a chain: x turns u three times as fast, and u turns y five times as fast, so x turns y fifteen times as fast. Rates multiply along a chain.
accompanying_text:
Nothing labels the inside for you. Two questions decide it:

**What is inside something?** (a bracket, a root, an exponent, a denominator)
**Is its derivative also present, up to a constant?**

If both answers are yes, that thing is u. If the second answer is no, substitution will not save you — and in this course, that means the integral is out of reach.

illustration_description: A curve and its inverse reflected across the line y equals x. A tangent of slope four on one becomes a tangent of slope one quarter on the other, because reflecting swaps rise and run.
accompanying_text:
And that is integration, in this course.

You can **define** an integral (the trap, squeezed shut), **interpret** it (a rate integrated gives a total), **compute** it (an antiderivative, evaluated twice), and **transform** it (substitution, the chain rule reversed).

What remains is not new machinery but new uses: areas between curves, volumes, average values. Those are the next course.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Draw a vertical strip through the region. Its top end sits on one curve and its bottom end on the other. **Height = top − bottom.** That height is what you integrate — and nothing else about the problem matters.

illustration_description: A thin rectangle standing under a curve, and the same rectangle after being spun about the axis: it has become a disc whose radius is the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
One curve gave you the area under it. **Two curves give you the area between them** — and the only thing that changes is the height of a strip.

Each strip runs from the **bottom** curve to the **top** one, so its height is **top − bottom**. Add the strips:

**Area = ∫ₐᵇ (top − bottom) dx**

That is the entire idea, and everything in this course is a variation on it.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
