Get the order wrong and the integral comes out **negative**. Area cannot be negative — so a negative answer is the integral telling you that you subtracted the wrong way round.

And if the curves **cross inside** the interval, the top and bottom SWAP. Split the integral at the crossing and do each piece separately, or you will silently subtract one region from the other.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: One strip, spun about the axis, sweeps out a coin. The coin's RADIUS is the height of the curve, f(x). Its FACE is πr². Its thickness is dx. Add up the coins and you have the solid.

illustration_description: A thin rectangle standing under a curve, and the same rectangle after being spun about the axis: it has become a disc whose radius is the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
Take the region under a curve and **spin it around the x-axis**. It sweeps out a solid.

Now take one thin strip of that region. What does IT sweep out? A **disc** — a coin of radius f(x) and thickness dx.

Its volume is **πr²·dx = π[f(x)]²·dx**. Add up the coins:

**V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx**

The integral has not changed. Only what you measure on the slice.

illustration_description: A thin rectangle standing under a curve, and the same rectangle after being spun about the axis: it has become a disc whose radius is the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
Notice how little actually changed.

**Area** — slice, measure the HEIGHT, add: ∫f dx.
**Volume** — slice, measure the DISC, add: ∫πf² dx.

Same slicing. Same summing. The only difference is what you measure on one slice. That single sentence is the whole of this course, and it is worth carrying into every problem you meet.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Two circles, one inside the other. Work out the BIG face, work out the HOLE, and subtract: π R² − π r². Squaring comes first and subtracting comes second — reversing them gives a different (and wrong) number.

illustration_description: A thin rectangle standing under a curve, and the same rectangle after being spun about the axis: it has become a disc whose radius is the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
Revolve the region **between two curves** and each strip sweeps out not a disc but a **washer** — a coin with a hole punched through it.

Outer radius R = the top curve. Inner radius r = the bottom one. The face is the big circle minus the small one:

**π(R² − r²)**

And once again: slice, measure the slice, add them up. Only the measurement changed.

illustration_description: A thin rectangle standing under a curve, and the same rectangle after being spun about the axis: it has become a disc whose radius is the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
So the whole course is one sentence, repeated:

**Slice the region. Measure ONE slice. Add them up.**

An area measures a slice's **height**. A disc measures **πr²**. A washer measures **π(R² − r²)**. The slicing never changes; the summing never changes. Only the measurement does — and that is the only thing you ever have to work out.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: What shape is standing on the slice, and what is its AREA? Write that in terms of x, then integrate it. The calculus does not care whether the shape is a circle, a square or a triangle — only you do.

illustration_description: A thin rectangle standing under a curve, and the same rectangle after being spun about the axis: it has become a disc whose radius is the height of the curve.
accompanying_text:
A solid does not have to be made by revolving anything. Stand a **square** on every slice of a flat region and you get a solid just as real — and just as easy.

The slice's area is whatever the cross-section's area is. If the side is s = f(x), a square slice is **s²**, and

**V = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx.**

And notice: **no π anywhere.** π only appeared because a disc is a circle.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
So the recipe is completely general:

**Work out the area of ONE cross-section, in terms of x.** Then integrate it.

Square → s². Equilateral triangle → (√3/4)s². Semicircle → (π/8)s². Circle → πr².

The calculus never notices which. It only ever adds up slices — and the geometry of the slice is your job, not the integral's.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text: Add up all the heights (that is the integral) and divide by how many there were (that is the width). The result is the height of the flat rectangle holding the same amount.

illustration_description: A table of powers and their derivatives: x gives one, x squared gives two x, x cubed gives three x squared. The exponent drops in front and the power falls by one.
accompanying_text:
What is the average height of a curve? You cannot add up infinitely many heights and divide.

But you CAN: add them with an integral, then divide by the width.

**f_avg = (1/(b − a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx**

Geometrically: it is the height of the **rectangle with the same area** as the region. Flatten the curve without spilling anything, and the level you end up at is the average.

illustration_description: The tangent to y equals x squared at the point three, nine has slope six, giving the line y equals six x minus nine.
accompanying_text:
So this is the **Mean Value Theorem for Integrals**, and it is the same theorem you already met, one level up.

**C3:** somewhere, the tangent's slope equals the secant's slope.
**Here:** somewhere, the function's value equals its average value.

Both say the same thing: *a continuous quantity must actually attain its own average at some instant.*

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text: Two questions, two integrals. **Where did it end up?** — integrate v, signs and all. **How far did it travel?** — integrate |v|, which means splitting at the sign changes and adding the magnitudes.

illustration_description: The curve y equals x squared on top, and its derivative two x plotted underneath as a straight line. The steeper the curve above, the higher the line below.
accompanying_text:
In C2 you split a journey into legs by hand, measured each one, and added the lengths as positive numbers. That was hard work.

Here is the machine that does it:

**Displacement = ∫ₐᵇ v dt** — where you ended up.
**Total distance = ∫ₐᵇ |v| dt** — every metre you actually covered.

The absolute value does *exactly* the leg-splitting you did by hand. It was never a different idea; it was the same idea, automated.

illustration_description: The cubic has a flat tangent at the origin but does not turn there — it keeps rising. A zero derivative does not guarantee a peak or a valley.
accompanying_text:
So the recipe for total distance is exactly the hand method, written down:

**Find where v = 0 and changes sign.** (the turns)
**Integrate v on each piece.**
**Add the ABSOLUTE VALUES.**

And that is why ∫|v| is not a strange new integral — it is three ordinary integrals with the minus signs stripped off.

illustration_description: A table showing x approaching 2 from the left (1.9, 1.99, 1.999) with f of x giving 3.9, 3.99, 3.999, and from the right (2.1, 2.01, 2.001) giving 4.1, 4.01, 4.001. Both columns close in on the limit value 4. A numerical table: f(x) approaches 4 as x approaches 2 from both sides.
accompanying_text: A **limit** asks a simple question: as x gets closer and closer to some value, what does f(x) head toward? We write lim(x→a) f(x) = L. The key idea is **approach** — we care where the function is GOING near a, not necessarily its value AT a.

illustration_description: The straight line y equals x plus 2 with an open circle at the point 2, 4, marking a hole. Both sides of the line approach height 4 at x equals 2, so the limit is 4 even though the function is undefined there. A graph with a hole where the limit still exists.
accompanying_text: Crucially, the limit can exist even where the function has a **hole**. For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), plugging in x = 2 gives 0/0 — undefined. But everywhere else f(x) = x + 2, so as x → 2 the outputs approach 4. The limit is 4 even though f(2) doesn't exist.

illustration_description: A table showing x approaching 2 from the left (1.9, 1.99, 1.999) with f of x giving 3.9, 3.99, 3.999, and from the right (2.1, 2.01, 2.001) giving 4.1, 4.01, 4.001. Both columns close in on the limit value 4. A numerical table: f(x) approaches 4 as x approaches 2 from both sides.
accompanying_text: A **numerical table** estimates a limit: evaluate f at x-values creeping toward a from both sides and watch the outputs settle. If both columns close in on the same number, that's the limit. Tables are how you probe a limit you can't yet solve by algebra.

illustration_description: The straight line y equals x plus 2 with an open circle at the point 2, 4, marking a hole. Both sides of the line approach height 4 at x equals 2, so the limit is 4 even though the function is undefined there. A graph with a hole where the limit still exists.
accompanying_text: On a **graph**, trace the curve toward x = a with your finger from each side. The limit is the y-height both fingers approach — even if there's an open circle (hole) there. A filled dot ON the curve gives the function's value; the limit is about the trend leading INTO the point.

illustration_description: A step function equal to 1 for x below zero and 2 for x at or above zero. The left piece ends in an open circle at 0, 1 and the right piece begins with a filled dot at 0, 2. Because the left approach 1 and the right approach 2 disagree, the limit at zero does not exist. A jump discontinuity where the two-sided limit does not exist.
accompanying_text: A limit **fails to exist** when the two sides disagree. If f approaches one value from the left and a DIFFERENT value from the right, there's no single number it heads toward — the limit does not exist (DNE). This is the story at a **jump**.

illustration_description: Two more ways limits fail: unbounded behavior, where the function shoots off toward infinity near a point.
accompanying_text: Two more ways limits fail: **unbounded** behavior (f shoots to +∞ or −∞ near a, as with 1/x² at 0) and wild **oscillation** that never settles. In each case there's no single finite value the function approaches, so the limit does not exist.

illustration_description: For most functions the limit is easy: if f is continuous at a, the limit is simply f of a.
accompanying_text: For most functions the limit is easy: if f is **continuous** at a (no hole, jump, or blow-up), then lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a). Just **substitute**. Polynomials are continuous everywhere, so lim(x→2)(3x + 1) = 3(2) + 1 = 7. Substitution is always the first thing to try.

illustration_description: The limit laws let you break a complicated limit into the limits of its parts, then combine.
accompanying_text:
The **limit laws** let you break a complicated limit into pieces:

lim(f + g) = lim f + lim g,  lim(f·g) = (lim f)(lim g),  lim(f/g) = lim f / lim g (if lim g ≠ 0).

Limits of sums, products, and quotients are the sums, products, and quotients of the limits — algebra distributes cleanly across the limit.

illustration_description: A four-stage pipeline for resolving an indeterminate limit: it starts at 0 over 0, then factor or rationalize, then cancel the shared factor, then substitute to reach the answer. Resolving a 0/0 indeterminate limit by factor-cancel-substitute.
accompanying_text: When substitution gives **0/0**, that's the **indeterminate form** — it doesn't mean the limit is 0 or undefined; it means 'more work needed.' The fix for rational functions: **factor** the numerator and denominator, **cancel** the shared factor causing the 0/0, then substitute into what remains.

illustration_description: Why cancelling is legal: for a limit x approaches two but never equals two, so a hole doesn't change the value.
accompanying_text: Why cancelling is legal: for a limit, x approaches 2 but never EQUALS 2, so x − 2 ≠ 0 the whole time and dividing it out is valid. The cancelled expression matches the original everywhere near 2 — exactly where the limit lives. The removed factor was just the hole.

illustration_description: A four-stage pipeline for resolving an indeterminate limit: it starts at 0 over 0, then factor or rationalize, then cancel the shared factor, then substitute to reach the answer. Resolving a 0/0 indeterminate limit by factor-cancel-substitute.
accompanying_text: When a **square root** causes the 0/0, factoring won't help — but **multiplying by the conjugate** does. For (√(x + 4) − 2)/x, multiply top and bottom by (√(x + 4) + 2). The numerator becomes a difference of squares, (x + 4) − 4 = x, which cancels the x below.

illustration_description: The conjugate trick works because root A minus B times root A plus B erases the root, clearing the indeterminate form.
accompanying_text: The trick works because (√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B² erases the root. That difference-of-squares in the numerator cancels the troublesome factor in the denominator, converting an indeterminate 0/0 into something you can finally substitute into.

illustration_description: A step function equal to 1 for x below zero and 2 for x at or above zero. The left piece ends in an open circle at 0, 1 and the right piece begins with a filled dot at 0, 2. Because the left approach 1 and the right approach 2 disagree, the limit at zero does not exist. A jump discontinuity where the two-sided limit does not exist.
accompanying_text: Sometimes a function behaves differently on each side of a. A **one-sided limit** looks at just one direction: lim(x→a⁻) approaches from the LEFT (smaller x), lim(x→a⁺) from the RIGHT. The two-sided limit exists **only if both one-sided limits agree**.

illustration_description: When the two one-sided limits agree, the two-sided limit exists and equals their shared value.
accompanying_text: When the two one-sided limits DO agree, the two-sided limit exists and equals their shared value. This is the precise rule: **lim(x→a) exists ⟺ lim(x→a⁻) = lim(x→a⁺)**. One-sided limits are the building blocks that decide whether the full limit lives.

illustration_description: A rational function curve that rises and then flattens out, approaching the horizontal dashed line y equals 3 as x grows large. The limit at infinity, 3, is exactly the horizontal asymptote. A curve approaching its horizontal asymptote as x grows without bound.
accompanying_text: A **limit at infinity** asks where f(x) heads as x grows without bound. For a rational function, compare the **degrees** of top and bottom. When they're **equal**, the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients — and that value is the **horizontal asymptote** (recall pra). The end behavior IS a limit.

illustration_description: The degree comparison has three cases: top less than bottom gives zero, equal gives the ratio of leads, top greater grows without bound.
accompanying_text:
The degree comparison has three cases:
• **top degree < bottom degree** → limit **0** (asymptote y = 0),
• **degrees equal** → ratio of leading coefficients,
• **top degree > bottom degree** → **±∞** (no horizontal asymptote; it grows without bound).

illustration_description: A rational function curve that rises and then flattens out, approaching the horizontal dashed line y equals 3 as x grows large. The limit at infinity, 3, is exactly the horizontal asymptote. A curve approaching its horizontal asymptote as x grows without bound.
accompanying_text: When the numerator's degree is **larger**, the fraction grows without bound: lim(x→∞) = +∞ or −∞, and there's **no horizontal asymptote**. The top overwhelms the bottom. Intuitively, the fastest-growing term wins the tug-of-war as x races off.

illustration_description: The full menu as x approaches infinity for a rational function: a horizontal asymptote, a slant, or unbounded growth.
accompanying_text: So the full menu, as x → ∞ for a rational function: a **horizontal asymptote** (degrees equal or top smaller) OR **unbounded growth** to ±∞ (top larger). The single tool — compare degrees, then leading coefficients — settles every case at both +∞ and −∞.

illustration_description: A checklist of the three conditions for a function to be continuous at x equals a: first, f of a is defined; second, the limit as x approaches a exists; third, the limit equals f of a. All three must hold. The three conditions for continuity at a point.
accompanying_text: A function is **continuous at x = a** if you can draw through that point without lifting your pen. Precisely, three things must ALL hold: (1) f(a) is defined, (2) the limit lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and (3) they're **equal**: lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a). Break any one and continuity fails.

illustration_description: For nice functions, polynomials and rational, root, and trig functions, continuity holds everywhere they're defined.
accompanying_text: For 'nice' functions — polynomials, and rational/root/trig functions where they're defined — continuity is automatic, so the limit is just **f(a)** by direct substitution (recall Ch2). Continuity is what MAKES substitution legal. The interesting points are exactly where one of the three conditions breaks.

illustration_description: Three kinds of discontinuity. Left: a removable discontinuity, a smooth line with a single open-circle hole. Middle: a jump, two level segments at different heights with open and closed endpoints. Right: an infinite discontinuity, a curve shooting up toward a vertical asymptote. Removable, jump, and infinite discontinuities.
accompanying_text: Discontinuities come in three flavors. A **removable** discontinuity is a single hole — the limit exists, but f(a) is missing or misplaced; you could 'fill it in.' A **jump** has the left and right limits disagree. An **infinite** discontinuity has the function blowing up to ±∞ (a vertical asymptote).

illustration_description: A jump occurs when the one-sided limits exist but disagree, leaving a step in the graph.
accompanying_text: A **jump** occurs when the one-sided limits exist but differ (recall Ch3): the graph leaps from one height to another, so no single limit exists. Common in piecewise functions and step functions — think of a price that jumps at a threshold.

illustration_description: A continuous curve rising from the point 1, negative 1 to the point 2, positive 2. Because it is continuous and changes sign, it must cross the horizontal zero line somewhere between, marking a guaranteed root at about x equals 1.41. The Intermediate Value Theorem forcing a root at a sign change.
accompanying_text: The **Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)**: if f is continuous on [a, b] and N is any value between f(a) and f(b), then f hits N somewhere in between — there's a c in (a, b) with f(c) = N. Continuity means the graph can't skip a value; it must pass through everything on the way.

illustration_description: The most common use is root-finding: if a continuous function changes sign across an interval, it must cross zero inside.
accompanying_text: The most common use is **root-finding**: if a continuous f changes sign on [a, b] — that is, f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs — then f must cross zero, so a root lives in (a, b). A sign change is a guarantee of a solution, even without solving.

illustration_description: A parabola y equals x squared. A secant line joins the points at x equals 1 and x equals 3, giving an average rate of change. A separate tangent line touches at x equals 2; as the two secant points slide together, the secant pivots into this tangent, whose slope is the derivative. A secant line pivoting into the tangent as the derivative.
accompanying_text:
The **average rate of change** of f over [a, b] is the slope of the **secant line** joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)):

(f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a).

It's the familiar rise-over-run (recall slope), now measuring how fast f changes on average across an interval — like average speed over a trip.

illustration_description: The average rate depends on the interval: the secant line's slope changes as the interval shifts.
accompanying_text: Notice the average rate DEPENDS on the interval: x² averaged 4 on [1, 3] but 7 on [2, 5] — steeper further right. A secant only reports the overall change between two points; it can't tell you the rate at a single instant. That gap is what the next lesson closes.

illustration_description: A parabola y equals x squared. A secant line joins the points at x equals 1 and x equals 3, giving an average rate of change. A separate tangent line touches at x equals 2; as the two secant points slide together, the secant pivots into this tangent, whose slope is the derivative. A secant line pivoting into the tangent as the derivative.
accompanying_text:
Let the step h shrink to zero. The secant pivots into the **tangent line**, and the difference quotient's LIMIT is the **instantaneous rate of change** — the **derivative**:

f′(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a)) / h.

This is the whole course's payoff: a single-point slope, defined by a limit.

illustration_description: The derivative reads as an instantaneous rate: as the interval shrinks to a point, the secant becomes the tangent line.
accompanying_text: The derivative reads as an **instantaneous** rate: the exact speed at one instant, the tangent's steepness at one point. Average rate needed two points; the derivative needs a limit to capture just one. This limit — the same tool from all of Chapter 1 — is the gateway to calculus.

illustration_description: A bar chart of the partial sums one half, three quarters, seven eighths, fifteen sixteenths, and thirty-one thirty-seconds, each taller than the last and closing in on a dashed horizontal line at 1, showing the infinite sum equals the limit of its running totals. Partial sums converging to the limit of an infinite series.
accompanying_text: One idea has run through this whole course — the **limit** — and it reaches beyond derivatives. An **infinite sum** is itself a limit: the value of the **partial sums** as you add more and more terms. Adding forever is really asking, 'what limit do the running totals approach?'

illustration_description: This is exactly the infinite geometric series from earlier: the partial sums approach a finite limit.
accompanying_text: This is exactly the infinite geometric series from earlier (recall the sum a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1). What that formula computes IS a limit of partial sums. For 1/2 + 1/4 + ⋯: a = 1/2, r = 1/2, so a/(1 − r) = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1 — the same 1 the totals crept toward.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: An equation is a **balance**: the two sides are equal, and any move you make must be done to BOTH sides to keep them equal. To solve, undo the operations around x one at a time until x stands alone.

illustration_description: Undoing in reverse order to solve 2x plus 3 equals 11: first subtract 3 from both sides to get 2x equals 8, then divide by 2 to get x equals 4. Undo in reverse: subtract, then divide.
accompanying_text: Undo in REVERSE order: the last thing done to x is undone first. In 4x + 8, x was multiplied by 4, then 8 was added — so subtract 8 first, then divide by 4. Each undo peels one layer.

illustration_description: A balance holds five x plus two on the left and three x plus ten on the right. Taking three x from both pans keeps it level, leaving two x plus two equals ten, so x equals four.
accompanying_text: When x sits on BOTH sides, like 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, first collect the x-terms on one side. Take 3x off both sides — the balance stays level — leaving 2x + 2 = 10. Then solve as usual.

illustration_description: Variables on both sides: from 5x plus 2 equals 3x plus 8, subtract the smaller 3x from both sides to reach 2x plus 2 equals 8, then solve x equals 3. Subtract the smaller x-term: x = 3.
accompanying_text: Subtract the SMALLER x-term to keep the coefficient positive. For 7x + 3 = 4x + 15, take 4x from both sides, giving 3x + 3 = 15 — easier than ending up with a negative x-term.

illustration_description: Distribute then solve: 2 times the quantity x plus 3 becomes 2x plus 6 equals 14, then subtract 6 and divide by 2 to get x equals 4. Distribute first: 2(x + 3) = 14 → x = 4.
accompanying_text: Clear parentheses FIRST using the distributive property: 3(x + 4) means the 3 multiplies BOTH parts, giving 3x + 12. Then solve the equation that remains. The 3 reaches every term inside the parentheses.

illustration_description: Distribute then solve: 2 times the quantity x plus 3 becomes 2x plus 6 equals 14, then subtract 6 and divide by 2 to get x equals 4. Distribute first: 2(x + 3) = 14 → x = 4.
accompanying_text: The classic slip is distributing to only the FIRST term: 3(x + 4) is NOT 3x + 4 — it's 3x + 12. The 3 must hit the 4 as well. Miss this and every later step is off.

illustration_description: Three outcomes for a one-variable equation. First, three x plus one equals x plus seven reduces to x equals three — one solution. Second, two x plus three equals two x plus five reduces to three equals five, which is false — no solution. Third, two x plus three equals two x plus three reduces to three equals three, always true — infinitely many solutions.
accompanying_text: Not every equation has an answer. When you solve and the variable DISAPPEARS, leaving a FALSE statement like 3 = 5, the equation has NO solution — no value of x could ever make it true.

illustration_description: Three outcomes for a one-variable equation. First, three x plus one equals x plus seven reduces to x equals three — one solution. Second, two x plus three equals two x plus five reduces to three equals five, which is false — no solution. Third, two x plus three equals two x plus three reduces to three equals three, always true — infinitely many solutions.
accompanying_text: This happens when both sides have the SAME x-coefficient but DIFFERENT constants — like two parallel lines that never meet. The x-terms cancel, and the leftover numbers can't be equal.

illustration_description: Infinitely many solutions: 2x plus 4 equals 2 times x plus 2 becomes 2x plus 4 equals 2x plus 4, a statement true for every x. Infinitely many: both sides are identical.
accompanying_text: The opposite case: when the variable cancels and leaves a TRUE statement like 3 = 3, EVERY value of x works — there are INFINITELY MANY solutions. Both sides are secretly the same expression.

illustration_description: Infinitely many solutions: 2x plus 4 equals 2 times x plus 2 becomes 2x plus 4 equals 2x plus 4, a statement true for every x. Infinitely many: both sides are identical.
accompanying_text: This happens when both sides are the SAME after simplifying — same x-coefficient AND same constant. It's like two lines drawn exactly on top of each other: they share every point.

illustration_description: Three outcomes for a one-variable equation. First, three x plus one equals x plus seven reduces to x equals three — one solution. Second, two x plus three equals two x plus five reduces to three equals five, which is false — no solution. Third, two x plus three equals two x plus three reduces to three equals three, always true — infinitely many solutions.
accompanying_text: Any linear equation falls into exactly three cases. Simplify both sides, then look: if x survives with a real value, ONE solution; if x cancels leaving a true statement, INFINITELY MANY; if x cancels leaving a false statement, NONE.

illustration_description: Three outcomes for a one-variable equation. First, three x plus one equals x plus seven reduces to x equals three — one solution. Second, two x plus three equals two x plus five reduces to three equals five, which is false — no solution. Third, two x plus three equals two x plus three reduces to three equals three, always true — infinitely many solutions.
accompanying_text: A quick shortcut: compare the simplified x-coefficients. DIFFERENT coefficients always give one solution (the lines cross). SAME coefficients give either none or infinitely many, decided by whether the constants match.

illustration_description: A system is two equations sharing the same two unknowns; its solution is the single pair of values that makes both true at once. A system: two equations, one shared solution.
accompanying_text: A **system** is two equations you solve at the same time. Its **solution** is the single point (x, y) that makes BOTH equations true at once — not just one of them. It's the point the two lines share.

illustration_description: A system is two equations sharing the same two unknowns; its solution is the single pair of values that makes both true at once. A system: two equations, one shared solution.
accompanying_text: To CHECK a proposed solution, substitute it into BOTH equations. The point counts only if it makes every equation true. A point on just one line is not a solution of the system.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: To solve a system BY GRAPHING: draw each line (start at its y-intercept, then step by its slope), and read off where they CROSS. That crossing point is the solution — the (x, y) that works in both.

illustration_description: Solving a system by graphing: two lines are drawn and their single crossing point at 2, 3 is the solution that satisfies both equations. Graphing a system: the crossing is the solution.
accompanying_text: You can also find the crossing without a perfect graph: set the two expressions for y EQUAL. For y = 2x and y = x + 3, solve 2x = x + 3 → x = 3, then y = 2(3) = 6. The crossing is (3, 6).

illustration_description: Three outcomes for a system of two lines. Crossing lines meet at one point — one solution. Parallel lines never meet — no solution. Two lines lying exactly on top of each other share every point — infinitely many solutions.
accompanying_text: Just like single equations, systems have three cases — and you can tell WHICH before solving by comparing the lines. DIFFERENT slopes → the lines cross → ONE solution. Same slope needs a closer look.

illustration_description: Three outcomes for a system of two lines. Crossing lines meet at one point — one solution. Parallel lines never meet — no solution. Two lines lying exactly on top of each other share every point — infinitely many solutions.
accompanying_text: When the slopes are EQUAL, the lines are parallel. If their y-intercepts DIFFER, they never meet — NO solution. If the y-intercepts are the SAME too, they're the same line — INFINITELY many solutions.

illustration_description: The substitution method in four steps: start with y equals two x minus one where y is alone, plug that into the other equation to get three x plus the quantity two x minus one equals nine, solve that for x to get x equals two, then back-substitute to find y equals three.
accompanying_text: Graphing is slow and imprecise. **Substitution** is exact. When one equation already says y = (something), replace y in the OTHER equation with that expression — now there's just one variable to solve.

illustration_description: The substitution method in four steps: start with y equals two x minus one where y is alone, plug that into the other equation to get three x plus the quantity two x minus one equals nine, solve that for x to get x equals two, then back-substitute to find y equals three.
accompanying_text: Worked all the way: y = 2x − 1 and 3x + y = 9. Substitute: 3x + (2x − 1) = 9 → 5x − 1 = 9 → 5x = 10 → x = 2. One variable, solved exactly — no graph needed.

illustration_description: Back-substituting: once substitution gives x equals 2, put it into y equals 2x minus 1 to find y equals 3, completing the pair. Back-substitute x = 2 to find y = 3.
accompanying_text: Substitution gives you x — but a system's solution is a POINT (x, y). To find y, **back-substitute**: plug your x back into the isolated equation (the easy y = one). Then the full solution is (x, y).

illustration_description: Back-substituting: once substitution gives x equals 2, put it into y equals 2x minus 1 to find y equals 3, completing the pair. Back-substitute x = 2 to find y = 3.
accompanying_text: Always back-substitute into the ISOLATED equation — it's already solved for y, so it's the easy one. Then CONFIRM the point in both equations to be sure. For x = 2 in y = 3x: y = 6, and (2, 6) checks in both.

illustration_description: A system is two equations sharing the same two unknowns; its solution is the single pair of values that makes both true at once. A system: two equations, one shared solution.
accompanying_text: Real problems often hide a system. When two quantities are related two different ways — like a total AND a difference — write one equation for each, then solve with substitution. Two facts, two equations, one solution.

illustration_description: Back-substituting: once substitution gives x equals 2, put it into y equals 2x minus 1 to find y equals 3, completing the pair. Back-substitute x = 2 to find y = 3.
accompanying_text: Once you have one unknown, back-substitute for the other, then answer the actual question. For x = 2 in y = 4x, the larger number is y = 8 — and 2 + 8 = 10 ✓, 8 = 4(2) ✓. Both facts check out.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: Slope measures a line's **steepness** as **rise ÷ run**: how far it climbs (rise) for how far it moves across (run). A gentle ramp has a small slope; a steep stair has a large one. Count the rise, count the run, and divide.

illustration_description: Slope is a rate of change: it says how much y changes each time x increases by one.
accompanying_text: Slope is a **rate of change**: it says how much y changes each time x increases by 1. A slope of 3 means y climbs 3 for every 1 step right. That steady rate is exactly what makes the graph a straight line.

illustration_description: The bigger the slope, the steeper the climb: slope five rises five for each step right.
accompanying_text: The **bigger** the slope, the **steeper** the climb. Slope 5 rises five units per step across; slope 2 rises only two. Same run, more rise means a steeper line.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Given two points, you don't need a grid to find slope. The **rise** is the change in y, and the **run** is the change in x. So slope = **(y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁)**. Subtract the y's on top, the matching x's on the bottom, and divide.

illustration_description: Keep the order matched: if the second point's y is on top of the fraction, the second point's x must be on the bottom.
accompanying_text: **Keep the order matched.** If you start with the second point's y on top, start with the second point's x on the bottom too. Mixing the orders flips the sign and gives the wrong slope.

illustration_description: A slope can be a fraction: a line that rises two over a run of three has slope two-thirds.
accompanying_text: A slope can be a **fraction**. If a line rises 2 over a run of 3, its slope is 2/3 — a real, valid slope, just shallower than 1. Leave it as a reduced fraction; don't round it away.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: Read the slope's **sign** from the line's direction. Going **uphill** left to right — y rising as x grows — gives a **positive** slope. Going **downhill** — y falling as x grows — gives a **negative** slope.

illustration_description: A horizontal line never rises: the y-values stay equal, so the rise is zero and the slope is zero.
accompanying_text: A **horizontal** line never rises: the y-values stay equal, so the rise is 0 and the slope is **0 ÷ run = 0**. Flat means a slope of zero — not 'no slope'.

illustration_description: A vertical line never runs: the x-values stay equal, so the run is zero and the slope is undefined.
accompanying_text: A **vertical** line never runs: the x-values stay equal, so the run is 0. Dividing by 0 is impossible, so a vertical line's slope is **undefined** — a different thing from zero.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: Most lines can be written in one tidy form: **y = mx + b**. The **m** is the **slope** — the number multiplied by x. The **b** is the **y-intercept** — the number added on, where the line crosses the y-axis. Read a line's equation and you already know how steep it is and where it starts.

illustration_description: b is the y-intercept because setting x to zero gives y equals m times zero plus b, which is b.
accompanying_text: Why is b the y-intercept? Set **x = 0**. Then y = m·0 + b = b. Every line hits the y-axis at x = 0, so the y-value there is always b. That's why b tells you where the line starts on the y-axis.

illustration_description: Both m and b can be negative or fractional, as in y equals one-half x minus three.
accompanying_text: Both m and b can be **negative** or **fractional**. In y = (1/2)x - 3, the slope is the fraction 1/2 and the y-intercept is -3. Read the coefficient of x for m, and the constant (with its sign) for b.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: You can graph **y = mx + b** without a table. **Step 1:** plot b on the y-axis — that's the point (0, b), where the line starts. **Step 2:** from there, use the slope as **rise over run** to step to the next point. **Step 3:** connect them into a line.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: The slope is your **step**. Slope 2 means **up 2, right 1**. Slope 1/3 means **up 1, right 3**. From the y-intercept, take that step to land on a second point — then a third. Same step each time keeps you on the line.

illustration_description: A negative slope steps down: for y equals negative x plus six, start at zero, six and step down one for each step right.
accompanying_text: A **negative** slope steps **down**. For y = -x + 6, start at (0, 6), then go down 1, right 1 to each next point. Positive slopes climb left-to-right; negative slopes descend.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: A slanted line crosses **both** axes. The **y-intercept** is where it crosses the y-axis — there **x = 0**, and the height is b. The **x-intercept** is where it crosses the x-axis — there **y = 0**. Two crossings, two different questions.

illustration_description: To find the x-intercept, set y to zero and solve for x, where the line crosses the horizontal axis.
accompanying_text: To find the **x-intercept**, set **y = 0** and solve for x. Take y = 2x - 8. Set 0 = 2x - 8, add 8 to get 2x = 8, divide by 2 to get x = 4. So the line crosses the x-axis at (4, 0).

illustration_description: You can build a line's equation: put the slope m in front of x, then add the intercept b.
accompanying_text: You can also **build** a line's equation. Put the slope m in front of x, and the y-intercept b at the end. Slope 3 and intercept -2 give **y = 3x - 2**. Slope first, intercept last.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: There's a form built for **one point and a slope**: **y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)**. Here (x₁, y₁) is a point the line passes through, and m is the slope. Know a point and a slope, and you can write the line straight away — the point's numbers slot into the blanks.

illustration_description: Building point-slope form: copy the point in with the same subtractions the form shows, y minus y-one equals m times x minus x-one.
accompanying_text: **Building it:** copy the point in with the same subtractions the form shows. A point (2, 5) with slope 3 becomes **y − 5 = 3(x − 2)**. The 5 and 2 are the point; the 3 is the slope out front.

illustration_description: Watch the inside signs: y plus two is really y minus negative two, so y-one is negative two.
accompanying_text: So watch the inside signs. **y + 2** is really y − (−2), so **y₁ = −2**. **x + 3** is x − (−3), so **x₁ = −3**. A plus sign inside the form is hiding a negative coordinate.

illustration_description: Point-slope and y equals m x plus b describe the same line in different clothing.
accompanying_text: Point-slope and y = mx + b describe the **same line** in different clothes. To convert, **distribute** the slope, then **add y₁** to both sides. The slope m never changes; only the constant becomes b. Shortcut: **b = y₁ − m·x₁**.

illustration_description: The shortcut in action: for y minus five equals two times x minus one, the slope stays two and b works out to three.
accompanying_text: The shortcut in action: for y − 5 = 2(x − 1), the slope stays 2 and **b = 5 − 2·1 = 3**. So the slope-intercept form is **y = 2x + 3** — no distributing needed once you trust the formula.

illustration_description: You can go backward too: given y equals m x plus b and any point the line passes through, recover point-slope form.
accompanying_text: You can go **backward** too. Given y = mx + b and any point the line passes through, write y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with that point. The y-intercept point (0, b) always works, but any known point does.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: A third way to write a line is **standard form: Ax + By = C**, with A, B, C whole numbers and A not negative. Both variables sit on the left. It hides the slope, but it makes the **intercepts** especially quick to find.

illustration_description: In standard form A x plus B y equals C, to find an intercept, zero the other variable: set y to zero for the x-intercept.
accompanying_text: The trick: to find an intercept, **zero the other variable**. Set y = 0 for the x-intercept (x = C/A); set x = 0 for the y-intercept (y = C/B). For 3x + 2y = 12: x-intercept 12/3 = 4, y-intercept 12/2 = 6.

illustration_description: To convert y equals m x plus b into standard form, move the x-term to the left so both variables sit on one side.
accompanying_text: To convert **y = mx + b into standard form**, move the x-term left and make A positive. From y = 2x − 5: subtract 2x → −2x + y = −5, then multiply by −1 → **2x − y = 5**. Clear any fractions so A, B, C are whole numbers.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: Give me one point and a slope, and I can write the whole line. The slope you're handed is already **m**. The only missing piece is **b**, and you get it from **b = y₁ − m·x₁**. Then write **y = mx + b**.

illustration_description: b can come out negative: for the point two, three with slope four, b equals three minus four times two, which is negative five.
accompanying_text: b can come out negative. For (2, 3) with slope 4: **b = 3 − 4·2 = −5**, so the line is **y = 4x − 5**. Check it — 4·2 − 5 = 3, which is the point's height. The point always lands back on the line.

illustration_description: One special case: slope zero makes a horizontal line, so b equals the y-value of the point.
accompanying_text: One special case: **slope 0** makes a **horizontal line**. Then b = y₁ − 0 = y₁, so the line is simply **y = y₁**. A line through (2, 5) with slope 0 is just **y = 5** — the same height everywhere.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Two points also fix a line. Work in order: first the **slope**, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Then use **either point** to get b = y₁ − m·x₁. Then write **y = mx + b**, and confirm both points fit.

illustration_description: Full example with the points one, one and four, ten: the slope is ten minus one over four minus one, which is nine over three, or three.
accompanying_text: Full example with (1, 1) and (4, 10): slope = (10 − 1)/(4 − 1) = **9/3 = 3**; then b = 1 − 3·1 = **−2**; so **y = 3x − 2**. Check the other point: 3·4 − 2 = 10. Both fit — the line is right.

illustration_description: Watch for a vertical line: if the two points share the same x, the run is zero and the slope is undefined.
accompanying_text: Watch for a **vertical line**: if the two points share the same x, the run is 0 and the slope is **undefined** — you can't divide by zero. The line is just **x = that value**, e.g. (3, 1) and (3, 6) give **x = 3**.

illustration_description: A rising line with a right triangle beneath a segment: the horizontal leg is the run, the vertical leg is the rise, and slope equals rise divided by run.
accompanying_text: Slope decides how two lines relate. **Parallel** lines never meet — they have the **same slope**. **Perpendicular** lines cross at a right angle — their slopes are **negative reciprocals** (flip the fraction, change the sign), so **m₁·m₂ = −1**.

illustration_description: Negative reciprocal is two moves: flip the fraction, then change the sign; two-thirds becomes negative three-halves.
accompanying_text: "Negative reciprocal" is two moves: **flip**, then **change the sign**. Slope 2 → flip to 1/2 → negate → **−1/2**. It works both ways: slope −1/2 → flip to −2 → negate → **2**. The product is always −1.

illustration_description: To write a parallel or perpendicular line through a point, pick the right slope, then plug the point into point-slope form.
accompanying_text: To **write** a parallel or perpendicular line through a point: pick the right slope (same for parallel, negative reciprocal for perpendicular), then find **b = y₁ − m·x₁** exactly as before. The point and the new slope give the full equation.

illustration_description: The four building blocks of geometry: a point is a dot, a line has arrows on both ends, a ray has one endpoint and one arrow, and a segment has two endpoints. Point, line, ray, and segment.
accompanying_text: Four building blocks of geometry. A **point** is an exact location — no size, just a spot, named with a capital letter. A **line** stretches forever in both directions. A **line segment** is a piece of a line with two definite endpoints. A **ray** starts at one point and shoots forever in a single direction.

illustration_description: The four building blocks of geometry: a point is a dot, a line has arrows on both ends, a ray has one endpoint and one arrow, and a segment has two endpoints. Point, line, ray, and segment.
accompanying_text: The endpoint count is the whole trick: **0 endpoints = line, 1 endpoint = ray, 2 endpoints = line segment.** Every shape's edge, every fence line, every beam of light fits one of these three.

illustration_description: Two rays sharing an endpoint form an angle; the shared point is the vertex and the angle opens between the two rays. Two rays from one vertex make an angle.
accompanying_text: You already measured angles in degrees. Now name their parts: an angle forms where two rays share a starting point, called the **vertex.** The two rays themselves are the angle's **sides.** Every angle you measured was really two rays meeting at a vertex.

illustration_description: Two rays sharing an endpoint form an angle; the shared point is the vertex and the angle opens between the two rays. Two rays from one vertex make an angle.
accompanying_text: Angles get precise names using three points: one on each ray, with the **vertex always in the middle.** Angle ABC means a ray toward A, the vertex at B, and a ray toward C. Swap the outer letters and it's still the same angle — but the vertex letter never moves from the middle.

illustration_description: Two rays sharing an endpoint form an angle; the shared point is the vertex and the angle opens between the two rays. Two rays from one vertex make an angle.
accompanying_text: Real figures mix every term you've learned: points, rays, angles, all at once. Reading one means checking each piece against what you know — how many endpoints, is there a shared vertex, what's the angle's name.

illustration_description: Two rays sharing an endpoint form an angle; the shared point is the vertex and the angle opens between the two rays. Two rays from one vertex make an angle.
accompanying_text: A figure can hide several angles at once. If three rays share vertex P, going toward Q, R, and S, that's actually THREE separate angles: QPR, RPS, and QPS (the two smaller ones combined).

illustration_description: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet, marked with matching arrowheads. Parallel lines never meet.
accompanying_text: **Parallel lines** stay exactly the same distance apart, forever — no matter how far you extend them, they never touch. Railroad tracks are the classic example: the two rails never get closer or farther apart, and never cross.

illustration_description: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet, marked with matching arrowheads. Parallel lines never meet.
accompanying_text: Diagrams mark parallel lines with matching arrow symbols — a single arrowhead (›) on each line in one parallel pair, double arrowheads (››) on a different pair. The matching arrows tell you which lines belong together.

illustration_description: Perpendicular lines cross at exactly a right angle, marked by a small square at the crossing. Perpendicular lines cross at a right angle.
accompanying_text: **Perpendicular lines** cross at exactly 90° — a right angle, the same benchmark from Course 9. Diagrams mark the crossing with a small square symbol, not an arrow. A plus sign (+) is the classic perpendicular shape.

illustration_description: Perpendicular lines cross at exactly a right angle, marked by a small square at the crossing. Perpendicular lines cross at a right angle.
accompanying_text: The word **'exactly'** matters, just like Course 9's angle boundaries. Two lines crossing at 89° are close, but not perpendicular — only a true 90° crossing counts. 'Almost perpendicular' isn't a real category.

illustration_description: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet, marked with matching arrowheads. Parallel lines never meet.
accompanying_text: Real figures often hide BOTH relationships at once. A rectangle's **opposite sides are parallel** (top-bottom, left-right); its **adjacent sides are perpendicular** (each corner is a 90° crossing). One shape, two relationships.

illustration_description: Perpendicular lines cross at exactly a right angle, marked by a small square at the crossing. Perpendicular lines cross at a right angle.
accompanying_text: A tic-tac-toe grid hides the same idea at a bigger scale: the 2 horizontal lines are parallel to each other, the 2 vertical lines are parallel to each other, and every horizontal-vertical crossing is perpendicular.

illustration_description: Three angle families: acute is under 90 degrees, right is exactly 90 degrees shown with a square corner mark, obtuse is over 90 degrees.
accompanying_text: A triangle's **largest angle** names its family, reusing the acute/right/obtuse vocabulary you already know. **Acute triangle:** every angle under 90°. **Right triangle:** one angle exactly 90°. **Obtuse triangle:** one angle over 90°.

illustration_description: A triangle can have at most one right or obtuse angle; the acute triangle has three sharp angles, the right triangle one square corner, the obtuse one wide angle. A triangle has at most one right or obtuse angle.
accompanying_text: A triangle can have **at most one** angle of 90° or more. Why? All three angles must add to 180° — if two angles were each 90° or more, they alone would total 180° or beyond, leaving nothing (or less) for the third.

illustration_description: A triangle's three angles always add to 180 degrees; torn off and placed together they form a straight line. A triangle's angles sum to 180°.
accompanying_text: Every triangle, no matter its shape, has three angles that add up to exactly **180°** — the same total as angles on a straight line. Tear off a triangle's three corners and line them up, and they form a straight line.

illustration_description: A triangle's three angles always add to 180 degrees; torn off and placed together they form a straight line. A triangle's angles sum to 180°.
accompanying_text: This works for **every** triangle — tiny or huge, acute, right, or obtuse. The 180° total never changes, even though the individual angles can be almost anything, as long as they add up right.

illustration_description: Four different four-sided shapes: a square, a rectangle, a trapezoid, and a slanted quadrilateral, all belonging to the quadrilateral family because each has four sides. The quadrilateral family: every shape has four sides.
accompanying_text: Remember shapes as members-only clubs with entry rules? A **rectangle's** entry rule is angle-based: **all four angles must be exactly 90°.** A quadrilateral missing that rule — even by one angle — doesn't get into the rectangle club, though it's still a quadrilateral.

illustration_description: Four different four-sided shapes: a square, a rectangle, a trapezoid, and a slanted quadrilateral, all belonging to the quadrilateral family because each has four sides. The quadrilateral family: every shape has four sides.
accompanying_text: A quadrilateral can have **any number** of right angles — zero, one, two, or four (never exactly three, since the fourth would then be forced to also equal 90° by the shape's angle total). Fewer than four just means a different family, not a failed shape.

illustration_description: A shape has a line of symmetry if folding along that line makes the two halves match; a heart folds evenly down the middle. A line of symmetry folds the halves to match.
accompanying_text: A shape has a **line of symmetry** if folding along that line makes both halves land exactly on top of each other — like a mirror. A square folded straight down the middle matches perfectly. A random scribbled shape usually doesn't.

illustration_description: A shape has a line of symmetry if folding along that line makes the two halves match; a heart folds evenly down the middle. A line of symmetry folds the halves to match.
accompanying_text: Not every line through a shape works. A square has SOME lines that produce a match (straight down the middle, or corner to corner) and infinitely many that don't (any random slanted line off-center). Only the special ones count as symmetry lines.

illustration_description: A regular shape has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides: a square has four and an equilateral triangle has three. A regular shape's symmetry lines equal its sides.
accompanying_text: A **regular shape** (every side and angle equal) has exactly as many symmetry lines as it has sides. An equilateral triangle: 3 sides, 3 symmetry lines. A square: 4 sides, 4 symmetry lines. A regular pentagon: 5 sides, 5 symmetry lines.

illustration_description: A regular shape has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides: a square has four and an equilateral triangle has three. A regular shape's symmetry lines equal its sides.
accompanying_text: Shapes that AREN'T regular can have fewer symmetry lines. A rectangle (unequal sides) has only **2** — the horizontal and vertical center lines. Its diagonals do NOT produce a match, since folding along one would need the two different side lengths to line up, which they can't.

illustration_description: Symmetry in letters: A has a vertical line of symmetry and folds to match, but N has no line of symmetry even though it looks balanced. Letter A is symmetric; N is not.
accompanying_text: Symmetry hides in everyday letters too. Using standard block capital letters: **A** has a vertical line of symmetry (left-right mirror). **H** has both a vertical AND a horizontal line. **F** has none at all.

illustration_description: Symmetry in letters: A has a vertical line of symmetry and folds to match, but N has no line of symmetry even though it looks balanced. Letter A is symmetric; N is not.
accompanying_text: Watch out for a trap: the letter **N** looks like it might have symmetry because spinning it 180° looks the same. But that's **rotational** symmetry (a spin), a completely different idea from **line** symmetry (a fold). No single fold line makes N's two halves match.

illustration_description: Two to the x equals eight solves by matching bases, but two to the x equals ten has no whole-number power, so it needs a logarithm.
accompanying_text: You can solve 2^x = 8 by matching bases. But 2^x = 10? No power of 2 matches. Math's answer is a new function: **log₂ 10 means 'the exponent that turns 2 into 10.'** In general: **log_b x = y  ⟺  b^y = x**. A logarithm IS an exponent — nothing more exotic.

illustration_description: Every log statement has a twin exponential statement: log base b of y equals x means b to the x equals y.
accompanying_text: Every log statement has a twin exponential statement, and converting between them is the core skill. log₅ 25 = 2 twins with 5² = 25. Going the other way: 3⁴ = 81 twins with log₃ 81 = 4. **Base stays the base; the log's output is the exponent.**

illustration_description: Three instant values every log shares: log base b of one is zero, log base b of b is one, and log base b of b to the x is x.
accompanying_text: Three instant values every log shares. **log_b 1 = 0** (anything to the 0 is 1). **log_b b = 1** (b¹ = b). And **log_b of a fraction can go negative**: log₂ (1/8) = −3 because 2⁻³ = 1/8. The log's output ranges over ALL real numbers — negatives included.

illustration_description: Two more families: base ten is the common log written just log, and base e is the natural log written l n.
accompanying_text: Two more families. **Base 10** is so common it hides its subscript: log 1000 = 3 (it's log₁₀). And fractional INSIDES pair with negative exponents: log₃ (1/9) = −2 since 3⁻² = 1/9. Fractional ANSWERS appear too: log₉ 3 = 1/2, because 9^(1/2) = √9 = 3 — rational exponents, straight from Radical Functions.

illustration_description: Two curves mirrored across the dashed diagonal line y equals x. The exponential y equals 2 to the x sweeps up steeply. Its reflection, y equals log base 2 of x, rises slowly to the right of its vertical asymptote at x equals 0. The point 1 comma 2 on the exponential mirrors to 2 comma 1 on the logarithm — inputs and outputs trade places.
accompanying_text: Because log₂ x undoes 2^x, its graph is the exponential's **mirror image across the line y = x** — inputs and outputs trade places. (1, 2) on the exponential becomes (2, 1) on the log. The mirror flips the exponential's horizontal asymptote into a **vertical asymptote at x = 0**.

illustration_description: The swap dictates everything: the log is the exponential's mirror across y equals x, trading domain for range.
accompanying_text: The swap dictates everything. The exponential's domain (all reals) becomes the log's **range** (all reals); the exponential's range (y > 0) becomes the log's **domain: x > 0**. Zero and negatives have no logarithm — no exponent turns 2 into −4 or into 0. The graph hugs its wall at x = 0, exactly like last course's vertical asymptotes.

illustration_description: Exponent rules become log rules, because logs are exponents in disguise.
accompanying_text: Exponent rules become log rules — because logs ARE exponents. Multiplying powers ADDS exponents (2³ · 2⁴ = 2⁷), so logs of products split into sums: **log_b (MN) = log_b M + log_b N**. Check: log₂ (8 · 4) = log₂ 32 = 5, and log₂ 8 + log₂ 4 = 3 + 2 = 5. ✓

illustration_description: The product property: the log of a product is the sum of the logs.
accompanying_text: The property runs both directions. **Expand:** log₂ (8x) = log₂ 8 + log₂ x = 3 + log₂ x. **Condense:** log 5 + log 20 = log (5 · 20) = log 100 = 2. Condensing often turns ugly pieces into a clean whole — 5 and 20 alone have messy logs; their product doesn't.

illustration_description: Division subtracts exponents, so the log of a quotient is a difference of logs.
accompanying_text: Two more exponent rules translate. Division subtracts exponents, so **log_b (M/N) = log_b M − log_b N**. And a power multiplies its exponent, so **log_b (Mᵖ) = p · log_b M** — the exponent inside marches out front. Check: log₂ (8²) = log₂ 64 = 6 = 2 · 3. ✓

illustration_description: The power property is the workhorse: the log of x to the n is n times the log of x.
accompanying_text: The power property is the workhorse of the whole subject: it drags an unknown **down from the exponent**. log₂ (x⁵) = 5 log₂ x — and later, taking log of both sides of 2^x = 10 will pull the x down where algebra can reach it. Special case: roots. log₉ (√9) = log₉ (9^(1/2)) = **1/2**.

illustration_description: Expanding unpacks one log into a sum or difference of simpler logs.
accompanying_text: **Expanding** unpacks one log into a sum/difference of simple logs — outside-in: quotient first, then products, then powers. **Condensing** reverses it — coefficients become powers FIRST, then sums merge into products and differences into quotients. Two directions, opposite orders.

illustration_description: Order matters when condensing: coefficients become exponents first, then combine into one log.
accompanying_text: Order matters when condensing: **coefficients become exponents before anything merges**. 3 log₂ x − log₂ y: first 3 log₂ x = log₂ (x³), then the difference divides: **log₂ (x³/y)**. Merging first (log₂(x/y) then cubing everything) would wrongly cube the y too.

illustration_description: Calculators offer only common log and natural log, so the change-of-base formula rewrites any base as a ratio.
accompanying_text: Calculators usually offer only log (base 10) and ln. The **change-of-base formula** unlocks every other base: **log_b x = (log x)/(log b)** — any base upstairs and downstairs, as long as they match. So log₂ 10 = (log 10)/(log 2) = 1/0.301 ≈ **3.32**.

illustration_description: Why it works: let y equal log base b of x, so b to the y is x; taking a log of both sides isolates y.
accompanying_text: Why does it work? Let y = log_b x, so bʸ = x. Take log (base 10) of both sides: y · log b = log x — the power property drags y down. Divide: y = (log x)/(log b). The formula is just the power property doing equation work — a preview of this whole chapter.

illustration_description: For two to the x equals ten, the tool is to take the log of both sides and bring the exponent down.
accompanying_text: Base-matching solved 2^x = 8. For 2^x = 10, the tool is **take the log of both sides**: log(2^x) = log 10, and the power property pulls x down — x · log 2 = log 10, so x = (log 10)/(log 2) ≈ **3.32**. Notice: that's exactly log₂ 10 by change of base. Same answer, two roads.

illustration_description: Full pipeline with a coefficient: five times two to the x equals eighty; isolate to get two to the x equals sixteen, so x is four.
accompanying_text: Full pipeline with a coefficient: 5 · 2^x = 80. **Isolate the power first** (divide by 5): 2^x = 16 — oh, that one matches bases: x = 4. But 5 · 2^x = 90 → 2^x = 18 → x = (log 18)/(log 2) ≈ 4.17. Isolate, then match if you can, log if you can't.

illustration_description: When the log holds the unknown, convert to exponential form to free it.
accompanying_text: When the LOG holds the unknown, **convert to exponential form**: log₂(x − 3) = 4 means x − 3 = 2⁴ = 16, so x = **19**. Check in the original: log₂ 16 = 4. ✓ One conversion, then ordinary algebra — the definition from Chapter 1 doing equation work.

illustration_description: Logs on both sides with the same base: equal logs mean equal arguments.
accompanying_text: Logs on **both sides** with the same base? Equal logs mean equal insides: log₅(2x − 1) = log₅(x + 4) forces 2x − 1 = x + 4, so x = 5. But logs bring their **domain**: every inside must end up **positive**. Candidates that leave any inside ≤ 0 are extraneous — the radical-equations discipline, back again.

illustration_description: Four bars show the value of one dollar after a year at 100 percent interest, compounded more and more often: yearly gives 2 dollars, quarterly about 2.44, monthly about 2.61, daily about 2.71. The bars rise toward — but never pass — a dashed line at e, approximately 2.718.
accompanying_text: Compound $1 at 100% interest: once a year gives $2. Twice a year: (1 + 1/2)² = $2.25. Monthly: ≈ $2.613. Daily: ≈ $2.7146. Compounding **continuously** — infinitely often — the value stops climbing at a specific number: **e ≈ 2.71828**, the natural base of growth.

illustration_description: Why care about one weird constant: e is the base of continuous growth, about two point seven one eight.
accompanying_text: Why care about one weird constant? Because e is the base of **smooth, continuous change** — populations, radioactive decay, cooling coffee, interest compounding every instant. The function f(x) = eˣ is an ordinary exponential (base ≈ 2.718 > 1: growth), sitting between 2ˣ and 3ˣ.

illustration_description: Every base gets a log, and e's is famous enough to earn its own name: the natural log, l n.
accompanying_text: Every base gets a log; e's is famous enough to earn its own name: **ln x = log_e x**, the natural log. Same machine as Chapter 1 — ln x asks 'e to what power gives x?' So **ln 1 = 0**, **ln e = 1**, and ln(e⁵) = 5. On calculators, ln sits right beside log.

illustration_description: Natural log and e to the x undo each other in both directions: l n of e to the x is x, and e to the l n x is x.
accompanying_text: ln and eˣ **undo each other in both directions**: ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x (for x > 0). And every property from Chapter 2 carries over unchanged: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b, ln(aⁿ) = n ln a. Nothing new to memorize — just a new base wearing a short name.

illustration_description: With the unknown in the exponent of e, take the natural log of both sides.
accompanying_text: Chapter 3's playbook, natural edition. Unknown in the **exponent**? Take ln of both sides: eˣ = 10 → x = **ln 10** (≈ 2.303). Unknown inside a **log**? Exponentiate: ln x = 2 → x = **e²** (≈ 7.389). Each tool summons its inverse.

illustration_description: With structure around the power, isolate the exponential first, then apply the natural log.
accompanying_text: With structure around the power, **isolate first** — the standing rule. 5e^(2x) = 20: divide by 5 → e^(2x) = 4 → take ln → 2x = ln 4 → x = (ln 4)/2. And since ln 4 = 2 ln 2, that's exactly **ln 2 ≈ 0.693**. The properties keep simplifying after the solve.

illustration_description: The all-purpose continuous model: amount equals principal times e to the rate times time.
accompanying_text: The all-purpose continuous model: **A = P·e^(rt)** — P the start, r the continuous rate (negative for decay), t the time. $500 at 6% for 10 years: A = 500·e^0.6 ≈ 500 · 1.822 = **$911**. Algebra 1's a·bˣ models, upgraded to compound every instant.

illustration_description: Read the anatomy: in A equals three hundred times e to the zero point zero eight t, the start is three hundred and the rate is eight percent.
accompanying_text: Read the anatomy: in A = 300·e^(0.08t), the start is **300** (t = 0 makes e⁰ = 1) and the continuous rate is **8%**. A negative rate flips it to decay: A = P·e^(−0.10t) shrinks continuously at 10%. Same skeleton either way — the exponent's sign tells the story.

illustration_description: Radioactive decay runs on a half-life: every half-life period the quantity halves.
accompanying_text: Radioactive decay runs on a **half-life** h: every h units of time, half the sample survives. The model: **N = N₀ · (1/2)^(t/h)**. Iodine-131's half-life is 8 days; 160 mg after 24 days is 3 half-lives: 160 → 80 → 40 → **20 mg**. The exponent t/h counts the halvings.

illustration_description: Fractional half-lives run through the formula's exponent: raise one-half to the number of half-lives elapsed.
accompanying_text: Fractional half-lives run through the formula's exponent. After 4 days with h = 8: N = 160·(1/2)^(4/8) = 160·(1/2)^(1/2) ≈ 160 · 0.707 ≈ 113 mg — about **71% survives** at the halfway mark, not 75%, because decay compounds. And 'how long?' questions fall to ln, exactly like every exponential equation.

illustration_description: A ladder comparing a log scale to the quantity it measures. Magnitudes 3, 4, 5, and 6 climb by equal steps of one, but the bars beside them grow by a factor of ten each step: times 1, times 10, times 100, times 1000. Equal steps on the scale mean equal multiplications underneath.
accompanying_text: Some quantities span such vast ranges that scientists measure their **logarithms** instead. On a log scale, **each step of 1 means ×10 underneath**: a magnitude-6 earthquake shakes 10 times harder than a magnitude 5, and 100 times harder than a magnitude 4. Equal steps, equal multiplications.

illustration_description: pH runs the same way: each pH step is a factor of ten in acidity, on a logarithmic scale.
accompanying_text: pH runs the same way (each pH step = ×10 in acidity, downward: pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4), and decibels use steps of 10 dB per ×10 of intensity. Converting is always the same move: **factor = 10^(difference in scale readings)** — and backwards, **difference = log(factor)**.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Before dividing by a two-digit number, size the answer with compatible numbers: 552 ÷ 24 is near 600 ÷ 25, which is 24.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Compatible numbers are chosen because they divide CLEANLY, not merely because they are round. That is what makes the estimate instant.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A divisor that is a multiple of ten splits into two easy steps: dividing by 30 is dividing by 3 and then by 10.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This is place value doing the work again — the same shortcut that makes multiplying by tens easy runs in reverse.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Partial quotients counts the groups in whatever batches are convenient: take 20 groups of 24, then 3 more, and total them.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The batches need not be equal or tidy. All that matters is that they are all counted, because the quotient is simply how many groups came out.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The standard algorithm counts the same groups, but fixes the batches by place value — one digit at a time, largest place first.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: That makes it compact and quick, and also less forgiving: a digit placed one column out is wrong by a factor of ten.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Trial digits with a two-digit divisor are guesses, and guessing too high is routine: if 4 × 24 = 96 exceeds the 88 available, lower the digit to 3.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Adjusting is part of the method, not a sign of failure. The algorithm never leaves a negative remainder.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The check has two halves: quotient times divisor plus remainder must rebuild the dividend, and the remainder must be smaller than the divisor.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: If the remainder reaches the divisor, another whole group fits and the quotient was too small — the second half of the check catches exactly that.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Objects hide many amounts at once: how LONG, how HEAVY, how MUCH they hold. Each amount is an attribute, and each can be measured.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Pick the attribute first, then the tool: a ruler for length, a seesaw for weight, a scoop for what fits inside.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Length wears many words: a snake is LONG, a tower TALL, a pencil stub SHORT. All describe one attribute — distance end to end.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Tall is length standing up; long is length lying down. Turn the tower sideways and tall becomes long.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Weight has its own words: HEAVY presses down hard, LIGHT barely presses at all. The seesaw turns that pressing into something you can see.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Down means heavier, up means lighter, level means equal — the seesaw's three answers.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Containers hold different amounts. HOLDS MORE and HOLDS LESS compare capacity — the room inside — which eyes alone often misjudge.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The fair test is filling: one same scoop, count the scoops each container swallows, compare the counts.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: To compare two lengths, put them side by side from ONE start line, then read the far ends: the one reaching farther is longer.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The unit ticks let you say by HOW MUCH: count each length in cubes and compare the counts.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: To compare two weights, load one on each pan and read the tilt: the sinking side is heavier, the rising side lighter.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A level beam is an answer too — it says the weights are EQUAL, neither side winning.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The oldest length trick: give one ribbon a head start and it LOOKS longer. Fair comparing means lining the starting ends up first.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
