accompanying_text: Align first, judge second. Once the starts agree, the far ends tell the truth.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Standing things compare by the same rule turned upright: same floor as the start line, and the top that reaches higher is TALLER.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The floor does the aligning for you — which is why towers are easy to compare and ribbons are not.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Sorting asks ONE question of every object — red or not? round or not? — and the answers build the groups.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Change the rule and the groups change: a red sock joins the red pile under a color rule, the clothing pile under a kind rule.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Size is a sorting rule too: BIG in one group, SMALL in the other. The rule must say where big begins before sorting.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Size-sorting is not length-measuring — it asks a yes-or-no question, not a how-many question.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: After the sort, count each group: touch and count the reds, then the blues. Each group earns its own number.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The counts turn piles into data — three groups become three numbers, ready for comparing.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: With every group counted, the last question answers itself: the group with the greatest count has the MOST; the least count, the FEWEST.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Sort, count, compare — the full chain. The counts do the comparing; the shapes' sizes never vote.

illustration_description: Metric prefix badges show a unit's size: kilo means one thousand, centi means one hundredth, and milli means one thousandth. Metric prefixes: kilo, centi, milli.
accompanying_text: Remember the kilo-badge from big numbers? A kilogram works exactly the same way: **kilo means ×1000.** 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams. The same badge that turned a thousand into 'kilo' on a big number now turns a thousand grams into one kilogram.

illustration_description: Metric prefix badges show a unit's size: kilo means one thousand, centi means one hundredth, and milli means one thousandth. Metric prefixes: kilo, centi, milli.
accompanying_text: Here's the useful part: the badge works **no matter what you're measuring.** Kilo means ×1000 whether it's attached to grams (mass), meters (length), or anything else. One badge system, many quantities — that's the whole point of the metric system.

illustration_description: The metric length ladder: 10 millimeters make a centimeter, 100 centimeters make a meter, and 1000 meters make a kilometer. The length ladder: mm, cm, m, km.
accompanying_text: The length ladder: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1,000 m = 1 km. Each step is its own badge. To convert, multiply when going from a bigger unit to a smaller one, and divide when going from smaller to bigger.

illustration_description: The metric length ladder: 10 millimeters make a centimeter, 100 centimeters make a meter, and 1000 meters make a kilometer. The length ladder: mm, cm, m, km.
accompanying_text: Some conversions need **two hops.** To go from meters to millimeters directly, combine both badges: 100 cm/m × 10 mm/cm = 1,000 mm per meter. So 1 km to cm hops through meters: 1 km = 1,000 m = 1,000×100 = 100,000 cm.

illustration_description: The kilo badge works for mass and volume too: 1000 grams make a kilogram and 1000 milliliters make a liter. Mass and volume: 1000 g = 1 kg, 1000 mL = 1 L.
accompanying_text: The same kilo badge you just used for length works for mass and volume too. **1,000 grams = 1 kilogram. 1,000 milliliters = 1 liter.** Same ×1000 rule, just measuring weight and liquid instead of distance.

illustration_description: The kilo badge works for mass and volume too: 1000 grams make a kilogram and 1000 milliliters make a liter. Mass and volume: 1000 g = 1 kg, 1000 mL = 1 L.
accompanying_text: Picking the right unit matters in real life. You'd measure an elephant's weight in **kilograms**, not grams (the number would be absurdly huge) — and a raindrop in **milliliters**, not liters (the number would be a tiny fraction). Choose the unit that keeps the number reasonable.

illustration_description: The area formula: for a rectangle, area equals length times width, so a 5 by 3 rectangle has an area of 15 square units. Area = length × width = 15.
accompanying_text: You already know area from counting unit squares tiled inside a rectangle. That counting has a name: the **AREA FORMULA — length × width.** An 8-by-6 rectangle has 8×6=48 unit squares, no counting required.

illustration_description: The area formula: for a rectangle, area equals length times width, so a 5 by 3 rectangle has an area of 15 square units. Area = length × width = 15.
accompanying_text: For bigger rectangles, reuse the break-apart trick from Course 6: split one side into tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add. 23×14 splits into 23×10 + 23×4 = 230+92 = **322.**

illustration_description: A rectangle with its four side lengths labelled and arrows walking around the edge, the perimeter being the total distance around. Perimeter is the distance around the edge.
accompanying_text: Remember walking the fence — tracing every side and adding the distances? That has a formula name too: **PERIMETER = 2 × (length + width).** For a 6-by-4 rectangle: 2×(6+4)=2×10=**20.** Two lengths, two widths, walked all the way around.

illustration_description: A rectangle with its four side lengths labelled and arrows walking around the edge, the perimeter being the total distance around. Perimeter is the distance around the edge.
accompanying_text: Area and perimeter move **independently.** A 3-by-8 rectangle and a 5-by-6 rectangle both have perimeter 22 — but their areas are 24 and 30. Same fence length, different amount of grass inside. One never tells you the other.

illustration_description: The area formula: for a rectangle, area equals length times width, so a 5 by 3 rectangle has an area of 15 square units. Area = length × width = 15.
accompanying_text: Word problems hide the formula in their verbs. **Covering, tiling, carpeting, painting** — that's surface, so it's **area.** **Fencing, framing, bordering, trimming** — that's the distance around, so it's **perimeter.** Spot the verb, pick the formula.

illustration_description: A rectangle with its four side lengths labelled and arrows walking around the edge, the perimeter being the total distance around. Perimeter is the distance around the edge.
accompanying_text: Fencing and framing signal perimeter instead. And for bigger dimensions, area calculations may need the break-apart trick from Course 6 — the story decides the formula, and the numbers decide whether you need to split them apart.

illustration_description: A degree measures an angle's turn: a full turn is 360 degrees, a quarter turn is a right angle of 90 degrees, and half of that is 45 degrees. A right angle is 90°; half is 45°.
accompanying_text: An angle's size is measured in **degrees.** A full turn all the way around is **360°.** Cut that turn exactly in half, and you get a **straight angle: 180°.** Cut it in half again, and you get a **right angle: 90°** — the same halving idea from fractions, now measuring a turn instead of a pizza.

illustration_description: A degree measures an angle's turn: a full turn is 360 degrees, a quarter turn is a right angle of 90 degrees, and half of that is 45 degrees. A right angle is 90°; half is 45°.
accompanying_text: The halving keeps going. Half of a right angle (90°) is **45°** — the diagonal angle you'd see cutting a square corner exactly in two. Same fraction-halving move, one more step down.

illustration_description: A protractor is a half-circle scale from 0 to 180 degrees; lining up the vertex and baseline reads an angle's exact degree measure. A protractor reads degrees from 0 to 180.
accompanying_text: A protractor counts the exact degrees between two rays. Here's a tool you already own: a **clock face.** A full trip around the clock is 360°, split into 12 equal hours — so each hour mark is 360÷12=**30°.** The angle from 12 to 3 o'clock spans 3 hours: 3×30=90°.

illustration_description: A protractor is a half-circle scale from 0 to 180 degrees; lining up the vertex and baseline reads an angle's exact degree measure. A protractor reads degrees from 0 to 180.
accompanying_text: A real protractor just measures more precisely than whole clock-hours — counting single degrees instead of 30° jumps. But the idea is identical: count how many degree-units fit between the two rays, whatever size those units are.

illustration_description: Four angle families sorted by size: acute is less than 90 degrees, right is exactly 90, obtuse is between 90 and 180, and straight is exactly 180. Acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles.
accompanying_text: Every angle sorts into one of four families, compared to two benchmarks — 90° and 180°. **Acute:** less than 90°. **Right:** exactly 90°. **Obtuse:** between 90° and 180°. **Straight:** exactly 180°.

illustration_description: Four angle families sorted by size: acute is less than 90 degrees, right is exactly 90, obtuse is between 90 and 180, and straight is exactly 180. Acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles.
accompanying_text: The boundaries are **exact**, not approximate. 90° is always right — never 'almost right.' 89° and 91° are both a full family away from 90°: acute and obtuse. One degree can flip the classification.

illustration_description: Two angles side by side sharing a ray add together: a 30 degree angle next to a 40 degree angle makes a 70 degree angle. Adjacent angles add: 30° + 40° = 70°.
accompanying_text: Two angles sitting side by side, sharing a ray, **add together** to make one bigger angle. A 30° angle next to a 60° angle makes a combined angle of 30°+60°=**90°.** Angles combine exactly like any other measurement — just add.

illustration_description: Two angles side by side sharing a ray add together: a 30 degree angle next to a 40 degree angle makes a 70 degree angle. Adjacent angles add: 30° + 40° = 70°.
accompanying_text: The combined angle can be **any size** — it doesn't have to land on a benchmark like 90° or 180°. A 25° angle next to a 35° angle simply makes 25°+35°=60°, nothing special required.

illustration_description: Finding a missing angle by subtracting: if a right angle of 90 degrees splits into 55 degrees and an unknown, the unknown is 90 minus 55 equals 35 degrees. Missing angle: 90° − 55° = 35°.
accompanying_text: Here's a named rule worth memorizing: **angles on a straight line always add up to 180°.** If you know one angle and the line's total, subtract to find what's missing. One angle is 110°: the other is 180−110=**70°.**

illustration_description: Finding a missing angle by subtracting: if a right angle of 90 degrees splits into 55 degrees and an unknown, the unknown is 90 minus 55 equals 35 degrees. Missing angle: 90° − 55° = 35°.
accompanying_text: The same subtracting move works for a **right angle split into two parts** — but now the target is 90°, not 180°. A right angle split with one part 35°: the other part is 90−35=**55°.**

illustration_description: Three benchmark angles form a toolkit: a right angle of 90 degrees, a straight angle of 180 degrees, and a full turn of 360 degrees. Benchmark angles: 90°, 180°, 360°.
accompanying_text: The pattern extends one more step: **angles all the way around a single point total 360°** — a full turn. Three known angles: 100°, 120°, and 90° sum to 310°; the missing fourth angle is 360−310=**50°.**

illustration_description: Three benchmark angles form a toolkit: a right angle of 90 degrees, a straight angle of 180 degrees, and a full turn of 360 degrees. Benchmark angles: 90°, 180°, 360°.
accompanying_text: Three benchmarks, one toolkit: a **right angle** totals 90°, a **straight line** totals 180°, and **all the way around a point** totals 360°. Reading the figure's description tells you which one applies.

accompanying_text: A ruler marked in eighths has a tick at every 1/8 inch: 1/8, 2/8, 3/8, all the way to 8/8 (one whole inch). Measuring means finding the **nearest** tick — the same rounding idea as whole numbers, just applied to eighth-inch marks.

illustration_description: A ruler marked in eighths: a measurement landing on the sixth tick reads six eighths, which simplifies to three fourths of an inch. Reading eighths: 6/8 = 3/4 inch.
accompanying_text: Once you've read the eighths, simplify if you can — reusing the greatest-common-factor skill. 6/8 shares a factor of 2 with 8, so it simplifies to **3/4.**

accompanying_text: A finished line plot answers real questions. Eight button widths were measured: 1/4 (×2), 3/8 (×1), 1/2 (×3), 5/8 (×1), 3/4 (×1). To answer 'how many,' count marks; to find a difference or a combined length, reuse fraction addition and subtraction.

accompanying_text: Finding the **difference** between the longest and shortest measurement reuses fraction subtraction from before: the longest button is 3/4, the shortest is 1/4, so 3/4−1/4=2/4, which simplifies to **1/2.**

accompanying_text: If A is longer than B, and B is longer than C, then A must be longer than C. The chain never breaks.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: To measure with units, lay same-size units end to end along the object, starting at its edge. The number of units is the length.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Measuring is covering: the units must start where the object starts and continue to where it ends.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Units must touch exactly: no gaps and no overlaps. A gap leaves length uncounted; an overlap counts the same length twice.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This is the rule that makes a count trustworthy. Break it and the number no longer describes the object.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Once the object is covered, the length is simply the number of units used. Count them carefully, one per placement.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The count is a description of the object: it says how many of that unit fit along it.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Cubes make good units because they are all the same size and stack end to end without gaps.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Any object can serve as a unit if every copy is identical — that sameness is what makes counting meaningful.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Paper clips work as units too, as long as every clip is the same size. The unit does not have to be a cube.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Different units give different counts for the same object — and both counts are correct, because each names its own unit.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.

accompanying_text: Liquid volume follows the pattern too: a liter holds 1,000 milliliters, so 4 L is 4,000 mL and 6,000 mL is 6 L.

accompanying_text: Time intervals work the same way: five shifts of 30 minutes is 150 minutes, and finishing 20 minutes early leaves 130.

accompanying_text: When the answer is wanted in hours, convert AFTER building the total — one conversion at the end beats several along the way.

accompanying_text: Money problems are measurement problems with dollars as the unit: nine passes at 25 dollars build 225, and a 40-dollar voucher leaves 185.

accompanying_text: The structure is identical to laps and shifts — equal groups first, single adjustment second.

accompanying_text: Measurements often land between whole units. A line plot in quarter-inches records eight marks at 1/4, and four of them rebuild one inch.

accompanying_text: Smaller pieces mean a bigger count — exactly the rule from converting units, now applied inside a single unit.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Multi-step measurement problems chain everything: build a total from equal groups, adjust it, then convert the result to the unit asked for.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Do the steps in that order and each one stays simple. Convert first and you carry awkward numbers through every later step.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A diagram makes the plan visible: equal parts for the groups, a crossed-off piece for what comes away, and a label for the unit.

accompanying_text: Where the crossing sits is the whole question — at the end of the bar it happens once, inside every part it happens to each group.

illustration_description: A clock at 3 o'clock with a short red hour hand pointing to 3 and a long blue minute hand pointing to 12. Two hands, two jobs: hour and minute.
accompanying_text: A clock has two hands with two different jobs. The **SHORT hand names the hour** — a slow walker, passing one number per hour. The **LONG hand counts minutes** — a fast walker, lapping the whole face every hour. Read short first, long second.

illustration_description: A clock whose numbers are relabelled in fives: 1 means 5 minutes, 2 means 10, up to 12 meaning 60, the minute hand's secret code. The minute code: each number counts by five.
accompanying_text: The minute hand has a secret code: the numbers 1–12 work **double shifts**. For the minute hand, each number is worth FIVE minutes — pointing at 3 means 15, at 6 means 30, at 9 means 45. Count by fives around the face.

illustration_description: The same moment named two ways: 7:50 is also ten minutes to eight, because 60 minus 50 equals 10. 7:50 is the same as ten to eight.
accompanying_text: Times have two ways of being said. **7:50 is also 'ten TO eight'** — ten minutes before the next hour. Early in the hour we count PAST the old hour; late in the hour we usually count TO the new one. Same moment, two names.

illustration_description: The same moment named two ways: 7:50 is also ten minutes to eight, because 60 minus 50 equals 10. 7:50 is the same as ten to eight.
accompanying_text: The switch has a formula: **minutes-to = 60 − minutes-past.** At 5:50, that's 60 − 50 = 10 to six. The minute hand shows it too — once it crosses the 6-mark into the clock's left half, counting down to the next hour is the shorter story.

illustration_description: A number line of time from 8:40 to 9:20 with a jump of 20 minutes to 9:00 and another 20 minutes to 9:20, totalling 40 minutes. Elapsed time on a number line: 40 minutes.
accompanying_text: How long is it from 8:40 to 9:20? Lay time on a number line and **JUMP**: a friendly hop to 9:00 (20 minutes), then a hop to 9:20 (20 more). Two hops, 40 minutes. The hour border is your stepping stone — always land on it first.

illustration_description: A number line of time from 8:40 to 9:20 with a jump of 20 minutes to 9:00 and another 20 minutes to 9:20, totalling 40 minutes. Elapsed time on a number line: 40 minutes.
accompanying_text: Why not just subtract the minute labels? Because **the hour rolls over at 60** — there is no 9:75 hiding after 9:59. Crossing an hour, label arithmetic breaks; the two-hop jump never does. That's the whole trick.

illustration_description: A balance scale weighing an apple at about 100 grams for light objects, with kilograms used for heavy objects. Grams for light, kilograms for heavy.
accompanying_text: Heaviness is measured in **grams (g)** for light things and **kilograms (kg)** for heavy ones. Anchors to keep in your pocket: a paperclip is about 1 gram; a bag of flour is about 1 kilogram. Pick the unit that keeps the number friendly.

illustration_description: The code word kilo means one thousand, so one kilogram equals one thousand grams. Kilo means 1000: 1 kg equals 1000 g.
accompanying_text: The two units are linked by a code word: **kilo means one thousand.** So **1 kilogram = 1,000 grams** — the kilo is a thousand-badge stamped on the gram. Going kg → g, stamp on three zeros; going g → kg, peel them off.

illustration_description: A measuring jug filled to the one-liter line, showing liters measure how much a container holds. Liters measure how much fits.
accompanying_text: Grams measure how HEAVY. **Liters (L) measure how MUCH liquid** — the space it fills, called capacity. Anchors: a juice carton holds about 1 liter; a big water bottle holds about 1 liter too. A bathtub? Many, many liters.

illustration_description: A measuring jug filled to the one-liter line, showing liters measure how much a container holds. Liters measure how much fits.
accompanying_text: Careful — pourable is not the same as light. **Flour pours, but recipes WEIGH it in grams; water pours and we measure it in liters.** The question isn't 'does it pour?' — it's 'am I measuring the AMOUNT (liters) or the HEAVINESS (grams)?'

illustration_description: A balance scale weighing an apple at about 100 grams for light objects, with kilograms used for heavy objects. Grams for light, kilograms for heavy.
accompanying_text: Now put the units to work. A measurement story is just arithmetic wearing a costume: **read what's being measured, pick the operation, keep the unit attached.** 'How much altogether' adds; 'how much is left' subtracts; 'how many fit' divides.

illustration_description: A measuring jug filled to the one-liter line, showing liters measure how much a container holds. Liters measure how much fits.
accompanying_text: Two-step stories chain the moves — and guard your answer with an estimate. Before trusting an exact number, ask: *is it even the right SIZE?* If you pour water OUT of a tank and get more than you started with, the answer is busted before you check a single digit.

illustration_description: A pictograph where each circle stands for two items; a row of three and a half circles means seven, read using the key. A pictograph: each symbol counts by the key.
accompanying_text: A pictograph draws data with pictures — but the pictures lie unless you read the **KEY** first. If the key says '🍎 = 2 votes,' then each apple is worth two, not one. The key is a secret multiplier: symbols × key = the real count.

illustration_description: A pictograph where each circle stands for two items; a row of three and a half circles means seven, read using the key. A pictograph: each symbol counts by the key.
accompanying_text: Sometimes a row ends in **half a symbol** — and half a symbol is worth half the key. With '⭐ = 10 points,' a half-star is 5. Pictographs use halves so they don't need a whole symbol for every in-between number.

illustration_description: A scaled bar graph with gridlines every five; a bar reaching the fifteen line reads fifteen, and a bar stopping between lines is read carefully. A scaled bar graph: read the gridline value.
accompanying_text: A bar graph shows amounts as bar heights — but read the **SCALE** first, just like a pictograph's key. If the grid lines climb 0, 2, 4, 6, each step is worth 2, not 1. A bar reaching the third line stands for 6, not 3.

illustration_description: A scaled bar graph with gridlines every five; a bar reaching the fifteen line reads fifteen, and a bar stopping between lines is read carefully. A scaled bar graph: read the gridline value.
accompanying_text: When a bar stops **between two grid lines**, it lands halfway. On a by-2 scale, halfway between the 4-line and the 6-line is 5 — an odd number the scale never labels. Between-lines reading is how bar graphs show numbers their scale skips.

illustration_description: A scaled bar graph with gridlines every five; a bar reaching the fifteen line reads fifteen, and a bar stopping between lines is read carefully. A scaled bar graph: read the gridline value.
accompanying_text: A graph isn't just a picture — it answers questions. **'How many more?' subtracts** two bars. **'How many in all?' adds** them. **'Which is most?' finds the tallest.** The trick is matching the question word to the right move.

illustration_description: A scaled bar graph with gridlines every five; a bar reaching the fifteen line reads fifteen, and a bar stopping between lines is read carefully. A scaled bar graph: read the gridline value.
accompanying_text: Watch a sneaky trap: the number of BARS and the HEIGHT of a bar answer different questions. Four bars might mean four days; each bar's height is that day's count. '4 bars' is not '4 books.' Always ask which one the question wants.

illustration_description: A line plot stacking X marks above a number line from zero to two, with tick marks at halves, showing how many measurements fall at each value. A line plot with halves.
accompanying_text: A **line plot** stacks an X above a number line for each measurement. When we measure lengths, the line is marked in **halves and quarters** — the very fourths you placed in the fractions course. Each X sits above the value it measured; taller stacks mean that value came up more often.

illustration_description: A line plot stacking X marks above a number line from zero to two, with tick marks at halves, showing how many measurements fall at each value. A line plot with halves.
accompanying_text: The marks between the whole numbers are fractions doing real work. A pencil measured at **2½ inches** lands its X on the halfway mark; one at **2¼** lands a quarter of the way past 2. The line plot is the fraction number line, wearing a lab coat.

illustration_description: A rectangle covered by a grid of unit squares with no gaps or overlaps; counting the squares gives the area. Area is the count of unit squares.
accompanying_text: **Area** is how much flat space a shape covers — and we measure it by counting **unit squares** that tile the shape with no gaps and no overlaps. Cover a rectangle in 1-cm squares, count them, and that count (in square cm) is its area.

illustration_description: A rectangle covered by a grid of unit squares with no gaps or overlaps; counting the squares gives the area. Area is the count of unit squares.
accompanying_text: Why SQUARES to measure with? Because they **tile perfectly** — full edge meets full edge, no gaps, no overlaps. Circles leave curved gaps; squares lock together like floor tiles. That gap-free locking is exactly why area is counted in *square* units.

illustration_description: A three by five array of squares labelled as three rows of five, so multiplying gives the area of fifteen. Rows times columns equals area.
accompanying_text: When the squares line up in **equal rows**, you don't have to count one by one. Equal rows are equal groups — so **area = rows × squares-per-row**. A rectangle 4 rows tall and 6 squares wide has 4 × 6 = 24 squares. Area is multiplication you can see.

illustration_description: A three by five array of squares labelled as three rows of five, so multiplying gives the area of fifteen. Rows times columns equals area.
accompanying_text: The **flip** works here too: 4 rows of 6 or 6 rows of 4 cover the exact same carpet — 4 × 6 = 6 × 4 = 24. Turning the rectangle sideways swaps rows and columns but never changes the squares inside.

illustration_description: A six by seven rectangle split into a six by five part and a six by two part, showing six times seven equals six times five plus six times two. Break apart: 6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 6 × 2.
accompanying_text: A wide rectangle can be **broken apart** into two friendlier ones. A 6-by-7 is hard? Slice the 7 into 5 + 2: now it's a 6-by-5 next to a 6-by-2. Find each area, add them — same total, easier math. Breaking apart never changes the covering.

illustration_description: A six by seven rectangle split into a six by five part and a six by two part, showing six times seven equals six times five plus six times two. Break apart: 6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 6 × 2.
accompanying_text: This is a hidden superpower: **6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 6 × 2.** Splitting one side and handing the other side to each piece is the same trick you use to break apart hard multiplication facts. The rectangle SHOWS why it works — the squares are just regrouped, never lost.

illustration_description: An L-shaped figure split into two rectangles; adding the two areas gives the total area of the odd shape. Odd shapes: add the rectangle pieces.
accompanying_text: An L-shape or a plus-sign isn't a rectangle — but it's **made of rectangles**. Cut it into rectangular pieces, find each area, and add them up. Any straight-sided shape surrenders to 'cut into rectangles, then add.'

illustration_description: An L-shaped figure split into two rectangles; adding the two areas gives the total area of the odd shape. Odd shapes: add the rectangle pieces.
accompanying_text: Sometimes SUBTRACTING is faster. Want the bare floor around a rug? Find the **whole room's area, then take away the rug's.** A big rectangle minus a rectangular bite is often quicker than adding up the leftover L-shaped strip piece by piece.

illustration_description: A rectangle with its four side lengths labelled and arrows walking around the edge, the perimeter being the total distance around. Perimeter is the distance around the edge.
accompanying_text: Area filled the inside; **perimeter walks the edge.** It's the total distance all the way around a shape — the length of fence it would take to enclose it. To find it, walk every side and add the lengths as you go.

illustration_description: A rectangle with its four side lengths labelled and arrows walking around the edge, the perimeter being the total distance around. Perimeter is the distance around the edge.
accompanying_text: A square makes it even easier: **all four sides match, so perimeter = 4 × side.** A square with 7 cm sides has a fence of 4 × 7 = 28 cm. One multiplication does the whole walk.

illustration_description: A rectangle where opposite sides match, so a missing side equals the side across from it, eight matches eight. Missing side: opposite sides match.
accompanying_text: Sometimes you know the fence but not every side. Work backwards: **take the known sides off the perimeter, and whatever's left belongs to the missing ones.** If the fence is 20 and three sides add to 14, the last side is 20 − 14 = 6.

illustration_description: A rectangle where opposite sides match, so a missing side equals the side across from it, eight matches eight. Missing side: opposite sides match.
accompanying_text: Rectangles hide a shortcut. Their sides come in **matching pairs**, so once you peel off BOTH known-length sides, split what's left between the two equal missing sides. And a square is simplest of all: **side = perimeter ÷ 4.**

illustration_description: Two shapes of the same area twelve: a compact three by four rectangle with perimeter fourteen and a skinny one by twelve with perimeter twenty-six. Same area, different perimeter.
accompanying_text: Here's the twist that ties the chapter together: **area and perimeter don't move together.** Two rectangles can share the SAME fence yet hold different amounts of space inside. The edge and the inside are genuinely separate measurements — knowing one never fixes the other.

illustration_description: Two shapes of the same area twelve: a compact three by four rectangle with perimeter fourteen and a skinny one by twelve with perimeter twenty-six. Same area, different perimeter.
accompanying_text: Why does the square win? A **skinny shape wastes fence** on its long sides while squeezing the inside thin. Pulling a rectangle toward a square shape packs the most area into a fixed fence. Long-and-thin spends the same fence on far less space.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Multiplying by 10, 100, or 1,000 does not need a new fact — it takes a fact you own and scales it. 3 × 4 = 12 gives 30 × 4 = 120.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The zeros are not decoration. Each ten in a factor multiplies the product by ten, so count the zeros the factors actually carry.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: An area model turns a hard product into easy ones: split a factor by place, multiply each piece, and the rectangle's regions add to the whole.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Splitting never changes the answer. 14 × 6 becomes 10 × 6 plus 4 × 6 — two facts you own, reassembled into one you did not.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The column algorithm is the area model written compactly: each place of the top number is multiplied by the single digit, and the pieces stack up.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Nothing new is happening — the partial products are still there, just written above one another instead of side by side.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A carry in multiplication is the same trade as in addition: when a column's product passes nine, the extra tens move left.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Strand a carry and the product drops by exactly that bundle. The carry is not scratch work — it is part of the answer.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: When both factors are two-digit, both split — and the rectangle gains four regions instead of two.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: 23 × 14 becomes 20×10, 20×4, 3×10 and 3×4. Miss one region and the product is short by exactly that rectangle.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Partial products write those four regions as four lines, then add them. The layout changes; the mathematics does not.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Keeping the places straight is the whole discipline: 20 × 10 is 200, not 30, and a misplaced zero costs the entire region.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Estimating a product rounds each factor to something friendly and multiplies those. It tells you the neighbourhood before you do the work.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: An estimate is a guard against the most expensive error in multiplication: a digit in the wrong place, which is wrong by a factor of ten.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Checking a product compares it to the estimate. Close means plausible; an answer ten times out is a misplaced digit, every time.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This check costs seconds and catches the errors that matter most — the ones where the digits are right but the places are not.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Division works from the LARGEST place downward — the opposite of addition. The first place that can be divided sets where the quotient begins.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: In 936 ÷ 3, nine hundreds split into three gives three hundreds, so the quotient opens in the hundreds place and 312 follows.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Partial quotients removes groups in whatever chunks are convenient, then adds the chunks up. 852 ÷ 4 can take 200 fours, then 13 more.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Any legal chunk works and the order never matters, because removing 200 groups then 13 removes exactly the same 213 groups.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Three-digit by one-digit division applies the same order every time: divide the place, write the digit, carry the leftover to the next place.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The leftover from one place does not vanish — it becomes tens or ones in the place below and gets divided there.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Four-digit dividends change nothing but the length of the work. The same place-by-place march produces the quotient.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Longer problems reward the estimate even more: knowing 3,612 ÷ 6 is near 600 tells you instantly whether the quotient has the right number of digits.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Most divisions leave something over. The remainder is what could not form another whole group — and it is always smaller than the divisor.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: If the remainder reached the divisor, one more group could be made. That is the test: a remainder at or above the divisor means the quotient is too small.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The same remainder answers different questions differently. Six full vans with five hikers left over means seven vans are needed — the leftover still has to travel.
