illustration_description: Walk the curve left to right: it climbs from negative infinity, crosses at each odd-multiplicity zero, and continues.
accompanying_text: Now walk the curve left to right: it climbs from −∞, **crosses** at −2, rises to a hilltop, comes back down to **bounce** at 1 (touching without crossing — f stays ≥ 0 nearby), then climbs to +∞. Between and around the zeros, the sign of f never changes without a crossing.

illustration_description: A turning point is where the graph switches direction, a local high or low; a degree-n graph has at most n minus one of them.
accompanying_text: A **turning point** is where the graph switches direction — a hilltop or valley floor. The rule from Chapter 1, now in reverse: degree n allows **at most n − 1** turning points, so a graph showing **4 turning points needs degree at least 5**. Wiggles put a floor under the degree.

illustration_description: Parity adds a clue: even-degree graphs have ends matching, both up or both down, while odd-degree graphs have ends opposite.
accompanying_text: Parity adds a second clue. **Even-degree** graphs (ends matching) have an **odd** number of turning points; **odd-degree** graphs (ends opposing) have an **even** number — 0, 2, 4, ... A cubic can run straight through with zero turns, but a parabola must turn exactly once.

illustration_description: Factored form runs backward beautifully: a monic polynomial with given zeros is the product of x minus each zero.
accompanying_text: Factored form runs backward beautifully: a monic polynomial with zeros −1, 2, and 3 is f(x) = **(x + 1)(x − 2)(x − 3)** — one factor per zero, signs flipped. Want a bounce at a zero? Square its factor. The blueprint IS the factorization.

illustration_description: Degree comes from the blueprint too: a zero of multiplicity two and another zero contribute degree three in total.
accompanying_text: Degree comes from the blueprint too: zeros 4 (multiplicity 2) and −1 (multiplicity 1) force degree **at least 3**, and f(x) = (x − 4)²(x + 1) is the smallest build. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees the accounting always balances: degree = total multiplicity.

illustration_description: Guessing zeros feels hopeless until the Rational Root Theorem lists candidates: plus or minus factors of the constant over factors of the lead.
accompanying_text: Guessing zeros of a cubic feels hopeless — until the **Rational Root Theorem** shrinks the haystack: any rational zero p/q (in lowest terms) must have **p dividing the constant term** and **q dividing the leading coefficient**. The theorem doesn't find roots; it writes the complete **candidate list**.

illustration_description: A leading coefficient bigger than one adds fractions to the candidate list.
accompanying_text: A leading coefficient bigger than 1 adds **fractions**: q ranges over its divisors. For g(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2, p ∈ {1, 2} and q ∈ {1, 2}, so p/q gives ±1, ±2, ±1/2 (±2/2 repeats ±1). Always reduce and drop duplicates.

illustration_description: A candidate c is a real zero exactly when f of c equals zero.
accompanying_text: A candidate c is a real zero exactly when **f(c) = 0** — the Factor Theorem's verdict: then (x − c) divides f. Testing is just evaluation, so be systematic: try the easy integers first (±1, ±2, …), and each **failure still helps** by shrinking the list.

illustration_description: One success changes the game: divide f by x minus c and the leftover quotient is one degree smaller.
accompanying_text: One success changes the game: **divide f by (x − c)** and the degree drops by one. Synthetic division does it fast (recall: bring down, multiply by c, add across). For a cubic, one found root leaves a **quadratic** — solvable by any method you like.

illustration_description: Four-stage pipeline for factoring a cubic: list the rational-root candidates, test until f of c equals zero, divide synthetically so the degree drops, then finish by solving the leftover quadratic. The list, test, divide, finish pipeline for factoring cubics.
accompanying_text: The complete method for factoring a cubic with no obvious pattern: **(1)** write the candidate list, **(2)** test until a zero appears, **(3)** divide it out synthetically, **(4)** the leftover **quadratic** finishes by factoring or the quadratic formula. Every zero of the original is either the found root or a zero of the quotient.

illustration_description: Always verify by multiplying the factors back to recover the original polynomial.
accompanying_text: Always **verify** by multiplying back: (x − 2)(x + 1)(x + 3) should rebuild x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6. First pair: (x + 1)(x + 3) = x² + 4x + 3; then (x − 2)(x² + 4x + 3) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6. ✔ A thirty-second check catches every division slip.

illustration_description: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: every degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots, counting complex ones and multiplicity.
accompanying_text: The **Fundamental Theorem of Algebra**: every degree-n polynomial has **exactly n zeros** in the complex numbers, as long as you count each zero by its **multiplicity**. No polynomial escapes — zeros the real line can't show are hiding in the complex plane.

illustration_description: When a graph shows fewer real zeros than the degree, the missing roots are complex.
accompanying_text: When a graph shows **fewer** real zeros than the degree, the FTA tells you exactly where the rest are: **off the real line**. A quartic crossing the x-axis only twice has 4 − 2 = **two non-real zeros** — invisible on the graph, guaranteed by the theorem.

illustration_description: Complex plane with the zero 3 plus 2i above the real axis and its conjugate 3 minus 2i below, connected by a dashed vertical segment showing mirror symmetry across the real axis. A conjugate pair mirrored across the real axis.
accompanying_text: For a polynomial with **real coefficients**, non-real zeros never travel alone: if a + bi is a zero, its **conjugate a − bi** is too. The pair is a mirror image across the real axis — one reflection the coefficients can't tell apart.

illustration_description: The pairing has muscle: non-real zeros come in twos, a complex number and its conjugate mirrored across the real axis.
accompanying_text: The pairing has muscle: non-real zeros come in **twos**, so a real-coefficient cubic can have **0 or 2** non-real zeros — never 1 or 3. Every odd-degree real polynomial is therefore forced to keep **at least one real zero**.

illustration_description: To build the minimal-degree real polynomial with given zeros, include each complex zero's conjugate partner.
accompanying_text: To build the **minimal-degree real polynomial** with given zeros: pair every non-real zero with its conjugate, turn each pair into a **real quadratic** using sum and product (recall: x² − (sum)x + product), attach one linear factor per real zero, and multiply.

illustration_description: Now multiply in the real zeros: the conjugate pair's quadratic times the real factors gives the polynomial.
accompanying_text:
Now multiply in the real zeros. With the pair's quadratic x² − 2x + 2 and the real zero 3:

(x² − 2x + 2)(x − 3) = **x³ − 5x² + 8x − 6**

— degree 3 is minimal: two slots for the forced pair, one for the real zero.

illustration_description: Horizontal asymptotes: when the top degree is below the bottom, the asymptote is y equals zero.
accompanying_text: Horizontal asymptotes (recall): top degree **below** bottom → y = 0; degrees **equal** → y = ratio of leading coefficients. But when the top degree is **exactly one more** than the bottom, the far-out graph follows a tilted line instead — a **slant (oblique) asymptote**. Two or more degrees over: no line at all.

illustration_description: Why one-degree-over means a line: dividing rewrites f as a line plus a vanishing remainder.
accompanying_text: Why one-over means a line: dividing gives f(x) = (**line**) + remainder/(bottom). The leftover fraction has bottom-heavy degrees, so it **dies to 0** far out — leaving only the line. The slant asymptote IS the quotient of the division.

illustration_description: To find a slant asymptote, divide top by bottom; the quotient line is the asymptote the curve hugs.
accompanying_text:
To find a slant asymptote, **divide** (long or synthetic — recall the mechanics) and keep the quotient:

f(x) = quotient + remainder/divisor

The far-out graph is the **quotient line y = mx + b**; the remainder term is the shrinking gap between curve and line.

illustration_description: Always verify by multiplying back: quotient times divisor plus remainder must rebuild the numerator.
accompanying_text: Always **verify by multiplying back**: quotient × divisor + remainder must rebuild the top. (x + 1)(x + 2) + 3 = x² + 3x + 2 + 3 = x² + 3x + 5 ✓. And notice: the remainder controls **which side** the curve approaches from — positive remainder means above the line for large positive x here.

illustration_description: Graph of the rational function x squared minus 4 over x minus 1 showing both branches, a dashed vertical asymptote at x equals 1, and a dashed slant asymptote y equals x plus 1 that the branches approach far out. Vertical asymptote and slant asymptote portrait of a rational function.
accompanying_text: A rational function's complete portrait has **two independent layers**: vertical asymptotes and holes come from the **bottom's zeros** (recall: common factor → hole, otherwise VA); the far-out line — horizontal or slant — comes from the **degree gap**. Find both layers separately, then draw.

illustration_description: The two layers never interfere: the curve can cross a horizontal or slant asymptote in the middle, only settling far out.
accompanying_text: The two layers never interfere: the curve can **cross a slant asymptote** near the middle of the graph (only VERTICAL asymptotes are uncrossable). Far out, though, the remainder term −3/(x − 1) pins the curve to the line: below it on the right (negative gap), above it on the left.

illustration_description: A sign chart for the product x plus 1 times x minus 2: the number line is cut at x equals negative 1 and x equals 2, with a plus sign on the left interval, a minus sign between the cuts, and a plus sign on the right interval. Sign chart with cuts at −1 and 2 showing the plus, minus, plus pattern.
accompanying_text: Where is (x + 1)(x − 2) **positive**? A polynomial can only switch sign by **passing through zero**, so its zeros chop the number line into intervals of constant sign. The **sign chart** records one test per interval — the whole inequality reads straight off it.

illustration_description: Strict versus inclusive matters only at the boundary points: whether the endpoints join the solution.
accompanying_text: Strict vs inclusive matters only at the **boundary points**: for f > 0 the zeros are excluded (f is 0 there, not positive); for f ≥ 0 they join the solution. The intervals themselves never change — only their endpoints.

illustration_description: Testing every interval is slow; the shortcut is a sign chart marking each factor's sign between the zeros.
accompanying_text: Testing every interval is honest but slow. The shortcut (recall bounce vs cross): at an **odd-multiplicity** zero the sign **flips**; at an **even-multiplicity** zero it **doesn't**. Find ONE interval's sign, then walk the chart flipping only at odd zeros.

illustration_description: Harvesting from a minus, plus, plus chart: g is greater than zero on the two positive intervals combined.
accompanying_text: Harvesting from −, +, +: g > 0 on (−2, 3) **and** (3, ∞) — but watch x = 3 itself: g(3) = 0, so for a **strict** inequality the point x = 3 is a **puncture** in an otherwise positive run.

illustration_description: Real problems arrive unfactored, like x squared minus x is at least six; move everything to one side first.
accompanying_text: Real problems arrive unfactored, like x² − x ≥ 6. The non-negotiable first move: **get zero on one side** — x² − x − 6 ≥ 0 — then factor and chart. Comparing to 6 directly is meaningless for signs; sign charts only speak the language of **zero**.

illustration_description: The classic trap: never divide both sides by a variable, because its sign is unknown and can flip the inequality.
accompanying_text: The classic trap: **never divide both sides by a variable expression**. In x³ ≥ 4x, dividing by x silently assumes x > 0 and throws away solutions. Instead: x³ − 4x ≥ 0, factor x(x − 2)(x + 2), chart with all THREE zeros.

illustration_description: Sign chart of x minus 3 over x plus 1 with cuts at negative 1 and 3 and signs plus, minus, plus. The cut at negative 1 is drawn as an open circle because the expression is undefined there; the cut at 3 is a closed dot because the expression equals zero there. Two kinds of cut points: an open excluded value and a closable zero.
accompanying_text: A rational expression can change sign at two kinds of places: where the **top is zero** (the expression is 0) and where the **bottom is zero** (the expression doesn't exist — recall excluded values). BOTH kinds cut the number line for the sign chart.

illustration_description: The bottom's zeros matter even though nothing is zero there: the expression can still flip sign across them.
accompanying_text: Why the bottom's zeros matter even though nothing is 'zero' there: crossing x = −1, the denominator flips sign, so the whole fraction can flip **without touching zero** — it jumps across the vertical asymptote instead. Skipping that cut merges intervals that have different signs.

illustration_description: With greater-or-equal or less-or-equal, boundary membership splits by kind: a top zero is included, a bottom zero excluded.
accompanying_text: With ≥ or ≤, boundary membership splits by KIND: a **top's zero** may join (the expression equals 0 there), but a **bottom's zero can never join any solution** — the expression has no value at all there (recall excluded values). Zeros close; excluded values stay open, always.

illustration_description: The second standing rule: a value making the denominator zero is always excluded from the solution.
accompanying_text: The second standing rule (recall from rational equations): **never multiply both sides by a variable denominator** in an inequality — its sign is unknown, so you don't know whether to flip the inequality. The sign chart needs no multiplication at all.

illustration_description: For x over x minus two at most three, the safe pipeline: subtract to get zero on one side, then combine into a single fraction.
accompanying_text: For x/(x − 2) ≤ 3, the safe pipeline: subtract to get zero on one side, **combine into a single fraction** over the common denominator, then chart. x/(x − 2) − 3 = (x − 3(x − 2))/(x − 2) = **(−2x + 6)/(x − 2)** — now the cuts are visible.

illustration_description: Why combine instead of just moving the three: cross-multiplying by an unknown-sign denominator can flip the inequality.
accompanying_text: Why combine instead of just moving the 3? Because the chart needs the expression's **zeros and excluded values in plain sight** — a difference of two terms hides them; a single fraction (top)/(bottom) displays both. Combine first, chart second, every time.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Subtracting a small amount works by counting back: start at the whole and hop backward once for each one taken away.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A double joins two equal groups: 4 + 4, 6 + 6, 8 + 8. Doubles are worth knowing by heart because so many other sums sit next to them.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Picture the double as two matching rows — every counter in one row has a partner in the other.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: When two addends differ by one, a known double is hiding inside: 6 + 7 is the double 6 + 6, plus one more.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Anchor on the smaller double, then add one. The double does most of the work.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A near-double can also lean on the bigger double: 6 + 5 is the double 6 + 6, minus one.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Both doors work — double the smaller and add one, or double the bigger and take one away. Use whichever double you know best.

accompanying_text: When a sum crosses ten, complete the ten first. Part of the second addend fills the frame to ten; the leftover rides on top.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Ten-and-some is easy to name — that is the whole point of the make-ten move.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Subtracting through ten works in two easy steps: first take away enough to land on ten, then take away the rest.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A related addition fact can check the answer: the part taken away plus the answer rebuilds the start.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Three numbers that add up make a family: the two parts and the whole. Knowing one fact in the family unlocks the others.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: If 9 + 4 = 13 is known, then 13 − 9 and 13 − 4 come free — the same three numbers, rearranged.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Different-looking sums can name the same total: 8 + 5 and 10 + 3 both make 13. Moving counters between the addends keeps the total steady.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This is why make-ten works — it slides the sum to an equivalent one that is easier to read.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Each strategy has a home: counting on for tiny add-ons, make-ten for sums that cross ten, doubles for near-equal addends.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Look at the numbers before starting — they point to the fastest tool.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Knowing WHY a strategy works matters as much as using it. Each strategy works because it protects the total while making the counting easier.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Swapping keeps the same groups; make-ten regroups without adding or removing; near-doubles adjust a known fact by exactly one.

illustration_description: One half mile in one quarter hour divides out to a unit rate of two miles per hour.
accompanying_text: A unit rate compares a quantity to **1 unit** of another. If a runner covers 1/2 mile in 1/4 hour, divide: (1/2) ÷ (1/4) = 2 miles per hour. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip (reciprocal).

illustration_description: One half mile in one quarter hour divides out to a unit rate of two miles per hour.
accompanying_text: The unit rate isn't always a whole number. If a hiker covers 3/4 mile in 1/2 hour: (3/4) ÷ (1/2) = (3/4) × 2 = 6/4 = 1 1/2 miles per hour.

illustration_description: Dividing by a fraction with keep-flip-multiply: three fourths divided by one half becomes three fourths times two over one, which is three halves. Keep, flip, multiply: ¾ ÷ ½ = 3⁄2.
accompanying_text: The recipe: keep the first fraction, flip the second, multiply. (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c). This works no matter which unit you're comparing.

illustration_description: One half mile in one quarter hour divides out to a unit rate of two miles per hour.
accompanying_text: Unit rates with fractions show up anywhere two quantities compare — laps around a track, cups in a recipe, minutes on a clock. The flip-and-multiply rule works the same way every time.

illustration_description: One half mile in one quarter hour divides out to a unit rate of two miles per hour.
accompanying_text: In a recipe, the unit rate tells you how much of one ingredient per single unit of another — useful for scaling a recipe up or down correctly.

illustration_description: A unit rate's label matches the question asked: miles per hour, cups per cup, or laps per hour all read as the first quantity per one of the second. The unit's label matches the question.
accompanying_text: The units always match the question: "laps per hour," "cups per cup," "miles per minute" — the unit rate's name tells you which quantity goes on top.

illustration_description: One half mile in one quarter hour divides out to a unit rate of two miles per hour.
accompanying_text: You now have one method for any unit rate with fractions: divide the two quantities by flipping the second fraction and multiplying. Mixed practice locks the method in.

illustration_description: Building a rate from a sentence: whichever quantity is named first goes on top, so miles per hour puts miles over hours. The first-named quantity goes on top.
accompanying_text: Whichever quantity comes first in the sentence goes on top — "miles per hour" means miles ÷ hours, always in that order.

illustration_description: Dividing by a fraction with keep-flip-multiply: three fourths divided by one half becomes three fourths times two over one, which is three halves. Keep, flip, multiply: ¾ ÷ ½ = 3⁄2.
accompanying_text: If you ever get confused about which fraction to flip, remember: you're always dividing the FIRST quantity by the SECOND — flip the second one, then multiply.

illustration_description: Two tables compared: one where every ratio equals three, so it is proportional, and one where the middle row breaks the pattern, so it is not proportional.
accompanying_text: A table is **proportional** if every pair has the same ratio y/x. For (2, 6), (3, 9), (5, 15): 6/2 = 3, 9/3 = 3, 15/5 = 3 — all equal, so it's proportional.

illustration_description: A table is not proportional if even one pair breaks the ratio: two pairs give a ratio of 3 but the third gives 4, so the whole table fails. One broken ratio fails the whole table.
accompanying_text: A table is NOT proportional if even one pair breaks the pattern. (2, 6), (3, 10), (5, 15): 6/2=3 and 15/5=3, but 10/3 isn't 3 — one broken ratio ruins it.

illustration_description: A table is not proportional if even one pair breaks the ratio: two pairs give a ratio of 3 but the third gives 4, so the whole table fails. One broken ratio fails the whole table.
accompanying_text: Checking every pair matters — skipping the middle row and only checking the first and last can hide a broken pattern.

illustration_description: Two tables compared: one where every ratio equals three, so it is proportional, and one where the middle row breaks the pattern, so it is not proportional.
accompanying_text: In a proportional table, the shared ratio y/x is called the **constant of proportionality**, k. For (2, 6), (3, 9), (5, 15): k = 6/2 = 3 — every y is 3 times its x.

illustration_description: Two tables compared: one where every ratio equals three, so it is proportional, and one where the middle row breaks the pattern, so it is not proportional.
accompanying_text: The constant of proportionality doesn't have to be a whole number. For (3, 2), (6, 4), (9, 6): k = 2/3 — a fraction, but still constant across every pair.

illustration_description: Using the constant of proportionality: once k is known, y equals k times x, so with k of 3 and x of 5, y is 15. y = kx: with k=3, x=5 gives y=15.
accompanying_text: Once you know k, you can find any missing value: y = k × x. If k = 3 and x = 10, then y = 30.

illustration_description: Two tables compared: one where every ratio equals three, so it is proportional, and one where the middle row breaks the pattern, so it is not proportional.
accompanying_text: Real situations give you a table to test: is pay proportional to hours? Is distance proportional to time? Check every ratio before deciding.

illustration_description: A taxi fare with a flat start fee is not proportional: its graph is a straight line that crosses the y-axis above zero instead of at the origin. A flat start fee: line misses the origin.
accompanying_text: Not every real table is proportional — a taxi fare with a flat starting fee, for instance, breaks the pattern because of that fixed extra amount.

illustration_description: Two tables compared: one where every ratio equals three, so it is proportional, and one where the middle row breaks the pattern, so it is not proportional.
accompanying_text: Once you've confirmed a table IS proportional, its constant of proportionality lets you predict any new value — a powerful shortcut for real problems.

illustration_description: A proportional line passing through the origin and the points one-two, two-four, and three-six, showing the unit rate two at the point one-two.
accompanying_text: A proportional relationship y = kx graphs as a **straight line through the origin (0, 0)**. For k = 2: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) all sit on the same line.

illustration_description: A proportional line passing through the origin and the points one-two, two-four, and three-six, showing the unit rate two at the point one-two.
accompanying_text: Any two points that fit y = kx will connect into a straight line — that's the visual signature of a proportional relationship.

illustration_description: A proportional graph is a straight line through the origin: the point 0, 0 always lies on it because zero of something costs zero. A proportional line passes through (0,0).
accompanying_text: The origin itself (0, 0) is always on the line too, even though the grid here starts counting at 1 — every proportional relationship passes through it.

illustration_description: A proportional line passing through the origin and the points one-two, two-four, and three-six, showing the unit rate two at the point one-two.
accompanying_text: The point **(1, k)** always shows the unit rate directly — when x = 1, y = k × 1 = k. Find where the line crosses x = 1, and its height IS the unit rate.

illustration_description: The unit-rate point on a proportional graph: the point where x is 1 shows the unit rate directly, so the point 1, 4 means a rate of 4. The point at x=1 shows the unit rate.
accompanying_text: Going the other way: if you're told the point (1, 4) is on the line, you instantly know the unit rate is 4 — no computation needed.

illustration_description: The unit-rate point on a proportional graph: the point where x is 1 shows the unit rate directly, so the point 1, 4 means a rate of 4. The point at x=1 shows the unit rate.
accompanying_text: For any OTHER point (x, y) on the line, the unit rate is still y/x — the point (1, k) is just the special case where the division is instant.

illustration_description: A proportional line passing through the origin and the points one-two, two-four, and three-six, showing the unit rate two at the point one-two.
accompanying_text: A graphed point tells a real story. The point (4, 20) on a pay graph means: after 4 hours, you've earned $20 — and the unit rate, $5 per hour, comes from 20 ÷ 4.

illustration_description: A proportional line passing through the origin and the points one-two, two-four, and three-six, showing the unit rate two at the point one-two.
accompanying_text: The x-value and y-value each have their own meaning in a story — x might be hours, y might be dollars. Keep track of which is which before dividing.

illustration_description: A proportional line passing through the origin and the points one-two, two-four, and three-six, showing the unit rate two at the point one-two.
accompanying_text: Once you know the rate, you can predict any point on the line — even ones you haven't plotted. That's the real power of recognizing proportionality.

illustration_description: Using the constant of proportionality: once k is known, y equals k times x, so with k of 3 and x of 5, y is 15. y = kx: with k=3, x=5 gives y=15.
accompanying_text:
You can already find the constant of proportionality in a table and spot it on a graph. The last step is to **write it down as an equation**.

Every proportional relationship has the same form: **y = kx**, where k is that constant. Once k is known the equation predicts any value at all — no table row required.

illustration_description: The same constant of proportionality of four shown three ways: as the ratio in a table, as the steepness of the graph, and as the number multiplying x in the equation y equals four x.
accompanying_text:
The constant is the same number wherever you look for it, and that is the point.

In a **table** it is y ÷ x for any row. On a **graph** it is the height at x = 1 — how steeply the line climbs. In the **equation** it is simply the number in front of x. Three representations, one number, and the equation is the most compact of the three.

accompanying_text: A decrease works the same way — the change is still (new − old), which comes out negative, showing the percent DROPPED.

illustration_description: Percent change uses the original as the base: the change divided by the original value, always dividing by the old amount, not the new one. Percent change = (new − old) ÷ original.
accompanying_text: Always use the ORIGINAL value as the base — never the new value. Dividing by the wrong number gives a different, incorrect percent.

illustration_description: A bar showing a principal of 500 dollars with a separate interest block of 60 dollars added on top, totalling 560 dollars.
accompanying_text:
Borrow money and you pay rent on it. That rent is **interest**, and the simple kind is a percent of the original amount, charged once per year.

The formula is just that sentence: **I = P · r · t** — principal times rate times time. Borrow $500 at 4% for 3 years and each year costs 4% of $500, which is $20, so three years cost $60.

illustration_description: Four bars showing interest growing in equal steps of twenty dollars per year, because simple interest is a fixed amount each year rather than a growing one.
accompanying_text:
"Simple" is doing real work in that name. The rate applies to the **principal** every single year, never to the money that has already piled up.

So the interest grows in equal steps — a straight staircase, $20 then $40 then $60. That is what separates it from compound interest, where each year's interest earns interest of its own.

illustration_description: A sale of 2000 dollars split into a 6 percent commission of 120 dollars for the seller and the remaining 1880 dollars.
accompanying_text:
A **commission** is a percent of a sale, paid to the person who made it. Sell $2,000 of equipment on 6% commission and you earn 0.06 × 2000 = $120.

The skill is old — it is *percent of a quantity* — but the trap is new: the percent is always of the **sale**, not of your existing pay and not of what is left over.

illustration_description: A taxi fare is not proportional: a fixed starting fee plus a per-mile rate means the line does not pass through the origin. A flat fee breaks proportionality.
accompanying_text:
A **fee** behaves differently from a commission, and the difference is proportionality.

A 6% commission doubles when the sale doubles — it is proportional. A flat $5 fee does not: it is the same on a $20 sale and a $2,000 one. Mixing the two gives a relationship that is *not* proportional, which is exactly why the graph of pay-plus-fee misses the origin.

illustration_description: A number line showing an actual value of 50 and an estimate of 44, with the six-unit gap divided by the actual value to give twelve percent error.
accompanying_text:
Guess 44 when the answer is 50 and you missed by 6. But *how badly* is 6?

**Percent error** answers that: the size of the miss divided by the actual value, as a percent. Here 6 ÷ 50 = 0.12, so 12% error. The denominator is always the actual value — the truth you are being judged against.

illustration_description: The same two-unit error compared against a measurement of ten and a measurement of one thousand: twenty percent error versus zero point two percent error.
accompanying_text:
Percent error exists because a raw miss means nothing on its own.

Missing by 2 when the answer is 10 is a 20% error — serious. Missing by 2 when the answer is 1,000 is 0.2% — barely worth mentioning. Same gap, completely different verdicts, and only the percent tells them apart.

illustration_description: An upward-opening parabola: its lowest point is the vertex, and the dashed vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, mirroring the two sides.
accompanying_text: The parent parabola y = x² is a U-shape. Its lowest point is the **vertex** at (0, 0), and the vertical line through it is the **axis of symmetry**. Vertex form y = (x − h)² + k slides that U so its vertex sits at **(h, k)**.

illustration_description: The sign inside flips intuition: x minus h shifts the parabola right by h.
accompanying_text: The sign inside flips your intuition: **(x − h) shifts right by h**. So y = (x − 3)² has its vertex at x = 3, not −3. Likewise (x + 1)² means x − (−1), so its vertex is at x = −1. Set the inside to zero to find the vertex x.

illustration_description: The axis of symmetry is the vertical line x equals h through the vertex, mirroring the two halves.
accompanying_text: The **axis of symmetry** is the vertical line x = h through the vertex — the parabola is a mirror image across it. For y = (x − 3)² + 2, the axis is x = 3. It always matches the vertex's x-coordinate.

illustration_description: An upward-opening parabola: its lowest point is the vertex, and the dashed vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, mirroring the two sides.
accompanying_text: In standard form y = ax² + bx + c, the axis of symmetry is **x = −b/(2a)**. That value is the vertex's x-coordinate; substitute it back into the equation to get the vertex's y-coordinate.

illustration_description: Graphing from standard form: for y equals x squared plus four x plus one, the axis is x equals negative four over two, which is negative two, and the vertex is negative two, negative three.
accompanying_text: Worked: y = x² + 4x + 1, so a = 1, b = 4. Axis: x = −4/(2·1) = **−2**. Vertex y: (−2)² + 4(−2) + 1 = 4 − 8 + 1 = **−3**. Vertex is (−2, −3). Always compute the axis first, then substitute.

illustration_description: The sign of a sets the shape: a greater than zero opens upward with a minimum vertex; a less than zero opens downward with a maximum.
accompanying_text: The sign of **a** sets the shape: a > 0 opens upward, so the vertex is the **minimum**; a < 0 opens downward, so the vertex is the **maximum**. A larger |a| makes the parabola narrower.

illustration_description: An upward-opening parabola: its lowest point is the vertex, and the dashed vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, mirroring the two sides.
accompanying_text: The number **a** in y = ax² reshapes the parent parabola: |a| > 1 makes it **narrower**, |a| < 1 makes it **wider**, and a negative a **flips** it to open downward. It never moves the vertex — only the width and direction change.

illustration_description: A vertical shift moves the whole parabola up or down: y equals x squared plus k has its vertex at zero, k.
accompanying_text: A **vertical shift** moves the whole parabola up or down: y = x² + k has vertex (0, k). Add to go up, subtract to go down. The shape and axis stay the same; only the height of the vertex changes.

illustration_description: A horizontal shift hides in the parentheses: y equals x minus h squared moves the parabola right by h.
accompanying_text: A **horizontal shift** hides in the parentheses: y = (x − h)² moves right by h. Combine everything into y = a(x − h)² + k — stretch/flip by a, shift right by h, shift up by k — and the vertex lands at (h, k).

illustration_description: A parabola crossing the horizontal x-axis at two points; those crossing points are the roots — the solutions where the expression equals zero.
accompanying_text: The **zero-product property**: if two things multiply to 0, at least one of them must be 0. So if (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, then x − 3 = 0 or x + 2 = 0. These solutions are the **roots** — where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

illustration_description: The zero-product property: set each factor to zero separately, so x minus three times x plus two equals zero splits into two equations.
accompanying_text: To solve, **set each factor to zero** separately. (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0 splits into x − 3 = 0 → x = 3, and x + 2 = 0 → x = −2. Each factor contributes exactly one root.

illustration_description: The root's sign is opposite the sign inside: x plus two equals zero gives x equals negative two.
accompanying_text: The root's sign is **opposite** the sign inside: x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2, while x − 5 = 0 gives x = 5. A factor (x − r) gives root r; a factor (x + r) gives root −r.

illustration_description: A parabola crossing the horizontal x-axis at two points; those crossing points are the roots — the solutions where the expression equals zero.
accompanying_text: To solve x² + bx + c = 0, **factor first**: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Write them as (x + p)(x + q), then use the zero-product property to read off the roots.

illustration_description: Factoring x squared minus seven x plus twelve: two numbers that multiply to twelve and add to negative seven are negative three and negative four.
accompanying_text: Worked: x² − 7x + 12. Two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to −7 are **−3 and −4**. So (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, giving x = 3 or x = 4. The signs of the numbers become the roots directly.

illustration_description: The signs guide the search: a positive constant with a negative middle term means both numbers are negative.
accompanying_text: The signs guide the search. Positive c with negative b → **both numbers negative**. A **negative c** → one positive and one negative, and the larger-magnitude number carries the sign of b.

illustration_description: A parabola crossing the horizontal x-axis at two points; those crossing points are the roots — the solutions where the expression equals zero.
accompanying_text: A **difference of squares** x² − a² = 0 factors as (x − a)(x + a) = 0, so x = a or x = −a. The two roots are mirror images across the axis of symmetry — the parabola crosses the x-axis symmetrically.

illustration_description: The roots are exactly where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
accompanying_text: The roots are exactly where the parabola **crosses the x-axis**. For x² − 9, the crossings are x = −3 and x = 3, symmetric about the axis x = 0. The vertex sits at the bottom, halfway between the two roots.

illustration_description: For x squared plus b x plus c with roots, the sum of the roots is negative b and the product of the roots is c.
accompanying_text: For x² + bx + c with roots r₁ and r₂: the **sum** of the roots is −b and the **product** is c. It's a quick check — if your two roots don't multiply to c and add to −b, refactor.

illustration_description: A parabola crossing the horizontal x-axis at two points; those crossing points are the roots — the solutions where the expression equals zero.
accompanying_text: When a quadratic is just x² = k (with k > 0), take the square root of both sides: **x = ±√k**. That ± gives two solutions, one positive and one negative. To solve x² − 49 = 0, isolate x² = 49, then x = ±7.

illustration_description: Never drop the negative root: x squared equals twenty-five has solutions x equals five and x equals negative five.
accompanying_text: Never drop the **negative** root: x² = 25 has solutions x = 5 **and** x = −5, because (−5)² = 25 as well. Forgetting the negative answer is the single most common square-root mistake.

illustration_description: Square-root solving works on a shifted square too: x minus three squared equals sixteen gives x equals seven or x equals negative one.
accompanying_text: Square-root solving also works on a **shifted** square: (x − 3)² = 16 → x − 3 = ±4 → x = 3 + 4 = 7 or x = 3 − 4 = −1. Take the root of both sides, then undo the shift on each branch.

illustration_description: A parabola crossing the horizontal x-axis at two points; those crossing points are the roots — the solutions where the expression equals zero.
accompanying_text: When factoring is hard, the **quadratic formula** solves any ax² + bx + c = 0: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a). Identify a, b, and c, substitute, and simplify. The ± gives the two roots.

illustration_description: Quadratic formula worked: for x squared minus two x minus three equals zero, the discriminant is sixteen, giving x equals three or x equals negative one.
accompanying_text: Worked: x² − 2x − 3 = 0, so a = 1, b = −2, c = −3. The part under the root is b² − 4ac = 4 − 4(1)(−3) = 4 + 12 = 16, and √16 = 4. Then x = (2 ± 4)/2 → x = 3 or x = −1.

illustration_description: The formula handles non-integer roots too: for two x squared minus seven x plus three equals zero, the discriminant is twenty-five, giving x equals three or one half.
accompanying_text: The formula handles **non-integer** roots too. For 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0: b² − 4ac = 49 − 24 = 25, √25 = 5, so x = (7 ± 5)/(2·2) = 12/4 or 2/4 → x = 3 or **x = 1/2**. A fraction is a perfectly valid root.

illustration_description: Three parabolas over a horizontal x-axis: when the discriminant is positive the curve crosses the axis at two points (two roots); when it is zero the curve just touches the axis (one root); when it is negative the curve stays above the axis (no real roots).
accompanying_text: The **discriminant** D = b² − 4ac — the part under the root — tells you how many real solutions a quadratic has before you solve it. **D > 0**: two real roots. **D = 0**: one (repeated) root. **D < 0**: no real roots.

illustration_description: A zero discriminant is the boundary case: for x squared minus six x plus nine equals zero, the discriminant is zero and the parabola touches the axis at one point.
accompanying_text: A **zero** discriminant is the boundary case. For x² − 6x + 9 = 0, D = 36 − 36 = 0. The parabola just touches the x-axis at its vertex, giving exactly one repeated solution, x = 3.

illustration_description: A negative discriminant means the parabola never reaches the x-axis, so there are no real roots.
accompanying_text: A **negative** discriminant means the parabola never reaches the x-axis, so there are no real solutions. For x² + x + 1 = 0, D = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0. (The solutions are complex numbers, a later topic.)

illustration_description: An upward-opening parabola: its lowest point is the vertex, and the dashed vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, mirroring the two sides.
accompanying_text: A thrown object traces a parabola. If its height after x seconds is h = −x² + 6x, it's on the ground when h = 0. Solving −x² + 6x = 0 (that is, x² − 6x = 0) gives the launch and landing times.

illustration_description: In projectile motion the two roots are the launch and landing times, and the vertex in between is the peak.
accompanying_text: The two roots are the launch and landing times; the **vertex** in between is the peak. For h = −x² + 6x, it launches at x = 0 and lands at x = 6, so it reaches its highest point halfway, at the axis x = −b/(2a) = 3.

illustration_description: Substitute the peak time back in for the maximum height: the vertex y-value is the greatest height reached.
accompanying_text: Substitute the peak time back in for the **maximum height**. For h = −x² + 6x at x = 3: h = −(3)² + 6(3) = −9 + 18 = 9. So the ball reaches 9 units at the top of its arc.

illustration_description: A rectangle three tall and x plus four wide splits into two parts: one three by x with area three x, one three by four with area twelve. So three times the quantity x plus four equals three x plus twelve.
accompanying_text: Area problems often become quadratics. A rectangle x wide and (x + 3) long with area 40 gives x(x + 3) = 40, which becomes x² + 3x − 40 = 0. Solve it, then keep the answer that makes sense as a length.

illustration_description: Only the positive root is a real length: x squared plus three x minus forty equals zero factors as x plus eight times x minus five, so x equals five.
accompanying_text: Only the **positive** root is a real length. x² + 3x − 40 = 0 factors as (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0, giving x = −8 or x = 5. A rectangle can't have width −8, so x = 5. Always discard the negative root in a measurement.

illustration_description: Check by plugging back: width five and length eight give area five times eight equals forty.
accompanying_text: Check by plugging back: width 5, length 8, area 5 × 8 = 40. ✓ A quick multiply confirms you picked the right root and set up the equation correctly — a habit worth keeping on every word problem.

illustration_description: An upward-opening parabola: its lowest point is the vertex, and the dashed vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, mirroring the two sides.
accompanying_text: Real problems ask you to **model, solve by the best method, and interpret**. Ground or break-even → set the quadratic to 0 and solve. A greatest or least value → use the vertex. Just counting solutions → check the discriminant.

illustration_description: Worked area problem: a rectangle x by x plus four with area forty-five gives x squared plus four x minus forty-five equals zero, so x equals five.
accompanying_text: Worked area: a rectangle x by (x + 4) with area 45 gives x² + 4x − 45 = 0 = (x + 9)(x − 5). The roots are −9 and 5; a length is positive, so x = 5. Length 9, and 5 × 9 = 45 checks out.

illustration_description: When a problem only asks how many solutions, the discriminant b squared minus four a c answers without solving.
accompanying_text: When a problem only asks **how many** solutions, the discriminant D = b² − 4ac answers instantly by its sign — two, one, or none — with no need to solve the whole thing.

illustration_description: Eight to the two-thirds is the cube root of eight, squared, which is four; now the base can be a variable.
accompanying_text: You know the numeric version: 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4. Now let the base be a **variable**: x^(m/n) = ⁿ√(xᵐ). The denominator is the root, the numerator is the power — so x^(3/2) = √(x³), and ∛(x²) = x^(2/3). Two notations, one object.

illustration_description: Going the other way is just as mechanical: x to the four-fifths is the fifth root of x to the fourth.
accompanying_text: Going the other way is just as mechanical: x^(4/5) = ⁵√(x⁴). And a unit fraction drops the power entirely: x^(1/2) = √x, x^(1/3) = ∛x. Exponent form is usually easier to **compute** with; radical form is easier to **read**.

illustration_description: Every exponent rule from Algebra 1 survives with fractions: add exponents when multiplying like bases.
accompanying_text: Every exponent rule from Algebra 1 survives with fractions. **Product:** x^(1/2) · x^(3/2) = x^(1/2 + 3/2) = x². **Quotient:** subtract. **Power of a power:** multiply — (x⁶)^(1/3) = x^(6/3) = x². Same three rules, fraction arithmetic inside. (Assume all variables are positive.)

illustration_description: Power of a power is the workhorse: x to the sixth, all to the one-third, multiplies the exponents to give x squared.
accompanying_text: Power-of-a-power is the workhorse: (x⁶)^(1/3) asks for a third of six x-factors — x². And it runs in reverse to **undo** exponents: raising x^(2/3) to the power 3/2 gives x^(2/3 · 3/2) = x¹ = x. Reciprocal exponents cancel — that's the key to solving equations later.

illustration_description: Exponent form makes variable radicals mechanical: the square root of x to the sixth is x to the six-halves, which is x cubed.
accompanying_text: Exponent form makes variable radicals mechanical: √(x⁶) = x^(6/2) = **x³**, and ∛(x¹²) = x^(12/3) = **x⁴**. When the root index divides the power evenly, the radical vanishes entirely. (Assume all variables are positive.)

illustration_description: Mixed radicands split into parts: the square root of fifty x to the fourth is five root two times x squared.
accompanying_text: Mixed radicands split into parts: √(50x⁴) = √50 · √(x⁴) = 5√2 · x² = **5x²√2**. Numbers get the largest-square-factor treatment from Algebra 1; variables get exponent division. Everything cleanly outside, leftovers under the root.

illustration_description: By convention, simplified form keeps radicals out of denominators; multiply by the radical over itself.
accompanying_text: By convention, simplified form keeps radicals **out of denominators**. The fix: multiply by a clever form of 1. For 1/√2, multiply by √2/√2: the bottom becomes √2 · √2 = 2, giving **√2/2**. Nothing changed in value — only in form.

illustration_description: With a coefficient: six over root three, times root three over root three, is six root three over three, which is two root three.
accompanying_text: With a coefficient: 6/√3 → multiply by √3/√3 → 6√3/3 = **2√3**. Always finish with the ordinary fraction reduction. And simplify the radical FIRST when you can: 4/√8 = 4/(2√2) = 2/√2 = **√2** — much less work than rationalizing √8 directly.

illustration_description: FOIL works on radicals unchanged: one plus root two times three plus root two equals five plus four root two.
accompanying_text: FOIL works on radicals unchanged. (1 + √2)(3 + √2) = 3 + √2 + 3√2 + √2·√2 = 3 + 4√2 + 2 = **5 + 4√2**. Radical terms combine like like-terms; √2 · √2 collapses to plain 2.

illustration_description: Squares follow the a plus b squared pattern: two plus root three squared equals seven plus four root three.
accompanying_text: Squares follow the (a + b)² pattern: (2 + √3)² = 4 + 2·2·√3 + 3 = **7 + 4√3**. The middle term 2ab is where dropped work shows — squaring is never term-by-term.

illustration_description: The conjugate of a plus root b is a minus root b: flip the radical's sign.
accompanying_text: The **conjugate** of a + √b is a − √b — flip the radical's sign. Their product needs no FOIL survivors: (3 + √2)(3 − √2) = 9 − 2 = **7**. The middle terms cancel and both leftovers are rational: (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b. Sound familiar? Complex conjugates play the same trick.

illustration_description: The conjugate is exactly the tool for a binomial denominator: multiply top and bottom by it to clear the radical.
accompanying_text: That's exactly the tool for a **binomial denominator**: for 4/(3 + √2), multiply by the conjugate over itself. Bottom: (3 + √2)(3 − √2) = 7. Top: 4(3 − √2) = 12 − 4√2. Result: **(12 − 4√2)/7** — radical evicted.

illustration_description: Five small graphs, one per parent function: a straight line for y equals x, an upward parabola for y equals x squared, a V shape for absolute value of x, a half curve starting at a point and rising to the right for the square root of x, and an S shaped curve for x cubed.
accompanying_text: Make the radical a **function**: f(x) = √x. It starts at the origin, rises forever, but slower and slower — a parabola lying on its side (just the top half). Inputs can't be negative and outputs never are: **domain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0**.

illustration_description: Why no negative inputs: the square root of negative four is not a real number, so the domain of the square-root function starts at zero.
accompanying_text: Why no negative inputs? √(−4) isn't a real number (that's i's territory, from complex numbers). And why no negative outputs? The √ symbol means the **principal** (nonnegative) root: √9 is 3, never −3. The graph lives entirely in the first quadrant.

illustration_description: The graph of y equals the square root of x minus 3. The curve starts at the point 3 comma 0 and rises to the right. The region left of x equals 3 is shaded to show it is excluded: inputs there would put a negative under the root. An arrow along the x axis marks the domain, x greater than or equal to 3.
accompanying_text: For any even root, the rule is one sentence: **the inside must be ≥ 0**. For f(x) = √(x − 3), solve x − 3 ≥ 0: domain **x ≥ 3**. The graph starts at (3, 0) and everything to the left is off-limits.

illustration_description: A coefficient makes it a one-step inequality: the radicand must be at least zero.
accompanying_text: A coefficient just makes it a one-step inequality: for √(2x − 8), solve 2x − 8 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 4. But **cube roots take anything**: ∛(x − 5) happily accepts x = 0, since ∛(−5) is a real number. Odd roots: domain all reals.

illustration_description: Transformation rules apply verbatim to the square-root curve: root of x minus two shifts the graph right by two.
accompanying_text: Your transformation rules apply verbatim to √x. f(x) = √(x − 2) + 1 is the parent graph slid **right 2, up 1** — its starting point moves from (0, 0) to **(2, 1)**. The start point travels exactly like a vertex.

illustration_description: Reflections work too: negative root x flips the curve below the axis.
accompanying_text: Reflections work too: −√x flips the curve **below** the axis (range y ≤ 0), and √(−x) flips it **leftward** (domain x ≤ 0). Shifts move the start point; flips choose which quadrant the curve sweeps into.

illustration_description: A radical equation traps x under a root; the escape move is to isolate the radical, then square both sides.
accompanying_text: A radical equation traps x under a root. The escape move: **isolate the radical, then square both sides**. √(x + 5) = 3 → square → x + 5 = 9 → **x = 4**. Verify: √9 = 3. ✓ Squaring undoes the root — as long as the root stood alone first.

illustration_description: Isolate first, because squaring a sum is a mess: root x plus two equals seven becomes root x equals five, so x is twenty-five.
accompanying_text: **Isolate first** — squaring a sum is a mess. For √x + 2 = 7, subtract 2 before squaring: √x = 5, so x = **25**. Squaring the original left side would give x + 4√x + 4, which still holds a radical: no progress.

illustration_description: Two graphs: the square root of x plus 7, and the line y equals x plus 1. They truly intersect once, at the point 2 comma 3, marked as the real solution. At the point negative 3 comma negative 2, the line is below the x axis where the square root cannot go — squaring both sides invents this phantom, the extraneous solution.
accompanying_text: Squaring has a blind spot: it erases signs, so it can **invent solutions**. Solve √(x + 7) = x + 1: squaring gives x + 7 = x² + 2x + 1 → x² + x − 6 = 0 → x = 2 or x = −3. Check both: √9 = 3 = 2 + 1 ✓, but √4 = 2 while −3 + 1 = **−2** ✗. The −3 is **extraneous**.

illustration_description: The picture explains extraneous solutions: the curve and the line cross only where a real solution exists.
accompanying_text: The picture explains it: the curve y = √(x + 7) and the line y = x + 1 truly cross **once**, at (2, 3). At x = −3 the line sits at −2 — the **mirror image** of the root's +2. Squaring can't tell y from −y, so it reports both. The check is how you un-blur them.

illustration_description: Radicals on both sides clear together with one square of the whole equation.
accompanying_text: Radicals on **both sides**? One square clears them together: √(2x + 3) = √(x + 7) → 2x + 3 = x + 7 → **x = 4**. Check: √11 = √11. ✓ With matching roots, the check rarely fails — but the domain still must admit the answer.

illustration_description: Cube roots are even friendlier: cubing never invents extraneous solutions, so no rejection step is needed.
accompanying_text: Cube roots are even friendlier: **cubing never invents solutions**, because cubing keeps signs (only even powers blur them). ∛(x − 4) = 2 → x − 4 = 8 → x = 12, no check drama. The extraneous risk belongs to EVEN powers alone.

illustration_description: Reciprocal exponents cancel: to undo a two-thirds power, raise to the three-halves power.
accompanying_text: Chapter 1 planted the key: **reciprocal exponents cancel**. To solve x^(3/2) = 8, raise both sides to the power 2/3: x = 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = **4**. One move undoes the exponent — no radical juggling required.

illustration_description: Check the reciprocal arithmetic: x to the three-halves, all to the two-thirds, has exponent one, giving x.
accompanying_text: Check the reciprocal arithmetic: (x^(3/2))^(2/3) = x^(3/2 · 2/3) = x¹. And evaluate the other side the easy way: 8^(2/3) roots first — ∛8 = 2, then 2² = 4. Verify the answer forward: 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8. ✓

illustration_description: Remember x squared equals nine giving plus or minus three: the same ghost haunts even numerators, which need plus or minus.
accompanying_text: Remember x² = 9 giving ±3? The same ghost haunts **even numerators**. Solve x^(2/3) = 9: the 2 up top squares — and squaring erases signs. Check both 27 and −27: 27^(2/3) = 9 ✓, and (−27)^(2/3) = (∛(−27))² = (−3)² = 9 ✓. **Two solutions: x = ±27.**

illustration_description: Odd numerators keep signs, so they stay single-answer: x to the three-fifths gives one solution.
accompanying_text: Odd numerators keep signs, so they stay single-answer: x^(3/5) = 8 has only x = 8^(5/3) = 32. The rule mirrors Chapter 4 exactly: **even powers blur signs (±), odd powers preserve them (one answer)**. Look at the numerator to know which world you're in.

illustration_description: Radicals model the real world whenever a quantity grows with a square root, flattening as it increases.
accompanying_text: Radicals model the real world whenever a quantity grows with a **square root**. Crash investigators use s = √(24d): skid length d feet predicts speed s mph. Skids of d = 6: s = √144 = **12 mph**. Quadruple the skid, only double the speed — that's √-growth.

illustration_description: Falling objects run on the same math: the drop time grows with the square root of the height.
accompanying_text: Falling objects run on the same math: dropping from height h feet takes t = √(h/16) = **√h/4 seconds**. From h = 64: t = 8/4 = 2 s. To ask 'what height gives a chosen time?', **solve the radical equation** — Chapter 4's skill, now employed.

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: The square root of a **perfect square** is a whole number: √49 = 7 because 7² = 49. The perfect squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, … Knowing them on sight is the key to radicals.

illustration_description: Not every number is a perfect square: root twenty is not whole, sitting between four and five on the number line.
accompanying_text: Not every number is a perfect square. √20 isn't whole — it sits between √16 = 4 and √25 = 5. But we can still simplify √20 using a perfect-square factor, which is the next idea.

illustration_description: To simplify a non-perfect square, find its largest perfect-square factor and split the radical there.
accompanying_text: To simplify a non-perfect-square, find its **largest perfect-square factor**. For 20, that's 4 (since 20 = 4 · 5). Scanning the perfect squares — 4, 9, 16, 25, … — for the biggest one that divides makes this quick.

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: Split off the perfect square using √(a · b) = √a · √b. So √72 = √(36 · 2) = √36 · √2 = 6√2. The root of the perfect square comes out front; the rest stays under the radical.

illustration_description: Worked: root fifty equals root of twenty-five times two equals root twenty-five times root two equals five root two.
accompanying_text: Worked: √50 = √(25 · 2) = √25 · √2 = 5√2. The number left under the root — here 2 — is the **radicand**, and it should have no perfect-square factors left.

illustration_description: Always pull out the largest square: root seventy-two is best split as root thirty-six times root two, giving six root two.
accompanying_text: Always pull out the **largest** square. √72 could start as √4 · √18 = 2√18, but √18 still simplifies. Using 36 directly gives 6√2 in one step — no perfect-square factor is left behind.

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: A radical is **fully simplified** when the radicand has no perfect-square factors left. √12 = 2√3 is done, since 3 is square-free. √3 is already simplified. Always ask: is any square still hiding under the root?

illustration_description: A coefficient already outside multiplies through: two root eight equals two times two root two, which is four root two.
accompanying_text: A coefficient already outside multiplies through. 2√8 = 2 · (2√2) = 4√2: simplify the radical to 2√2, then multiply the outside numbers 2 · 2 = 4. Handle the radical first, then the coefficients.

illustration_description: The final answer has the coefficient out front and a square-free radicand with no perfect-square factors left.
accompanying_text: The final answer has the coefficient out front and a square-free radicand. After each step, check: is there any perfect square still under the root? If yes, keep simplifying until there isn't.

illustration_description: Adding like radicals: two copies of root three plus five copies of root three make seven copies of root three, just like counting groups of the same thing.
accompanying_text: **Like radicals** have the same radicand and combine like terms: 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3. Add the coefficients and keep the radical. Unlike radicals — such as √2 + √3 — cannot be combined at all.

illustration_description: Adding like radicals: the coefficients add or subtract while the radical is a label that must match.
accompanying_text: The coefficients add or subtract; the radical is a label that must match. 4√2 + 3√2 = 7√2, but 4√2 + 3√5 stays as it is — different radicals can't be merged, just like 4x + 3y can't.

illustration_description: Sometimes simplify first to reveal like radicals: root eight plus root two becomes two root two plus root two, which is three root two.
accompanying_text: Sometimes you must **simplify first** to reveal like radicals. √8 + √2 looks unlike, but √8 = 2√2, so it becomes 2√2 + √2 = 3√2. Simplify each radical, then combine the ones that match.

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: Multiply radicals by multiplying the radicands: √a · √b = √(ab). So √2 · √3 = √6. When the product is a perfect square, it becomes a whole number: √2 · √8 = √16 = 4.

illustration_description: Coefficients out front multiply separately: two root three times four root two equals eight root six.
accompanying_text: Coefficients out front multiply separately: 2√3 · 4√2 = (2 · 4)√(3 · 2) = 8√6. Multiply the outside numbers together, and the inside numbers together — two independent multiplications.

illustration_description: Multiply first, then simplify the result: root six times root two is root twelve, which simplifies to two root three.
accompanying_text: Multiply first, then simplify the result. √6 · √2 = √12 = 2√3. Combine everything under one root, then pull out any perfect square that appears.

illustration_description: Adding like radicals: two copies of root three plus five copies of root three make seven copies of root three, just like counting groups of the same thing.
accompanying_text: Distribute a radical over a sum just like a number: √2 · (√3 + √5) = √6 + √10. Multiply the outside radical into each term inside the parentheses, one at a time.

illustration_description: Distribute, then simplify each product, often to a whole number.
accompanying_text: Distribute, then simplify each product — often to a whole number. √3 · (√3 + √12) = √9 + √36 = 3 + 6 = 9. Each piece can collapse to an integer when the radicands multiply to a perfect square.

illustration_description: After distributing, combine like radicals if any match.
accompanying_text: After distributing, **combine like radicals** if any match. √2 · (√6 + √2) = √12 + √4 = 2√3 + 2. Simplify each product, then merge anything with the same radicand.

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: A fractional exponent is a root: a^(1/n) means the n-th root of a. So a^(1/2) = √a and a^(1/3) = ∛a. For example, 16^(1/2) = 4 because 4² = 16, and 27^(1/3) = 3 because 3³ = 27.

illustration_description: Roots as exponents: the denominator picks the root, so one-fourth means the fourth root and one-fifth the fifth root.
accompanying_text: The **denominator picks the root**: 1/4 means the fourth root, 1/5 the fifth root. So 81^(1/4) = 3 because 3⁴ = 81. Ask yourself: what number, raised to the n-th power, gives a?

illustration_description: This works for any perfect power: thirty-two to the one-fifth is two, because two to the fifth is thirty-two.
accompanying_text: This works for any perfect power. 32^(1/5) = 2 because 2⁵ = 32. A rational exponent is just a root written as a fraction — the two notations mean exactly the same thing.

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: A^(m/n) means take the n-th root, then raise to the m-th power: a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m. For 8^(2/3): ∛8 = 2, then 2² = 4. Take the root first — it keeps the numbers small — then apply the power.

illustration_description: Taking the root first keeps arithmetic easy: twenty-seven to the two-thirds is the cube root of twenty-seven squared, which is three squared, nine.
accompanying_text: Taking the root first keeps the arithmetic easy. 27^(2/3) = (∛27)² = 3² = 9, much simpler than 27² = 729 and then cube-rooting. Same answer, far less work.

illustration_description: Read the fraction as instructions: the numerator is the power and the denominator is the root.
accompanying_text: Read the fraction as instructions: the **numerator is the power**, the **denominator is the root**. For 32^(2/5): the fifth root of 32 is 2, and 2² = 4. Denominator down (root), numerator up (power).

illustration_description: Simplifying the square root of 72 by splitting 72 into 36 times 2: the square root of the perfect square 36 is 6, which comes out in front, leaving 6 times the square root of 2.
accompanying_text: A negative exponent means **reciprocal**: a^(−1/n) = 1/(ⁿ√a). So 8^(−1/3) = 1/∛8 = 1/2. Take the root as usual, then flip the result to make it a fraction below 1.

illustration_description: Negative rational exponents combine all three parts: the root from the denominator, the power from the numerator, and the reciprocal from the sign.
accompanying_text: Combine all three parts: root (denominator), power (numerator), reciprocal (negative sign). For 27^(−2/3): ∛27 = 3, then 3² = 9, then flip to get 1/9.

illustration_description: The sign tells which side of one the answer lands on: a positive exponent gives a value above one, a negative one below.
accompanying_text: The sign tells you which side of 1 the answer lands on. A **positive** rational exponent grows the base; a **negative** one shrinks it to a fraction below 1. The size of the fraction comes from the root and power.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse c satisfies c² = a² + b², so c = √(a² + b²). For legs 3 and 4: c = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Square each leg, add, and take the root.

illustration_description: The Pythagorean theorem for any right triangle: legs five and twelve give hypotenuse root of twenty-five plus one hundred forty-four, which is root one hundred sixty-nine, thirteen.
accompanying_text: It works for any right triangle. Legs 5 and 12: c = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13. As long as the sum of the squares is a perfect square, the hypotenuse is a whole number.

illustration_description: You can also find a missing leg: subtract the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the root.
accompanying_text: You can also find a **missing leg**: if the hypotenuse and one leg are known, a = √(c² − b²). For c = 13 and b = 5: a = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12. Subtract the squares this time.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: Often the hypotenuse is irrational and stays as a simplified radical. Legs 2 and 2: c = √(4 + 4) = √8 = 2√2. Compute c² first, then simplify the radical the way we did in Chapter 1.

illustration_description: When the answer is a radical: legs two and four give c squared equals twenty, so c is root twenty, which simplifies to two root five.
accompanying_text: Worked: legs 2 and 4. c² = 4 + 16 = 20, and c = √20 = 2√5. Add the squares to get c², then pull out the largest perfect-square factor to simplify.

illustration_description: Some hypotenuses are already simplified: legs one and two give c equals root of one plus four, which is root five.
accompanying_text: Some hypotenuses are already simplified. Legs 1 and 2 give c = √(1 + 4) = √5, and 5 is square-free, so √5 is the final answer — nothing to pull out.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: The distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle: d = √((Δx)² + (Δy)²), where Δx and Δy are the horizontal and vertical gaps. From (0, 0) to (3, 4): d = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

illustration_description: Distance between points not at the origin: subtract the coordinates to get the legs, then apply the Pythagorean theorem.
accompanying_text: When the points aren't at the origin, **subtract the coordinates** to get the legs. From (1, 2) to (4, 6): Δx = 4 − 1 = 3 and Δy = 6 − 2 = 4, so d = √(9 + 16) = 5. The differences are the triangle's legs.

illustration_description: When the distance is not a whole number, simplify the radical to its cleanest form.
accompanying_text: When the distance isn't a whole number, simplify the radical. From (0, 0) to (2, 2): d = √(4 + 4) = √8 = 2√2. Same steps as before, ending in a simplified radical.

illustration_description: A rational expression is a fraction of polynomials, one polynomial over another.
accompanying_text: A **rational expression** is a fraction of polynomials, like (x + 2)/(x − 5). It behaves like any fraction with one iron rule: **the denominator can't be zero**. Here x = 5 would divide by zero, so 5 is an **excluded value** — the expression's domain is every real number except 5.

illustration_description: Factored denominators hand you every excluded value at once: any input making the denominator zero is banned.
accompanying_text: Factored denominators hand you every excluded value at once: for x/((x − 2)(x + 3)), the denominator dies at x = 2 **and** x = −3 — two exclusions. A zero **numerator** is harmless: 0 divided by something is just 0. Only the bottom can break the expression.

illustration_description: Simplifying works exactly like six-eighths equals three-quarters: cancel a common factor.
accompanying_text: Simplifying works exactly like 6/8 = 3/4 — cancel a **common factor**. With polynomials, factor first: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = ((x − 3)(x + 3))/(x + 3) = **x − 3**. The shared factor (x + 3) cancels. Factoring is the price of admission.

illustration_description: Only factors cancel, never terms: in x plus four over x, the x's do not cancel because x is a term, not a factor.
accompanying_text: Only **factors** cancel — never terms. In (x + 4)/x, the x's do NOT cancel: x is a term of the top, not a factor of it. Test with a number: at x = 2, (2 + 4)/2 = 3, but the illegal cancel would claim 4. One substitution exposes the fraud.

illustration_description: x minus three and three minus x look like a match but are opposites, differing by a factor of negative one.
accompanying_text: (x − 3) and (3 − x) look like a match but aren't — they're **opposites**: 3 − x = −(x − 3). Check x = 5: the first gives 2, the second −2. So (3 − x)/(x − 3) doesn't cancel to 1 — it cancels to **−1**, at every legal x.

illustration_description: The mechanical move: rewrite one opposite as negative one times the other, then the factors cancel.
accompanying_text: The mechanical move: rewrite one opposite as −1 times the other. (5 − x)/(x² − 25) = −(x − 5)/((x − 5)(x + 5)) = **−1/(x + 5)**. Factor, flip the backwards one with a −1, cancel as usual. The −1 rides out front.

illustration_description: Multiply like numeric fractions: tops together and bottoms together.
accompanying_text: Multiply like numeric fractions — tops together, bottoms together — but **factor first and cancel across**. (x + 2)/x · x/(x − 1): the x's cancel diagonally, leaving (x + 2)/(x − 1). Cancel before multiplying and nothing ever grows.

illustration_description: The full pipeline: factor every level, then cancel any top with any bottom before multiplying.
accompanying_text: The full pipeline: **factor every level, cancel any top with any bottom, multiply what's left.** (x² − 4)/(x + 1) · (x + 1)/(x + 2) = ((x−2)(x+2)(x+1))/((x+1)(x+2)) = **x − 2**. Diagonal cancels are legal because multiplication is one big fraction.

illustration_description: Division is the same fraction rule you have always used: keep, change, flip.
accompanying_text: Division is the same fraction rule you've always used: **keep, change, flip**. Keep the first, change ÷ to ·, flip the second. (x/(x+1)) ÷ (x/(x+3)) = (x/(x+1)) · ((x+3)/x) = **(x + 3)/(x + 1)** after the x's cancel.

illustration_description: After the flip it becomes the multiply lesson again: factor and cancel.
accompanying_text: After the flip, it's Chapter 2 Lesson 1: factor and cancel. (x² − 4)/(x + 3) ÷ (x − 2)/(x + 3) → flip → ((x−2)(x+2)/(x+3)) · ((x+3)/(x−2)) = **x + 2**. Both (x + 3) and (x − 2) cancel across.

illustration_description: Real problems chain operations; the bookkeeping rule is that every excluded input stays excluded throughout.
accompanying_text: Real problems chain operations. The bookkeeping rule: an input is banned if it breaks **any stage** — every original denominator, every divisor's numerator (it flips underneath), and nothing gets un-banned by cancellation. Collect exclusions as you go, not at the end.

illustration_description: Chains simplify left to right, or all at once as one big fraction.
accompanying_text: Chains simplify left to right (or all at once as one big fraction). (x²−1)/x · x/(x+1) ÷ (x−1)/2: flip the last, factor, and the big fraction ((x−1)(x+1) · x · 2) / (x · (x+1) · (x−1)) collapses to **2**. Constants can be the final answer — the exclusions are what remember the journey.

illustration_description: Same denominator, same rule as always: add the tops and keep the common denominator.
accompanying_text: Same denominator? Same rule as always: **add the tops, keep the bottom**. (3x)/(x + 2) + 5/(x + 2) = (3x + 5)/(x + 2). The denominator is a label — it never adds to itself.

illustration_description: Subtraction has one famous trap: the minus sign hits the entire second numerator, so distribute it to every term.
accompanying_text: Subtraction has one famous trap: **the minus hits the entire second numerator**. (5x)/(x+3) − (x − 2)/(x+3) = (5x − (x − 2))/(x+3) = (5x − x + 2)/(x+3) = **(4x + 2)/(x+3)**. Parentheses first, then distribute the minus — the −2 becomes +2.

illustration_description: Unlike denominators need the least common denominator, built from every distinct factor.
accompanying_text: Unlike denominators need the **least common denominator** — with polynomials, take **each distinct factor at its highest power**. For (x + 1) and x(x + 1): factors x and (x + 1), so LCD = **x(x + 1)**. Never multiply blindly; collect factors.

illustration_description: Factor before collecting: for one over x squared minus four and one over x plus two, factor x squared minus four to reveal the shared factor.
