illustration_description: Twenty intervals, one per poll. Nineteen of them reach across the true value and one misses it. Ninety-five percent describes how often the method captures the truth, not how likely any single interval is to be right.
accompanying_text: Think of a machine that stamps out intervals. About 19 in 20 of its intervals contain the truth. You pull one out of the machine. You cannot say your interval has a 95% chance of being right — you can say the machine is right 95% of the time, and you trust the machine.

illustration_description: Twenty intervals, one per poll. Nineteen of them reach across the true value and one misses it. Ninety-five percent describes how often the method captures the truth, not how likely any single interval is to be right.
accompanying_text:
Here is the sentence almost everyone gets wrong:

*"There is a 95% chance the truth is inside this interval."*

The truth is a fixed number. It is either inside your interval or it is not — there is no chance about it. The 95% describes the **method**: run it many times and about 95% of the intervals it makes will capture the truth.

illustration_description: Twenty intervals, one per poll. Nineteen of them reach across the true value and one misses it. Ninety-five percent describes how often the method captures the truth, not how likely any single interval is to be right.
accompanying_text:
Raising the confidence level widens the interval. There is no free lunch:

**99%** — catches the truth almost always, but the band may be so wide it rules nothing out.
**80%** — a tight, decisive-looking band that misses one time in five.

95% is a convention, not a law of nature. It is a chosen trade between being right often and saying something useful.

illustration_description: Two candidates at forty-eight and forty-five percent, each with a three point margin. Their bands overlap heavily, so the lead is inside the wobble and the race is a statistical tie.
accompanying_text: Draw both bands before you say anything. If they share any ground, the poll cannot tell you which one is really higher. If they are cleanly apart, it can.

illustration_description: Two candidates at forty-eight and forty-five percent, each with a three point margin. Their bands overlap heavily, so the lead is inside the wobble and the race is a statistical tie.
accompanying_text:
"A leads B, 48% to 45%." With a margin of ±3, A's band runs 45–51 and B's runs 42–48. They overlap.

So a truth of 47% for both is perfectly consistent with this poll. The lead is **inside the wobble** — which is what commentators mean, when they are careful, by a statistical tie.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text:
Three questions to ask any poll, in order:

**Who was asked, and how were they chosen?** (bias — the margin cannot see it)
**How many?** (the margin — how much wobble)
**Is the effect bigger than the margin?** (whether the finding survives its own uncertainty)

Skip the first and the other two are decoration.

illustration_description: The pile of gaps that random relabelling produces, centred on zero. The gap actually observed sits far out in the tail, where chance almost never reaches.
accompanying_text: The scores never change. Only the labels move. If the treatment truly did nothing, then the labels are just stickers — and any gap you see is an accident of which scores happened to get which sticker. Shuffling shows you every accident that was available.

illustration_description: The pile of gaps that random relabelling produces, centred on zero. The gap actually observed sits far out in the tail, where chance almost never reaches.
accompanying_text:
Two groups differ. Before you celebrate, ask the only question that matters:

**Could chance alone have produced a gap this big?**

To answer it, you need to know what gaps chance *does* produce. So build them: shuffle the labels at random, keeping the same scores, and record the gap. Do it hundreds of times.

illustration_description: The pile of gaps that random relabelling produces, centred on zero. The gap actually observed sits far out in the tail, where chance almost never reaches.
accompanying_text:
Now compare. The real gap was **4**. In the pile of chance gaps, almost nothing reaches out that far — in the exact count, 6 of the 252 possible splits, about **2%**.

So either something unusual happened by luck (about a 1-in-50 event), or the method really did something. That comparison is the whole logic of a significance test.

illustration_description: The pile of gaps that random relabelling produces, centred on zero. The gap actually observed sits far out in the tail, where chance almost never reaches.
accompanying_text: Read the p-value in one direction only: given no effect, how often would chance hand me data this extreme? It never tells you the probability that there is no effect. Swapping those two is the same reversal error as confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A).

illustration_description: The pile of gaps that random relabelling produces, centred on zero. The gap actually observed sits far out in the tail, where chance almost never reaches.
accompanying_text:
Count the tail. Of all the gaps chance produced, what fraction reached as far as the one you actually saw?

That fraction is the **p-value**: the chance of data at least this extreme *if the no-effect story were true*.

Small p-value → the no-effect story explains your data badly.

illustration_description: A tiny effect measured on a huge sample can be statistically significant and still be far too small to matter. Significance answers whether the effect is real; effect size answers whether it is worth anything.
accompanying_text:
How small is small enough? By convention, **p < 0.05** — a result that chance would produce less than 1 time in 20 gets called *statistically significant*.

That 5% is a custom, not a discovery. It buys you a mistake rate: even when nothing is going on, about 1 study in 20 will clear the bar by luck alone.

illustration_description: A tiny effect measured on a huge sample can be statistically significant and still be far too small to matter. Significance answers whether the effect is real; effect size answers whether it is worth anything.
accompanying_text: Ask two questions of every finding, never one. **Is it real?** — that is the p-value's job. **Is it big?** — that is the effect size's job, measured in the units of the problem. A yes to the first and a no to the second means: real, and not worth doing.

illustration_description: A tiny effect measured on a huge sample can be statistically significant and still be far too small to matter. Significance answers whether the effect is real; effect size answers whether it is worth anything.
accompanying_text:
"Significant" answers exactly one question: **could chance alone have done this?**

It does not answer:

– Is the effect **big**?
– Does it **matter**?
– Is it **true**?

With a large enough sample, an effect of 0.3 points on a 100-point test becomes significant. It is real, and it is worthless.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text:
Three more things a significant result does not give you:

**Proof.** About 1 significant result in 20 is a fluke when nothing is going on.
**Generalisation.** It applies to the population you sampled, not to everyone.
**Cause** — unless the treatment was randomly assigned. Significance and causation are different questions with different guardians.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text: Run two checks on any headline. Was the treatment assigned by a coin? If not, delete every causal verb from the sentence. Was the sample drawn at random from the population being talked about? If not, shrink the sentence to the people who were actually studied.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text:
Every claim has a design underneath it, and the design is a ceiling.

A voluntary online poll supports almost nothing. An observational study supports association. A random sample supports a population estimate. A randomised experiment supports cause.

A claim can travel **down** this ladder. It can never climb it.

illustration_description: Three study designs side by side. A sample survey uses random sampling and can generalise to a population. An observational study can only report association. An experiment uses random assignment and is the only design that can establish cause.
accompanying_text:
Two more questions the design answers, and the headline usually hides:

**Who was in it?** A drug tested only on men aged 20–35 is a drug tested only on men aged 20–35.
**Compared with what?** "Improves memory" — compared with a placebo? With nothing? With a rival product?

A claim with no comparison group is not a weak claim. It is not a claim at all.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text: Ask two questions of any conclusion. **Who does it speak for?** Only the people who could have been sampled. **Where does it apply?** Only inside the range of the data. A conclusion that leaves either boundary is no longer supported by the study.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text:
The arithmetic can be perfect while the sentence is false. Three ways it happens:

**Reach** — the claim covers people the sample never included.
**Extrapolation** — the claim runs past the range of the data.
**Swapped conditional** — P(A | B) reported as P(B | A).

Each one is a failure of *interpretation*, not of computation.

illustration_description: A tiny effect measured on a huge sample can be statistically significant and still be far too small to matter. Significance answers whether the effect is real; effect size answers whether it is worth anything.
accompanying_text:
The third failure is the reversal you met in probability.

"95% of people with the disease test positive" is P(positive | disease).
"95% of positive tests mean disease" is P(disease | positive).

When the disease is rare, these two numbers are wildly different — and the second one is usually the false claim in the headline.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text: Take the questions in order and stop at the first failure. A claim that fails question 1 cannot be rescued by a beautiful p-value at question 4 — the later answers are only meaningful once the earlier ones pass.

illustration_description: A ladder of study designs. The stronger the design, the stronger the claim it can carry: a voluntary poll supports almost nothing, an observational study supports association, a random sample supports a population estimate, and only a randomised experiment supports a causal claim.
accompanying_text:
You now have five questions, and in this order they catch almost everything:

1. **How was the data made?** (design → ceiling)
2. **Who was left out?** (bias — the margin cannot see it)
3. **How much wobble?** (margin of error)
4. **Is the effect bigger than the wobble?** (significance)
5. **Is it big enough to matter?** (effect size)

illustration_description: A poll result of forty-eight percent with a three point margin either side, shown as a band from forty-five to fifty-one percent. Every value inside the band is a plausible truth; the single number is only the middle of it.
accompanying_text:
Two habits worth keeping for life:

**Ask what was randomised** before you read anything else. It is one question and it settles what the claim may say.

**Read the band, not the number.** Every estimate is a range, every gap has its own wobble, and every "significant" finding still owes you an effect size.

illustration_description: Drawing sample after sample and stacking each statistic builds a mound: the sampling distribution.
accompanying_text: Chapter 2 showed the statistic wobbling from sample to sample. Now stack those wobbles up: draw sample after sample and pile each proportion on a line. The pile that grows has a shape — and it is always the same shape.

illustration_description: The mound has a name: the normal distribution, which appears whenever many small chances add together.
accompanying_text: This mound has a name: the normal distribution. It appears whenever many small chances add up — sample proportions, measurement errors, heights. Same curve, different rulers: what changes is only its center (the mean) and its width (the standard deviation).

illustration_description: Every normal curve keeps the same promise: about sixty-eight percent of values within one standard deviation, ninety-five within two, and ninety-nine point seven within three.
accompanying_text: Every normal curve keeps the same promise, whatever its center μ and width σ: about 68% of values land within one σ of μ, about 95% within two, about 99.7% within three. Scores on a test with μ = 100, σ = 10 will be our running example.

illustration_description: Symmetry lets you split the leftover: five percent lies outside two standard deviations, so each tail takes exactly half of it, two and a half percent.
accompanying_text: Notice what just happened: symmetry let you split the leftover. Outside two σ is 5%; each tail takes exactly half. Every region under the bell is reachable from the three memorized numbers plus halving.

illustration_description: The z-score gives the idea its own number: z equals x minus mu over sigma, asking how many standard deviations x sits from the centre.
accompanying_text: 'Within two σ' keeps coming up — so give the idea its own number. z = (x − μ) / σ asks: how many widths is x from the center? z = 0 is the mean itself; z = 2 is the edge of the 95% country; the sign says which side.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: A **system** is two equations you solve at the same time. Its **solution** is the single point (x, y) that makes **both** equations true at once. On a graph, that's exactly where the two lines **cross**.

illustration_description: To check a proposed solution, substitute it into both equations; it must make each one true.
accompanying_text: To **check** a proposed solution, substitute it into **both** equations. For (2, 3) with y = x + 1: 3 = 2 + 1 ✓. With y = −x + 5: 3 = −2 + 5 ✓. Both come out true, so (2, 3) really is the solution.

illustration_description: A solution must satisfy every equation in the system at once.
accompanying_text: That's the heart of it: a solution must satisfy **every** equation at once, not just one. A point can sit on one line and still miss the system entirely. Only the shared point — the crossing — counts.

illustration_description: A slanted line crossing both axes: the point where it crosses the y-axis is the y-intercept (there x is 0), and where it crosses the x-axis is the x-intercept (there y is 0).
accompanying_text: To solve a system **by graphing**: draw each line (start at its y-intercept, then step by its slope), and find where they **cross**. That crossing point is the solution — read off its x and y, then confirm by substitution.

illustration_description: Graphing y equals two x and y equals x plus three, the two lines cross at the point three, six, which is the solution.
accompanying_text: Worked example: **y = 2x** and **y = x + 3**. Plot both and they cross at **(3, 6)**. Check by substituting: 2·3 = 6 ✓ and 3 + 3 = 6 ✓. When the crossing lands on grid lines, graphing reads the solution right off the page.

illustration_description: Always check the crossing by substituting into both equations, since a graph can only be read approximately.
accompanying_text: Always **check the crossing** by substituting into both equations. A graph read by eye can land a little off, especially between grid lines; the substitution is what proves the point is exactly right.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: You can tell how many solutions a system has **before** solving, by comparing the lines. **Different slopes** → they cross once → **one solution**. **Same slope, different intercept** → parallel → **no solution**. **Same slope and intercept** → the same line → **infinitely many**.

illustration_description: Parallel lines are the no-solution case: equal slopes tilt the lines the same way so they never cross.
accompanying_text: **Parallel** is the no-solution case. Equal slopes tilt the lines the same way; different y-intercepts start them at different heights. They march alongside each other forever and never cross — so there's no point that satisfies both.

illustration_description: When both equations describe the same line, every point on it is a solution, giving infinitely many.
accompanying_text: When both equations describe the **same line**, every point on it satisfies both — **infinitely many** solutions. Watch for equations that look different but are the same line in disguise; comparing slope and intercept settles it.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Graphing is slow and imprecise. **Substitution** is exact. When one equation already says **y = (something)**, replace y in the *other* equation with that something. Now it has only x — solve it, then use y = (something) to find y.

illustration_description: Substitution worked: with y equals two x minus one and three x plus y equals nine, substitute to get five x minus one equals nine, so x equals two.
accompanying_text: Worked all the way: **y = 2x − 1** and **3x + y = 9**. Substitute: 3x + (2x − 1) = 9 → 5x − 1 = 9 → 5x = 10 → **x = 2**. Then back-substitute: y = 2·2 − 1 = **3**. Solution **(2, 3)**.

illustration_description: Back-substitute into the already-isolated equation, since it is solved for the other variable.
accompanying_text: Back-substitute into the **isolated** equation — it's already solved for y, so it's the easy one. Then confirm the point in **both** equations. If either fails, a sign slipped during the substitution.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Often nothing is isolated yet. Then **solve one equation for a variable first** — pick one with a coefficient of 1 so you avoid fractions. From x + y = 7 you get **y = 7 − x**. Now substitute that into the other equation, exactly as before.

illustration_description: Isolate first: from x plus y equals eight and three x minus y equals four, write y equals eight minus x and substitute to find x equals three.
accompanying_text: Worked: **x + y = 8** and **3x − y = 4**. From the first, y = 8 − x. Substitute: 3x − (8 − x) = 4 → 4x − 8 = 4 → **x = 3**, then y = 8 − 3 = **5**. Solution **(3, 5)** — check both to be sure.

illustration_description: Guard the sign: when substituting into a minus y term, wrap the whole expression in parentheses before distributing.
accompanying_text: Guard the **sign**. When you substitute into a **−y** term, wrap the expression in parentheses: −(8 − x) = −8 + x. Skip the parentheses and you'll flip the sign of the second piece — the most common substitution mistake.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Substitution solves **any** system, whether or not the graph is clear. The full method: isolate a variable if needed, substitute into the other equation, solve for one variable, back-substitute for the other, and check the point in both equations.

illustration_description: Substitution in action: with y equals two x minus three and x plus y equals nine, x plus two x minus three equals nine gives x equals four.
Checking into both equations is not a formality: if the point fails either one, the answer is wrong.
accompanying_text: The check into **both** equations isn't a formality. If the point fails one equation, a sign slipped during substitution — most often forgetting to distribute a minus into a substituted expression. Re-check that step first.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: **Elimination** combines the two equations so one variable disappears. If a variable has **opposite** coefficients (+y in one, −y in the other), **add** the equations — it cancels. If it has **matching** coefficients, **subtract**. Either way you're left with one variable to solve.

illustration_description: Add to eliminate: with x plus y equals eight and x minus y equals two, the y-terms are opposites, so adding gives two x equals ten and x equals five.
accompanying_text: Worked: **x + y = 8** and **x − y = 2**. The y-coefficients are opposite, so add: (x + y) + (x − y) = 8 + 2 → 2x = 10 → **x = 5**. Back-substitute: 5 + y = 8 → **y = 3**. Solution **(5, 3)**.

illustration_description: Matching coefficients means subtract, but subtract carefully: the minus sign distributes to every term of the second equation.
accompanying_text: Matching coefficients → **subtract**. But subtract carefully: the minus applies to **every** term of the second equation. (2x + y) − (x + y) = 2x + y − x − y = x. A sign dropped here is the usual elimination mistake.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: When no coefficients line up, **multiply one whole equation** by a number so a coefficient matches the other. Then add or subtract as usual. Multiplying every term of an equation by a nonzero number keeps it the same line — it just rescales it.

illustration_description: Scale one equation first: with two x plus y equals seven and x plus three y equals eleven, multiply the second by two to make the x-coefficients match.
accompanying_text: Worked: **2x + y = 7** and **x + 3y = 11**. Multiply the second by 2 → 2x + 6y = 22. Subtract the first: (2x + 6y) − (2x + y) = 22 − 7 → 5y = 15 → **y = 3**, then **x = 2**. Solution **(2, 3)**.

illustration_description: Pick the variable easiest to match, usually one with a coefficient of one or a small factor apart.
accompanying_text: Pick the variable that's easiest to match — usually one with a coefficient of 1, since you just multiply by the other equation's coefficient. Scale only the equation that needs it; leave the other alone.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Sometimes **both** equations need scaling. Multiply each by its own number so one variable's coefficients match, then subtract (or add). It's the same method with one extra multiplication — aim for the least common multiple of the two coefficients you're matching.

illustration_description: Scale both: with two x plus three y equals thirteen and three x plus two y equals twelve, multiply the first by three and the second by two to match x, giving the solution two, three.
accompanying_text: Worked: **2x + 3y = 13** and **3x + 2y = 12**. First×3 → 6x + 9y = 39. Second×2 → 6x + 4y = 24. Subtract: 5y = 15 → **y = 3**, then **x = 2**. The 6 is the LCM of 2 and 3 — the smallest match to aim for.

illustration_description: Elimination exposes special cases: if both variables cancel, a false statement means no solution and a true one means infinitely many.
accompanying_text: Elimination also exposes the **special cases**. If both variables cancel and you're left with a **false** statement like 0 = 7, the lines are parallel — **no solution**. If you're left with a **true** one like 0 = 0, they're the same line — **infinitely many**.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Word problems become systems: **name each unknown**, then write **one equation per fact**. A total gives x + y = (sum). A difference — "x is k more than y" — gives x − y = k. Two facts, two equations, one solvable system.

illustration_description: Totals and differences: two numbers sum to twenty and one is six more than the other, giving x plus y equals twenty and x minus y equals six.
accompanying_text: Worked: two numbers sum to 20, and one is 6 more than the other. Let x be the larger: **x + y = 20** and **x − y = 6**. Add: 2x = 26 → **x = 13**, then **y = 7**. Check: 13 + 7 = 20 and 13 − 7 = 6. Both facts hold.

illustration_description: Mind the direction of more than: x is six more than y means x minus y equals six.
accompanying_text: Mind the **direction** of "more than": "x is 6 more than y" means **x − y = 6**, not y − x = 6. Assign x to the larger quantity so the difference stays positive and the equation reads the way the sentence does.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: Two-category problems give two equations: a **count** equation (how many of each — x + y = total) and a **value** equation (what they're worth — price·x + price·y = total worth). Coins, tickets, and stamps all follow this pattern.

illustration_description: Counts and values: with x adult tickets at eight dollars and y child tickets at five dollars and nine tickets total, one equation counts and one totals the money.
accompanying_text: Worked: x adult tickets at $8, y child tickets at $5, **9 tickets** for **$57**. Count: x + y = 9. Value: 8x + 5y = 57. Substitute y = 9 − x: 8x + 5(9 − x) = 57 → 3x + 45 = 57 → **x = 4**, **y = 5**.

illustration_description: Keep the two equations distinct: the count equation adds the items while the value equation adds their worth.
accompanying_text: Keep the two equations distinct. The **count** equation just adds the items, so its coefficients are 1. The **value** equation weights each item by its price. Mixing a price into the count equation (or vice versa) is the usual slip.

illustration_description: The coordinate plane: x-axis right, y-axis up, origin at (0, 0); the point (3, 2) is reached by going 3 right, then 2 up.
accompanying_text: With three methods available, pick the easiest: **substitution** when a variable is already isolated (or easy to isolate), **elimination** when coefficients line up or scale cleanly, graphing only for a rough read. Then do the last step everyone forgets — **answer the question actually asked**.

illustration_description: Elimination shines when a variable cancels directly, as when the coefficients already match or oppose.
accompanying_text: Elimination shines when a variable cancels directly. For **3x + 2y = 12** and **3x − y = 3**, both have 3x — subtract to cancel it: (3x + 2y) − (3x − y) = 12 − 3 → 3y = 9 → **y = 3**, then **x = 2**. Choosing the fitting method saves steps.

illustration_description: Then interpret: the solution is a pair of numbers, but the question may ask for just one of them or a combination.
accompanying_text: Then **interpret**. The solution is a pair of numbers, but the question asks for one specific thing. If x = adult tickets and the question asks how many children, report **y**. Re-read the question before writing the final answer.

accompanying_text: Ten single ones bundle together to make one ten. A "ten" is just 10 ones grouped into a rod. So 3 tens is the same as 30 ones — three groups of ten.

illustration_description: Forty loose ones bundle into four tens, because forty is four groups of ten.
accompanying_text: Going the other way, 40 ones make 4 tens, because 40 is 4 groups of ten. To find how many tens, count the groups of ten.

illustration_description: One ten is always ten ones, whether shown as a rod or as ten loose cubes.
accompanying_text: A bundle keeps its size: 1 ten is always 10 ones, whether you see a rod or ten loose cubes. Bundling into tens makes big counts quick to read.

illustration_description: Base-ten blocks showing forty-six: four ten-rods make forty, and six one-cubes make six, together forty-six.
accompanying_text: A two-digit number is made of tens and ones. In 46, the 4 means 4 tens and the 6 means 6 ones. The left digit counts the tens; the right digit counts the ones.

illustration_description: Four tens and six ones build the number forty-six: put the tens count first, then the ones.
accompanying_text: You can build a number from its parts: 4 tens and 6 ones make 46. Put the tens count on the left and the ones count on the right.

illustration_description: In seventy-two there are seven tens and two ones; in thirty there are three tens and zero ones.
accompanying_text: The same works for any two-digit number. In 72 there are 7 tens and 2 ones. In 30 there are 3 tens and 0 ones — the 0 means no extra ones.

illustration_description: Base-ten blocks showing forty-six: four ten-rods make forty, and six one-cubes make six, together forty-six.
accompanying_text: Base-ten blocks show a number: each rod is a ten and each cube is a one. So 3 rods and 5 cubes means 3 tens and 5 ones, which is 35. Count the rods, then the cubes.

illustration_description: Five rods and no cubes is five tens and zero ones, which is fifty.
accompanying_text: Count the tens first, then the ones. 5 rods and 0 cubes is 5 tens and 0 ones, which is 50 — no cubes means the ones digit is 0.

illustration_description: Rods come first because tens are worth more: six rods and four cubes is six tens and four ones, which is sixty-four.
accompanying_text: Rods always come first because tens are worth more. 6 rods and 4 cubes is 6 tens and 4 ones, which is 64.

illustration_description: Expanded form: forty-six equals forty plus six — the four tens are worth forty and the six ones are worth six.
accompanying_text: Expanded form breaks a number into its tens value and ones value. 46 = 40 + 6: the 4 tens are worth 40 and the 6 ones are worth 6. Add them back to get 46.

illustration_description: The tens part is the tens digit times ten: in seventy-two the seven tens are worth seven times ten, which is seventy.
accompanying_text: The tens part is the tens digit times ten. In 72, the 7 tens are worth 7 × 10 = 70. The digit is 7, but its value is 70 because it sits in the tens place.

illustration_description: Putting the parts back together checks the number: seventy plus two equals seventy-two.
accompanying_text: Put the parts back together to check: 70 + 2 = 72. Expanded form and the number are just two ways to write the same amount.

illustration_description: Expanded form: forty-six equals forty plus six — the four tens are worth forty and the six ones are worth six.
accompanying_text: Read expanded form by adding the parts. 40 + 6 = 46. The tens part tells you the left digit, and the ones part tells you the right digit.

illustration_description: The tens part is a multiple of ten: eighty plus five equals eighty-five.
accompanying_text: The tens part is always a multiple of ten. 80 + 5 = 85. If the ones part is 0, the number ends in 0: 60 + 0 = 60.

accompanying_text: Expanded form can be written in either order, but the value is the same: 6 + 40 still makes 46. Add the tens and ones however they appear.

illustration_description: In thirty-three both digits are three, but they are worth different amounts: the left three is worth thirty and the right three is worth three.
accompanying_text: In 33 both digits are 3, but they're worth different amounts: the left 3 is worth 30 and the right 3 is worth 3. The place, not the digit, decides the value.

illustration_description: Place matters: forty is bigger than four, because the four in forty sits in the tens place and is worth forty.
accompanying_text: This is why 40 is bigger than 4: the 4 sits in the tens place in 40, worth 40, but stands alone as 4 ones in 4. Place is everything.

illustration_description: Base-ten blocks showing forty-six: four ten-rods make forty, and six one-cubes make six, together forty-six.
accompanying_text: Adding 10 adds one ten, so only the tens digit goes up by 1. 34 + 10 = 44 — the 4 ones stay the same. Subtracting 10 takes one ten away: 34 − 10 = 24.

illustration_description: Adding ten keeps the ones digit: thirty-four plus ten is forty-four, and the four ones stay the same.
accompanying_text: The ones digit never changes when you add or subtract ten. In 34 + 10, the 4 ones stay; only the tens move. That's why the answer ends in the same digit.

illustration_description: For one ten, move the tens digit by one: up for plus ten, down for minus ten, while the ones stay put.
accompanying_text: So for one ten, just move the tens digit by one: up for plus, down for minus. The ones ride along unchanged.

illustration_description: Base-ten blocks showing forty-six: four ten-rods make forty, and six one-cubes make six, together forty-six.
accompanying_text: Adding 20 adds two tens, so the tens digit goes up by 2. 40 + 30 = 70: 4 tens plus 3 tens is 7 tens. The ones stay the same.

illustration_description: Adding tens: twenty-six plus forty adds four tens, so two tens plus four tens is six tens, making sixty-six.
accompanying_text: Count the tens you're adding. 26 + 40 adds four tens: 2 tens + 4 tens = 6 tens, so 66. The ones digit (6) rides along unchanged.

illustration_description: Tens add just like small numbers: five tens plus three tens is eight tens, so fifty-five plus thirty is eighty-five.
accompanying_text: The tens add just like small numbers: 5 tens + 3 tens = 8 tens, so 55 + 30 = 85. Add the tens, keep the ones.

illustration_description: Base-ten blocks showing forty-six: four ten-rods make forty, and six one-cubes make six, together forty-six.
accompanying_text: Subtracting tens takes whole tens away. 65 − 30 = 35: 6 tens minus 3 tens is 3 tens, and the 5 ones stay. The tens digit drops by the number of tens removed.

illustration_description: The ones stay put: in ninety minus forty the zero ones stay zero, and nine tens minus four tens is five tens, making fifty.
accompanying_text: The ones digit stays put. In 90 − 40, the 0 ones stay 0; 9 tens minus 4 tens is 5 tens, so 50.

illustration_description: Counting down by tens: sixty-five, fifty-five, forty-five, thirty-five is minus three tens.
accompanying_text: You can count down by tens if it helps: 65, 55, 45, 35 is minus three tens. Or just drop the tens digit by 3. Same result.

illustration_description: Two stacks of ten-rods compared: forty-five has four tens and fifty-two has five tens, so the taller stack fifty-two is greater — forty-five is less than fifty-two.
accompanying_text: To compare two-digit numbers, look at the tens first. 45 vs 52: 4 tens is less than 5 tens, so 45 < 52. More tens means a bigger number. The sign < points to the smaller one.

illustration_description: The number with more tens is greater even if its ones are smaller: forty has more tens than thirty-nine, so forty is greater.
accompanying_text: The number with more tens is greater, even if its ones are smaller. 40 has more tens than 39, so 40 > 39 — even though 0 ones is less than 9 ones.

illustration_description: The symbol opens toward the bigger number: greater-than means the left is bigger, less-than means the left is smaller.
accompanying_text: The symbol opens toward the bigger number: > means the left is greater, < means the left is smaller. 28 < 71 because 2 tens is less than 7 tens.

illustration_description: Two stacks of ten-rods compared: forty-five has four tens and fifty-two has five tens, so the taller stack fifty-two is greater — forty-five is less than fifty-two.
accompanying_text: When two numbers have the same tens, compare the ones. 63 vs 67: both have 6 tens, so look at the ones — 3 is less than 7, so 63 < 67.

illustration_description: When the tens match, the ones decide: seventy-one and seventy-six both have seven tens, so six ones beats one one and seventy-six is greater.
accompanying_text: Always check the tens first; only when they match do the ones decide. 71 and 76 both have 7 tens, so 1 < 6 means 71 < 76.

illustration_description: If the tens and the ones are both the same, the numbers are equal: forty-five equals forty-five.
accompanying_text: If the tens and the ones are both the same, the numbers are equal. 45 = 45. That's when you use the = sign.

illustration_description: Two stacks of ten-rods compared: forty-five has four tens and fifty-two has five tens, so the taller stack fifty-two is greater — forty-five is less than fifty-two.
accompanying_text: To compare any two two-digit numbers: check the tens. If they differ, more tens wins. If they're equal, more ones wins. That one rule handles every pair.

illustration_description: A bigger ones digit does not win if the tens are smaller: thirty-nine has a big nine but only three tens, so forty-one is greater.
accompanying_text: Watch out: a bigger ones digit doesn't win if the tens are smaller. 39 vs 41: 9 ones looks big, but 3 tens is less than 4 tens, so 39 < 41.

illustration_description: The first place that differs decides: fifty-two and fifty-eight share the tens, so the ones place two versus eight decides that fifty-eight is greater.
accompanying_text: Equal numbers have the same tens and ones. Otherwise, the first place that differs decides it — always starting from the tens.

illustration_description: A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction a over b with integers and a nonzero denominator, like one half, negative three, or 0.25. A rational number is a fraction a/b.
accompanying_text: A **rational number** is any number that can be written as a fraction a/b of two integers (b ≠ 0). That includes whole numbers (5 = 5/1), negatives (-2 = -2/1), and familiar decimals (0.5 = 1/2). Every rational number, in decimal form, either stops or repeats forever.

illustration_description: Dividing 1 by 3: bring down a zero to make 10, divide to get digit 3 with remainder 1, and that remainder 1 is exactly what started — so the same digit 3 repeats forever.
accompanying_text: Why do rational decimals always stop or repeat? Long division only ever produces remainders smaller than the divisor — so dividing by 3, the only possible remainders are 0, 1, or 2. Eventually a remainder must repeat, and once it does, the digits after it repeat too.

illustration_description: Predicting a decimal: after simplifying, a denominator built only from 2s and 5s terminates, while any other prime factor makes it repeat. Denominator of only 2s and 5s terminates.
accompanying_text: You can predict the pattern before dividing: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (since our number system is base ten = 2×5). 1/4 terminates because 4 = 2². 1/3 repeats because 3 is neither a 2 nor a 5.

illustration_description: Predicting a decimal: after simplifying, a denominator built only from 2s and 5s terminates, while any other prime factor makes it repeat. Denominator of only 2s and 5s terminates.
accompanying_text: Always simplify first! 3/6 looks like it has a factor of 3 in the denominator, but 3/6 = 1/2 — after simplifying, the 3 cancels away and only a 2 remains, so it terminates.

illustration_description: Converting a repeating decimal to a fraction: let x equal 0.4545 repeating, multiply by 100, subtract to clear the repeat, giving 99x equals 45, so x is 45 over 99, which is 5 over 11. 0.45 repeating = 45/99 = 5/11.
accompanying_text: To turn a repeating decimal into a fraction: let x equal the decimal, multiply by a power of 10 that shifts one full repeating block to the left of the decimal point, then subtract the original x. The repeating parts cancel, leaving a simple equation to solve for x.

illustration_description: Converting a repeating decimal to a fraction: let x equal 0.4545 repeating, multiply by 100, subtract to clear the repeat, giving 99x equals 45, so x is 45 over 99, which is 5 over 11. 0.45 repeating = 45/99 = 5/11.
accompanying_text: For a TWO-digit repeating block, multiply by 100 instead of 10, so the whole block shifts past the decimal point. Example: x = 0.454545…, so 100x = 45.4545…, and 100x − x = 45, giving 99x = 45, so x = 45/99 = 5/11 once simplified.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: Draw a square with side length 1. Its diagonal has length c, where 1² + 1² = c² (the Pythagorean theorem), so c² = 2. No fraction, when squared, lands on exactly 2 — this diagonal's length is called an **irrational number**, written √2.

illustration_description: The real numbers split into rationals and irrationals: rationals include integers and terminating or repeating decimals, while irrationals like root two and pi never terminate or repeat. Real numbers: rational or irrational.
accompanying_text: Compare with √4: since 4 = 2², √4 = 2 exactly — a whole number, so it's rational. But √2, √3, √5, and √7 are irrational, because none of 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … (the perfect squares) equals 2, 3, 5, or 7.

illustration_description: The real numbers split into rationals and irrationals: rationals include integers and terminating or repeating decimals, while irrationals like root two and pi never terminate or repeat. Real numbers: rational or irrational.
accompanying_text: Every real number is either rational (a fraction a/b — its decimal terminates or repeats a block forever) or irrational (its decimal never terminates and never settles into a repeating block — π, √2, and √3 are classic examples).

illustration_description: The real numbers split into rationals and irrationals: rationals include integers and terminating or repeating decimals, while irrationals like root two and pi never terminate or repeat. Real numbers: rational or irrational.
accompanying_text: A repeating decimal like 0.4545… IS rational (it equals 5/11) — it just looks messy. What makes π different is that its digits never lock into ANY repeating block, no matter how far you go — 3.14159265358979…, forever unpatterned.

illustration_description: The real number line has no gaps: between any two different numbers such as 0.3 and 0.4 there is always another, like 0.35, and this never ends. Between any two numbers lies another.
accompanying_text: Between ANY two different numbers on the number line — no matter how close together — there's always another number hiding in between. Rational and irrational numbers are mixed together everywhere on the line; there are no empty patches.

illustration_description: The real number line has no gaps: between any two different numbers such as 0.3 and 0.4 there is always another, like 0.35, and this never ends. Between any two numbers lies another.
accompanying_text: This matters for locating √2: since 1.4² = 1.96 and 1.5² = 2.25, √2 must be trapped between 1.4 and 1.5. We can keep narrowing forever without ever landing on a clean decimal, because √2 truly never terminates or repeats.

illustration_description: A number line showing an unknown value between two consecutive whole numbers n and n+1; a zoomed-in strip below shows the same interval split into tenths, narrowing down closer to exactly where the value sits.
accompanying_text: To estimate √n, find the two perfect squares n sits between. For √50: 49 < 50 < 64, and 49 = 7², 64 = 8², so 7 < √50 < 8 — √50 is trapped between the whole numbers 7 and 8.

illustration_description: A number line showing an unknown value between two consecutive whole numbers n and n+1; a zoomed-in strip below shows the same interval split into tenths, narrowing down closer to exactly where the value sits.
accompanying_text: Once you know the two whole numbers, decide which one it's closer to by comparing how far n is from each perfect square. Since 50 is very close to 49, √50 is much closer to 7 than to 8.

illustration_description: A number line showing an unknown value between two consecutive whole numbers n and n+1; a zoomed-in strip below shows the same interval split into tenths, narrowing down closer to exactly where the value sits.
accompanying_text: Once √n sits between two whole numbers, narrow further with decimals — testing 7.0², 7.1², 7.2²… — the same squeezing idea, one decimal place at a time.

illustration_description: A number line showing an unknown value between two consecutive whole numbers n and n+1; a zoomed-in strip below shows the same interval split into tenths, narrowing down closer to exactly where the value sits.
accompanying_text: The same idea applies to π: since π ≈ 3.14159…, at one decimal place π ≈ 3.1. We could keep narrowing to as many decimal places as we want — the digits just never stop or repeat.

illustration_description: Estimating with irrationals: since pi is about 3.14, pi squared is about 3.14 squared, roughly 9.87, which sits just below 10. Estimate π² ≈ 3.14² ≈ 9.87.
accompanying_text: To compare irrationals and rationals fairly, convert everything to decimals first. Notation (radicals, fractions, decimals) can trick the eye — decimals put every number on equal footing for comparison.

illustration_description: Estimating with irrationals: since pi is about 3.14, pi squared is about 3.14 squared, roughly 9.87, which sits just below 10. Estimate π² ≈ 3.14² ≈ 9.87.
accompanying_text: To estimate an expression like π², use a rational approximation for π — like 3.14 — and compute: 3.14² ≈ 9.86, so π² ≈ 9.86. That estimate is close to, but never exactly, the true (irrational) value of π² itself.

illustration_description: Three rigid motions. A translation slides a triangle to a new spot. A reflection flips it across a line like a mirror. A rotation turns it around a point. In every case the moved copy is the same size and shape as the original.
accompanying_text: A **translation** slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction — no turning, no flipping. On the grid, add the slide to each point: sliding right 4 and down 1 sends (x, y) to (x + 4, y − 1).

illustration_description: Translation directions: moving right or up uses positive numbers, while moving left or down uses negative numbers. Right/up are positive; left/down negative.
accompanying_text: Right and up are POSITIVE moves; left and down are NEGATIVE. Sliding left 3 subtracts 3 from x; sliding down 2 subtracts 2 from y. Apply the same shift to every point, and the shape arrives unchanged in size and shape.

illustration_description: Three rigid motions. A translation slides a triangle to a new spot. A reflection flips it across a line like a mirror. A rotation turns it around a point. In every case the moved copy is the same size and shape as the original.
accompanying_text: A **reflection** flips a shape across a line, like a mirror. Reflecting across the **x-axis** keeps x and flips the sign of y: (x, y) → (x, −y). Reflecting across the **y-axis** flips x: (x, y) → (−x, y).

illustration_description: Three rigid motions. A translation slides a triangle to a new spot. A reflection flips it across a line like a mirror. A rotation turns it around a point. In every case the moved copy is the same size and shape as the original.
accompanying_text: The mirror line is what you flip ACROSS. Points keep their distance from the line but land on the opposite side. Across the x-axis, a point 5 above lands 5 below. The shape's size never changes.

illustration_description: Three rigid motions. A translation slides a triangle to a new spot. A reflection flips it across a line like a mirror. A rotation turns it around a point. In every case the moved copy is the same size and shape as the original.
accompanying_text: A **rotation** turns a shape around a center point by an angle. Around the origin, a **180° turn** flips both signs: (x, y) → (−x, −y). A point and its 180° image sit on opposite sides of the center.

illustration_description: A 90 degree counterclockwise rotation about the origin sends a point at 3, 1 to negative 1, 3. 90° counterclockwise: (3,1) → (−1,3).
accompanying_text: A **90° turn counterclockwise** around the origin sends (x, y) → (−y, x): swap the coordinates, then flip the sign of the new first one. For (2, 3): swap to (3, 2), flip the first to get (−3, 2).

illustration_description: A triangle slid three right and two up, with each vertex labelled to show that the rule adds three to x and two to y.
accompanying_text:
You have slid shapes around already. Now write down exactly what a slide **does to the numbers**.

Move three right and two up and every point obeys the same instruction: (x, y) → (x + 3, y + 2). Not the vertices you happen to notice — every point, the same shift. That sentence is the whole transformation.

illustration_description: Translations chain: doing plus two, minus five and then minus seven, plus one adds up to a single combined shift.
accompanying_text:
Because a translation is just addition, two of them in a row simply add up.

Slide (+2, −5) and then (−7, +1) and the net effect is (−5, −4) — one slide doing the work of two. No shape has changed at any stage, which is the deeper point: translations preserve every distance and every angle.

illustration_description: A point at three, two reflected across the y-axis to negative three, two, and across the x-axis to three, negative two, showing which coordinate changes sign.
accompanying_text:
A flip changes exactly one coordinate's sign, and which one depends on the mirror.

Across the **y-axis**, left and right swap: (x, y) → (−x, y). Across the **x-axis**, up and down swap: (x, y) → (x, −y). The coordinate that changes is the one measured *perpendicular* to the mirror line.

illustration_description: Reflections are functions too, using sign flips instead of shifts: across the x-axis, y changes sign.
accompanying_text:
Reflections are rigid, and that has a consequence worth noticing: they preserve every length and every angle, yet they reverse **orientation**.

Trace the vertices of the original in order and then trace the image. What ran clockwise now runs anticlockwise. That is the one thing a translation can never do, and it is what distinguishes a flip from a slide.

illustration_description: A triangle dilated from the origin by a scale factor of two, with rays from the origin through each vertex extended to double the distance.
accompanying_text:
Translations and reflections are rigid: they move a shape without resizing it. A **dilation** is the one that changes size.

From the origin with scale factor k, the rule is (x, y) → (kx, ky). Every distance from the centre is multiplied by k, so the shape is preserved exactly while the size is not.

illustration_description: A dilation from a center point: rays from the center pass through the small pre-image triangle and out to the larger image triangle, scaled by factor one-and-a-half Dilation by a scale factor
accompanying_text:
A dilation is **not** rigid, and that is exactly its job: it produces a **similar** figure — same angles, all lengths multiplied by k.

That is the difference the whole chapter turns on. Translations, reflections and rotations give congruence; dilations give similarity. And an area does not scale by k, but by k² — doubling the lengths quadruples the space inside.

illustration_description: Congruent shapes have the same size and shape: one triangle maps exactly onto another by a slide, flip, or turn, so all sides and angles match. Congruent: same size and shape.
accompanying_text: Two shapes are **congruent** when one can be moved onto the other using only rigid motions — translations, reflections, and rotations. Since those never change size or shape, congruent shapes are identical: same side lengths, same angles.

illustration_description: Congruent shapes have the same size and shape: one triangle maps exactly onto another by a slide, flip, or turn, so all sides and angles match. Congruent: same size and shape.
accompanying_text: To show two shapes are congruent, describe a SEQUENCE of rigid motions that maps one exactly onto the other — for example, 'translate, then rotate.' If such a sequence exists, they're congruent.

illustration_description: A dilation from a center point. Rays drawn from the center through each corner of a small triangle are extended to twice the distance, producing a larger triangle of the same shape. The two triangles are similar but not congruent.
accompanying_text: A **dilation** resizes a shape by a **scale factor** from a center point. From the origin, multiply each coordinate by the scale factor: factor 2 sends (x, y) → (2x, 2y). The shape keeps its proportions but changes size.

illustration_description: A dilation from a center point. Rays drawn from the center through each corner of a small triangle are extended to twice the distance, producing a larger triangle of the same shape. The two triangles are similar but not congruent.
accompanying_text: A scale factor bigger than 1 enlarges; a factor between 0 and 1 shrinks. Factor ½ sends (6, 8) → (3, 4), shrinking to half. Whatever the factor, the shape's angles and proportions stay the same.

illustration_description: A dilation from a center point. Rays drawn from the center through each corner of a small triangle are extended to twice the distance, producing a larger triangle of the same shape. The two triangles are similar but not congruent.
accompanying_text: Two shapes are **similar** when one maps onto the other by a dilation, possibly combined with rigid motions. Similar shapes have the SAME ANGLES but PROPORTIONAL side lengths — same shape, possibly different size.

illustration_description: A dilation from a center point. Rays drawn from the center through each corner of a small triangle are extended to twice the distance, producing a larger triangle of the same shape. The two triangles are similar but not congruent.
accompanying_text: In similar shapes, the ratio between matching sides is the same everywhere — that's the scale factor. If a 3-side matches a 6-side (ratio 2), then a 4-side matches an 8-side, and a 5-side matches a 10-side.

illustration_description: Two parallel lines crossed by a slanted transversal. At each crossing the same pattern of angles appears. Angles in matching positions (corresponding angles) are equal, and alternate interior angles are equal too — shown here by shared colors.
accompanying_text: When a line (a **transversal**) crosses two **parallel** lines, it makes eight angles — but only two different sizes. **Corresponding angles** (same position at each crossing) are equal, and **alternate interior angles** (opposite sides, between the lines) are equal too.

illustration_description: A transversal crossing two parallel lines makes equal angle pairs; angles in the same position at each crossing are equal. A transversal makes equal angle pairs.
accompanying_text: Angles that sit together on a straight line are **supplementary** — they add to 180°. So next to a 70° angle, the angle completing the straight line is 110°. Co-interior angles (same side, between the lines) are supplementary this way.

illustration_description: Three angle families: acute is under 90 degrees, right is exactly 90 degrees shown with a square corner mark, obtuse is over 90 degrees.
accompanying_text: The three angles inside ANY triangle always add up to **180°**. Know two of them and you can find the third by subtracting from 180. This holds for every triangle, no matter its shape.

illustration_description: A triangle's three angles always add to 180 degrees; torn off and placed together they form a straight line. A triangle's angles sum to 180°.
accompanying_text: This works even for right triangles. A right triangle has one 90° angle, so the other two must add to 90°. If one of them is 35°, the last is 90 − 35 = 55°.

illustration_description: Three angle families: acute is under 90 degrees, right is exactly 90 degrees shown with a square corner mark, obtuse is over 90 degrees.
accompanying_text: Two triangles are **similar** if just TWO pairs of their angles match. Since all three angles of any triangle sum to 180°, matching two forces the third to match too — so the triangles have the same shape. This is the **angle-angle (AA)** rule.

illustration_description: Three angle families: acute is under 90 degrees, right is exactly 90 degrees shown with a square corner mark, obtuse is over 90 degrees.
accompanying_text: Why does two force the third? Because the three must total 180°. If two triangles share two angles, their third angles are both 180 minus the same sum — so those match automatically. Equal angles mean the same shape.

illustration_description: A 3-4-5 right triangle with a square drawn on each side. The square on the leg of length 3 has area 9, the square on the leg of length 4 has area 16, and the square on the hypotenuse of length 5 has area 25. Since 9 plus 16 equals 25, the two leg-squares' areas add up to the hypotenuse-square's area.
accompanying_text: In a right triangle, name the two short sides (the **legs**) a and b, and the long side opposite the right angle (the **hypotenuse**) c. The **Pythagorean theorem** says a² + b² = c². Build a square on each side to see why.

illustration_description: A 3-4-5 right triangle with a square drawn on each side. The square on the leg of length 3 has area 9, the square on the leg of length 4 has area 16, and the square on the hypotenuse of length 5 has area 25. Since 9 plus 16 equals 25, the two leg-squares' areas add up to the hypotenuse-square's area.
accompanying_text: That area picture is the proof: for ANY right triangle, the squares built on the two legs have areas a² and b², and together they exactly fill the square built on the hypotenuse, whose area is c². So a² + b² = c² always holds.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: To find the hypotenuse, add the leg-squares and take the square root: c = √(a² + b²). For legs 3 and 4: c = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Here every answer comes out a whole number.

illustration_description: Finding a missing leg with the Pythagorean theorem: subtract the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square, so 5 squared minus 3 squared is 16, and the leg is 4. Missing leg: √(5² − 3²) = 4.
accompanying_text: To find a missing LEG instead, subtract: a = √(c² − b²). If the hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5, then a = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12. Subtract because the hypotenuse-square is the biggest.

illustration_description: A right triangle with the two legs a and b meeting at the right angle, and the hypotenuse c opposite it; the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
accompanying_text: The theorem runs backward too — the **converse**: if a triangle's sides satisfy a² + b² = c² (with c the longest), then it's a RIGHT triangle. Test any triangle by checking whether the two smaller squares add to the biggest.

illustration_description: The converse of the Pythagorean theorem: if the two smaller squares' areas add to the largest square's area, the triangle is right; if not, it isn't. Converse: a² + b² = c² means a right angle.
accompanying_text: If the two smaller squares DON'T add to the biggest, the triangle is NOT right. For 5, 6, 7: 25 + 36 = 61, but 7² = 49. Since 61 ≠ 49, it fails the test — not a right triangle.

illustration_description: Three round solids with their volume formulas. A cylinder has volume pi times r squared times h. A cone with the same base and height has one-third that volume: one-third pi r squared h. A sphere has volume four-thirds pi r cubed.
accompanying_text: A **cylinder** is a can: a circle stacked into a column. Its volume is the base circle's area times the height: **V = πr²h**. Because answers involve π, we leave them as a number times π (exact) unless asked to round.

illustration_description: The volume of a cylinder is the base circle's area times the height: pi times radius squared, times height, giving 45 pi for radius 3 and height 5. Cylinder volume = πr²h = 45π.
accompanying_text: The key is squaring the radius FIRST, then multiplying by the height. For r = 5, h = 2: r² = 25, then 25 × 2 = 50, so V = 50π. Squaring the radius is the step most people rush.

illustration_description: Three round solids with their volume formulas. A cylinder has volume pi times r squared times h. A cone with the same base and height has one-third that volume: one-third pi r squared h. A sphere has volume four-thirds pi r cubed.
accompanying_text: A **cone** with the same base and height as a cylinder holds exactly **one-third** as much. So its volume is **V = ⅓πr²h** — the cylinder formula times a third. Three cones fill one matching cylinder.

illustration_description: A cone with the same base and height as a cylinder holds exactly one third as much, so its volume is one third pi r squared h, giving 15 pi. Cone volume = ⅓πr²h = 15π.
accompanying_text: The reliable method: find the matching cylinder's volume (πr²h) first, then divide by 3. For r = 6, h = 5: cylinder is 36 × 5 = 180, and the cone is 180 ÷ 3 = 60, so V = 60π.

illustration_description: Three round solids with their volume formulas. A cylinder has volume pi times r squared times h. A cone with the same base and height has one-third that volume: one-third pi r squared h. A sphere has volume four-thirds pi r cubed.
accompanying_text: A **sphere** is a perfect ball. Its volume uses the radius cubed: **V = 4⁄3 πr³**. Cube the radius first (r × r × r), multiply by 4, then divide by 3 — leaving the answer as a number times π.

illustration_description: The volume of a sphere is four thirds pi times the radius cubed; for a radius of 3 this gives 36 pi. Sphere volume = 4⁄3·πr³ = 36π.
accompanying_text: The order that avoids mistakes: cube the radius, multiply by 4, then divide by 3. For r = 6: r³ = 216, times 4 = 864, divided by 3 = 288, so V = 288π. Cubing (not squaring) is the key difference from cylinders and cones.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SSS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SSS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: Congruence means a rigid motion maps one triangle onto another — but checking all **six** parts (three sides, three angles) is a lot. The good news: a triangle is rigid, so a few parts LOCK the rest. A **congruence criterion** is a shortcut — a small set of equal parts that GUARANTEES the motion exists, no need to check the other three.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SAS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SAS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: **SAS** works too: two sides with the **included** angle (the one BETWEEN them). Fix two sticks and the hinge angle between them, and the third side has nowhere to go — it snaps to one length. Included is the key word: the angle must sit between the two sides you're using.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the ASA congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks ASA congruence criterion
accompanying_text: **ASA** flips it: two angles with the **included** side between them. Fix two angles and the side joining their vertices, and the other two sides must meet at exactly one point — one triangle. And because a triangle's angles sum to 180°, knowing two angles gives the third for free.

illustration_description: The ambiguous SSA case: from vertex A a fixed angle and side AB are drawn, and a swing arc of the second side length crosses the base ray at two points, giving two different possible triangles SSA ambiguous case
accompanying_text: Not every arrangement locks a triangle. **SSA** — two sides and a NON-included angle — can leave TWO different triangles. Swing the second side from its fixed angle and, for the right lengths, it can reach the base line at two different points. Both fit the given parts; both are legal. So SSA is NOT a congruence criterion.

illustration_description: Three equal angles fix the shape but not the size, so angle-angle-angle proves similarity, not congruence.
accompanying_text: The same logic exposes **AAA**: three equal angles fix the SHAPE but not the SIZE. A triangle and a scaled-up copy have identical angles yet different side lengths — they're **similar**, not congruent. Angles alone never guarantee congruence; you always need at least one side.

illustration_description: The valid congruence criteria are exactly side-side-side, side-angle-side, angle-side-angle, and angle-angle-side.
accompanying_text: So the valid criteria are exactly **SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS** — each with at least one side, each locking size AND shape. The two impostors are **SSA** (ambiguous — two triangles) and **AAA** (similar — any size). Memorize the winners; recognize the two traps.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SAS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SAS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: Now put criteria to work. A congruence proof has two acts: FIRST prove the triangles congruent by a criterion (SSS/SAS/ASA/AAS); THEN, because congruent triangles match in every part, read off whatever equal side or angle you need. That second act has a name: **CPCTC** — Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent.

illustration_description: Choosing a criterion is a matching game: inventory what you are given, sides and angles, then pick the criterion that fits.
accompanying_text: Choosing the criterion is a matching game: inventory what you're GIVEN (and what's free — shared sides are reflexive, vertical angles are equal), then pick the criterion whose pattern you can complete. Given two sides and the angle between? SAS. Two angles and a side? ASA or AAS. Three sides? SSS.

illustration_description: Letter order encodes correspondence: in triangle A B C congruent to triangle D E F, A matches D, B matches E, and C matches F.
accompanying_text: One caution graders love: **letter order encodes correspondence.** In △ABC ≅ △DEF, A↔D, B↔E, C↔F. So AB corresponds to DE — not to EF. When you apply CPCTC, match parts by POSITION in the statement, never by how the triangle happens to look.

illustration_description: Two right triangles sharing a right-angle mark, with equal-hypotenuse ticks and one equal-leg tick, illustrating the hypotenuse-leg congruence criterion HL congruence criterion
accompanying_text: Right triangles get a fifth criterion the others don't: **HL** — hypotenuse and one leg. Given a right angle, an equal hypotenuse, and one equal leg, the triangles are congruent. It looks like the forbidden SSA (two sides + a non-included angle), but the right angle rescues it — the second leg is forced by the Pythagorean theorem.

illustration_description: Two right triangles sharing a right-angle mark, with equal-hypotenuse ticks and one equal-leg tick, illustrating the hypotenuse-leg congruence criterion HL congruence criterion
accompanying_text: HL is really SAS-in-disguise once you compute. Fix the right angle and the two legs (one given, one recovered by Pythagoras) and you have two sides plus the included right angle — the very pattern of SAS. So HL isn't a loophole; it's SAS wearing the right angle as its included angle.

illustration_description: The hypotenuse-leg criterion needs the hypotenuse specifically, plus one leg, on a right triangle.
accompanying_text: One guardrail: HL needs the **hypotenuse** specifically, plus a leg. Two legs and the right angle would just be SAS. A leg and the hypotenuse with the right angle is HL. But a NON-right angle with two sides is back to ambiguous SSA — the right angle is non-negotiable for HL.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SSS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SSS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: CPCTC is the workhorse for proving parts equal that you can't measure directly. The strategy never changes: find two triangles containing the target parts, prove those triangles congruent by a criterion, then release the part you want with CPCTC. The art is spotting WHICH two triangles hold your target.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SAS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SAS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: Watch for the hidden free parts, they turn a two-given problem into a full criterion. **Shared sides** are reflexively equal. **Vertical angles** at a crossing are equal. **Right angles** are all equal to each other. Each is a part you didn't have to be handed — spot them before declaring a criterion incomplete.

illustration_description: You may use corresponding parts of congruent triangles only for parts not already used to prove the triangles congruent.
accompanying_text: A subtle rule: you may use CPCTC only for parts NOT already used to prove the congruence. You prove the triangles congruent with SOME parts, then CPCTC unlocks the REMAINING ones. It never re-proves a part you already assumed — that would be circular.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the ASA congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks ASA congruence criterion
accompanying_text: The trickiest proofs hide the triangles: they **overlap**, sharing a side or angle. The move is to mentally pull them apart into two separate triangles, then look for the shared part — which is reflexively equal. Once separated, the usual criteria apply as normal.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SSS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SSS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: Some conclusions need **two congruences in sequence**. First prove one pair of triangles congruent to get an intermediate equal part by CPCTC; then USE that part to prove a SECOND pair congruent, and CPCTC again for the final goal. Each CPCTC feeds the next proof — a relay.

illustration_description: Two congruent triangles marked to illustrate the SAS congruence criterion, with matching sides and angles tagged by identical tick and arc marks SAS congruence criterion
accompanying_text: A planning tip for these: work BACKWARD from the goal. Ask 'which two triangles contain my target part?' Then 'what do I need to prove those congruent?' If a needed part isn't given, ask 'which earlier congruence could CPCTC it?' Backward planning turns a maze into a checklist.

illustration_description: An isosceles triangle with its two equal legs marked by single ticks and its two equal base angles marked by matching single arcs Isosceles base angles theorem
accompanying_text: An **isosceles** triangle has two equal sides — the **legs** — and the angles opposite them, the **base angles**, turn out equal too. This is the Base Angles Theorem: equal legs force equal base angles. It's not obvious from looking; it earns its certainty from a congruence proof.

illustration_description: An isosceles triangle with its two equal legs marked by single ticks and its two equal base angles marked by matching single arcs Isosceles base angles theorem
accompanying_text: The bisector does triple duty. In an isosceles triangle, the segment from the apex is at once the **angle bisector**, the **perpendicular bisector of the base**, the **median**, and the **altitude** — all the same line. That coincidence is special to isosceles (and equilateral) triangles.

illustration_description: In an isosceles triangle, equal legs guarantee equal base angles.
accompanying_text: Equal legs guarantee equal base angles — a one-way street for now. The reverse question (do equal base angles guarantee equal legs?) is the CONVERSE, and it deserves its own proof. That's the next lesson. For now: whenever you see two equal sides, you may immediately mark the base angles equal.

illustration_description: An isosceles triangle with its two equal legs marked by single ticks and its two equal base angles marked by matching single arcs Isosceles base angles theorem
accompanying_text: The **converse** of the Base Angles Theorem: if two base angles are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal — the triangle is isosceles. Unlike some converses, this one is TRUE, and it's the tool you use to PROVE a triangle isosceles from its angles.

illustration_description: An isosceles triangle with its two equal legs marked by single ticks and its two equal base angles marked by matching single arcs Isosceles base angles theorem
accompanying_text: Push both theorems to the limit with the **equilateral** triangle. All three sides equal means (by the Base Angles Theorem, applied to each pair) all three angles equal — **equiangular**. And each angle is 180 ÷ 3 = **60°**. The converse runs backward: three equal angles ⇒ three equal sides.

illustration_description: For triangles, equilateral and equiangular are the same thing: equal sides force equal angles of sixty degrees each.
accompanying_text: So for triangles, **equilateral and equiangular are the same thing** — each implies the other. This tidy equivalence is special to triangles; for polygons with more sides (like a rectangle: equiangular but not equilateral), the two properties can part ways.

illustration_description: A triangle with the midpoints of two sides joined by a midsegment, drawn parallel to the base and marked as half its length Triangle midsegment
accompanying_text: Join the **midpoints** of two sides of a triangle and you get a **midsegment** with two striking properties: it's **parallel** to the third side, and it's exactly **half** its length. One little segment, two guarantees — proved with congruent triangles or coordinates.

illustration_description: A triangle with the midpoints of two sides joined by a midsegment, drawn parallel to the base and marked as half its length Triangle midsegment
accompanying_text: Why half and parallel? Coordinates make it clean: place the base on the x-axis and compute the two midpoints. Their difference is exactly half the base vector, and its y-component is zero — so the midsegment is parallel and half-length. A congruence proof reaches the same conclusion.

illustration_description: The three midsegments split a triangle into four smaller triangles, all congruent to one another.
accompanying_text: The three midsegments split a triangle into **four** smaller triangles, all congruent to each other and each **similar** to the original at half scale. The middle one is flipped; the three corner ones are translates. It's a tidy self-similar tiling that the midsegment properties guarantee.

illustration_description: A triangle with its circumcenter marked, where the three defining lines meet at a single point Triangle circumcenter
accompanying_text: Three lines of the same type in a triangle often meet at a single point — they're **concurrent**. The **circumcenter** is where the three **perpendicular bisectors** of the sides meet. Because every point on a side's perpendicular bisector is equidistant from that side's two endpoints, the meeting point is equidistant from all three vertices.

illustration_description: A triangle with its incenter marked, where the three defining lines meet at a single point Triangle incenter
accompanying_text: The **incenter** is the other equidistance center: where the three **angle bisectors** meet. Every point on an angle's bisector is equidistant from the two SIDES forming that angle, so the common point is equidistant from all three sides — the center of the inscribed circle that just touches each side.

illustration_description: Two centers compared: the circumcenter comes from perpendicular bisectors and is equidistant from the vertices; the incenter comes from angle bisectors and is equidistant from the sides.
accompanying_text: A tale of two centers: **circumcenter** = perpendicular bisectors = equidistant from VERTICES = circle AROUND. **Incenter** = angle bisectors = equidistant from SIDES = circle INSIDE. The incenter always sits inside the triangle; the circumcenter can fall outside (for an obtuse triangle) since it only cares about vertex distances.

illustration_description: A triangle with its centroid marked, where the three defining lines meet at a single point Triangle centroid
accompanying_text: The **centroid** is where the three **medians** meet — a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. It's the triangle's balance point (center of mass), and it always lands inside. Its coordinates are just the **average** of the three vertices' coordinates.

illustration_description: A triangle with its orthocenter marked, where the three defining lines meet at a single point Triangle orthocenter
accompanying_text: The **orthocenter** is where the three **altitudes** meet — an altitude drops from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side. Unlike the balance-point centroid, the orthocenter has no averaging or equidistance property; it's purely the altitudes' intersection, and it can land outside an obtuse triangle.

illustration_description: A beautiful bonus: for any triangle the circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter all sit on one straight line called the Euler line.
