accompanying_text: A beautiful bonus: for ANY triangle the **circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter are collinear** — they lie on one line, the **Euler line**, with the centroid always between, twice as close to the circumcenter as to the orthocenter. (The incenter generally sits off this line.)

illustration_description: A triangle with its circumcenter marked, where the three defining lines meet at a single point Triangle circumcenter
accompanying_text: Four centers, four jobs. **Circumcenter** (perpendicular bisectors) — equidistant from vertices. **Incenter** (angle bisectors) — equidistant from sides. **Centroid** (medians) — balance point. **Orthocenter** (altitudes) — altitudes' meeting. Knowing the defining LINES and PROPERTY of each is the whole chapter.

illustration_description: A memory hook by the lines: perpendicular bisectors give the circumcenter, angle bisectors give the incenter, medians give the centroid, and altitudes give the orthocenter.
accompanying_text: A quick memory hook by the LINES: **perpendicular bisectors → circumcenter**, **angle bisectors → incenter**, **medians → centroid**, **altitudes → orthocenter**. And by PROPERTY: two are equidistance centers (circum from vertices, in from sides), the centroid is the balance point, and the orthocenter is the odd one out with no special distance property.

illustration_description: Only two centers are guaranteed to stay inside every triangle: the centroid and the incenter.
accompanying_text: Only two centers are guaranteed to stay INSIDE every triangle: the **centroid** and the **incenter**. The **circumcenter** and **orthocenter** slip outside when the triangle is obtuse. For a right triangle, the circumcenter lands exactly on the hypotenuse's midpoint — a handy special case.

illustration_description: Two triangles with the same two side lengths; the one with the larger included angle has the longer third side, illustrating the hinge theorem Hinge theorem
accompanying_text: Not every trio of lengths makes a triangle. The **Triangle Inequality** says the sum of any two sides must **exceed** the third. If two sides can't reach across the gap left by the third, they never meet — the triangle collapses flat or fails entirely. Check all three pairings to be safe.

illustration_description: Two triangles with the same two side lengths; the one with the larger included angle has the longer third side, illustrating the hinge theorem Hinge theorem
accompanying_text: The inequality also **bounds the third side**. Given two sides, the third must be more than their **difference** and less than their **sum**: |a − b| < third < a + b. Too short and the sides overlap; too long and they can't close. That window is exactly the buildable range.

illustration_description: Sides and angles line up in order: the largest angle sits opposite the largest side.
accompanying_text: Sides and angles line up in order: the **largest angle sits opposite the largest side**, the smallest opposite the smallest. So in a 5-6-7 triangle, the biggest angle faces the 7. This side-angle ranking lets you order a triangle's angles just by glancing at its sides.

illustration_description: Two triangles with the same two side lengths; the one with the larger included angle has the longer third side, illustrating the hinge theorem Hinge theorem
accompanying_text: Picture a door hinge with two fixed arms. Open it wider and the gap between the arm-ends grows. That's the **Hinge Theorem**: if two triangles share two pairs of equal sides, the one with the **larger included angle** has the **longer third side**. Same two sides, bigger angle, bigger opposite side.

illustration_description: Two triangles with the same two side lengths; the one with the larger included angle has the longer third side, illustrating the hinge theorem Hinge theorem
accompanying_text: The Hinge Theorem is really the **SAS inequality** — a cousin of SAS congruence. SAS congruence: equal sides AND equal included angle ⇒ equal third sides (congruent). The hinge: equal sides but a BIGGER included angle ⇒ a bigger third side. Equal angle gives equal; bigger angle gives bigger.

illustration_description: The hinge theorem, like a door: with two fixed side lengths, a wider hinge angle opens to a longer far side.
accompanying_text: A neat door analogy seals it: the two door edges are the fixed sides; the hinge is the included angle; the gap you'd measure between the door's free edge and the frame is the third side. Swing the door open wider, the gap widens. Close it, the gap shrinks toward zero.

illustration_description: Two triangles with the same two side lengths; the one with the larger included angle has the longer third side, illustrating the hinge theorem Hinge theorem
accompanying_text: Congruence proofs conclude parts are EQUAL; inequality proofs conclude one part is GREATER. The tools mirror each other: instead of SAS congruence you reach for the **hinge theorem**, instead of the base-angles theorem you use **bigger side ⇒ bigger opposite angle**. The proof shape is the same; only the relation changes from = to >.

illustration_description: Two triangles with the same two side lengths; the one with the larger included angle has the longer third side, illustrating the hinge theorem Hinge theorem
accompanying_text: The **Exterior Angle Inequality** adds another tool: an exterior angle of a triangle is **greater than either** of the two remote interior angles. (In fact it EQUALS their sum, so it must exceed each.) It's handy for proving one angle bigger than another across a figure.

illustration_description: To prove one segment or angle bigger than another, find the triangle that contains both and apply the side-angle inequality.
accompanying_text: Putting it together: to prove one segment or angle bigger than another, find the triangle (or two triangles) linking them, then apply the matching inequality — hinge for two triangles sharing sides, side-angle ordering within one triangle, or the exterior-angle inequality across a vertex. Same detective work as congruence, aimed at > instead of =.

illustration_description: A 3-4-5 right triangle with the angle theta at the left vertex. The side opposite theta, of length 3, is drawn in berry red. The side adjacent to theta, of length 4, is drawn in leaf green. The hypotenuse, of length 5, is drawn in sky blue. Callouts read: sine of theta equals opposite over hypotenuse equals 3 fifths; cosine equals adjacent over hypotenuse equals 4 fifths; tangent equals opposite over adjacent equals 3 fourths.
accompanying_text: Stand at an acute angle θ of a right triangle. The side across from you is the **opposite**; the side touching you (not the hypotenuse) is the **adjacent**; the longest side, across from the right angle, is the **hypotenuse**. Three ratios of these sides get names: **sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj** — SOH-CAH-TOA.

illustration_description: Move to the other acute angle and the legs swap jobs: what was opposite becomes adjacent.
accompanying_text: Move to the OTHER acute angle and the legs swap jobs: what was opposite becomes adjacent and vice versa — the hypotenuse never moves. That swap is why **sin θ = cos(90° − θ)**: one angle's opposite is its complement's adjacent.

illustration_description: Scale the triangle and the ratios stay the same, which is why the ratios deserve names.
accompanying_text: Why do the ratios deserve names? **Scale the triangle and they don't change.** Double 3-4-5 into 6-8-10: the sides all doubled, but opp/adj is still 6/8 = 3/4. Similar triangles share every ratio — so sin, cos, and tan depend only on the ANGLE. Tan even has a physical reading: rise over run, the steepness.

illustration_description: Know an angle and one side, and a ratio hands you the others by multiplying.
accompanying_text: Know an angle and one side? A ratio hands you the others. Pick the ratio that links the side you KNOW to the side you WANT. Hypotenuse 20, θ = 30°, want the opposite: sine links them — sin 30° = opp/20, so opp = 20 · sin 30° = 20 · 0.5 = 10. Known hypotenuse ⇒ multiply.

illustration_description: Flip the knowns and the operation flips: when the opposite is known and you want the hypotenuse, divide.
accompanying_text: Flip the knowns and the operation flips. If the OPPOSITE is known and the hypotenuse is wanted, sin θ = opp/hyp rearranges to **hyp = opp / sin θ** — divide. Sanity check every answer: the hypotenuse is the longest side, so it must come out BIGGER than the known leg.

illustration_description: Choosing the ratio is a matching game: which two sides are involved picks sine, cosine, or tangent.
accompanying_text: Choosing the ratio is a matching game: **which two sides are in play?** Opposite-and-hypotenuse → sine. Adjacent-and-hypotenuse → cosine. Opposite-and-adjacent → tangent — the go-to whenever the hypotenuse isn't part of the story at all.

illustration_description: Sides known and the angle missing: run the ratio backward with an inverse trig function.
accompanying_text: Sides known, angle missing — run the ratio BACKWARD. If sin θ = 0.5, then θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°: the inverse function asks “which angle has this sine?” One notation warning: **sin⁻¹ is NOT 1/sin** — the −1 marks an inverse function, not a reciprocal.

illustration_description: Which inverse: the same matching game, identify which two sides you have.
accompanying_text: Which inverse? Same matching game as before: identify WHICH two sides you hold, and take that ratio's inverse. Opposite-and-hypotenuse → sin⁻¹. Adjacent-and-hypotenuse → cos⁻¹. The two legs → tan⁻¹. The sides choose the function for you.

illustration_description: Built-in check: a right triangle's two acute angles always total ninety degrees.
accompanying_text: Built-in check: a right triangle's two acute angles always total 90°. Find one with an inverse and the other is 90° minus it — 36.9° pairs with 53.1°. If your two inverses don't add to 90°, a ratio got flipped somewhere.

illustration_description: A circle with radius 52 units. A straight radius segment is shown in sky blue, and an arc of the same length is highlighted in tangerine along the rim, spanning exactly one radian. Tick marks show the radius-length arc stepping around the circle six times with a small piece left over, illustrating that a full circle holds 2 pi, about 6.28, radians. A caption reads: arc length s equals r times theta.
accompanying_text: Degrees are a human invention — 360 slices because ancient astronomers liked the number. The circle offers its own unit: bend one RADIUS along the rim, and the angle it spans is **one radian**. Since the full rim is 2π radii long, a full turn holds 2π ≈ 6.28 radians.

illustration_description: Radians are the circle's native unit: the full circle is two pi radians.
accompanying_text: Why bother? Because radians are the circle's NATIVE unit: they're a pure ratio (arc length ÷ radius), no unit attached — and every clean circle formula, starting with arc length s = rθ next lesson, works **only** when θ is in radians. Degrees always need converting first.

illustration_description: Converting hinges on one anchor: one hundred eighty degrees equals pi radians.
accompanying_text: Converting hinges on one anchor: **180° = π radians**. Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180. Radians to degrees: multiply by 180/π. Keep the anchor in view and the factor's direction is never in doubt — the 180 sits opposite the π.

illustration_description: The angles you meet constantly are clean fractions of pi, like pi over six, pi over four, and pi over three.
accompanying_text: The angles you'll meet constantly are clean fractions of the anchor: **30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2**. The pattern: the denominator tells how many copies fit in 180°. Six 30s, four 45s, three 60s, two 90s — the smaller the angle, the BIGGER the denominator.

illustration_description: Reading pi-fractions back is the same skill reversed: treat pi as one hundred eighty degrees.
accompanying_text: Reading π-fractions BACK is the same skill reversed: treat the denominator as a step size and count. π/6 steps are 30° each, so 5π/6 is five 30° steps: 150°. No formula grinding — just steps of a known size.

illustration_description: Angles don't stop at one lap, and a negative angle turns clockwise instead of counterclockwise.
accompanying_text: Angles don't stop at one lap. A negative angle turns CLOCKWISE, and an angle past 2π keeps spinning — a full turn plus a quarter turn lands exactly where the quarter turn does. The landing spot repeats every 2π; the total rotation is what the number records.

illustration_description: One radian of angle spans exactly one radius of arc along the circle.
accompanying_text: Here's what radians buy you. Since 1 radian of angle spans 1 radius of arc, **θ radians span θ radii**: arc length **s = rθ**. One multiplication, no circumference fractions, no 360s — provided θ is in radians.

illustration_description: The classic wreck is feeding degrees into arc length equals r theta; theta must be in radians.
accompanying_text: The classic wreck: feeding DEGREES into s = rθ. Radius 4, angle 90° — plugging 90 straight in claims a 360-unit arc on a circle whose whole rim is only about 25. Convert first: 90° = π/2, then s = 4 · π/2 = 2π ≈ 6.28.

illustration_description: Arc length is also the rolling law: a wheel of radius r that turns theta radians rolls forward r theta.
accompanying_text: s = rθ is also the **rolling** law. A wheel of radius r that turns through θ radians rolls exactly s = rθ along the ground — the rim unspools onto the road. Every odometer is quietly computing rθ.

illustration_description: A unit circle with x and y axes. A point at 150 degrees is marked in berry red at coordinates negative square root of three over two, one half. Its reference angle of 30 degrees to the negative x axis is shaded in tangerine, and the matching first-quadrant 30 degree angle is shown dashed. Quadrant labels read A, S, T, C for all, sine, tangent, cosine positive. A caption notes that cosine is the x coordinate and sine is the y coordinate.
accompanying_text: Right triangles cap θ below 90° — the unit circle removes the cap. Draw a circle of radius 1 and rotate a point θ from the positive x-axis: **cos θ is the point's x-coordinate, sin θ is its y-coordinate.** For acute θ this reproduces the old ratios (hypotenuse 1) — but now EVERY angle, any size, any sign, has a sine and cosine.

illustration_description: Signs come free from the quadrant: in quadrant one x and y are both positive, and each quadrant flips a sign.
accompanying_text: Signs now come free from the QUADRANT. Q1: x and y both positive — everything positive. Q2: x < 0 — only sine positive. Q3: both negative — only tangent (y/x) positive. Q4: y < 0 — only cosine positive. The classic mnemonic, counterclockwise from Q1: **A-S-T-C** — All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine.

illustration_description: Tangent rides along: tangent theta equals sine over cosine equals y over x.
accompanying_text: Tangent rides along: **tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = y/x** — the SLOPE of the radius line. Its sign follows the quadrant rules, and it has a failure mode the others don't: wherever x = 0 (straight up at 90°, straight down at 270°), the division breaks.

illustration_description: Every angle on the circle leans on quadrant one through its reference angle, the acute gap to the x-axis.
accompanying_text: Every angle on the circle leans on Quadrant I. The **reference angle** is the acute angle between the terminal side and the X-AXIS — and the point at any angle has the SAME coordinates as its reference point, up to sign. Size from the reference, sign from the quadrant: that's the whole system.

illustration_description: Three rules, one per outer quadrant, all measuring the gap to the x-axis.
accompanying_text: Three rules, one per outer quadrant — all measuring the gap to the nearest x-axis crossing. **Q2: 180 − θ. Q3: θ − 180. Q4: 360 − θ.** In radians the same shapes: π − θ, θ − π, 2π − θ. Locate the quadrant first; the rule follows.

illustration_description: Now compute anything: the magnitude comes from the reference angle and the sign from the quadrant.
accompanying_text: Now compute anything: **magnitude from the reference angle, sign from A-S-T-C.** cos 150°: reference 30° gives magnitude cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87; Quadrant II makes cosine negative. Answer: −0.87. Two lookups, one sign check — the whole circle from one quadrant's table.

illustration_description: Two special triangles hand you exact values forever: the thirty-sixty-ninety and the forty-five-forty-five-ninety.
accompanying_text: Two special triangles hand you exact values forever. The half-equilateral (30-60-90) and half-square (45-45-90) give: **sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2** — and cosines run the same list BACKWARD. Memory device: √1/2, √2/2, √3/2 — sine climbs the roots as the angle grows.

illustration_description: Combine the special-triangle table with reference angles and the whole circle opens up.
accompanying_text: Combine the table with reference angles and the WHOLE circle is exact. cos 300°: quadrant IV (the C quadrant — cosine positive), reference 360 − 300 = 60°, magnitude cos 60° = 1/2. So cos 300° = **+0.5**. Reference for size, A-S-T-C for sign, table for the number.

illustration_description: Radians change nothing but the labels: the sine of pi over six is still one half.
accompanying_text: Radians change nothing but the labels: **sin(π/6) = 1/2, sin(π/4) = √2/2, sin(π/3) = √3/2.** The denominator names the family — 6 for the 30s, 4 for the 45s, 3 for the 60s — and reference-angle rules run in π-form exactly as before.

illustration_description: Let the angle run and track sine as the unit circle's height: it climbs, peaks, and falls into a wave.
accompanying_text: Let θ run and track sin θ — the unit circle's HEIGHT. It climbs 0 → 1 (top), falls back through 0, dips to −1 (bottom), and returns: one full lap, one full **wave**. And because lap θ + 2π revisits the same point, the wave repeats forever: sine is **periodic with period 2π**.

illustration_description: Cosine draws the same wave from the x-coordinate, identical but shifted a quarter turn.
accompanying_text: Cosine draws the SAME wave from the x-coordinate — identical shape, different starting pose. At θ = 0 the point is (1, 0): so **cosine starts at its peak** (cos 0 = 1) while **sine starts at the midline, rising** (sin 0 = 0). One wave, two entrances.

illustration_description: Real waves rarely swing between plus and minus one; the amplitude a stretches the height.
accompanying_text: Real waves rarely swing between ±1 — but two reads recover any wave's anatomy. **Midline = (max + min)/2** — the horizontal center the wave oscillates around. **Amplitude = (max − min)/2** — how far it swings from that center. Average for the center, half-the-span for the swing.

illustration_description: One full cycle of the wave y equals 2 sine x plus 1. A dashed leaf-green horizontal midline sits at y equals 1. A berry-red double arrow from the midline up to the peak marks the amplitude of 2. A tangerine bracket under one complete cycle marks the period of 2 pi. The wave rises to 3, returns through the midline, dips to negative 1, and comes back.
accompanying_text: You already own these moves from function transformations: in **y = a sin x + d**, the a is a vertical STRETCH and the d a vertical SHIFT. Trig gives them names: |a| is the **amplitude**, y = d the **midline**. The figure's y = 2 sin x + 1 swings 2 around a center of 1: top 3, bottom −1.

illustration_description: Reading runs backward too: a graph hands you the rule by reading its amplitude and period.
accompanying_text: Reading runs backward, too: a graph hands you the rule. Read the **midline** off the center — that's d. Read the **amplitude** off the swing — that's a. A wave oscillating between 10 and 2 centers on (10+2)/2 = 6 and swings (10−2)/2 = 4: y = 4 sin x + 6.

illustration_description: A negative amplitude is the transformation you'd expect: a reflection of the wave across the midline.
accompanying_text: A negative a is the transformation you'd expect: a **reflection over the midline** (the vertical flip). y = −3 sin x starts at the midline heading DOWN instead of up. The amplitude stays |a| = 3 — amplitude is a distance, and distances don't carry signs.

illustration_description: The last dial sits inside: y equals sine of b x, where b is a horizontal stretch or squeeze setting the period.
accompanying_text: The last dial sits INSIDE: y = sin(bx). The b is a horizontal squeeze — at b = 2 the input races twice as fast, finishing a full lap in half the room. The rule: **period = 2π/b**. Bigger b, faster wave, SHORTER period.

illustration_description: Designing a wave runs the rule backward: b equals two pi over the period.
accompanying_text: Designing a wave runs the rule backward: **b = 2π/period**. Want a wave that repeats every π/2? Then b = 2π ÷ (π/2) = 4. The check never lies: b × period must equal 2π, always.

illustration_description: All three dials assemble into y equals a sine of b x plus d: amplitude, period, and vertical midline shift.
accompanying_text: All three dials assemble into **y = a sin(bx) + d**: amplitude → a, midline → d, period → b = 2π/period. Given any wave description, fill the three slots in that order — each read is independent of the others.

illustration_description: A ferris wheel of radius 20 feet whose center sits 25 feet above the ground, next to a graph of a rider's height over one full turn. The height curve is a cosine-shaped wave running from a low of 5 feet up to a high of 45 feet and back, with a dashed leaf-green midline at 25 feet. A berry-red dot on the wheel rim matches a berry-red dot on the curve at the same height, tying the rotating position to the wave.
accompanying_text: Circular motion IS a wave — watch a rider's HEIGHT. A wheel of radius 20 ft with its axle 25 ft up, boarding at the bottom, gives **h(t) = 25 − 20 cos t**: axle height as the midline, radius as the amplitude, and −cos because the ride STARTS at its lowest point.

illustration_description: Every part of the formula is a part of the wheel: the midline d is the axle height the wave oscillates around.
accompanying_text: Every part of the formula is a part of the wheel. **Midline = axle height** (the center of the motion). **Amplitude = radius** (how far the rider swings from it). And the entrance: boarding at the BOTTOM means starting at the minimum — exactly what −cos does (it opens at −1).

illustration_description: Any oscillating data fits the same anatomy: amplitude, period, and midline.
accompanying_text: Any oscillating data fits the same anatomy from last chapter: **midline = (max + min)/2, amplitude = (max − min)/2**. A tide running between 8 ft and 2 ft centers on 5 ft and swings 3 — the wheel's logic, without the wheel.

illustration_description: Temperatures, tides, and daylight hours: anything that cycles fits a sine model.
accompanying_text: Temperatures, tides, daylight hours — anything that cycles fits y = a sin(bt) + d (or its −cos twin). The data hands you two of the dials immediately: a day running from 10° up to 30° has **amplitude (30 − 10)/2 = 10** and **midline (30 + 10)/2 = 20**.

illustration_description: The third dial comes from the real-world repeat time: b equals two pi over the period.
accompanying_text: The third dial comes from the real-world REPEAT time: **b = 2π/period**, exactly as in the graphs chapter — except now the period arrives in hours or seconds. A tide repeating every 12 hours takes b = 2π/12 = π/6 ≈ 0.52.

illustration_description: Assembled, the model predicts: plug in a time and get a value.
accompanying_text: Assembled, the model PREDICTS: plug in a time, get a value. h(t) = 3 sin(πt/6) + 5 models the tide — at t = 3 hours the inside is π/2, sine hits its peak 1, and the tide reads 3 · 1 + 5 = 8 ft: high tide, right on schedule.

illustration_description: Every point on the unit circle satisfies the Pythagorean identity: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one.
accompanying_text: One last gift from the unit circle. Every point on it satisfies x² + y² = 1 — that's the Pythagorean theorem on a radius-1 triangle. But x = cos θ and y = sin θ, so for EVERY angle: **sin²θ + cos²θ = 1**. Not an equation to solve — an identity, true always.

illustration_description: The identity hands you one from the other: cosine squared theta equals one minus sine squared theta.
accompanying_text: The procedure has one subtlety. **cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ** hands you a square, and the root offers TWO candidates: ±. The identity can't tell them apart — the QUADRANT does. Chapter 3's sign rules return: locate θ, then pick.

illustration_description: Fractions run the same machine, and old friends surface, like a three-four-five ratio inside the identity.
accompanying_text: Fractions run the same machine — and old friends surface. cos θ = 5/13 gives sin²θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169, so sin θ = ±12/13: the 5-12-13 triple, living inside the identity. Every Pythagorean triple is a (cos, sin) pair in disguise.

illustration_description: The sine curve and the same curve shifted right by pi over 2. The original peak at x equals pi over 2 slides to x equals pi; a horizontal arrow between the two peaks shows the phase shift. A sine wave and its phase-shifted copy, peaks joined by a shift arrow.
accompanying_text: You already move waves UP (midline) and STRETCH them (amplitude, period). The last motion is SIDEWAYS: y = sin(x − C) slides the whole wave **C to the right** — the **phase shift**. Inside the parentheses, minus means right (the same inside-flip as every function shift).

illustration_description: With a period change, read the horizontal shift only after factoring B out of the inside.
accompanying_text: With a period change, read the shift ONLY after factoring: y = sin(2x − π/3) = sin(2(x − **π/6**)) — the shift is π/6, not π/3. The B multiplies the whole inside, so the raw constant overstates the slide by a factor of B.

illustration_description: Every sinusoid is y equals A sine of B times x minus C, plus D: amplitude, period, phase shift, and midline.
accompanying_text: Every sinusoid is y = **A** sin(**B**(x − **C**)) + **D**: amplitude A (recall), period 2π/B (recall), phase shift C (new), midline D (recall). Four independent dials. To graph: draw the midline, mark the amplitude band, start a sine shape at x = C, and fit one period of length 2π/B.

illustration_description: Reading a graph, use the landmarks: the peak and trough give amplitude and midline, the repeat gives the period.
accompanying_text: Going the other way — **reading a graph** — use the landmarks in this order: midline D = (max + min)/2; amplitude A = (max − min)/2; period from repeat-distance, then B = 2π/period; finally C = where a rising midline-crossing sits.

illustration_description: To sketch cleanly, plot the five key points across one period: start, peak, mid, trough, end.
accompanying_text: To sketch y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D cleanly, plot the **five key points** of one period: start (midline, rising) at x = C, then quarter-period steps — peak, midline falling, trough, midline rising again. Five dots, one smooth wave through them.

illustration_description: A negative A flips the pattern: negative A sine starts by going down instead of up.
accompanying_text: A **negative A** flips the pattern: y = −A sin(…) starts at the midline heading **down** — the five points run start, trough, midline, peak, close. Same dots' x-positions, swapped heights. (Recall reflections: the minus mirrors across the midline.)

illustration_description: Cosine draws the same wave shape as sine with one difference: it starts at a peak.
accompanying_text: Cosine draws the SAME wave shape as sine with one difference: it **starts at the peak**. cos 0 = 1 (recall the unit circle: the point starts at (1, 0), and cosine reads the x-coordinate). Five key points for cos x: peak, midline falling, trough, midline rising, peak.

illustration_description: All four dials work identically on cosine: y equals A cosine of B times x minus C, plus D.
accompanying_text: All four dials work identically on cosine: y = A cos(B(x − C)) + D has amplitude A, period 2π/B, shift C, midline D. Only the **starting posture** differs — cos begins at the top of its band instead of mid-climb.

illustration_description: Slide the sine wave left by pi over two and it starts at a peak, exactly matching cosine.
accompanying_text:
Slide the sine wave LEFT by π/2 and it starts at a peak — exactly cosine's posture. That's an identity:

**cos x = sin(x + π/2)**  and equally  **sin x = cos(x − π/2)**

Every sinusoid can wear either name; only the phase constant changes.

illustration_description: Choosing a name is about convenience: if a graph's rising point sits at the origin, sine is simplest.
accompanying_text: Choosing a name is about **convenience**: if a graph's rising midline-crossing is easiest to spot, write it as sine from there; if a **peak** is the clean landmark, write cosine with C at the peak. Same curve, cheaper bookkeeping.

illustration_description: A half-period slide flips a wave upside down: sine of x plus pi equals negative sine x.
accompanying_text: A HALF-period slide flips a wave upside down: **sin(x + π) = −sin x** and **cos(x + π) = −cos x**. So reflection (the outside minus, recall) and a π-slide are the SAME motion for sinusoids — one graph can wear rules that look wildly different.

illustration_description: Equivalence is testable: two rules name the same wave if and only if they match at every point.
accompanying_text: Equivalence is testable: two rules name the same wave iff they agree on the **landmarks** — same midline, amplitude, period, and same value-and-direction at one x. Checking a single well-chosen point (plus the dials) beats expanding identities.

illustration_description: Three climbing branches of the tangent function with dashed vertical asymptotes at negative pi over 2 and pi over 2; each branch rises from negative infinity through zero to positive infinity, and the pattern repeats every pi. Tangent's ladder of climbing branches between vertical asymptote walls.
accompanying_text: Tangent is a QUOTIENT: tan x = sin x / cos x. Wherever **cos x = 0**, the quotient blows up — a **vertical asymptote** (recall the portrait rule: bottom's zeros build walls). Between walls, tangent sweeps from −∞ up through 0 to +∞: a climbing branch, repeated forever.

illustration_description: Tangent's period is pi, not two pi: after half a turn both sine and cosine flip sign, so their ratio repeats.
accompanying_text: Tangent's period is **π**, not 2π: after half a turn, BOTH sin and cos flip sign (recall sin(x + π) = −sin x, cos(x + π) = −cos x), and the two minuses cancel in the quotient. So walls stand at π/2 + kπ, and each branch is one π-wide copy.

illustration_description: Tangent's exact values come straight from the ratio of the exact sine and cosine values.
accompanying_text: Tangent's exact values come straight from the ratio of the exact sin/cos values you know: tan(π/6) = (1/2)/(√3/2) = **1/√3 ≈ 0.58**, tan(π/4) = 1, tan(π/3) = (√3/2)/(1/2) = **√3 ≈ 1.73**. The trio 0.58, 1, 1.73 climbs — as every tangent branch does.

illustration_description: Pressed against the wall, tangent is one-sided: approaching pi over two, it shoots to positive infinity from the left.
accompanying_text: Pressed against a wall, tangent is one-sided: approaching π/2 **from the left**, cos shrinks through tiny POSITIVE values while sin ≈ 1, so tan → **+∞**; from the right, cos is tiny and NEGATIVE, so tan → **−∞**. Each branch exits its wall at opposite infinities.

illustration_description: Tangent takes the same dials with a twist: its period is pi over the absolute value of B.
accompanying_text: Tangent takes the same dials with two twists. **Period:** y = tan(Bx) has period **π/B** (the base period is π, not 2π). **No amplitude:** a branch already spans −∞ to +∞, so A in y = A tan x only steepens the climb — there is no max to scale.

illustration_description: Slides work unchanged: y equals tangent of x minus C moves every zero and every asymptote by C.
accompanying_text: Slides work unchanged: y = tan(x − C) moves every zero and every wall right by C, spacing intact. To find any wall of a transformed tangent, set the whole **inside equal to π/2 + kπ** and solve — one equation covers stretch and slide at once.

illustration_description: The full sine wave drawn faintly, with the single climbing branch from negative pi over 2 to pi over 2 highlighted in bold; closed dots mark its endpoints at heights negative 1 and 1. This restricted branch is one-to-one and defines the arcsine function. The one-to-one sine branch kept to define arcsine.
accompanying_text: sin x fails the horizontal line test spectacularly — every output is hit infinitely often — so, recall the rescue: **restrict the domain**. Keep only **[−π/2, π/2]**, one clean climb from −1 to 1. THAT piece is one-to-one, and its inverse is **arcsin** (also written sin⁻¹).

illustration_description: Domain and range swap for the inverse: arcsine's domain is negative one to one, its range the branch from negative pi over two to pi over two.
accompanying_text: Domain and range swap (recall): sin on the branch has domain [−π/2, π/2] and range [−1, 1], so **arcsin has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]**. Inputs beyond ±1 are meaningless — no angle has sine 2.

illustration_description: Cosine can't use sine's branch: on zero to pi it falls steadily, one-to-one, so that is arccosine's branch.
accompanying_text: Cosine can't use sine's branch: on [−π/2, π/2] cosine rises then falls — it repeats outputs (cos(−π/3) = cos(π/3)), failing the line test. Cosine's clean one-to-one run is **[0, π]**, a pure descent from 1 to −1. So **arccos has range [0, π]** — never negative.

illustration_description: Tangent's turn: one full climbing branch on negative pi over two to pi over two, is arctangent's branch.
accompanying_text: Tangent's turn: one full climbing branch, **(−π/2, π/2)** — OPEN, because the walls are excluded values. **arctan** inverts it: domain ALL reals (each branch spans −∞ to +∞), range (−π/2, π/2), and the walls become **horizontal asymptotes** of arctan: y → ±π/2 as x → ±∞. (Recall: inverses swap domain and range — so vertical walls swap into horizontal ones.)

illustration_description: Each inverse graph is its branch reflected across the line y equals x.
accompanying_text: Each inverse graph is its branch **reflected across y = x** (recall the mirror). Arcsine: an S-shaped climb from (−1, −π/2) to (1, π/2). Arccosine: a descent from (−1, π) to (1, 0). Arctangent: a flattening climb pinched between the lines y = ±π/2.

illustration_description: Arctangent's mirror inherits tangent's landmarks: horizontal asymptotes at plus and minus pi over two.
accompanying_text: Arctangent's mirror inherits tangent's landmarks: the branch's center (0, 0) stays put, its steepness flattens (steep sections mirror into flat ones), and the vertical walls x = ±π/2 mirror into the **horizontal fences y = ±π/2** that arctan approaches forever.

illustration_description: One composition direction is always safe: sine of arcsine v equals v for v in the domain.
accompanying_text: One composition direction is always safe: **sin(arcsin v) = v** for every v in [−1, 1] — arcsin outputs a branch angle, and sine happily eats it. The reverse, **arcsin(sin x)**, equals x ONLY when x already lies in the branch [−π/2, π/2]. Outside it, the round trip returns a different angle (recall the same one-way trap from verifying inverses).

illustration_description: The general rule: arcsine of sine x answers which branch angle shares x's sine, not necessarily x itself.
accompanying_text: The general rule: **arcsin(sin x)** answers *"which BRANCH angle has the same sine as x?"* For second-quadrant x, that's the mirror **π − x**; the same logic gives arccos(cos x) = the [0, π] angle sharing x's cosine. Compositions of DIFFERENT functions, like cos(arcsin v), come next.

illustration_description: What is cosine of arcsine three-fifths? Name the hidden angle whose sine is three-fifths in a three-four-five triangle; its cosine is four-fifths.
accompanying_text: What is cos(arcsin(3/5))? Name the hidden angle: θ = arcsin(3/5) means **sin θ = 3/5 with θ in the branch**. Draw the helper right triangle — opposite 3, hypotenuse 5 — and the missing leg is 4 (recall 3-4-5). So cos θ = **4/5**, no calculator, exactly.

illustration_description: The identity route gives the same answer: use sine squared plus cosine squared equals one to find the cosine.
accompanying_text: The identity route (recall sin²θ + cos²θ = 1) gives the same answer: cos θ = ±√(1 − v²), and the **branch chooses the sign** — arcsin's outputs in [−π/2, π/2] always have cos θ ≥ 0, so cos(arcsin v) = **+√(1 − v²)** for every valid v, even negative ones.

illustration_description: Sine x equals one half has infinitely many solutions where the wave crosses the level, but arcsine hands back just one.
accompanying_text: sin x = 1/2 has infinitely many solutions, but **arcsin hands you exactly one**: x₁ = arcsin(1/2) = π/6. The rest come from the circle (recall reference angles): sine repeats its value at the **supplement π − x₁**, and everything recurs every 2π. On [0, 2π): x = π/6 and 5π/6.

illustration_description: Tangent is easiest: its period pi means solutions come one per period, spaced pi apart.
accompanying_text: Tangent is easiest: period π means solutions come **one per branch** — x₁ = arctan(v), then x₁ + π, x₁ + 2π, … On [0, 2π), tan x = 1 gives π/4 and π/4 + π = 5π/4. The pairing rule depends on the FUNCTION: supplement for sine, reflection for cosine, +π for tangent.

illustration_description: Left: a unit circle with the twin angles pi over 6 and 5 pi over 6 marked at the same height, one half, showing they share the same sine. Right: a number line where each twin seeds its own ladder of solutions spaced two pi apart. Twin base solutions on the circle, each seeding a plus two pi k ladder.
accompanying_text:
On [0, 2π), sin x = 1/2 gave two solutions (recall the twins π/6 and 5π/6). But sine repeats every 2π forever, so EVERY solution is one of those two **plus any whole number of turns**:

x = π/6 + 2πk or x = 5π/6 + 2πk, k any integer.

Two families capture infinitely many answers.

illustration_description: Why two families: two-pi-stepping from pi over six never reaches five pi over six, so each needs its own family.
accompanying_text: Why two families and not one? Because 2π-stepping from π/6 never reaches 5π/6 (they differ by 2π/3, not a multiple of 2π). The complete answer is always: **each [0, 2π) solution founds its own +2πk family**. Same recipe for cosine with its twins x₁ and 2π − x₁.

illustration_description: Tangent's period is pi, so its general solution steps by pi, needing only one family.
accompanying_text: Tangent's period is **π** (recall), so its general solution needs only **one family with a π step**: tan x = 1 gives x = π/4 + **πk** — no twin required, because the twin (5π/4) is just the k = 1 rung. A denser ladder from a shorter period.

illustration_description: Sine and cosine families can also merge when the two twin solutions are evenly spaced.
accompanying_text: Sine and cosine families can ALSO merge when the twins are exactly π apart. cos x = 0 has base solutions π/2 and 3π/2 — a π gap — so the two 2πk families collapse into the single dense family **x = π/2 + πk**. Always check the twin gap before writing two ladders.

illustration_description: For sine of two x equals one half, solve for the inside first: two x equals pi over six plus two pi k, then divide.
accompanying_text:
For sin(2x) = 1/2, solve for the INSIDE first: 2x = π/6 + 2πk or 2x = 5π/6 + 2πk. Then divide EVERYTHING — including the 2πk — by 2:

x = π/12 + **πk** or x = 5π/12 + **πk**.

The ladder step shrinks with the period: dividing by B compresses the spacing too.

illustration_description: The full recipe for A times trig of B times x minus C equals v: isolate the trig, solve the inside, then undo the transformations.
accompanying_text: The full recipe for A·trig(B(x − C)) = v: **(1)** isolate the trig; **(2)** write the inside's general ladder from the base twins; **(3)** solve the linear equation inside = ladder for x — dividing or shifting the ENTIRE expression, k-term included.

illustration_description: A reference diagram: sine and cosine at the center, with tangent shown as sine over cosine, and secant, cosecant, and cotangent shown as the reciprocals of cosine, sine, and tangent respectively. The six trig functions built from sine and cosine.
accompanying_text: Every trig function is built from sine and cosine. The **quotient** identity (recall the ratio observation): tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. The three **reciprocals** name the flips: **sec θ = 1/cos θ**, **csc θ = 1/sin θ**, **cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ**. Learn the pairings, not six separate objects.

illustration_description: Identities also simplify expressions: sine theta times secant theta collapses to tangent theta.
accompanying_text: These identities also **simplify** expressions. sin θ · sec θ = sin θ · (1/cos θ) = sin θ/cos θ = **tan θ**. The trick is always the same: rewrite everything in sines and cosines, then cancel. Complicated-looking products collapse.

illustration_description: From the one identity you know, sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, divide through to get the others.
accompanying_text:
From the one identity you know — **sin²θ + cos²θ = 1** (recall) — two more appear by division. Divide every term by **cos²θ**:

tan²θ + 1 = **sec²θ**.

Divide instead by **sin²θ**:

1 + cot²θ = **csc²θ**.

Three identities, one parent.

illustration_description: These shine when simplifying: secant squared theta minus one collapses straight to tangent squared theta.
accompanying_text: These shine when **simplifying**: sec²θ − 1 collapses straight to **tan²θ**, and 1 − sin²θ becomes **cos²θ**. Spotting a Pythagorean pair inside a messy expression is the single most useful move in identity work.

illustration_description: To prove an identity, transform one side until it matches the other; never move terms across the equals sign.
accompanying_text: To PROVE an identity, transform **one side** until it matches the other — never move terms across the equals sign (that assumes what you're proving). The reliable strategy: pick the messier side, **convert to sines and cosines**, and simplify using the toolkit.

illustration_description: A harder pattern: combine fractions over a common denominator, then apply a Pythagorean identity.
accompanying_text: A harder pattern: combine fractions over a common denominator, then look for a Pythagorean collapse. To prove **(1 − cos²θ)/sin θ = sin θ**: the numerator 1 − cos²θ is sin²θ, so the fraction is sin²θ/sin θ = sin θ. Recognizing the identity BEFORE grinding saves all the algebra.

illustration_description: A unit circle showing 75 degrees built as 45 degrees plus 30 degrees: a first arc sweeps from the x-axis to a 45-degree ray, and a second larger arc sweeps 30 degrees further to the 75-degree ray, illustrating the sum formula. Seventy-five degrees decomposed as forty-five plus thirty.
accompanying_text:
You know exact values at 30°, 45°, 60°. The **sum and difference formulas** unlock their combinations — 75° = 45° + 30°, 15° = 45° − 30°:

sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Note cosine's sign **flips**: plus-angle uses minus in the formula.

illustration_description: Cosine's sign flip is the classic trap: cosine of A plus B equals cosine A cosine B minus sine A sine B.
accompanying_text: Cosine's sign flip is the classic trap: cos(A + B) = cos A cos B **−** sin A sin B. The plus-angle takes a minus. So cos 75° = cos45°cos30° − sin45°sin30° = (√6 − √2)/4 ≈ 0.2588 — a small positive, as a 75° cosine should be.

illustration_description: Tangent has its own formula, all tangents: tangent of A plus or minus B equals tangent A plus or minus tangent B over one minus or plus their product.
accompanying_text:
Tangent has its own formula, all tangents:

tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) / (1 ∓ tan A tan B).

The denominator's sign is OPPOSITE the numerator's. For tan 75° = tan(45° + 30°): (1 + 1/√3)/(1 − 1·1/√3), which simplifies to **2 + √3 ≈ 3.732**.

illustration_description: Cofunctions: sine and cosine are the same wave a quarter turn apart, so sine theta equals cosine of ninety minus theta.
accompanying_text: **Cofunctions**: sin and cos are the SAME wave a quarter-turn apart (recall cos x = sin(x + π/2)), which means **sin(90° − θ) = cos θ** and cos(90° − θ) = sin θ. 'Co' literally means *complementary*: each function of an angle equals its cofunction of the complement.

illustration_description: Read backwards, the formulas compress: spot the sum pattern and fold it into a single trig term.
accompanying_text: Read backwards, the formulas COMPRESS. Spot the pattern sin A cos B + cos A sin B and rewrite it as the single **sin(A + B)**. This collapses scary expressions: sin 40° cos 10° + cos 40° sin 10° is just **sin 50° ≈ 0.766** — no evaluation of the parts needed.

illustration_description: A recurring simplification: sine of x plus pi equals negative sine x falls right out of the sum formula.
accompanying_text: A recurring simplification: **sin(x + π) = −sin x** falls right out of the sum formula (sin x cos π + cos x sin π = sin x·(−1) + 0 = −sin x). Every reflection and shift identity from the graphing chapter is really a sum formula in disguise.

illustration_description: Set A equal to B equal theta in the sum formulas and the double-angle identity appears: sine two theta equals two sine theta cosine theta.
accompanying_text:
Set A = B = θ in the sum formulas and the **double-angle** identities fall out:

sin 2θ = **2 sin θ cos θ**
cos 2θ = **cos²θ − sin²θ**

These turn a doubled angle into single-angle pieces — the key to both evaluating and later un-doubling.

illustration_description: Sign warning: cosine two theta can be negative even when theta is acute.
accompanying_text: **Sign warning:** cos 2θ can be negative even when θ is acute — it flips once θ passes 45°. And sin 2θ depends on θ's quadrant through cos θ: if θ sits in Quadrant II with sin θ = 3/5, then cos θ = −4/5 and sin 2θ = 2·(3/5)·(−4/5) = **−24/25**.

illustration_description: Three equal forms of cosine of two theta shown side by side: cosine squared minus sine squared, one minus two sine squared labeled sine-only, and two cosine squared minus one labeled cosine-only. The three equal faces of cosine of two theta.
accompanying_text:
Using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cos 2θ wears **three equal forms**:

cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = **1 − 2sin²θ** = **2cos²θ − 1**.

Each is best in a different situation: pick the one matching what you're GIVEN or what you want to CANCEL.

illustration_description: Read backwards, these give the crucial power-reduction formula: sine squared theta equals one minus cosine two theta, over two.
accompanying_text:
Read backwards, these give the crucial **power-reduction** formulas — the way to lower an exponent:

sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2,  cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2.

They trade a squared single-angle for a first-power double-angle — indispensable in calculus and for solving certain equations.

illustration_description: Double-angle identities solve and prove: sine two theta over sine theta simplifies to two cosine theta.
accompanying_text: Double-angle identities SOLVE and PROVE. To prove sin 2θ/sin θ = 2 cos θ: expand the top — 2 sinθ cosθ/sinθ = 2 cos θ. The sin θ cancels. Whenever a '2θ' meets a 'θ', expand the double angle so everything speaks one angle.

illustration_description: For equations, expanding a double angle turns a mixed-angle equation into one angle you can solve.
accompanying_text: For EQUATIONS, expanding turns a mixed-angle equation into one solvable angle. sin 2x = sin x becomes 2 sinx cosx = sinx, then **2 sinx cosx − sinx = 0**, factor **sinx(2cosx − 1) = 0** — two simple equations (recall zero-product).

illustration_description: A solution tree: the equation two sine squared x minus sine x minus one equals zero factors into two branches. The left branch, two sine x plus one equals zero, gives sine x equals negative one half with solutions seven pi over six and eleven pi over six. The right branch, sine x minus one equals zero, gives sine x equals one with solution pi over two. Factoring a trig quadratic into two solution branches.
accompanying_text: Many trig equations are **quadratics wearing a trig coat**: 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 is just 2u² − u − 1 = 0 with u = sin x. Factor as usual — (2sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0 — then solve each simple trig equation with the twin/ladder rules (recall).

illustration_description: Watch for branches with no solution: if a factor forces sine above one, that branch is rejected.
accompanying_text: Watch for branches with **no solution**: if a factor gives sin x = 2, discard it — sine never exceeds 1 (recall arcsin's domain). Only real, in-range values survive to the twin/ladder step.

illustration_description: When an equation mixes sine and cosine with different powers, substitute an identity to make one function.
accompanying_text: When an equation mixes sin AND cos with different powers, **convert to one function** using an identity. For 2cos²x + 3sin x − 3 = 0, replace cos²x with 1 − sin²x (Pythagorean): the equation becomes all-sine, then factors as a quadratic in sin x.

illustration_description: Choose the substitution that leaves the lowest power, keeping the resulting equation simplest.
accompanying_text: Choose the substitution that leaves the LOWEST power: if the equation has sin²x and cos x, replace **sin²x = 1 − cos²x** to get an all-cosine quadratic. Converting toward the linear term's function keeps the algebra a clean quadratic.

illustration_description: Squaring both sides can invent extraneous solutions, so every answer must be checked.
accompanying_text: Two operations create traps. **Squaring** both sides can invent **extraneous** roots — always substitute back and discard failures. **Dividing** by a trig factor can DELETE roots — factor instead of dividing (recall). Both traps come from operations that aren't reversible.

illustration_description: The dividing trap: solving sine x cosine x equals sine x by dividing by sine x loses the solutions where sine x is zero.
accompanying_text: The dividing trap: solving sin x cos x = sin x by DIVIDING by sin x gives only cos x = 1 — losing every solution where sin x = 0. Factor instead: sin x(cos x − 1) = 0 keeps BOTH branches. Never divide away a factor that can equal zero.

illustration_description: A sign rule table: positive times positive is positive, positive times negative is negative, negative times positive is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
accompanying_text: Distributing works the same way with a **negative** multiplier — every term still gets multiplied, sign included. -3(x + 2) = -3x + (-3)(2) = -3x − 6.

illustration_description: Checking a distribution by evaluating both forms: negative 2 times the quantity x plus 3 and negative 2x minus 6 both give negative 8 when x is 1. Check by evaluating both forms at x = 1.
accompanying_text: Check any distribution by evaluating both the original and expanded form at the same x — they must match at EVERY value, not just one.

illustration_description: A sign rule table: positive times positive is positive, positive times negative is negative, negative times positive is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
accompanying_text: Two negatives multiply to a positive — the same sign rule from the last course applies here too. -2(x − 6) = -2x + 12.

illustration_description: A sign rule table: positive times positive is positive, positive times negative is negative, negative times positive is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
accompanying_text: Combining like terms works the same with negative coefficients — add the coefficients using the signed-number rules you already know. -3x + 5x: different signs, so 5-3=2, keep positive: 2x.

illustration_description: Combining like terms keeps constants separate from x-terms: 5x minus 2x plus 3 combines the x-terms into 3x, leaving 3x plus 3. Combine like terms: 5x − 2x + 3 = 3x + 3.
accompanying_text: Constants (plain numbers) stay separate from x-terms. Simplify each group on its own: 4n + 3 + 2n = (4n+2n) + 3 = 6n + 3.

illustration_description: Simplifying in order: first distribute the multiplication, then combine like terms, turning 2 times x plus 3 plus 4x into 6x plus 6. Distribute first, then combine: 6x + 6.
accompanying_text: You can distribute first, then combine — 2(x+3)+4x becomes 2x+6+4x, and combining the x-terms gives 6x+6.

illustration_description: A sign rule table: positive times positive is positive, positive times negative is negative, negative times positive is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
accompanying_text: You now have every tool for simplifying linear expressions: distribute using the sign rule, then combine like terms using the signed-number rules.

illustration_description: Simplifying in order: first distribute the multiplication, then combine like terms, turning 2 times x plus 3 plus 4x into 6x plus 6. Distribute first, then combine: 6x + 6.
accompanying_text: The order of operations always matters: distribute (multiply into the parentheses) before you combine (add matching terms together).

illustration_description: Simplifying in order: first distribute the multiplication, then combine like terms, turning 2 times x plus 3 plus 4x into 6x plus 6. Distribute first, then combine: 6x + 6.
accompanying_text: Practice noticing which pattern you're facing — pure distribution, pure combining, or both together — before you start computing.

illustration_description: A rectangle of tiles three rows tall and five columns wide, split into a block of three x-tiles and a block of twelve unit tiles, showing that 3x plus 12 is three rows of one x and four units.
accompanying_text:
Distributing takes 3(x + 4) apart into 3x + 12. **Factoring** runs the same road the other way: it takes 3x + 12 and finds the equal groups hiding inside it.

The question factoring asks is always the same — *what does every term share?* Here both 3x and 12 are divisible by 3, so three equal rows of (x + 4) can be built.

illustration_description: The expression 12x plus 18 factored two ways: 2 times the quantity 6x plus 9, which still has a common factor of 3 left inside, and 6 times the quantity 2x plus 3, where nothing is left to pull out.
accompanying_text:
A common factor is not always **the** common factor. 12x + 18 really does equal 2(6x + 9) — but a 3 is still hiding inside that bracket, so the job is half done.

Taking out the *greatest* common factor, 6, leaves 6(2x + 3) with nothing left to pull. That is what "fully factored" means.

illustration_description: Two routes from a price to the same increased price: adding five percent of the price in two steps, and multiplying by 1.05 in one step.
accompanying_text:
Raise a price *a* by 5% and the natural way to write it is two moves: the price, plus 5% of the price. That is a + 0.05a.

But a is really 1a, so a + 0.05a is 1a + 0.05a — like terms. Combined, they are **1.05a**. Same value, one move instead of two.

illustration_description: Adding a percent in one step: multiplying a twenty-dollar price by one plus fifteen hundredths gives twenty-three dollars. $20 × 1.15 = $23 in one step.
accompanying_text:
The multiplier form is not merely shorter — it is more **useful**. Two increases in a row become 1.05 × 1.05 instead of a two-line calculation done twice, and a decrease of 20% becomes × 0.80.

That is what the standard means by rewriting an expression to shed light: the second form makes the rate visible as a single number.

illustration_description: One quantity written three equivalent ways, each form answering a different question: the total, the per-item cost, and the discount rate.
accompanying_text:
8n + 8 and 8(n + 1) are the same number for every n. They are not equally **useful**.

If you want the total cost, 8n + 8 is already arithmetic you can do. If you want to know how many things were bought at $8 each, 8(n + 1) says it outright: n + 1 of them. The question picks the form.

illustration_description: Testing equivalence: substituting x equals 4 into 2 times x plus 2 gives 10, and into 2x plus 4 also depends — matching values at a test point suggests equivalence. Test equivalence by substituting a value.
accompanying_text:
There is a test, and it is not opinion: two forms are equivalent when they agree for **every** value of the variable, not just the one you tried.

One substitution can fool you — 2x and x² both give 4 at x = 2. Distributing or factoring is what proves equivalence; substitution only ever disproves it.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: A two-step equation like 3x + 4 = 19 needs two undo-moves: first subtract 4 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both sides by 3 (x = 5).

illustration_description: Two-step order: undo addition or subtraction first because it is outermost, then undo the multiplication, so 2x plus 3 equals 11 gives x equals 4. Undo +/− first, then ×/÷: x = 4.
accompanying_text: The order matters: undo addition/subtraction FIRST (it's outside the multiplication), then undo the multiplication last.

illustration_description: Checking a distribution by evaluating both forms: negative 2 times the quantity x plus 3 and negative 2x minus 6 both give negative 8 when x is 1. Check by evaluating both forms at x = 1.
accompanying_text: Always check your answer by substituting it back into the ORIGINAL equation — if both sides match, you solved it correctly.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: When the x-coefficient is negative, the same two steps work — undo addition/subtraction, then divide by the negative coefficient, using the signed-number rules you already know.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: The result can also come out negative — different signs give a negative quotient, exactly as you learned before.

illustration_description: A sign rule table: positive times positive is positive, positive times negative is negative, negative times positive is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
accompanying_text: Always check your work carefully with negative coefficients — a sign slip anywhere gives a completely wrong answer.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: Real problems translate into two-step equations. A cab charges $3 plus $4 per mile; a $19 fare means 4m + 3 = 19, so m = 4 miles.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: A temperature-drop story can involve a negative coefficient — the same two-step method still applies, using the sign rules you know.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: Whatever the story — fares, temperatures, savings — translate it into px+q=r, then solve with the same two steps.

illustration_description: A balanced scale holding 2x plus 3 on the left and 11 on the right. Taking 3 from one pan only tips the scale; taking 3 from both pans keeps it level.
accompanying_text: An equation is a balanced scale: 2x + 3 = 11 says the two pans weigh the same. You can take tiles away — but only if you take the SAME amount off BOTH pans. Take from one side only and the beam tips: the two sides stop being equal, and the equation you're holding is no longer the one you started with.

illustration_description: Two x-tiles beside three loose unit tiles cannot be split into equal groups; once the three units are removed from both sides, the two x-tiles share the remaining eight evenly as four each.
accompanying_text: Notice the order the balance forces on you. You can't share the pans into equal groups while loose unit tiles sit next to the x-tiles — so the units must be cleared FIRST, and the splitting comes LAST. That is exactly why, on paper, you subtract before you divide.

illustration_description: Forward, x is multiplied by 5 then 3 is added, giving 28. The undo track runs the other way: subtract 3 first, then divide by 5, recovering x equals 5.
accompanying_text: An equation like 5x + 3 = 28 is a machine: x goes in, the machine multiplies by 5, then adds 3, and 28 comes out. Solving it means UNDOING the machine. And undoing has a rule: the LAST thing the machine did is the FIRST thing you undo. The + 3 happened last, so it goes first — subtract 3, then divide by 5.

illustration_description: The undo track for 6x minus 5 equals 25: twenty-five enters, adding 5 gives 30, dividing by 6 gives x equals 5. Each stage shows the running value.
accompanying_text: Once the undo machine is built, solving is just feeding it the answer-side number. For 6x − 5 = 25: send 25 through the undo track — add 5 to get 30, divide by 6 to get x = 5. Every two-step equation you've solved was secretly this: build the undo, run the number through it.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: An equation like 3(x + 2) = 18 has parentheses first — distribute across them before solving. 3(x+2)=18 becomes 3x+6=18, then solve the usual way: x=4.

illustration_description: Distribute then solve: 2 times the quantity x plus 3 becomes 2x plus 6 equals 14, then subtract 6 and divide by 2 to get x equals 4. Distribute first: 2(x + 3) = 14 → x = 4.
accompanying_text: The parentheses can hold a subtraction too — distribute the same way, watching the signs carefully.

illustration_description: Two-step order: undo addition or subtraction first because it is outermost, then undo the multiplication, so 2x plus 3 equals 11 gives x equals 4. Undo +/− first, then ×/÷: x = 4.
accompanying_text: After distributing, the equation looks exactly like the two-step equations from the last chapter — the same undo-moves apply.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: When the multiplier outside the parentheses is negative, distribute using the sign rule, then solve as usual. -2(x + 5) = -6: distribute to -2x-10=-6, then solve: x=-2.

illustration_description: Distribute then solve: 2 times the quantity x plus 3 becomes 2x plus 6 equals 14, then subtract 6 and divide by 2 to get x equals 4. Distribute first: 2(x + 3) = 14 → x = 4.
accompanying_text: A negative multiplier with a subtraction inside gives a positive constant when distributed — same signs multiply to positive.

illustration_description: A sign rule table: positive times positive is positive, positive times negative is negative, negative times positive is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
accompanying_text: Always double-check the distribution step first — a sign error there carries through the entire solve.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: You now handle any parenthesized equation: distribute using the sign rule, then solve the two-step equation that results — whatever the multiplier's sign.

illustration_description: Distribute then solve: 2 times the quantity x plus 3 becomes 2x plus 6 equals 14, then subtract 6 and divide by 2 to get x equals 4. Distribute first: 2(x + 3) = 14 → x = 4.
accompanying_text: The very first move is always the same: identify the multiplier outside the parentheses, and distribute it across every term inside.

illustration_description: Solving three x plus four equals nineteen in two steps: subtract four from both sides to get three x equals fifteen, then divide both sides by three to get x equals five.
accompanying_text: Practice catching your own errors: if your final answer doesn't satisfy the ORIGINAL equation when substituted back, retrace your distribution step.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: Solving a two-step inequality uses the same undo-moves as an equation — with a POSITIVE coefficient, the direction never changes. 3x + 2 > 14: subtract 2, divide by 3: x > 4.

illustration_description: Testing an inequality solution: for x greater than 2, a value inside like 3 makes 3 greater than 2 true, while a value outside like 0 makes it false. Test a value: x=3 works, x=0 fails.
accompanying_text: Check a solved inequality by testing a number from the solution set — plug it into the ORIGINAL inequality and confirm it holds true.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: The comparator (>, <, ≥, ≤) stays exactly the same throughout, as long as you never multiply or divide by a negative number.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: Dividing an inequality by a NEGATIVE number flips the direction. -2x + 5 > -3: subtract 5 (-2x>-8), divide by -2 — and FLIP: x < 4.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: The rule only triggers when you multiply or divide by a negative — adding or subtracting a negative number never flips anything.

illustration_description: Testing an inequality solution: for x greater than 2, a value inside like 3 makes 3 greater than 2 true, while a value outside like 0 makes it false. Test a value: x=3 works, x=0 fails.
accompanying_text: A useful check: pick a number in your solution set and test it in the ORIGINAL inequality — if it works, you flipped correctly.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: Real problems translate into inequalities too. A budget story: saving $5 a week plus $20 already saved, wanting at least $50 — 5x + 20 >= 50 — solves to x >= 6 weeks.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: The first move for any story problem is the same: identify the constant fee, the per-unit rate, and the target — then write px+q [comparator] r.

illustration_description: A number line showing the solution x less than 4 as an open circle at four with an arrow extending left, the result of dividing an inequality by a negative number and flipping its direction.
accompanying_text: Whatever the story — savings, cost limits, temperature — the same two rules apply: undo addition/subtraction first, then divide, flipping only for a negative.

accompanying_text: Fractions add by counting pieces — but only when the pieces are the same size. Halves and thirds cannot be counted together any more than metres and inches can.

accompanying_text: This is why 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5. Adding across ignores the piece sizes entirely, and produces an answer smaller than one of the parts.

accompanying_text: A common denominator is a piece size both fractions can be cut into. Any shared multiple of the two denominators will do.

accompanying_text: Renaming does not change either fraction — it re-cuts the same amount into finer pieces, which is exactly what scaling top and bottom accomplishes.

accompanying_text: Any common multiple works, but the LEAST one keeps the numbers smallest and the simplifying lightest.

accompanying_text: For fourths and sixths, both 24 and 12 are shared sizes. Twelve is the least, so it is the one worth choosing.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: 1/4 and 1/6 into twelfths: the first scales by 3, the second by 2. Different factors, same destination.

accompanying_text: Once both fractions wear the same denominator, addition is pure counting: the pieces match, so the totals simply combine.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The denominator does not add. It names the piece size, and the pieces stayed the same size throughout.

accompanying_text: Subtraction runs the same course: rename to a shared size, then take one count from the other.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The demand is identical — matching pieces — because you cannot remove thirds from halves any more than you can add them.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Mixed numbers carry wholes and parts at once. Add the fraction parts and the whole parts separately, then reassemble.

accompanying_text: If the fraction parts pass one whole, the extra whole moves across — the same carrying that whole-number addition uses.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Subtracting mixed numbers works the same way — provided the top fraction is big enough to subtract from.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Converting both to improper fractions sidesteps the question entirely: with everything in pieces, there are no wholes to trade.

accompanying_text: When the top fraction is smaller than the bottom one, trade a whole: 4 1/8 becomes 3 9/8, because one whole is eight eighths.

accompanying_text: This is the fraction version of borrowing, and it obeys the same law — the amount is unchanged, only its packaging moves.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Simplifying divides top and bottom by their greatest common factor. The value does not move; the numbers just get smaller.

accompanying_text: It is the exact inverse of renaming: one scales up to make pieces match, the other scales down once counting is done.

accompanying_text: A reasonable answer sits where the parts put it: a sum must exceed each part it was built from, and two proper fractions cannot exceed two.
