accompanying_text: Renaming at every step wastes work and invites mistakes. One shared size carries the whole chain.

illustration_description: The vector 3, 4 drawn from the origin, with a horizontal leg of 3 and a vertical leg of 4 shown dashed, forming a right triangle whose hypotenuse has magnitude 5, and an arc marking the direction angle of about 53 degrees. A vector shown by its components, magnitude, and direction angle.
accompanying_text: A **vector** carries two facts at once: a **magnitude** (how much) and a **direction** (which way). In components, v = ⟨a, b⟩ means 'go a right and b up.' Unlike a plain number — a scalar — a vector points somewhere. Velocity, force, and displacement are all vectors.

illustration_description: Magnitude is pure Pythagoras: the length of vector a b is the square root of a squared plus b squared.
accompanying_text: Magnitude is pure Pythagoras: |⟨a, b⟩| = √(a² + b²). The components are the legs of a right triangle; the vector is the hypotenuse. That's why ⟨3, 4⟩, ⟨5, 12⟩, and ⟨6, 8⟩ have the clean lengths 5, 13, and 10 — they're the Pythagorean triples.

illustration_description: A vector's direction angle theta is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.
accompanying_text: A vector's **direction angle** θ is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis. Find it from the components: θ is the angle whose tangent is b/a — **with a quadrant check** (recall the arctan trap from polar). For ⟨1, √3⟩: |v| = 2 and tan θ = √3, so θ = 60° in Quadrant I.

illustration_description: Reverse the process to build a vector from its size and angle: components are magnitude times cosine and sine.
accompanying_text:
Reverse the process to BUILD a vector from its size and angle — the polar→rectangular formulas (recall):

a = |v| cos θ,  b = |v| sin θ.

A vector of magnitude 10 at 30° is ⟨10cos30°, 10sin30°⟩ = ⟨5√3, 5⟩ ≈ ⟨8.66, 5⟩.

illustration_description: Two points A at 1,2 and B at 4,6 on a grid, with an arrow from A to B representing the displacement vector 3, 4, found by subtracting A's coordinates from B's. The displacement vector from point A to point B.
accompanying_text:
A vector from point A to point B is the **displacement** — subtract tail from tip, coordinate by coordinate:

AB = ⟨x_B − x_A, y_B − y_A⟩.

From A(1, 2) to B(4, 6): ⟨4 − 1, 6 − 2⟩ = ⟨3, 4⟩. The vector records the trip, not the starting spot.

illustration_description: Two vectors are equal if they have the same components, regardless of where they start.
accompanying_text: Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same components — regardless of where they're drawn. The displacement ⟨3, 4⟩ starting at the origin and the same ⟨3, 4⟩ starting at (10, 10) are the SAME vector: identical magnitude and direction. Position is not part of a vector's identity.

illustration_description: Tip-to-tail vector addition: a vector 3, 0 along the x-axis, then a vector 0, 4 placed at its tip, with the resultant 3, 4 drawn from the start to the end, forming a right triangle of hypotenuse 5. Tip-to-tail addition producing the resultant vector.
accompanying_text:
To **add** vectors, add matching components:

⟨a, b⟩ + ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a + c, b + d⟩.

Geometrically, place the second vector's tail at the first's tip — the sum runs from the very start to the very end. This **tip-to-tail** picture is why forces and displacements combine the way they do.

illustration_description: Subtraction is adding the opposite: a b minus c d equals a minus c, b minus d.
accompanying_text: **Subtraction** is adding the opposite: ⟨a, b⟩ − ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a − c, b − d⟩. Geometrically, u − v points **from the tip of v to the tip of u** — exactly the displacement idea (recall). Order matters: u − v and v − u are opposites.

illustration_description: Multiplying a vector by a scalar k scales every component, stretching or shrinking the arrow.
accompanying_text: Multiplying a vector by a **scalar** k scales every component: k⟨a, b⟩ = ⟨ka, kb⟩. This **stretches** the vector's length by |k| and keeps its direction — unless k is negative, which **flips** it to point the opposite way. The direction is preserved (k > 0) or reversed (k < 0), never rotated.

illustration_description: A unit vector has length one; build one by dividing a vector by its own magnitude.
accompanying_text: A **unit vector** has length 1. To build one pointing along v, divide by the magnitude: **û = v/|v|**. For ⟨6, 8⟩ (length 10): û = ⟨6/10, 8/10⟩ = ⟨0.6, 0.8⟩ — same direction, length exactly 1. Unit vectors capture pure direction.

illustration_description: Any vector splits into length times direction: v equals its magnitude times its unit vector.
accompanying_text: Any vector splits into **length × direction**: v = |v|·û. This lets you REBUILD a vector at a chosen length: to get a vector of length 15 along ⟨3, 4⟩, take 15·û = 15·⟨0.6, 0.8⟩ = ⟨9, 12⟩. Unit vectors are the 'pure direction' you scale to any size.

illustration_description: Vectors shine for combining motions: a boat heading across a current follows the sum of the two velocity vectors.
accompanying_text: Vectors shine for **combining motions**. A boat heads across a river at ⟨0, 4⟩ (m/s) while the current pushes ⟨3, 0⟩. Its true velocity is the sum ⟨3, 4⟩ — speed 5 m/s, angled downstream. The components handle each direction independently, then combine.

illustration_description: Two vectors from the origin: u equals 3,4 and v equals 5,0 along the x-axis, with an arc marking the angle between them and a dashed shadow showing the projection of u onto v, illustrating that the dot product measures alignment. The angle between two vectors and the projection of one onto the other.
accompanying_text:
The **dot product** multiplies two vectors into a single NUMBER (a scalar):

⟨a, b⟩ · ⟨c, d⟩ = ac + bd.

Multiply matching components, then add. ⟨3, 4⟩ · ⟨1, 2⟩ = 3·1 + 4·2 = 11. The result isn't a vector — it measures how much the two vectors point the same way.

illustration_description: The sign of the dot product reveals the rough angle: positive is acute, zero is perpendicular, negative is obtuse.
accompanying_text: The sign of the dot product reveals the rough angle: **positive** if the vectors point generally the same way (< 90° apart), **zero** if perpendicular, **negative** if generally opposite (> 90°). This is the dot product's superpower — it detects alignment.

illustration_description: The dot product also encodes the exact angle: u dot v equals the product of magnitudes times cosine theta.
accompanying_text:
The dot product also encodes the exact **angle** between vectors:

cos θ = (u · v) / (|u| |v|).

Divide the dot product by the product of magnitudes to get the cosine, then take arccos (recall). This one formula turns component arithmetic into geometry.

illustration_description: When cosine theta equals one the vectors are parallel, pointing the same direction.
accompanying_text: When cos θ = 1 the vectors are **parallel** (same direction, 0°); when cos θ = −1 they're **antiparallel** (opposite, 180°). Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other, so their dot product equals the full product of magnitudes — no 'wasted' perpendicular part.

illustration_description: Two vectors from the origin: u equals 3,4 and v equals 5,0 along the x-axis, with an arc marking the angle between them and a dashed shadow showing the projection of u onto v, illustrating that the dot product measures alignment. The angle between two vectors and the projection of one onto the other.
accompanying_text:
In physics, **work** = force · displacement — literally the dot product:

W = F · d.

Only the part of the force ALONG the motion does work. A force ⟨6, 8⟩ N moving an object ⟨10, 0⟩ m does W = 6·10 + 8·0 = **60 joules** — the vertical 8 contributes nothing to horizontal motion.

illustration_description: The projection idea underlies this: the dot product measures how much of one vector lies along the other.
accompanying_text: The **projection** idea underlies this: u · v = |u| |v| cos θ picks out the shadow of one vector on the other. When they align (θ = 0°), the dot product is maximal (full |u||v|); at 90° it's zero. Work measures exactly the force's shadow along the path.

illustration_description: The unit square of area 1 shown small at the origin, and its image under a 2 by 2 matrix: a larger parallelogram whose area equals the absolute value of the determinant, here 5. The basis vectors map to the parallelogram's two edges. A 2×2 matrix maps the unit square to a parallelogram of area |det|.
accompanying_text:
A **2×2 matrix** is a square of four numbers, [[a, b], [c, d]]. Add matrices entry by entry, and scale by multiplying every entry. The real power is the **matrix-vector product**, which sends a vector to a new vector:

[[a, b], [c, d]]·⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨ax + by, cx + dy⟩.

illustration_description: Each output component is a row of the matrix dotted with the input vector.
accompanying_text: Each output component is a **row of the matrix dotted with the vector** (recall the dot product). The top row makes the new x; the bottom row makes the new y. A matrix is a machine that recombines a vector's coordinates by fixed recipes — the rows.

illustration_description: The determinant of a two by two matrix is a d minus b c, and it equals the area of the parallelogram the columns span.
accompanying_text: The **determinant** of [[a, b], [c, d]] is **ad − bc** — a single number measuring how the matrix scales area (recall the unit square). det[[1, 2], [3, 4]] = 1·4 − 2·3 = −2. Its sign tells orientation; its size tells the area factor; **zero means the matrix collapses the plane** (no inverse).

illustration_description: When the determinant is not zero, the inverse exists: swap a and d, negate b and c, and divide by the determinant.
accompanying_text:
When det ≠ 0, the **inverse** exists:

[[a, b], [c, d]]⁻¹ = (1/det)·[[d, −b], [−c, a]].

Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant. The inverse UNDOES the matrix: M⁻¹(M·v) = v.

illustration_description: A linear system is a matrix equation: the coefficient matrix times the unknown vector equals the constants.
accompanying_text: A linear system is a matrix equation. The system 2x + y = 5, x + 3y = 10 becomes [[2, 1], [1, 3]]·⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨5, 10⟩ — recall solving these by elimination (se). Now: multiply both sides by the **inverse** to isolate ⟨x, y⟩ = M⁻¹·⟨5, 10⟩. Same answers, matrix machinery.

illustration_description: When the determinant is zero, the matrix method signals no unique solution: the columns collapse onto one line.
accompanying_text: When the determinant is **zero**, the matrix method signals trouble: the system has either **no solution** (parallel lines) or **infinitely many** (the same line). A zero determinant is exactly the algebraic sign that elimination would stall — the two viewpoints agree (recall se's special cases).

illustration_description: The unit square with basis vectors i pointing right and j pointing up is transformed by a 2 by 2 matrix into a parallelogram; i lands on the matrix's first column and j on its second column, showing the columns are the images of the basis vectors. A matrix transformation carries the basis vectors to its columns.
accompanying_text: A matrix is a **transformation of the plane**: feed it every point ⟨x, y⟩ and it maps them to new points ⟨x′, y′⟩ (recall the mapping notation from geometry). The matrix-vector product IS the rule (x, y) → (x′, y′). Scaling, reflecting, and rotating all become single matrices.

illustration_description: The key to reading a transformation matrix: its columns are the images of the basis vectors after the transformation.
accompanying_text: Here's the key to READING a transformation matrix: its **columns are the images of the basis vectors**. The first column is where ⟨1, 0⟩ lands; the second is where ⟨0, 1⟩ lands. Know where the two arrows go, and you know the whole matrix — every other point follows.

illustration_description: A vector 3,2 and its image under a 90 degree counterclockwise rotation, the vector negative 2, 3, with a curved arrow showing the quarter turn. Both vectors have the same length, since rotation preserves magnitude. A 90-degree rotation preserving the vector's length.
accompanying_text:
Rotation by angle θ (counterclockwise, about the origin) is the matrix

[[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].

Its columns are where the basis vectors swing to: ⟨1, 0⟩ → ⟨cos θ, sin θ⟩ and ⟨0, 1⟩ → ⟨−sin θ, cos θ⟩ (recall the unit circle). Every point rotates rigidly around the origin.

illustration_description: Special rotations are clean: one hundred eighty degrees is the matrix negative one, zero, zero, negative one, flipping every vector.
accompanying_text: Special rotations are clean: **180°** is [[−1, 0], [0, −1]] (negate everything — point reflection through the origin), and **360°** returns the identity [[1, 0], [0, 1]]. Rotation preserves length and angle: it's a **rigid motion** (recall geometry), so magnitudes never change.

illustration_description: A three-stage pipeline: the vector 1,0 is reflected over the line y equals x to become 0,1, then reflected over the x-axis to become 0, negative 1. The two reflections together equal a single 90 degree clockwise rotation. Composing two reflections into one rotation.
accompanying_text:
To do one transformation **then** another, **multiply the matrices**. For 'apply B, then A,' the combined matrix is A·B (the second one goes on the LEFT). Matrix product:

[[a, b], [c, d]]·[[e, f], [g, h]] = [[ae+bg, af+bh], [ce+dg, cf+dh]].

Each entry is a row of A dotted with a column of B.

illustration_description: Order matters: A times B and B times A usually differ, because doing transformations in a different order lands elsewhere.
accompanying_text: **Order matters**: A·B and B·A usually differ, because doing a reflection then a rotation is not the same as rotation then reflection. This mirrors geometry — the sequence of rigid motions changes the outcome. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**.

illustration_description: Metric units step by powers of ten: a kilometer is 1000 meters and a meter is 100 centimeters, so bigger to smaller multiplies.
accompanying_text: Metric units step by powers of ten. A kilometer is 1000 meters, a meter is 100 centimeters, a kilogram is 1000 grams, a liter is 1000 milliliters. Going from a **bigger** unit to a **smaller** one, multiply: 3 km = 3 × 1000 = 3000 m.

illustration_description: Going from a smaller unit to a bigger one, divide: 3500 grams is 3500 divided by 1000, which is 3.5 kilograms.
accompanying_text: Going the other way — **smaller** unit to **bigger** — divide. 3500 grams in kilograms: 3500 ÷ 1000 = 3.5 kg. The number gets smaller because each bigger unit holds many small ones. Multiply going down the ladder, divide going up.

illustration_description: Customary units use their own factors, not tens: a foot is 12 inches and a yard is 3 feet.
accompanying_text: Customary units use their own factors — not tens. A foot is 12 inches, a yard is 3 feet, a pound is 16 ounces, a gallon is 4 quarts. The direction rule still holds: bigger unit to smaller, multiply. 3 feet = 3 × 12 = 36 inches.

illustration_description: Going from a smaller unit up to a bigger one, divide: 48 ounces is 48 divided by 16, which is 3 pounds.
accompanying_text: Going from a smaller unit up to a bigger one, divide. 48 ounces in pounds: 48 ÷ 16 = 3 lb. Same as before — down the ladder multiply, up the ladder divide — only the factor changes with each pair of units.

illustration_description: Multi-step conversions jump through a middle unit: yards to inches goes through feet, so one yard is three feet is thirty-six inches.
accompanying_text: Some conversions need two jumps through a middle unit. Yards to inches goes through feet: 3 yd = 3 × 3 = 9 ft, then 9 × 12 = 108 in. Plan the chain first — name the middle unit — then convert one rung at a time.

illustration_description: Capacity chains work the same way: gallons to cups goes through quarts, so one gallon is four quarts is sixteen cups.
accompanying_text: Capacity chains work the same way. Gallons to cups goes through quarts: 1 gal = 4 qt, and 1 qt = 4 cups. So 1.5 gal = 1.5 × 4 = 6 qt, then 6 × 4 = 24 cups. Write the middle unit down — most multi-step mistakes are a skipped rung.

illustration_description: A line plot stacks an X above a number line for each measurement.
accompanying_text: A line plot stacks an X above a number line for each measurement. When we measure lengths in fractions of a foot, the line is marked in quarters. Here are eight ribbons: 1/4 → XX, 1/2 → XXX, 3/4 → X, 1 → XX. Each X is one ribbon measured at that length.

illustration_description: Two readings from a plot: the total number measured is all the X's added up, and the range is the biggest value minus the smallest.
accompanying_text: Two more readings. The **total** number measured is all the X's added up. The **range** is the longest minus the shortest length on the plot. On our plot the shortest is 1/4 and the longest is 1, so the spread runs from 1/4 to 1 foot.

illustration_description: To find the total length from a line plot, multiply each value by how many X's it has, then add.
accompanying_text: A line plot isn't just for reading — you can compute with it. To find the **total** length, multiply each measurement by how many X's it has, then add. For the plot 1/4 → XX, 1/2 → XXX, 3/4 → X, that's 2×(1/4) + 3×(1/2) + 1×(3/4).

illustration_description: The difference between the longest and shortest measurement is the biggest value minus the smallest.
accompanying_text: Two more questions a plot answers. The **difference** between the longest and shortest is a subtraction (3/4 − 1/4). And if you pooled everything and split it **equally** among the items, each share is the total ÷ the number of items. Both are just fraction arithmetic on the data.

illustration_description: A single unit cube: each edge is 1 unit long, and it fills exactly 1 cubic unit of space.
accompanying_text: **Volume** is the amount of space a solid shape fills. To measure it, we fill the shape with **unit cubes** — little cubes that are 1 unit long on every edge. One unit cube takes up exactly **1 cubic unit** of space. So volume is really just a count: how many unit cubes fit inside?

illustration_description: When a cube is one centimeter on every edge, its volume is one cubic centimeter.
accompanying_text: When the cubes have real sizes, the count gets a label. If each cube is 1 centimeter on every edge, one cube is **1 cubic centimeter (cm³)**, and the volume in cm³ equals the number of cubes. Bigger cubes give bigger units: **cubic inches (in³)** or **cubic meters (m³)**. The little **3** means three dimensions — length, width, and height.

illustration_description: Shortcut for a packed box: the number of cubes is length times width times height, not counted one by one.
accompanying_text: Counting cubes one by one is slow for a big box. Here's the shortcut: a box packed with cubes is made of equal **layers**. Count the cubes in **one layer**, then multiply by the **number of layers**. If the bottom is 3 cubes long and 2 cubes wide, each layer holds 3 × 2 = 6 cubes. Four such layers hold 6 × 4 = 24 cubes.

illustration_description: You can slice a box into layers from any direction and get the same cube count.
accompanying_text: You can slice a box into layers from any direction and get the same count. That's why volume is just **length × width × height**. Take a box 2 cubes long, 2 wide, and 3 tall: one layer is 2 × 2 = 4 cubes, and 3 layers give 4 × 3 = 12. Multiplying all three edges — 2 × 2 × 3 — gives the same 12.

illustration_description: A box built from unit cubes: a base layer of 3 by 2 cubes, stacked 3 layers high; the highlighted bottom layer shows the base.
accompanying_text: Last chapter's shortcut has a name. The cubes covering the bottom of a box form the **base layer**, and the number of cubes in it is the **area of the base** — a 4-by-3 base holds 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. Stack that layer once per unit of height: 5 layers hold 12 × 5 = 60 cubes.

illustration_description: You need not count the base cube by cube: if the base area is ten square units and the box is three high, the volume is ten times three, thirty.
accompanying_text: You don't have to count the base cube by cube. If the **base area** is known — say 10 square units — then 10 cubes fit in each layer, and the volume is simply **base area × number of layers**. Area covers the floor; height repeats it upward.

illustration_description: The layer method in one line: the base layer holds length times width cubes, and there are height layers, so volume equals length times width times height.
accompanying_text: The layer method fits in one line. The base layer holds **length × width** cubes, and there are **height** layers. So the volume of a box is **V = l × w × h** — multiply the three edge lengths. A box 6 long, 3 wide, and 2 tall: V = 6 × 3 × 2 = 36 cubic units.

illustration_description: If the edges are in centimeters, the volume is in cubic centimeters, written cm cubed.
accompanying_text: Two useful facts. **Units:** if the edges are in centimeters, the volume is in **cm³** — a 4 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm box holds 24 cm³, the same as 24 one-centimeter cubes. **Order:** multiplying in any order gives the same result, so (4 × 2) × 3 and 4 × (2 × 3) both equal 24. Pick the easiest pairing.

illustration_description: Group the formula differently: in V equals length times width times height, the first pair length times width is the area of the base, so V equals base times height.
accompanying_text: Group the formula differently. In V = l × w × h, the first pair l × w is the **area of the base, B**. So the same formula reads **V = B × h**: base area times height. If a problem hands you B directly — "the base area is 15 square units" — skip straight to B × h. One formula, two groupings.

illustration_description: When the base is not given, compute it first: a base six units by two units has base area twelve, then multiply by the height.
accompanying_text: When B isn't given, compute it first. A base 6 units by 2 units has B = 6 × 2 = 12; with height 3, V = 12 × 3 = 36. Check the other grouping: 6 × 2 × 3 = 36 too. **Both routes always land on the same number** — choose whichever grouping the problem hands you.

illustration_description: Many solids are boxes glued together, and volume is additive: add the volume of each box.
accompanying_text: Not every solid is a single box — but many are **boxes glued together**. Volume is **additive**: if a solid is made of two boxes that don't overlap, its volume is the first volume **plus** the second. Box A at 4 × 2 × 3 = 24 joined to box B at 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 makes a solid of 24 + 12 = 36 cubic units.

illustration_description: The one rule: the pieces must not overlap, so every unit cube is counted exactly once.
accompanying_text: The one rule: the pieces must **not overlap**, so every unit cube is counted exactly once. Then combining is always **addition** — never multiplication. And order doesn't matter: A + B equals B + A, just like any sum.

illustration_description: An L-shaped solid is not a single box, so cut it into two boxes and add their volumes.
accompanying_text: An **L-shaped** solid isn't a box, so no single l × w × h fits it. The trick: **cut it into boxes yourself**. Our L: a bottom slab 5 units long, 2 wide, 2 tall, with a 2 × 2 × 2 block sitting on top of its left end. Cut along the block's base, find each box's volume, add.

illustration_description: An L-shaped solid cut two ways: a horizontal cut gives pieces of 20 and 8 cubic units; a vertical cut gives 16 and 12. Both totals are 28.
accompanying_text: Here's the satisfying part: **a different cut gives the same answer**. Slice the same L straight down at the block's edge instead. Now the pieces are a tall box 2 long, 2 wide, 4 tall, and a short box 3 long, 2 wide, 2 tall. Every cube still gets counted exactly once — so any legal split must agree.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Volume is a count: each unit cube fills one unit of space, so the number of cubes that pack a solid IS its volume.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This is the same idea as area, one dimension further on. Area counts equal squares covering a surface; volume counts equal cubes filling a space.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A prism is layers of the same base stacked up. Each layer is a complete copy, so the height MULTIPLIES rather than adds.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A base of 12 cubes, four layers tall, holds 48 cubes — not 16. That distinction is the whole of the volume formula.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: V = l × w × h records the counting in order: l × w builds one layer, and h stacks it.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The formula is not a rule to memorise separately from the cubes — it IS the cube count, organised so you never have to draw them.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: V = B × h says the same thing more generally: whatever shape the base is, find its area and stack it.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: For a rectangular prism B is just l × w, so the two formulas agree. But B × h keeps working when the base is a triangle or an L-shape.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: If the volume and the base are known, the height follows by division: how many base-layers fit inside the volume?

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: This is the formula run in reverse, and it is the same move as recovering a missing side from an area.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Composite solids are built from simple ones: find the full block, then subtract what has been cut away.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A notch is space removed, so every cube it takes lowers the count by one. The subtraction happens once, on the whole solid.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Volume word problems name the dimensions in words. Find the base, find the height, and the plan writes itself.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: The commonest slip is stopping at the base area — a flat answer to a question about space.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Two solids can be compared without imagining either one: compute both volumes and the larger count wins.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: Different shapes can hold identical volumes, which is exactly why the count settles the question and appearances do not.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
accompanying_text: A two-step problem hides a question inside itself. The story never states the middle quantity — you have to build it before the real question can be answered.

illustration_description: A number line from 0 to 10. A blue dot sits on 4. Three orange hops step to 5, 6, then 7, where a green dot lands. The caption reads four plus three equals seven.
